🏆 Skills You'll Master

❌ BEFORE — Common Beginner Struggles
  • "Where do I store database passwords?" → .env files in git
  • "K8s secrets are base64 — that's secure, right?" → NO!
  • "How do pods authenticate to Vault?" → No idea
  • "What's the difference between KV v1 and v2?" → Huh?
  • "Vault is sealed — what does that mean?" → Panic
  • "Token? Lease? Policy?" → All sound the same
✅ AFTER — Skills This Guide Builds
  • Configure Vault from scratch: init → unseal → audit → use
  • Deploy Vault HA on K8s with Helm in <10 minutes
  • Write policies granting LEAST PRIVILEGE to every app
  • Set up dynamic DB secrets: zero hardcoded passwords
  • Configure K8s auth: pods auto-login via ServiceAccount
  • Backup/restore Vault with Raft snapshots
  • Set up DR replication across regions
  • Encrypt any data with Transit engine (never store keys)
  • Issue TLS certificates dynamically with PKI engine
  • Audit every request and detect suspicious patterns

🎯 Vault Associate Exam Strategy & Battle Plan

⏱️ The First 5 Minutes — Your Setup Ritual

Terminal — First 5 Minutes 
# 0:00-0:30 — Verify Vault is reachable
export VAULT_ADDR='https://127.0.0.1:8200'
vault status
# → Sealed: false, Initialized: true

# 0:30-1:00 — Authenticate
vault login <method>

# 1:00-2:00 — Survey the environment
vault secrets list      # What engines are enabled?
vault auth list         # What auth methods exist?
vault policy list       # What policies are available?

# 2:00-5:00 — Scan ALL 60 questions
# Mark each as: 🟢 Easy  🟡 Medium  🔴 Hard

🚨 Critical Do's & Don'ts During the Exam

✅ DO THIS
  • ✅ Use vault path-help <path> — it's your built-in docs!
  • ✅ Run vault status FIRST — sealed Vault = 0 points
  • ✅ Remember KV v2 data path: /secret/data/<path>
  • ✅ Test policies: vault token capabilities <token> <path>
  • ✅ Use -format=json for parsing
  • ✅ Flag hard questions, return with fresh eyes
  • ✅ Use tab completion: vault <TAB><TAB>
❌ DON'T DO THIS
  • ❌ Don't guess API paths — KV v2 is /data/ not //
  • ❌ Don't assume Vault is unsealed. VERIFY.
  • ❌ Don't write to /secret/ directly (v2 needs /data/ prefix!)
  • ❌ Don't assume a policy works — TEST IT.
  • ❌ Don't manually count fields in text output
  • ❌ Don't spend >2 min on any single question
  • ❌ Don't type full paths repeatedly

⚡ Exam Day Cheat Sheet — Your Aliases & Commands

Critical Commands — Type From Memory 
export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
export VAULT_TOKEN='s.xxxxxxxxxx'

vault status                   # Check seal state
vault operator init            # Initialize Vault
vault operator unseal          # Unseal (3 keys needed)
vault login                    # Authenticate
vault secrets list             # List all engines
vault auth list                # List auth methods
vault policy list              # List policies
vault token lookup             # Inspect current token
vault lease renew              # Renew a lease
vault lease revoke             # Revoke a lease

# Quick policy write:
vault policy write app-policy - <<EOF ... EOF

# Quick KV operations:
vault kv put secret/anihpj db_user=anihpj
vault kv get secret/anihpj
vault kv list secret/
vault kv delete secret/anihpj

📖 Complete Guide Overview — Your Vault Learning Roadmap

This document is a complete, self-contained HashiCorp Vault Associate (003) certification preparation system. It takes you from absolute beginner to exam-ready through 12 structured parts, 27 chapters, 270 practice questions, 50 mock exam questions, and 14 quick-reference appendices — all built around the anihpj/jobpost Django-on-Kubernetes project as a real-world demonstration.

📚
12 Parts · 27 Chapters

Structured from Foundation → Secrets Engines → Auth → Tokens → Policies → K8s → Operations → Exam Prep

📝
320 Questions

270 chapter practice questions + 50-question mock exam — all with detailed answers and explanations

14 Appendices

Answer keys, CLI cheatsheets, policy templates, decision trees, API refs, glossary, cram sheet

🎯 How to Use This Guide — Three Learning Paths

🚀
Path 1: The Cram (2 Weeks)

For: Experienced engineers who need the exam fast.

1Read Part 1 (Ch 1-3) — Foundation
2Skim Parts 2-5 (Ch 4-13) — Core concepts
3Deep-dive Part 5 (Ch 12) — Policies (28%!)
4Take Mock Exam (Ch 27) — Identify gaps
5Review Part 12 Appendices — Cram sheet
📖
Path 2: The Deep Dive (6 Weeks)

For: Engineers who want mastery, not just certification.

1Work through Parts 1-11 sequentially
2Complete ALL 270 practice questions
3Run every lab drill with anihpj/jobpost
4Re-read deep-dive sections (marked 🔬)
5Mock exam → Review gaps → Retake
🔐
Path 3: The Authorship Track

For: Engineers aiming for Vault Authorship certification.

1Complete Path 2 (Deep Dive) first
2Master Ch 26 (Plugins) + Appendix N
3Build a custom plugin with Go SDK
4Study Vault source code (reference plugins)
5Take Authorship Certification exam

🟢 Part 1: Foundation — What is Vault?

Chapter 1: The Secret Problem — Why Vault Exists

Every application has secrets — database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, tokens. Without a centralized system to manage them, secrets sprawl across .env files, config files, CI/CD pipelines, and even source code repositories. This chapter explores the secret sprawl nightmare, introduces HashiCorp Vault as the solution, and sets up anihpj/jobpost as your hands-on learning project.

1.1 The Secret Sprawl Nightmare

Before we understand why Vault exists, we need to understand the problem it solves. In modern software, a "secret" is any piece of sensitive information that an application needs to function — passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, database credentials, encryption keys, tokens. Without a central management system, these secrets end up scattered everywhere — a phenomenon called "secret sprawl."

🔍 How Secret Sprawl Happens — A Day in the Life

Imagine you're a developer on the anihpj team. Your Django app needs a database password to connect to PostgreSQL. You add it to settings.py for local testing — "I'll fix it before production." But the deadline looms, and the password gets committed to Git. A colleague needs it for their local setup, so you Slack it to them. The DevOps engineer copies it into a Kubernetes Secret YAML. Six months later, the password is in 5 different places, nobody knows who has access, and it hasn't been rotated since day one. This is secret sprawl.

The average organization has thousands of secrets spread across source code, CI/CD pipelines, config files, cloud consoles, and chat messages. Manual management doesn't scale — you can't audit who accessed what, you can't rotate secrets without breaking things, and a single leaked credential can compromise your entire infrastructure.

💡 COMMON PATTERN

Secrets in CODE/REPOS = DISASTER. Every single one of these breaches could have been prevented with centralized secret management.

🔴 Before Vault vs ✅ After Vault

🔴 BEFORE VAULT

Secrets in .env files → committed to git by accident

Hardcoded passwords → leaked when repo is public

Same password for 3 years → never rotated, everyone uses the same admin password

No idea who accessed what → zero visibility, zero logs

Manual secret distribution → copy-paste into Slack/email

K8s Secrets = base64 → NOT encryption, anyone with kubectl can decode

✅ AFTER VAULT

Secrets encrypted at rest → AES-256-GCM96 in Vault storage

Dynamic DB credentials → auto-generated, short-lived (TTL)

Auto-rotated secrets → PKI certs, DB creds auto-renewed

Full audit trail → every request logged (who, what, when)

Apps pull secrets automatically → via Vault Agent/CSI

Vault encrypts at rest → AES-256-GCM96, only Vault can decrypt

🔑 THE KEY INSIGHT

Vault doesn't just STORE secrets — it MANAGES their entire LIFECYCLE: Creation → Distribution → Rotation → Revocation → Audit. Every step is automated and logged. This is the paradigm shift.

📚 Vault Terminology — Your First 8 Words

🔐
Secret

Any sensitive data: password, key, token, certificate. The "what" that Vault protects.

🔌
Secrets Engine

A plugin that manages secrets. Like an "app" inside Vault. KV, DB, PKI, Transit are engines.

🪪
Auth Method

How you prove your identity to Vault. Token, AppRole, K8s SA, LDAP, JWT/OIDC.

🎫
Token

The result of authentication. Every Vault request includes a token. "The currency of Vault."

📜
Policy

ACL rules defining WHO can do WHAT on WHICH path. Written in HCL. Default: DENY ALL.

⏱️
Lease

A time-limited permission. Dynamic secrets have leases. Expired lease = secret revoked.

🔒
Seal / Unseal

Vault starts SEALED (encrypted, inaccessible). Must be UNSEALED with Shamir keys or auto-unseal.

📋
Audit Device

Logs every Vault request. File, socket (→ Splunk), syslog (→ SIEM). Tamper-proof record.

1.2 What is HashiCorp Vault? (The Simple Answer)

HashiCorp Vault is a centralized secrets management platform. At its core, Vault is a tool for securely accessing secrets. It encrypts data at rest, controls access via policies, audits every interaction, and can even generate and auto-rotate secrets dynamically.

📖 Quick Facts

Built by: HashiCorp (creators of Terraform, Consul, Nomad, Boundary)
Written in: Go | License: MPL 2.0 (open-source) | Enterprise: Available
Used by: Adobe, SAP, eBay, Splunk, Barclays, Comcast, Robinhood

🧠 The Philosophy Behind Vault

Vault was born from a simple insight: secrets should never be stored alongside the code that uses them. This principle — separation of secrets from application logic — is the foundation of modern security architecture. Vault doesn't just encrypt secrets; it acts as a trusted intermediary between applications and their sensitive data. Every interaction goes through Vault's policy engine, which answers one question: "Should THIS caller be allowed to do THAT operation?"

Think of Vault as a central bank for secrets. Just as you don't carry your life savings in cash everywhere, your applications shouldn't carry credentials. They go to the "bank" (Vault), prove their identity (authenticate), and withdraw only what they're authorized to access (policy check). Every transaction is recorded (audit), and some "currencies" even expire automatically (dynamic secrets with TTL). This is fundamentally different from the .env file approach where secrets sit in plaintext on every developer's laptop.

THE PORT ANALOGY — How Vault Works (Novice-Friendly)

💡 Ships don't carry their own cargo manifests — they
   check in, get what they need, and leave. That's Vault!

Just like ships at a seaport don't carry their own cargo manifests — they check in at the security checkpoint, get authorized, pick up what they need from the warehouse, and leave — applications don't carry their own secrets. They authenticate to Vault, get authorized via policies, and retrieve the secrets they need.

🏢 Where Vault Fits in the HashiCorp Ecosystem

Vault is part of HashiCorp's infrastructure automation suite. Understanding where it fits helps you see the bigger picture:

🏗️
Terraform

Provision infrastructure as code. Terraform can use Vault to retrieve secrets during provisioning — no hardcoded credentials in .tf files.

🔐
Vault

Secure secrets and protect sensitive data. THIS is what you're learning now — the central security layer.

📦
Nomad

Orchestrate workloads (alternative to K8s). Nomad integrates with Vault for secret injection into jobs.

🌐
Consul

Connect services with networking + service mesh. Consul can use Vault for TLS certificate management.

🛡️
Boundary

Access infrastructure without exposing credentials. Boundary integrates with Vault for credential brokering.

☸️
Vault + Kubernetes

Vault is the most popular secret manager for Kubernetes. Helm charts, sidecar injector, CSI, and VSO make integration seamless.

📖 The HashiCorp Philosophy

HashiCorp's suite follows the pattern: Provision → Secure → Connect → Run. Vault is the Secure layer — it sits between provisioning (Terraform) and runtime (Nomad/K8s), ensuring that secrets never appear in plaintext at any stage of the infrastructure lifecycle.

1.3 The 4 Pillars of Vault — Visual Overview

Vault's architecture rests on four foundational pillars that together create a complete secrets management solution:

🔐
PILLAR 1: Secure Secret Storage

AES-256-GCM96 encryption at rest. Data is NEVER stored as plaintext on disk. An encryption barrier ensures all data is encrypted before touching storage. "Like a bank vault — everything locked inside."

🔑
PILLAR 2: Access Control

Identity-based ACL policies with per-path control. Default is DENY ALL. Policies use HCL syntax. Multiple policies combine as a UNION (most permissive wins). Supports templated policies for dynamic access. "Like a security guard checking every ID badge."

📋
PILLAR 3: Audit Everything

Every single request is logged — who, what, when. Tamper-proof audit trail. Multiple audit devices: file, socket (→ Logstash/Splunk), syslog (→ SIEM). "Like CCTV cameras recording every interaction."

🔄
PILLAR 4: Automate Rotation

Dynamic DB credentials with TTL — auto-expire. Auto-renew leases. Zero-touch certificate rotation via PKI. Root credential rotation. "Like a self-cleaning system — nothing stale."

🎓 EXAM TIP

Remember the 4 Pillars in order: Storage → Access → Audit → Rotation. A common exam question asks "Which Vault feature ensures credentials are automatically changed?" — The answer is Dynamic Secrets with TTL/Lease (Pillar 4).

🔗 How the 4 Pillars Work Together

These pillars are not independent — they form a chain of trust. Pillar 1 (Secure Storage) ensures secrets are encrypted, but without Pillar 2 (Access Control), anyone could decrypt them. Pillar 2 controls access, but without Pillar 3 (Audit), you'd never know if someone abused their access. Pillar 3 records everything, but without Pillar 4 (Rotation), a compromised secret remains valid indefinitely. All four are required for a complete security posture. This is why Vault is fundamentally different from a password manager or a KMS — it's not just about storing secrets; it's about managing their entire lifecycle with cryptographic guarantees at every stage.

🎯 When to Use Which — Decision Scenarios

🏠
Solo Developer, Hobby Project

Use .env files. Vault is overkill for a single dev with one app and no compliance needs. Add secrets to .gitignore and use environment variables.

☸️
K8s-Only, One Cluster

K8s Secrets + etcd encryption may suffice if you don't need dynamic secrets, cross-cluster sharing, or audit trails. Add Vault when you outgrow this.

☁️
AWS-Only, Serverless

AWS Secrets Manager is simpler if you're fully on AWS. But costs scale with API calls, and you're locked into one cloud. Vault is cloud-agnostic.

🏢
Multi-Cloud, Multi-Team

HashiCorp Vault is the clear winner. Dynamic secrets, multi-cloud, per-path ACLs, full audit, and self-hosted. This is anihpj's use case.

1.5 How Vault Fits With Kubernetes

Kubernetes has a built-in Secrets resource — but it's only base64 encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with kubectl access can decode them. This is where Vault comes in, providing three integration patterns for Kubernetes:

VAULT ON KUBERNETES — 3 Integration Patterns
PATTERN 1: SIDECAR INJECTOR
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POD                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐    │
│  │ anihpj   │  │ Vault Agent      │    │
│  │ Container│  │ Container        │    │
│  │          │  │ 1. Auth (K8s SA) │    │
│  │ Reads    │  │ 2. Fetch secrets │    │
│  │ from     │  │ 3. Render to     │    │
│  │ /vault/  │  │    shared volume │    │
│  │ secrets/ │  │                  │    │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────────────┘    │
│       └──────────────┬─────────────────┘
│              ┌───────▼───────┐
│              │ Shared Volume  │
│              │ /vault/secrets │
│              └───────────────┘
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

PATTERN 2: CSI PROVIDER
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POD → CSI Driver (DaemonSet) → Vault   │
│  Mounts secrets as Kubernetes Volumes    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

PATTERN 3: VAULT SECRETS OPERATOR (VSO)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  VSO watches Vault → Syncs to K8s Secret│
│  App reads K8s Secret (native, no sidecar)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ IMPORTANT

Kubernetes Secrets are base64 encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with kubectl get secret -o yaml can decode them. Vault encrypts secrets with AES-256-GCM96 and provides full access control and audit — things K8s Secrets alone cannot do.

🔬 Why K8s Secrets Alone Are Insufficient

Let's be concrete. If you store your database password in a K8s Secret and run kubectl get secret db-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d, you get the plaintext password. Anyone with kubectl access to that namespace can read it. Moreover, K8s Secrets have no concept of dynamic generation (you can't create temporary database users on-demand), no automatic rotation (passwords never change unless you manually update them), and no cross-cluster sharing (a secret in cluster A stays in cluster A). Vault addresses ALL of these limitations while still running natively on Kubernetes.

       │  ✅    ││  ✅    ││   ❌    │ │encrypt  │
       └────────┘└────────┘└─────────┘ └─────────┘
💡 Rule of Thumb

If you have secrets AND multiple services or team members → USE VAULT. It pays for itself fast. For a single hobby app with one developer, .env files or cloud KMS may be sufficient.

⚖️ Vault Cost vs Benefit — Quick Assessment

✅
USE Vault When...

Multiple services need secrets • Compliance requires audit trails • Secrets must be rotated automatically • Multi-cloud or hybrid infrastructure • Team of 5+ developers sharing credentials • Need dynamic database credentials

❌
Skip Vault When...

Single developer hobby project • No compliance/audit requirements • All infrastructure on one cloud (use native KMS) • Team lacks operational capacity • Simple static secrets that rarely change • Pod with 2 env vars total

1. Pod starts → Vault Agent sidecar auths via K8s SA
2. Agent fetches: DB creds (dynamic), API keys (KV v2),
   TLS cert (PKI), encrypted config (Transit)
3. Agent renders secrets to /vault/secrets/ as files
4. Django reads files → connects to DB, Redis, sends email
5. Agent auto-renews tokens + leases in background

Secrets needed by anihpj/jobpost: Database password, Redis password, Django SECRET_KEY, Email API key, SMS API key, TLS certificates for HTTPS. Throughout this guide, we'll configure Vault to manage ALL of these securely.

🌅 A Day in the Life — How anihpj Uses Vault

1
Pod Starts

anihpj Pod scheduled on K8s node. Vault Agent sidecar starts alongside Django container.

2
Authenticate

Vault Agent reads Pod's ServiceAccount JWT → calls Vault K8s auth → receives token.

3
Fetch Secrets

Agent uses token to fetch: DB creds (dynamic), API keys (KV v2), TLS cert (PKI).

4
Render Files

Agent renders secrets to /vault/secrets/ as .env file. Django reads it on startup.

5
Live & Renew

Django connects to DB with dynamic creds. Agent auto-renews tokens + leases in background.

This flow happens automatically — zero human intervention after initial setup. If a pod restarts, the process repeats seamlessly. If credentials are compromised, they auto-expire within their TTL. This is the power of Vault in production.

By the end of this guide, you'll be able to set up this entire flow for the anihpj/jobpost application. Every chapter builds toward this goal — the architecture diagram above is your "north star" for understanding how all the pieces fit together.

📝 Chapter 1 Practice Questions — Secret Sprawl & Vault Fundamentals

Q1
What is "secret sprawl" and why is it a security risk?
Show Answer
Answer

Secret sprawl is the uncontrolled distribution of secrets (passwords, API keys, tokens) across multiple locations — .env files, config files, CI/CD pipelines, source code repositories, and hardcoded in application code. It's a security risk because: (1) no one knows who has access, (2) there's no audit trail of when secrets were used, (3) rotation is manual and often forgotten, and (4) secrets can be committed to git and exposed publicly.

Explanation

The average cost of a data breach caused by exposed secrets is $4.45M (IBM 2024). Real examples include Uber (AWS creds in GitHub → 77K records exposed) and Toyota (DB password in public repo → 300K emails exposed for 5+ years). Vault solves this by centralizing and encrypting all secrets with full audit logging.

Q2
In one sentence, what is HashiCorp Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

HashiCorp Vault is a centralized secrets management platform that securely stores, controls access to, audits, and automatically rotates secrets such as passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, and database credentials.

Explanation

Vault's official tagline: "A tool for securely accessing secrets." Built by HashiCorp (Terraform, Consul), written in Go, open-source under MPL 2.0. Used by Adobe, SAP, eBay, Splunk, and many more.

Q3
What are the 4 Pillars of HashiCorp Vault? Name them and describe each in one line.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Secure Secret Storage: AES-256-GCM96 encryption at rest — data never stored as plaintext on disk.
2. Access Control: Identity-based ACL policies with per-path control — default DENY ALL.
3. Audit Everything: Every request logged (who, what, when) — tamper-proof audit trail.
4. Automate Rotation: Dynamic secrets with TTL, auto-renew leases, zero-touch certificate rotation.

Explanation

These four pillars form the complete secrets management lifecycle. Remember the order: Storage → Access → Audit → Rotation. Without any one pillar, the system is incomplete. For example, storing secrets securely (Pillar 1) without auditing access (Pillar 3) means you can't detect breaches.

Q4
Why are Kubernetes Secrets alone NOT sufficient for production secret management?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes Secrets are only base64 encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with kubectl access can decode them with a simple command. They provide no dynamic secret generation, no automatic rotation, no audit trail, and no cross-cluster or multi-cloud secret management.

K8s Secrets are NOT encrypted
# Anyone with kubectl can decode K8s secrets:
kubectl get secret my-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
# → Outputs the plaintext password!
Explanation

While Kubernetes Secrets can be encrypted at rest with etcd encryption, they still lack dynamic secrets, automatic rotation, fine-grained ACL policies (beyond RBAC), and comprehensive audit logging. Vault complements K8s by providing all of these capabilities.

Q5
Name the 3 integration patterns for running Vault with Kubernetes.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Sidecar Injector: Vault Agent runs as a sidecar container in the same Pod, authenticates via K8s ServiceAccount, fetches secrets, and renders them to a shared volume.
2. CSI Provider: A DaemonSet that mounts secrets as Kubernetes Volumes — no sidecar needed.
3. Vault Secrets Operator (VSO): A Kubernetes operator that watches Vault and syncs secrets into native K8s Secret resources.

Explanation

Sidecar is the most common pattern (feature-rich, supports templates). CSI is simpler (no sidecar container overhead). VSO is the newest pattern (applications read standard K8s Secrets, VSO handles sync). Each has different trade-offs in complexity, resource usage, and security model.

Q6
Which of the following is NOT one of Vault's 4 Pillars? A) Secure Secret Storage B) Access Control C) Container Orchestration D) Audit Everything
Show Answer
Answer

C) Container Orchestration is NOT one of Vault's 4 Pillars. The 4 Pillars are: Secure Secret Storage, Access Control, Audit Everything, and Automate Rotation.

Explanation

Container orchestration is a Kubernetes function, not a Vault function. Vault focuses on secrets management, not running containers.

Q7
What is the difference between static secrets and dynamic secrets in Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

Static secrets are pre-existing values (like an API key or password) that Vault stores and retrieves — they don't change unless manually rotated. Dynamic secrets are generated on-demand by Vault when requested (like database credentials), have a TTL (time-to-live), and are automatically revoked when the TTL expires.

Explanation

Static = you give Vault a password to store (KV v1/v2). Dynamic = Vault creates a temporary database user for you with a short TTL, then automatically deletes it. Dynamic secrets are more secure because even if leaked, they expire quickly.

Q8
The anihpj/jobpost application needs to store the following: DB password, Redis password, Django SECRET_KEY, Email API key, TLS certificates. Which Vault engines would you use for each?
Show Answer
Answer

DB password: Database Secrets Engine (dynamic, auto-rotated)
Redis password: KV v2 Secrets Engine (static, encrypted at rest)
Django SECRET_KEY: KV v2 Secrets Engine (static)
Email API key: KV v2 Secrets Engine (static)
TLS certificates: PKI Secrets Engine (dynamic, auto-issued, short-lived)

Explanation

The Database Secrets Engine is ideal for DB credentials because it creates unique, time-limited credentials per request. PKI is ideal for TLS certs because it issues short-lived certificates (72h default). KV v2 handles all other static secrets with versioning and encryption.

Q9
When should you NOT use HashiCorp Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

You should consider NOT using Vault when: (1) you have a single application with a single developer, (2) you have no compliance requirements for audit trails, (3) your team lacks the operational expertise to manage Vault, or (4) the complexity overhead outweighs the security benefits for your use case (e.g., a small hobby project).

Explanation

Vault has an operational cost — it needs to be installed, configured, backed up, and monitored. For very simple setups, .env files with proper file permissions or cloud KMS may be sufficient. The tipping point is typically when you have multiple services or team members needing access to shared secrets.

Q10
Explain the "shipping port" analogy for understanding how Vault works. Map each part to a Vault component.
Show Answer
Answer

The Sea: Your network/infrastructure where applications run
Ships (Applications): Your apps that need secrets — they don't carry secrets, they request them
Security Checkpoint: Vault Authentication — "Who are you? Show your papers!" (AppRole, K8s SA)
Warehouse: Vault Secrets Engines — KV (static secrets), DB (dynamic secrets), PKI (certificates)
Cargo Manifest: Policies — defines what each ship (app) is allowed to access
Security Cameras: Audit Devices — logs every interaction

Explanation

Just like ships don't carry their own cargo manifests, applications shouldn't carry their own secrets. They authenticate at the checkpoint, get authorized by their manifest (policy), pick up what they need from the warehouse (secrets engine), and every interaction is recorded by the cameras (audit).

🏋️ Chapter 1 Lab Drill — Your First Vault Interaction (5 min)
⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes | 🎯 Goal: Start Vault dev server, login, write & read your first secret
Lab Steps — Type These Commands
# Step 1: Start Vault in dev mode (in-memory, pre-unsealed, root token = "root")
vault server -dev -dev-root-token-id=root &

# Step 2: Set environment variables
export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
export VAULT_TOKEN='root'

# Step 3: Check Vault status
vault status
# Expected: Sealed: false, Initialized: true

# Step 4: Enable your first secrets engine (KV v2)
vault secrets enable -path=anihpj kv-v2

# Step 5: Write your first secret
vault kv put anihpj/hello greeting="Hello from Vault" target="anihpj jobpost app"

# Step 6: Read it back
vault kv get anihpj/hello

# Step 7: List all enabled engines
vault secrets list

# Step 8: Stop the dev server
pkill vault

Drill Check: Can you explain what happened in each step? Step 3 verifies Vault is running. Step 4 creates a storage engine. Steps 5-6 demonstrate the fundamental secret write/read cycle. Step 7 shows you all active engines. This 8-step flow is the foundation of EVERY Vault interaction you'll ever do.

2.1 Vault's Core Architecture — The Big Picture

Vault is a single Go binary. Since Raft was integrated (Vault 1.4+), there are zero external dependencies for production use. Understanding Vault's layered architecture is key to passing the exam.

HASHICORP VAULT — ARCHITECTURE DEEP DIVE
┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐
│ vault   │  │ HTTP    │  │ Python  │  │ Go      │
│ CLI     │  │ API     │  │ SDK     │  │ SDK     │
└────┬────┘  └────┬────┘  └────┬────┘  └────┬────┘
     └────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘
                      │  HTTPS (TLS 1.2+)
     ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
     │         LISTENERS                │
     │   (TCP, TLS, rate limiting)      │
     └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                      │
     ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
     │            CORE                  │
     │                                  │
     │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │
     │  │     AUTH METHODS           │ │ ← "WHO are you?"
     │  │  AppRole │ K8s │ Userpass  │ │
     │  └────────────┬───────────────┘ │
     │  ┌────────────▼───────────────┐ │
     │  │     TOKEN STORE            │ │ ← Session tokens
     │  │  Service │ Batch │ Periodic│ │
     │  └────────────┬───────────────┘ │
     │  ┌────────────▼───────────────┐ │
     │  │     POLICY ENGINE (ACL)    │ │ ← "CAN you do it?"
     │  │  Default: DENY ALL         │ │
     │  └────────────┬───────────────┘ │
     │  ┌────────────▼───────────────┐ │
     │  │     SECRETS ENGINES        │ │ ← DO the work
     │  │  KV │ DB │ PKI │ Transit   │ │
     │  └────────────┬───────────────┘ │
     │  ┌────────────▼───────────────┐ │
     │  │     AUDIT BROKER           │ │ ← "What happened?"
     │  │  → File, Socket, Syslog    │ │
     │  └────────────────────────────┘ │
     └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                      │
     ┌────────────────▼────────────────┐
     │    ENCRYPTION BARRIER            │
     │    AES-256-GCM96 encryption      │
     │    ALL data encrypted before     │
     │    touching storage              │
     └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                      │
     ┌────────────────▼────────────────┐
     │      STORAGE BACKEND             │
     │  Raft │ Consul │ Filesystem      │
     │  (All data encrypted at rest)    │
     └─────────────────────────────────┘

The Encryption Barrier is the security foundation — ALL data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM96 before it touches any storage backend. The master key exists ONLY in memory (never on disk).

🧱 Understanding Each Layer

Vault's architecture follows the separation of concerns principle. Listeners handle the network (TCP, TLS, rate limiting) — they're the "front door." The Core is a pipeline: Auth Methods verify identity (WHO you are), the Token Store creates a session token, the Policy Engine checks authorization (WHAT you can do), and Secrets Engines perform the actual work. The Audit Broker logs everything in parallel (non-blocking). Finally, the Encryption Barrier ensures that even if an attacker gains physical access to storage, all data is encrypted. Storage Backends only ever see encrypted blobs. This layered design means security is not a single point but a defense in depth system where each layer independently contributes to security.

🩺 What Happens When Each Component Fails

Understanding failure modes solidifies your architectural knowledge:

🔌
Listener Failure

Vault unreachable but data safe. External — no impact on stored secrets.

🪪
Auth Method Misconfig

New logins fail. Existing tokens continue working until TTL expires.

🎫
Token Store Failure

New tokens can't be created. Existing tokens remain valid in memory.

📜
Policy Engine Error

Unknown policy = DENY ALL. Vault fails CLOSED (secure), never OPEN.

🔧
Secrets Engine Crash

Only that engine affected. Others continue operating normally.

📋
Audit Device Full

ALL requests blocked until space freed. Critical to monitor disk usage!

🛡️
Encryption Barrier

Master key lost = ALL operations halt. Must unseal to recover.

💾
Storage Unavailable

All writes fail. Reads may work from cache. HA with Raft prevents this.

2.2 The Seal/Unseal Mechanism (EXAM CRITICAL) 🎯

When Vault starts, it's SEALED — the master key is NOT in memory, and ALL operations (except status and unseal) are blocked. This is Vault's strongest security guarantee.

🔐 Why the Seal State Matters

The seal state is Vault's ultimate security control. When Vault is sealed, the encrypted data sits on disk but is mathematically impossible to decrypt without the master key — and the master key exists nowhere in the system. It must be reconstructed through the unseal process. This means: (1) a stolen hard drive with Vault data is useless without unseal keys, (2) a compromised Vault process can be instantly locked down with vault operator seal, and (3) Vault restarts are safe — data remains protected until explicitly unsealed. This is fundamentally different from a typical database that auto-decrypts on startup. Vault refuses to operate until enough key holders explicitly authorize it.

THE SEAL/UNSEAL LIFECYCLE
STEP 1: VAULT PROCESS STARTS
$ vault server -config=vault.hcl
→ Vault starts, loads encrypted data from storage
→ Cannot decrypt: Master Key NOT in memory
                         │
                         ▼
STEP 2: VAULT IS "SEALED" 🔒
$ vault status → Sealed: true
→ ALL operations BLOCKED except: status, unseal
                         │
         ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
         │   HOW TO UNSEAL?              │
         │                               │
         │ OPTION A: SHAMIR KEYS         │  OPTION B: AUTO-UNSEAL
         │ vault operator unseal <key1>  │  Vault → Cloud KMS
         │ vault operator unseal <key2>  │  (AWS KMS / Azure / GCP)
         │ vault operator unseal <key3>  │  → Automatic on startup
         │ → Need 3 of 5 keys            │
         └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
STEP 3: VAULT IS "UNSEALED" 🔓
$ vault status → Sealed: false
→ Master Key in MEMORY (never to disk)
→ ALL operations now available

Shamir's Secret Sharing — Visual Explanation

🔑
Key Shares (N=5)

Master key split into 5 shares. Each key holder gets one. Any 3 (K=3) can reconstruct the master key. Having 2 or fewer = useless.

🛡️
Separation of Duties

No single person can unseal Vault alone. Requires collaboration of 3 key holders. Even if 2 keys are lost, 3 remain safe.

Auto-Unseal (Cloud KMS)

Instead of manual Shamir keys, Vault can use cloud KMS to automatically decrypt the master key on startup. Supported: AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP Cloud KMS, and Transit (self-referential auto-unseal).

🔬 Understanding Recovery Keys vs Unseal Keys

This distinction is heavily tested on the exam. Unseal keys reconstruct the master key — they let Vault decrypt data. Recovery keys are used to regenerate the root token or rotate the underlying encryption key. They serve different purposes: unseal keys = "open the vault," recovery keys = "reset the admin password." In auto-unseal setups, you don't have unseal keys (the cloud KMS handles that), but you still get recovery keys during initialization. If you lose recovery keys AND the root token, you lose administrative access permanently — even though Vault is unsealed and operational.

🎓 EXAM TIP

Shamir keys = manual, need K of N. Auto-Unseal = automatic via cloud KMS. Recovery Keys are DIFFERENT from unseal keys — they regenerate the root token, not the master key. This is a common exam trick!

2.3 Storage Backends — Where Data Lives 🎯

FEATURERAFT (Integrated)CONSUL (External)FILESYSTEMCLOUD (DynamoDB)
HA Support✅ Built-in✅ Yes❌ No✅ Yes
External Deps❌ None needed✅ Consul cluster❌ None✅ Cloud account
Setup Complexity🟢 Easy🟡 Medium🟢 Trivial🟢 Easy
Production Ready✅ Yes✅ Yes❌ NEVER!✅ Yes
Recommended SinceVault 1.4Vault 0.xN/AVault 1.x
Auto Snapshot✅ Yes✅ Yes❌ No✅ Yes
💡 Recommendation

For NEW deployments: Use RAFT (integrated, no external deps). For EXISTING Consul infra: Use CONSUL. For DEV/TESTING only: Use FILESYSTEM or INMEM.

🔍 Storage Backend Selection — Decision Guide

Raft is integrated directly into the Vault binary — when you run Vault, you're also running Raft. This eliminates the operational complexity of managing a separate Consul cluster. Raft handles leader election automatically: if the active Vault node fails, Raft elects a new leader from the remaining followers within milliseconds. Consul is still valuable if you already have a Consul cluster for service mesh or service discovery — Vault can use it as an external storage backend. However, this adds a dependency: if Consul goes down, Vault can't persist data. Filesystem and Inmem are development-only: they have no HA, no replication, and no data durability guarantees. A single disk failure or process restart means total data loss. The exam expects you to know which backends are production-ready (Raft, Consul, integrated cloud backends) and which are not (Filesystem, Inmem).

2.4 High Availability (HA) Mode 🎯

VAULT HA CLUSTER — Production Topology
                   CLIENT REQUESTS
                        │
               ┌────────▼────────┐
               │  LOAD BALANCER   │  ← Health checks /v1/sys/health
               │  (HAProxy/Nginx) │     Routes to ACTIVE only
               └────────┬────────┘
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼               ▼
┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
│  VAULT-1     │ │  VAULT-2     │ │  VAULT-3     │
│  🟢 ACTIVE   │ │  ⚪ STANDBY  │ │  ⚪ STANDBY  │
│ Handles ALL  │ │ Forwards ALL │ │ Forwards ALL │
│ read + write │ │ to Active    │ │ to Active    │
└──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘
       └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                        │
               ┌────────▼────────┐
               │   RAFT CLUSTER   │
               │ Leader: Vault-1  │ ← handles all writes
               │ Follower: Vault-2│ ← replicates from Leader
               │ Follower: Vault-3│
               └─────────────────┘

🔄 FAILOVER: Active crashes → Raft elects new Leader
→ LB detects unhealthy → Routes to new Active → <5s downtime

⚡ Why HA Matters for anihpj

If the anihpj job board is running in production and its Vault instance goes down, every pod that needs secrets will fail to start or refresh its credentials. New deployments stall because database credentials can't be generated. TLS certificates expire without renewal.

<5sFailover Time
3Min Nodes (HA)
99.99%Target Uptime
0Data Loss on Failover

In HA mode with 3 replicas, any single node failure is transparent — the load balancer routes to the new active, and the application never notices. The Raft consensus algorithm ensures that even during a leader election, no data is lost and no inconsistent state is possible.

2.5 Vault's Request Lifecycle — 10 Steps

REQUEST LIFECYCLE — What Happens When You Run vault kv get
$ vault kv get secret/anihpj
     │
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. PARSE: CLI → HTTP GET /v1/secret/data/anihpj  │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. TLS: TLS 1.2+ encryption, cert verification   │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. PARSE TOKEN: Extract X-Vault-Token from header│
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. VERIFY TOKEN: Check validity, TTL, parent     │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. LOAD POLICIES: Get all policies on token      │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 6. ACL CHECK: "read" on secret/data/anihpj? → YES│
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 7. ROUTE: Send to KV v2 secrets engine           │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 8. DECRYPT: Barrier decrypts data from storage   │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 9. AUDIT LOG: Log request+response               │
└────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 10. RESPONSE: { "data": { "db_user": "anihpj" }}│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⏱️ Total time: 5-15ms | 💡 Steps 4-6 = 90% of errors

🪵 Debugging Permission Denied — Using the Lifecycle

When you see 403 Permission Denied, the lifecycle tells you exactly where to look: Step 4 (Token invalid or expired?), Step 5 (Correct policies attached?), or Step 6 (Policy covers this path with the right capability?). Use vault token lookup to check TTL and policies. Use vault token capabilities <token> <path> to test exactly what a token can do on a given path without actually making the request. This command is your #1 debugging tool and is frequently tested on the exam. The audit log (Step 9) also records every denied request with the exact reason — check it first when troubleshooting.

⚡ Performance Implications of the Lifecycle

Each of the 10 steps adds latency. In a typical production setup, the full roundtrip is 5-15ms. Storage backend choice has the biggest impact — Raft adds sub-millisecond overhead for reads (from followers) but requires a quorum write to the leader (1-3ms). The TLS handshake (Step 2) is amortized over persistent connections. Policy evaluation (Step 6) is extremely fast because policies are compiled and cached in memory. The audit broker (Step 9) is non-blocking — Vault doesn't wait for audit writes before responding. For high-throughput scenarios (>10K requests/sec), consider using batch tokens (lighter verification) and enabling performance standbys (Enterprise) to distribute read load.

1️⃣ParseCLI→HTTP
→
2️⃣TLSEncrypt
→
3️⃣TokenExtract
→
4️⃣VerifyTTL/Parent
→
5️⃣PoliciesLoad ACLs
→
6️⃣ACL CheckAllow/Deny
→
7️⃣RouteTo Engine
→
8️⃣DecryptBarrier
→

🔟ResponseReturn Data

📝 Chapter 2 Practice Questions — Vault Architecture

Q1
What is the Encryption Barrier in Vault and why is it critical?
Show Answer
Answer

The Encryption Barrier is Vault's security foundation — ALL data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM96 before it touches any storage backend. The master key exists ONLY in memory, never on disk. This means even if an attacker gains access to the physical storage, the data is encrypted and useless without the master key.

Explanation

This is the reason Vault must be "unsealed" — the master key needs to be reconstructed in memory before any data can be decrypted. When Vault is sealed, ALL operations (except status and unseal) return errors.

Q2
What is Shamir's Secret Sharing and how does it work in Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

Shamir's Secret Sharing is a cryptographic algorithm that splits the master key into N shares (e.g., 5), where K shares (e.g., 3) are needed to reconstruct it. Each key holder gets one share. No single person can unseal Vault alone — it requires collaboration of K key holders.

Explanation

This provides both security (2 keys = useless) and fault tolerance (2 keys can be lost, 3 remain). The command is: vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3. This is called "M of N" or "threshold cryptography."

Q3
What is the difference between Shamir Unseal and Auto-Unseal?
Show Answer
Answer

Shamir: Manual — requires K of N key holders to enter their keys via vault operator unseal. Auto-Unseal: Automatic — Vault uses a cloud KMS (AWS, Azure, GCP) to decrypt the master key on startup. No manual intervention needed.

Explanation

Auto-unseal is preferred for production because it eliminates the manual unseal process on restart. However, it requires a cloud KMS dependency and additional cost. Important: Recovery Keys (for root token regeneration) are DIFFERENT from unseal keys.

Q4
Which storage backend is recommended for new Vault deployments and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Raft (integrated) is recommended for all new deployments since Vault 1.4. It requires zero external dependencies, supports HA natively, provides automatic snapshots, and is simpler to operate than Consul-backed deployments.

Explanation

Consul is still supported and recommended if you already have a Consul cluster running. Filesystem should NEVER be used in production (single point of failure, no HA). Inmem is dev-only (data lost on restart).

Q5
In a Vault HA cluster with Raft, what happens when the Active node crashes?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Raft detects the leader failure and elects a new leader from the standby nodes. 2. The load balancer detects the old active as unhealthy. 3. ALL traffic is routed to the new active. Total downtime: typically <5 seconds.

Explanation

Standby nodes forward ALL requests to the active node during normal operation. After failover, the newly elected active starts handling reads and writes directly. This is why the load balancer must point to /v1/sys/health which returns 200 only for the active node.

Q6
List the 10 steps of a Vault request lifecycle in order.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Parse, 2. TLS, 3. Parse Token, 4. Verify Token, 5. Load Policies, 6. ACL Check, 7. Route, 8. Decrypt, 9. Audit Log, 10. Response. Steps 4-6 are where 90% of permission errors occur.

Explanation

Understanding this lifecycle helps you debug "permission denied" errors. If you get a 403, the issue is in steps 4-6 (token invalid, TTL expired, policies don't allow the operation, or ACL denied it).

Q7
What does "vault operator seal" do and when would you use it?
Show Answer
Answer

vault operator seal is an emergency lockdown command. It wipes the master key from memory, putting Vault back into the sealed state. ALL operations are immediately blocked. Use it when you suspect a security breach.

Explanation

After sealing, Vault must be unsealed again (via Shamir keys or auto-unseal) to resume operations. This is Vault's "big red button" — it instantly protects all secrets when you detect suspicious activity.

Q8
Can the Filesystem storage backend be used in production?
Show Answer
Answer

NO — NEVER use Filesystem in production. It's a single point of failure with no HA support. If the disk fails, all Vault data is lost. Production requires Raft (integrated) or Consul (external) with multiple nodes.

Explanation

Filesystem is acceptable for development and testing only. Even then, inmem (dev mode) is often more convenient. The exam may ask which storage backends are production-ready — the answer is Raft, Consul, and cloud backends (DynamoDB, GCS, etc.).

Q9
How does the Audit Broker work in Vault's architecture?
Show Answer
Answer

The Audit Broker sits inside Vault's Core and logs EVERY request — including who made it, what path was accessed, what operation was performed, and the response. It supports multiple audit devices simultaneously: File (local disk), Socket (→ Logstash/Splunk), and Syslog (→ SIEM).

Explanation

Audit logging is non-blocking — if an audit device fails, Vault continues to operate. However, if ALL audit devices fail, Vault will eventually block requests (configurable). Sensitive data in audit logs is HMAC'd (hashed) by default.

Q10
Explain the flow when the anihpj pod requests a database credential from Vault. Which components are involved and in what order?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Vault Agent sends request with K8s SA JWT → 2. Auth Method (K8s) validates JWT via TokenReview API → 3. Token Store creates a token with policies → 4. Policy Engine checks ACL → 5. DB Secrets Engine generates dynamic credentials on PostgreSQL → 6. Encryption Barrier encrypts audit log → 7. Audit Broker logs the request → 8. Response returned to pod.

Explanation

This is the full production flow for anihpj/jobpost. The DB Secrets Engine creates a temporary PostgreSQL user with a TTL, the credentials are returned to the pod, and when the TTL expires, Vault automatically drops the database user. Every step is audited.

🏋️ Ch 2 Lab Drill — Init, Unseal & Architecture (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Production init, unseal, explore components
# 1. Start production Vault
vault server -config=vault-config.hcl &
# vault-config.hcl: storage "raft" { path="/tmp/vault-data" }

# 2. Init (SAVE the 5 keys + root token!)
export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3

# 3. Unseal 3 times (Shamir K=3 of N=5)
vault operator unseal <key1>
vault operator unseal <key2>
vault operator unseal <key3>

# 4. Login + enable audit (ALWAYS first!)
export VAULT_TOKEN='<root_token>'
vault audit enable file file_path=/tmp/vault_audit.log

# 5. Explore: secrets list, auth list, policy list, health
vault secrets list && vault auth list && vault policy list
curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health | jq

Drill Check: Why 3 keys? (Shamir K-of-N). Why audit FIRST? (No unlogged ops). Why does status show 0/3 before unseal? (Master key not in memory).

Chapter 3: Installing and Running Vault — Your First Vault Server

Time to get hands-on! This chapter walks you through installing Vault, running it in dev mode for quick experiments, setting up production mode with proper init/unseal, and deploying Vault on Kubernetes with Helm — all using the anihpj/jobpost project as your target environment.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔧 Hands-On 🏗️ Lab

  • ✅ Run Vault in Dev Mode and write your first secret

  • ✅ Deploy Vault HA on Kubernetes with Helm for anihpj

3.1 Installation Methods — Choose Your Path

Vault is distributed as a single Go binary. You can install it via package managers, download it directly, run it in Docker, or deploy it on Kubernetes with Helm. Choose based on your environment:

🐧
Linux Server (Production)

apt install vault or download binary. Best for dedicated VMs/bare metal. Use systemd to manage the Vault service.

🍎
macOS (Development)

brew install vault. Great for local dev and testing. Use dev mode for quick experiments.

🪟
Windows (Development)

choco install vault or download binary. Works with PowerShell. Dev mode supported.

🐳
Docker (Quick Test)

docker run -d --cap-add=IPC_LOCK vault. Fastest way to test. Data lost on container removal unless volumes are configured.

☸️
Helm on K8s (Production)

helm install vault hashicorp/vault. HA with Raft, StatefulSet, persistent storage. Best for cloud-native deployments.

📦
Binary Download (Any OS)

Download from releases.hashicorp.com. Single binary, zero dependencies. Extract and run.

3.2 Your First Vault — Dev Mode Quick Start 🏗️

Dev mode is the fastest way to get hands-on with Vault. It starts an in-memory, pre-unsealed Vault instance — perfect for learning.

1
Start Server

vault server -dev
Auto-inits + unseals

2
Set Env Vars

VAULT_ADDR +
VAULT_TOKEN=root

3
Check Status

vault status
→ Sealed: false

4

secret/anihpj ...

5

Terminal — Dev Mode
# Terminal 1: Start Vault in dev mode
$ vault server -dev
==> Vault server started! Log data will stream in below:

# Terminal 2: Set environment and write your first secret
$ export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
$ export VAULT_TOKEN='root'  # Dev mode root token

$ vault status
Key             Value
---             -----
Seal Type       shamir
Initialized     true
Sealed          false  ← Already unsealed in dev mode!
Version         1.18.x
Storage Type    inmem  ← Data gone on restart!

$ vault kv put secret/anihpj db_user=anihpj db_pass=s3cr3t
======= Secret Path 'secret/data/anihpj' ========
========== Secret Version 1 ==========

$ vault kv get secret/anihpj
======= Secret Path 'secret/data/anihpj' ========
Key        Value
---        -----
db_pass    s3cr3t
db_user    anihpj

🎉 CONGRATULATIONS! You just wrote your first Vault secret!
⚠️ DEV MODE WARNING

Dev mode stores data in memory only — all data is lost when the server stops. NEVER use dev mode for production data. It auto-unseals and uses a root token of "root" for convenience.

🧪 What Dev Mode Actually Does

Behind the scenes, vault server -dev does several things automatically that you'll later do manually in production: it initializes Vault (generates the master key and root token), unseals it (reconstructs the master key in memory), enables the KV v2 secrets engine at secret/, and prints the root token. It also uses an in-memory storage backend — meaning when you stop the server, everything disappears.

⚖️ Dev Mode vs Production Mode — Side by Side

🧪 DEV MODE

🔓 Auto-unsealed on startup

🔑 Root token = "root"

💾 In-memory storage (lost on restart)

🔌 No TLS required

📋 Single key share, no threshold

⚡ 1 command: vault server -dev

🏭 PRODUCTION MODE

🔐 Must be manually unsealed (K of N keys)

🔑 Unique root token, store securely

💾 Persistent storage (Raft/Consul)

🔒 TLS 1.2+ required on all listeners

📋 Configurable shares + threshold

📝 Config file + init + unseal flow

3.3 Production Mode — The Real Setup 🎯

Production mode requires proper initialization and unseal. The master key is split into shares using Shamir's Secret Sharing, and you must provide enough keys to unseal.

🔄 Production Setup Sequence

1️⃣Configvault.hcl
→
2️⃣Startvault server
→
3️⃣Init5 keys/3 threshold
→
4️⃣DistributeKeys to holders
→
5️⃣Unseal3 key holders
→
6️⃣LoginRoot token
→
7️⃣AuditEnable first!
Terminal — Production Setup
# Initialize Vault with 5 key shares, 3 required to unseal
$ vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3

Unseal Key 1: abc123...  ← GIVE TO Alice (Security Lead)
Unseal Key 2: def456...  ← GIVE TO Bob (SRE Lead)
Unseal Key 3: ghi789...  ← GIVE TO Carol (CTO)
Unseal Key 4: jkl012...  ← STORE IN SAFE (backup)
Unseal Key 5: mno345...  ← STORE IN BANK VAULT (backup)

Initial Root Token: hvs.xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
← STORE THIS SECURELY! (Use for initial setup only!)

# Unseal: 3 key holders must provide their keys
$ vault operator unseal <key1>  # Alice
$ vault operator unseal <key2>  # Bob
$ vault operator unseal <key3>  # Carol
→ Sealed: false  ← Vault is now operational!

$ vault login <root-token>

# FIRST THING: Enable audit logging
$ vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log
🎓 EXAM TIP

The first command after unsealing in production should ALWAYS be enabling an audit device. The exam expects you to know: vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log

📝 The vault.hcl Production Config File

The production Vault server is configured via an HCL file (typically /etc/vault.d/vault.hcl). Here are the essential stanzas you need to understand for the exam:

/etc/vault.d/vault.hcl — Production Config
storage "raft" {
  path = "/opt/vault/data"    # Where Raft stores data
  node_id = "vault-1"          # Unique ID for this node
}

listener "tcp" {
  address     = "0.0.0.0:8200"
  tls_cert_file = "/etc/vault.d/cert.pem"
  tls_key_file  = "/etc/vault.d/key.pem"
}

api_addr = "https://vault-1:8200"   # Advertised to other nodes
cluster_addr = "https://vault-1:8201" # For Raft replication

ui = true  # Enable the Vault Web UI

# Optional: Auto-unseal via cloud KMS
# seal "awskms" {
#   region     = "us-east-1"
#   kms_key_id = "12345678-..."
# }

Key takeaways: storage defines where data lives (Raft/Consul/Filesystem), listener defines how clients connect (always use TLS in production), api_addr is the address other Vault nodes use to forward requests, and cluster_addr is used for Raft replication traffic. These must be unique per node in a cluster.

3.6 Practice Lab — Deploy Vault for anihpj/jobpost on K8s 🏗️

☸️ Helm — Deploy Vault HA on K8s
# Step 1: Add Helm repo
$ helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
$ helm repo update

# Step 2: Create namespace
$ kubectl create namespace vault

# Step 3: Install Vault (HA mode with Raft, 3 replicas)
$ helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault \
    --set server.ha.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.raft.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.replicas=3

# Step 4: Wait for pods
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/vault-0 -n vault

# Step 5: Init Vault
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator init \
    -key-shares=3 -key-threshold=2
→ SAVE THE OUTPUT! Unseal keys + root token

# Step 6: Unseal all 3 pods
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <key1>
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <key2>
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-1 -- vault operator unseal <key1>
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-1 -- vault operator unseal <key2>
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-2 -- vault operator unseal <key1>
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-2 -- vault operator unseal <key2>

# Step 7: Verify
$ kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault status
→ Sealed: false  ← Vault is ready on Kubernetes!
🏗️ anihpj Integration

This Vault instance will serve as the secrets backend for our anihpj/jobpost application. In later chapters, we'll configure the Kubernetes auth method, enable the database secrets engine for PostgreSQL, and set up the Vault Agent sidecar to inject secrets into the anihpj pods.

☸️ Understanding the K8s Deployment

The Helm chart creates a StatefulSet (not a Deployment) because each Vault pod needs a stable identity and persistent storage for its Raft data. Each pod gets a PersistentVolumeClaim automatically. The pods are named vault-0, vault-1, vault-2 — these names are stable across restarts, which is critical for Raft cluster membership. The Helm values we used (server.ha.enabled=true, server.ha.raft.enabled=true) tell Vault to form a Raft cluster instead of using external storage. Each pod must be unsealed individually because each has its own memory space — the unseal keys provide the same master key to each pod, but the reconstruction happens independently in each pod's memory.

🔍 Verifying Your Deployment

After deploying, run these checks to confirm everything is working:

Verification Commands
# Check pod status — all 3 should be Running
kubectl get pods -n vault
# vault-0   1/1   Running   0   2m
# vault-1   1/1   Running   0   2m
# vault-2   1/1   Running   0   2m

# Check Raft peers — should show leader + 2 followers
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator raft list-peers
# Node       Address              State       Voter
# vault-0    vault-0.vault:8201   leader      true
# vault-1    vault-1.vault:8201   follower    true
# vault-2    vault-2.vault:8201   follower    true

# Check Vault status on each pod
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault status
# Initialized: true  Sealed: false  ← All good!

# Check the Vault UI (if enabled):
kubectl port-forward -n vault svc/vault 8200:8200
# Open https://localhost:8200 in browser

📝 Chapter 3 Practice Questions — Installation & Setup

Q1
What is the difference between Vault Dev Mode and Production Mode?
Show Answer
Answer

Dev Mode: In-memory storage (data lost on restart), pre-unsealed, root token = "root", no TLS, single key share. For development only. Production Mode: Persistent storage (Raft/Consul), requires init + unseal, proper TLS, multiple key shares with threshold. For real workloads.

Explanation

Dev mode is started with vault server -dev. Production mode requires a config file: vault server -config=vault.hcl. The exam expects you to understand that dev mode should NEVER be used for production data.

Q2
What command initializes Vault with 5 key shares and a threshold of 3?
Show Answer
Answer
vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3
Explanation

This creates 5 unseal keys, and any 3 of them are needed to unseal Vault. The output includes the unseal keys and the initial root token. These must be stored securely — they cannot be recovered if lost.

Q3
What is the first thing you should do after unsealing Vault in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Enable an audit device: vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log. This ensures all requests are logged from the very beginning. Without audit logging, you have no record of who accessed what.

Explanation

This is a production best practice AND an exam topic. After enabling audit, you should also create non-root policies and tokens — never use the root token for day-to-day operations.

Q4
How do you deploy Vault on Kubernetes with Helm in HA mode?
Show Answer
Answer
helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault \
    --set server.ha.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.raft.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.replicas=3
Explanation

This deploys 3 Vault pods in HA mode with Raft as the storage backend. Each pod needs to be unsealed individually after initialization. Use kubectl exec to run vault commands inside the pods.

Q5
Where should unseal keys and the root token be stored after vault operator init?
Show Answer
Answer

Unseal keys should be distributed to different trusted individuals (security lead, SRE lead, CTO). Backup keys should be stored in physically separate, secure locations (safe, bank vault). The root token should be stored securely and used only for initial setup — create non-root tokens for daily use.

Explanation

Never store all unseal keys together — that defeats the purpose of Shamir's Secret Sharing. Never commit keys or tokens to git. Use Vault's own KV store or a physical safe for backup keys.

Q6
What happens if you lose all unseal keys for a Vault instance?
Show Answer
Answer

All data is permanently inaccessible. There is no "forgot password" mechanism. The master key cannot be reconstructed without enough key shares, and without it, the encrypted data cannot be decrypted. This is why key management is critical.

Explanation

This is by design — Vault's security model ensures that even HashiCorp cannot recover your data. Always distribute keys to multiple trusted holders and store backups in secure, separate locations. For auto-unseal, the cloud KMS key becomes the critical recovery dependency.

Q7
How do you verify that Vault is running and unsealed?
Show Answer
Answer
vault status
# Key             Value
# Seal Type       shamir
# Initialized     true
# Sealed          false  ← Must be false for Vault to work
# Version         1.18.x

# Or check health endpoint:
curl https://vault:8200/v1/sys/health
# 200 = OK (initialized, unsealed, active)
Explanation

vault status is always available (even when sealed). The health endpoint returns 200 for active, 429 for standby, and 501 for not initialized. Use both for monitoring.

Q8
What's the difference between vault operator unseal and vault operator seal?
Show Answer
Answer

unseal: Provides a key share to reconstruct the master key in memory → transitions from SEALED to UNSEALED. seal: Emergency lockdown — wipes the master key from memory → transitions from UNSEALED to SEALED. All operations immediately blocked.

Explanation

Unseal requires K key shares. Seal requires just the command — it's instantaneous. Used when you suspect a security breach and need to immediately protect all secrets.

Q9
Why do you need to unseal EACH Vault pod individually in a Kubernetes HA deployment?
Show Answer
Answer

Each Vault pod is a separate process with its own memory space. The master key must be reconstructed in each pod's memory independently. Raft replicates the encrypted data, but the decryption key (master key) must be provided to each node via unseal.

Explanation

With auto-unseal, each pod automatically contacts the cloud KMS on startup, so no manual intervention is needed. Without auto-unseal, you must run kubectl exec -n vault vault-X -- vault operator unseal for each pod after every restart.

Q10
After deploying Vault on K8s for anihpj, what are the next steps to integrate it with the application?
Show Answer
Answer

1. Enable Kubernetes auth method (vault auth enable kubernetes) 2. Configure K8s auth role bound to anihpj ServiceAccount 3. Enable database secrets engine (vault secrets enable database) 4. Configure PostgreSQL connection 5. Create DB role for anihpj 6. Write policy granting read access to DB creds 7. Configure Vault Agent sidecar with template to render secrets.

Explanation

These are the topics of Chapters 4-8 and 14-16. Chapter 3 gets Vault running; subsequent chapters configure it for the anihpj application.

🏋️ Ch 3 Lab — Install & Deploy Vault (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Install Vault, run dev + production mode, deploy on K8s
# 1. Check Vault installation
vault version
# Expected: Vault v1.16+ (or latest)

# 2. Run dev server (in-memory, auto-unsealed)
vault server -dev -dev-root-token-id=root &
export VAULT_ADDR='http://127.0.0.1:8200'
export VAULT_TOKEN=root
vault status   # Sealed: false ✓

# 3. Kill dev, create production config
pkill vault
mkdir -p /tmp/vault-data
cat > /tmp/vault-config.hcl <<EOF
storage "raft" { path="/tmp/vault-data" node_id="node1" }
listener "tcp" { address="127.0.0.1:8200" tls_disable=true }
ui=true
EOF

# 4. Start production server + init
vault server -config=/tmp/vault-config.hcl &
vault operator init -key-shares=3 -key-threshold=2

# 5. Unseal + login
vault operator unseal <key1>
vault operator unseal <key2>
vault login <root_token>

# 6. K8s: Deploy via Helm
helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
helm install vault hashicorp/vault --set server.ha.enabled=true --set server.ha.replicas=3

Drill Check: Dev vs Prod: what stays after restart? (Dev=NOTHING lost, Prod=encrypted data persists, needs unseal). Minimum K8s replicas for HA? (3).

🟢 Part 2: Secrets Engines — Storing and Generating Secrets

Chapter 4: KV Secrets Engine — The Foundation of Vault

The KV (Key-Value) Secrets Engine is the most fundamental and most-used engine in Vault. It stores arbitrary secrets as key-value pairs — think of it as an encrypted, audited, version-controlled dictionary. Understanding KV v1 vs v2 is critical for the exam — the path differences, versioning, and deletion behavior are frequently tested.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔧 Hands-On 🎯 EXAM CRITICAL

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What Secrets Engines are and how to manage them
  • ✅ KV v1 — simple key-value storage with basic operations
  • ✅ KV v2 — versioned secrets with soft delete, destroy, metadata, and patch
  • ✅ The critical differences between KV v1 and KV v2 paths and behaviors
  • ✅ Setting up KV v2 for anihpj/jobpost secrets
🎓 VAULT ASSOCIATE RELEVANCE
Domain 2: Secrets Engines 25%

4.1 What Are Secrets Engines?

Secrets engines are Vault's plugin system — each engine handles a specific type of secret. Think of them as "apps" inside Vault: the KV engine stores static secrets, the Database engine generates dynamic credentials, the PKI engine issues certificates, and the Transit engine performs encryption-as-a-service.

VAULT SECRETS ENGINES — The Plugin Ecosystem
          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
          │       VAULT CORE              │
          │                               │
          │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐    │
          │  │ KV  │ │ DB  │ │ PKI │    │
          │  │v1/v2│ │Post- │ │Cert │    │
          │  │     │ │gres │ │Auth │    │
          │  └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘    │
          │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐    │
          │  │Trans│ │ SSH │ │TOTP │    │
          │  │it   │ │ OTP │ │ 2FA │    │
          │  └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘    │
          │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐    │
          │  │AWS  │ │Azure│ │ GCP │    │
          │  │IAM  │ │SP   │ │ SA  │    │
          │  └─────┘ └─────┘ └─────┘    │
          └──────────────────────────────┘

Each engine is ENABLED at a PATH:
$ vault secrets enable -path=anihpj kv-v2
→ Now anihpj/ is a KV v2 store for anihpj secrets

🔧 Managing Secrets Engines

🔌
Enable

vault secrets enable <type> — activates an engine. Use -path=NAME to customize the mount path. Multiple instances of the same engine type can run at different paths.

📋
List

vault secrets list — shows all enabled engines, their types, and mount paths. Essential for surveying what's configured.

⚙️
Tune

vault secrets tune <path> — adjust engine configuration like default TTL, max TTL, and visibility settings.

🗑️
Disable

vault secrets disable <path> — removes the engine and ALL its data. This is irreversible — use with caution!

4.2 KV v1 — Simple Key-Value Storage

KV v1 is the original, simpler version of the KV engine. It stores secrets at the path you specify — no versioning, no soft delete, no metadata. What you write is what you get. It's still available for backward compatibility but KV v2 is the default since Vault 1.0.

KV v1 Operations
# Enable KV v1
vault secrets enable -version=1 kv

# Write (path is direct — no /data/ prefix)
vault kv put kv/anihpj db_user=anihpj db_pass=s3cr3t

# Read (same path)
vault kv get kv/anihpj

# Delete (permanent — no recovery!)
vault kv delete kv/anihpj
# → Data is GONE. No undelete. No versioning.
⚠️ KV v1 Limitations

No version history, no soft delete, no metadata tracking, no patch (partial update), no Check-And-Set. For all new deployments, use KV v2 unless you have a specific reason to use v1.

4.3 KV v2 — Versioned Key-Value Store (EXAM CRITICAL) 🎯🎯🎯

KV v2 is the #1 most tested topic on the Vault Associate exam. The critical difference: v2 paths use /data/ between the mount path and your secret path. If you enable KV v2 at secret/, you write to and read from secret/data/your-path.

KV v2 SECRET LIFECYCLE — Complete Visual
CRITICAL: KV v2 paths use /secret/DATA/<path> format!

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. CREATE / UPDATE                               │
│ vault kv put secret/anihpj db_user=anihpj        │
│ → Creates Version 1 at secret/data/anihpj        │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. UPDATE (creates NEW version)                  │
│ vault kv put secret/anihpj db_pass=NEWPASS       │
│ → Creates Version 2 (v1 still exists!)           │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. READ LATEST / SPECIFIC VERSION                │
│ vault kv get secret/anihpj  → Version 2          │
│ vault kv get -version=1 secret/anihpj → v1       │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. SOFT DELETE (recoverable)                     │
│ vault kv delete secret/anihpj                    │
│ → Marked DELETED but recoverable via "undelete"  │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. UNDELETE (recover)                            │
│ vault kv undelete -versions=2 secret/anihpj      │
│ → Version 2 is back!                             │
└────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                     │
┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│ 6. PERMANENT DESTROY (unrecoverable!)            │
│ vault kv destroy -versions=2 secret/anihpj       │
│ → Version 2 is GONE FOREVER                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📊 METADATA: vault kv metadata get secret/anihpj
→ Shows: created_time, versions, deletion_time, destroyed

📋 KV v1 vs KV v2 — Complete Comparison

FEATUREKV v1KV v2
API Path/secret/<path>/secret/DATA/<path>
Versioning❌ No✅ 10 versions default
Soft Delete❌ No✅ Yes (recoverable)
Destroy❌ N/A✅ Permanent delete
Metadata❌ No✅ Yes (created_time, versions)
Undelete❌ No✅ Yes
Patch❌ No✅ Partial update
CAS❌ No✅ Check-And-Set
Enable Commandkv (v1)kv-v2 (default since 1.0)

⚠️ EXAM GOTCHA

  • Writing to secret/anihpj in v2 creates at secret/data/anihpj
  • vault read secret/anihpj — WRONG for v2!
  • vault kv get secret/anihpj — CORRECT (CLI handles /data/)
  • API calls MUST include /data/: GET /v1/secret/data/anihpj

4.4 KV v1 vs v2 — Choosing the Right Engine

KV v1 — When to Use

Legacy compatibility with older Vault versions. Simple use cases where versioning is not needed. When you want direct path access without /data/ prefix.

KV v2 — Recommended

All new deployments should use KV v2. Versioning prevents accidental data loss. Soft delete with undelete provides safety net. Metadata tracks who changed what and when.

4.5 KV v2 Setup for anihpj/jobpost 🏗️

Setting up KV v2 for anihpj
# Enable KV v2 at a dedicated path for anihpj
vault secrets enable -path=anihpj kv-v2

# Store anihpj application secrets
vault kv put anihpj/database \
    db_host=postgres.anihpj.svc \
    db_port=5432 \
    db_name=anihpj

vault kv put anihpj/django \
    secret_key="django-insecure-abc123..." \
    debug=false \
    allowed_hosts="anihpj.local,api.anihpj.local"

vault kv put anihpj/email \
    api_key="sg.xxxxxxxxxx" \
    from_email="noreply@anihpj.local"

# Verify
vault kv get anihpj/database
vault kv list anihpj/
🏗️ anihpj Integration

These KV v2 secrets will be read by the Vault Agent sidecar and rendered as environment variables or files for the Django application. Each secret path is organized by concern (database, django, email) — this makes it easy to write targeted policies that grant access to specific secret groups only.
