│  → token_policies: ["anihpj-policy", "default"]                   │
│  → token_ttl: 20m                                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 SECURITY: RoleID can be in config/CI. SecretID is the         │
│     actual secret — distribute via Vault Agent or response wrap.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8.4 Kubernetes Auth Configuration — Full Production Setup 🎯🏗️

Complete Kubernetes auth configuration for the anihpj namespace. This section covers everything from enabling the auth method to testing from inside a pod, including common pitfalls.

Bash — Kubernetes Auth Full Configuration
# ===== STEP 1: Enable Kubernetes auth =====
vault auth enable kubernetes
# Success! Enabled kubernetes auth method at: kubernetes/

# ===== STEP 2: Configure K8s API connection =====
# Vault needs to call K8s TokenReview API
# When Vault runs INSIDE K8s (recommended):
vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    kubernetes_host="https://kubernetes.default.svc:443" \
    token_reviewer_jwt="$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt"

# When Vault runs OUTSIDE K8s:
vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    kubernetes_host="https://k8s-api.company.com:6443" \
    token_reviewer_jwt="@vault-reviewer-sa.jwt" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@k8s-ca.pem"

# ===== STEP 3: Create roles for different workloads =====
# Role for anihpj application pods
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj-app \
    bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    policies=anihpj-policy \
    ttl=1h \
    max_ttl=4h

# Role for jobpost application pods (same namespace, different SA)
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/jobpost-app \
    bound_service_account_names=jobpost-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    policies=jobpost-policy \
    ttl=30m

# Role with audience binding
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/audience-role \
    bound_service_account_names="*" \
    bound_service_account_namespaces="*" \
    audience="vault-custom-audience" \
    policies=default \
    ttl=1h

# ===== STEP 4: Test from inside a pod =====
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj -- sh -c '
  VAULT_ADDR=http://vault.vault.svc:8200 \
  vault login -method=kubernetes role=anihpj-app
'
# Success! You are now authenticated.
# token: s.A1b2C3d4E5f6G7h8I9j0K1l2
# token_policies: ["anihpj-policy","default"]
# token_ttl: 1h
📋bound_service_account_namesWhich ServiceAccounts can use this role. Use ["*"] for all (less secure) or list specific SAs. Required parameter.
📂bound_service_account_namespacesWhich namespaces' pods can use this role. Use ["*"] for all namespaces or specify exact namespaces. Required parameter.
👂audienceThe JWT aud claim to validate. The pod's SA JWT audience must match this value. Default is "vault" if not specified.
🏷️alias_name_sourceWhat to use as the entity alias name: serviceaccount_uid (unique, stable) or serviceaccount_name (human-readable).
⚠️ COMMON EXAM PITFALL: If Vault is deployed OUTSIDE the Kubernetes cluster (e.g., on a VM), you MUST provide kubernetes_host pointing to the K8s API server's external endpoint. You also need a long-lived ServiceAccount JWT for the token_reviewer_jwt parameter. Many exam questions test this external-Vault scenario!

8.5 JWT/OIDC Auth Configuration

JWT/OIDC auth allows Vault to accept tokens from any OIDC-compliant identity provider (Okta, Auth0, Azure AD, Google, etc.). Vault validates the JWT signature against the provider's JWKS endpoint and checks bound claims before issuing a Vault token.

Bash — JWT/OIDC Configuration
# Enable JWT auth (or 'oidc' — functionally identical)
vault auth enable jwt

# Configure with OIDC discovery (auto-fetches JWKS, issuer, etc.)
vault write auth/jwt/config \
    oidc_discovery_url="https://accounts.google.com" \
    default_role="gcp-user"

# Or configure manually (without OIDC discovery)
vault write auth/jwt/config \
    jwt_validation_pubkeys=@public-key.pem \
    issuer="https://my-idp.company.com"

# Create role with bound claims
vault write auth/jwt/role/my-role \
    role_type="jwt" \
    user_claim="sub" \
    bound_claims='{"group":"engineering","email_verified":true}' \
    bound_audiences="vault-audience" \
    policies="eng-policy" \
    ttl=1h \
    max_ttl=8h

# Login with JWT
vault write auth/jwt/login role=my-role jwt="eyJhbGci..."
# Returns Vault token with eng-policy attached
🔑 Key Parameters: user_claim — which JWT claim identifies the user (typically "sub" or "email"). bound_claims — JSON map of required claim values (all must match). bound_audiences — which aud values are accepted. oidc_discovery_url — auto-configures issuer, JWKS endpoint, and algorithms from OIDC discovery document.

8.6 Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) 🔐

MFA adds a second layer of authentication on top of any auth method. After successful primary authentication, Vault requires a second factor (TOTP code, Duo push, Okta verify) before issuing a token. MFA is configured per mount accessor — each auth method mount has its own MFA configuration.

Bash — MFA Configuration Examples
# Enable TOTP MFA for the userpass auth method
# First, get the mount accessor for userpass
vault auth list -format=json | jq '."userpass/".accessor'

# Create TOTP MFA method enforcement
vault write identity/mfa/method/totp/admin-totp \
    issuer=vault \
    period=30 \
    key_size=20 \
    algorithm=SHA256 \
    digits=8

# Enforce MFA on userpass login
vault write identity/mfa/login-enforcement/admin-mfa \
    mfa_method_ids=admin-totp \
    auth_method_accessors="auth_userpass_xxx" \
    auth_method_types=userpass

# Now, users authenticating via userpass must also
# provide a valid TOTP code to complete login

# Supported MFA types:
# - TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password)
# - Okta (Push notification + verify)
# - Duo (Push, phone call, passcode)
# - PingID (Push, OTP)
⚠️ IMPORTANT: MFA login enforcement applies to all login attempts on the specified auth method. There's no per-user MFA — it's all-or-nothing per auth method mount. To have different MFA policies for different users, mount the same auth type at multiple paths with different MFA configs.
🏗️ PRODUCTION MFA STRATEGY — Multi-Mount Approach

Since MFA is per-mount (not per-user), here's how to implement tiered MFA for the anihpj team:

# Strategy: Mount userpass at TWO paths with different MFA requirements

# Admin mount — REQUIRES TOTP MFA
vault auth enable -path=admin-userpass userpass
vault write auth/admin-userpass/users/admin password="s3cur3"
vault write identity/mfa/login-enforcement/admin-mfa \
    mfa_method_ids=admin-totp \
    auth_method_accessors=$(vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '."admin-userpass/".accessor')

# Developer mount — NO MFA (or lighter MFA like Duo)
vault auth enable -path=dev-userpass userpass
vault write auth/dev-userpass/users/dev1 password="d3vP@ss"
# No MFA enforcement on this mount

# Now:
# vault login -method=userpass -path=admin-userpass → prompts for TOTP
# vault login -method=userpass -path=dev-userpass  → no MFA required

This pattern lets you enforce strict MFA for privileged accounts while keeping developer access friction-free. Each mount can have different TTLs, policies, and MFA requirements — all using the same underlying userpass auth type.

📝 Chapter 8 Practice Questions — Auth Configuration

Q71
What happens when you disable an auth method with vault auth disable <path>?
Show Answer
Answer

All configuration, roles, and data under that auth path are permanently and irreversibly deleted. However, tokens that were already issued via that auth method continue to work until they expire or are revoked — disabling an auth method does NOT revoke existing tokens. Users/applications can no longer authenticate via that method.

Explanation

This is a critical distinction: disabling the auth method removes the "door" (no new entries), but doesn't kick out people already inside (existing tokens still work). To also revoke all tokens from that auth method, you must revoke them separately via vault token revoke -mode=path auth/approle/.

Q72
What's the difference between vault token create and vault write auth/token/create/<role>?
Show Answer
Answer

vault token create uses the root/sudo privilege path — it bypasses token roles entirely. vault write auth/token/create/<role> goes through the Token auth method and respects the role's restrictions (allowed_policies, explicit_max_ttl, orphan, etc.). The second approach is for delegating controlled token creation to non-administrators.

Explanation

Think of it as: vault token create = "I'm the admin, give me whatever token I want." vault write auth/token/create/<role> = "I'm a user, give me a token within these role-defined limits."

Q73
How do you configure AppRole with SecretID single-use and a 10-minute TTL?
Show Answer
Answer
vault write auth/approle/role/my-app \
    secret_id_ttl=10m \
    secret_id_num_uses=1 \
    token_policies=my-policy \
    token_ttl=30m
Explanation

secret_id_ttl=10m: The SecretID expires 10 minutes after generation. secret_id_num_uses=1: The SecretID can only be used once — after a successful login, it's consumed. This is the most secure configuration: the credential is short-lived AND single-use.

Q74
What is bind_secret_id in AppRole and what are its security implications?
Show Answer
Answer

When bind_secret_id=true (default), the resulting Vault token is cryptographically bound to the specific SecretID used for login. If that SecretID is later revoked, the token becomes invalid. When bind_secret_id=false, the token is independent of the SecretID — revoking the SecretID doesn't affect the token. Always use bind_secret_id=true for production. Set to false only when SecretID is unavailable at token usage time.

Explanation

Security recommendation: bind_secret_id=true + secret_id_num_uses=1 + secret_id_ttl=10m = maximum security. The SecretID is single-use, short-lived, and the resulting token is bound to it.

Q75
What are the three critical parameters for Kubernetes auth when Vault is OUTSIDE the cluster?
Show Answer
Answer

1. kubernetes_host: The external K8s API server URL (e.g., https://k8s-api.company.com:6443). 2. token_reviewer_jwt: A long-lived ServiceAccount JWT that Vault uses to call the TokenReview API. 3. kubernetes_ca_cert: The K8s API server's CA certificate for TLS verification. All three are REQUIRED when Vault is outside the cluster.

Explanation

When Vault is inside the cluster, these values auto-resolve from the service account mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/. Outside the cluster, you must provide them explicitly, and the K8s API must be network-reachable from Vault.

Q76
How does JWT/OIDC auth validate a token from an external identity provider?
Show Answer
Answer

Vault fetches the OIDC provider's JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) from the discovery URL, then uses the provider's public keys to verify the JWT signature. After signature verification, Vault checks: (1) iss claim matches configured issuer, (2) aud claim is in bound_audiences, (3) All bound_claims match the JWT claims, (4) JWT is not expired (exp claim). If all checks pass, Vault issues a token with the role's policies.

Explanation

This is a multi-layer validation: cryptographic (signature), temporal (expiration), and semantic (claims matching). Vault never sees the user's password — it trusts the OIDC provider's assertion.

Q77
What parameters can you tune on an existing auth method with vault auth tune?
Show Answer
Answer

vault auth tune can modify: -default-lease-ttl (default token TTL), -max-lease-ttl (maximum token TTL), -audit-non-hmac-request-keys (which request keys to log in plaintext), -audit-non-hmac-response-keys (which response keys to log in plaintext), -description (human-readable description), -listing-visibility (whether path listing is visible). You cannot change the auth method type — to change type, disable and re-enable.

Explanation
# Increase default TTL and set description
vault auth tune \
    -default-lease-ttl=2h \
    -max-lease-ttl=12h \
    -description="Production AppRole for anihpj" \
    approle/
Q78
How does MFA enforcement work in Vault and what MFA types are supported?
Show Answer
Answer

MFA is enforced at the auth method mount level (not per-user). After primary authentication succeeds, Vault requires the MFA challenge before issuing the token. Supported types: TOTP (time-based codes like Google Authenticator), Okta Verify (push notification), Duo (push/call/passcode), PingID (push/OTP). MFA is configured via identity/mfa/ paths and enforced via identity/mfa/login-enforcement/.

Explanation

Key exam point: MFA is per-mount, not per-user. All users of a specific auth method mount are subject to the same MFA requirement. For different MFA policies, mount the same auth type at different paths.

Q79
How do you test Kubernetes auth from a specific pod?
Show Answer
Answer
# From inside the pod:
vault login -method=kubernetes role=anihpj-app

# Or from outside, using kubectl exec:
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj -- \
    vault login -method=kubernetes role=anihpj-app

# Verify the token:
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj -- \
    vault token lookup

The pod must have: (1) The correct ServiceAccount (anihpj-sa), (2) VAULT_ADDR set to Vault's address, (3) The SA JWT auto-mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token.

Q80
Configure a complete Kubernetes auth role for anihpj with strict security: only the anihpj-sa ServiceAccount in the anihpj namespace, 1-hour TTL, and custom audience.
Show Answer
Answer
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj-secure \
    bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    audience="vault-anihpj-prod" \
    policies=anihpj-policy \
    ttl=1h \
    max_ttl=4h \
    token_bound_cidrs="10.244.0.0/16" \
    token_no_default_policy=false
Explanation

This configuration: (1) Only the anihpj-sa SA in the anihpj namespace can authenticate, (2) JWT must have audience "vault-anihpj-prod", (3) Token has 1h TTL with 4h max, (4) Token is CIDR-bound to the pod network, (5) The default policy IS attached (set to false to exclude). For even stricter security, set token_no_default_policy=true and define all permissions explicitly in anihpj-policy.

🏋️ Ch 8 Lab — Auth Tuning & Token Restrictions (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Tune auth mount, create restricted tokens, test CIDR binding
# 1. Tune auth mount defaults
vault auth tune -default-lease-ttl=30m -max-lease-ttl=2h approle/

# 2. Create AppRole with token restrictions
vault write auth/approle/role/restricted \
    token_ttl=15m token_max_ttl=1h \
    token_bound_cidrs=10.0.0.0/8 \
    token_no_default_policy=true \
    token_policies=restricted-app

# 3. Test: create token and verify restrictions
ROLE_ID=$(vault read -field=role_id auth/approle/role/restricted/role-id)
SECRET_ID=$(vault write -f -field=secret_id auth/approle/role/restricted/secret-id)
TOKEN=$(vault write -field=token auth/approle/login role_id=$ROLE_ID secret_id=$SECRET_ID)
vault token lookup $TOKEN
# Check: ttl=15m, policies=[restricted-app], bound_cidrs=[10.0.0.0/8]

# 4. Verify CIDR binding (token fails from outside 10.0.0.0/8)
vault token capabilities $TOKEN secret/data/test
# Succeeds only if request comes from 10.x.x.x IP

# 5. Check config without knowing token
ACCESSOR=$(vault token lookup $TOKEN | grep accessor | awk '{print $2}')
vault token lookup -accessor $ACCESSOR
vault token revoke -accessor $ACCESSOR  # Revoke by accessor!

Drill Check: Can you revoke a token if you only know its accessor? (YES). Does CIDR binding protect against token theft? (YES — stolen token useless from attacker's IP). What does token_no_default_policy do? (Removes the default policy — token gets ONLY explicit policies).

Chapter 9: Identity — Entities, Groups, and Aliases 🎯🔐

VA Exam Weight: 20% (Auth Methods domain — Identity sub-system)

Here's a problem: Alice authenticates via userpass in the morning and via LDAP in the afternoon. Are these two "different" people to Vault? Without the Identity system — yes. With Identity — no. Vault's Identity system unifies multiple auth methods under a single Entity, organizes entities into Groups, and maps auth-specific identities to entities via Aliases. This is the bridge between Part 3 (Authentication) and Part 5 (Policies).

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Understand the Vault Identity system: Entities, Groups, Aliases
  • Create and manage entities that unify multiple auth methods
  • Organize entities into internal and external groups
  • Map auth method identities to entities using aliases
  • Understand how group policies flow to entity tokens
  • Apply Identity concepts to anihpj/jobpost team structure

9.1 Vault Identity System Overview — The Unified Identity Layer

The Identity system answers a fundamental question: "How does Vault recognize that Alice-logging-in-via-userpass is the same person as Alice-logging-in-via-LDAP?" Without Identity, each auth method creates a separate, unrelated identity. With Identity, they're unified under one Entity.

👥 VAULT IDENTITY SYSTEM — Complete Relationship Map
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           👥 VAULT IDENTITY SYSTEM — Entity/Group/Alias Map       │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                 ENTITY: "Alice"                               │ │
│  │                 ────────────────                               │ │
│  │                 id: entity_abc123                             │ │
│  │                 name: alice                                   │ │
│  │                 metadata: { dept: "engineering" }              │ │
│  │                 policies: [] (via groups only)                │ │
│  └──────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘  │
│             │                     │                                │
│   ┌─────────▼────────┐   ┌───────▼─────────┐                     │
│   │  ALIAS 1          │   │  ALIAS 2         │                    │
│   │  ──────────────── │   │  ─────────────── │                    │
│   │  Auth: userpass   │   │  Auth: LDAP      │                    │
│   │  Name: alice      │   │  Name: alice.s   │                    │
│   │  Mount: userpass/ │   │  Mount: ldap/    │                    │
│   │  Accessor: auth_  │   │  Accessor: auth_ │                    │
│   │    userpass_xxx   │   │    ldap_yyy      │                    │
│   └───────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘                    │
│                                                                    │
│  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  GROUP: "engineering-team"                                    │ │
│  │  ─────────────────────────────                                 │ │
│  │  id: group_xyz789                                             │ │
│  │  type: internal                                               │ │
│  │  policies: ["eng-policy", "db-read-policy"]                  │ │
│  │  metadata: { cost_center: "CC-1234" }                        │ │
│  │                                                               │ │
│  │  Members:                                                     │ │
│  │  ├── Entity: Alice (entity_abc123)                            │ │
│  │  ├── Entity: Bob (entity_def456)                              │ │
│  │  └── Entity: Charlie (entity_ghi789)                          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                    │
│  🔗 HOW POLICIES FLOW TO TOKENS:                                  │
│  ───────────────────────────────                                  │
│  Alice logs in via userpass → Token is created                    │
│                                                                   │
│  Token's effective policies =                                     │
│    Alice's ENTITY policies                                        │
│    + engineering-team GROUP policies                              │
│    + Token's own policies (from auth method role)                 │
│    + default policy                                               │
│                                                                   │
│  → UNION of ALL applicable policies (most permissive wins)       │
│                                                                   │
│  💡 KEY INSIGHT: Alice can auth via userpass OR LDAP, but Vault  │
│     recognizes her as the SAME entity with SAME group policies    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏷️ Entity

A single identity in Vault. Represents a person or machine. Has a unique ID, name, metadata, and can be a member of groups. Entities don't have policies directly — they inherit them from groups.

🔗 Alias

A mapping from an auth method identity to an Entity. Each alias says: "When someone logs in as 'alice' via userpass, they are Entity Alice." One entity can have many aliases (one per auth method).

👥 Group

A collection of entities. Groups hold policies. When an entity is a member of a group, tokens created for that entity inherit the group's policies. Two types: Internal (managed in Vault) and External (managed by LDAP/Okta, synced to Vault).

📋 Mount Accessor

Each auth method mount has a unique accessor (UUID). Aliases use the accessor to identify WHICH auth method mount they belong to. Even if two userpass mounts exist (prod-userpass, dev-userpass), each has a different accessor.

🎯 EXAM TIP: The Identity system is a bridge topic between Auth Methods (Part 3) and Policies (Part 5). Expect questions like: "Alice authenticates via LDAP. How do you ensure she has the same permissions as when she authenticates via userpass?" Answer: Create an entity with aliases for both auth methods, add the entity to a group with the required policies.

9.2 Entities — Deep Dive

An Entity is the canonical representation of an identity in Vault. It's the anchor point that all aliases point to. Entities can be created manually, or Vault can auto-create them when entity_alias is configured on the auth method role.

Bash — Entity CRUD Operations
# CREATE an entity
vault write identity/entity name="alice" \
    metadata=department=engineering \
    metadata=team=platform

# READ an entity
vault read identity/entity/name/alice
# Key        Value
# ---        -----
# id         f5a8b3c2-1d4e-5f6a-7b8c-9d0e1f2a3b4c
# name       alice
# metadata   map[department:engineering team:platform]

# LIST all entities
vault list identity/entity/name
# Keys
# ----
# alice
# bob
# charlie

# UPDATE entity metadata
vault write identity/entity/name/alice \
    metadata=department=engineering \
    metadata=team=platform \
    metadata=title=senior_engineer

# DELETE an entity (requires entity ID)
vault delete identity/entity/id/f5a8b3c2-1d4e-5f6a-7b8c-9d0e1f2a3b4c

# MERGE two entities (all aliases from source → destination)
vault write identity/entity/merge \
    from_entity_ids="entity_old123" \
    to_entity_id="entity_new456"
# ⚠️ Source entity is DELETED after merge!
Entity NameUnique per namespace
Entity IDUUID, auto-generated
MetadataArbitrary key-value
DisabledSoft-delete flag

9.3 Groups — Organizing Entities and Inheriting Policies

Groups are how you assign policies to multiple entities at once. Instead of attaching policies to each entity individually, you add the entity to a group, and the group carries the policies. This is the Identity system's answer to RBAC at scale.

FeatureInternal GroupExternal Group
Managed byVault (manually)External system (LDAP/Okta)
MembershipManually add/remove entitiesAuto-synced from external directory
PoliciesAssigned directly to groupAssigned directly to group
Use caseSmall teams, custom groupsEnterprise, existing LDAP groups
SyncN/A (manual)Periodic or on-login
Bash — Group Management
# CREATE an internal group
vault write identity/group name="engineering-team" \
    type=internal \
    policies="eng-policy,db-read-policy" \
    metadata=department=engineering

# ADD entity as member
vault write identity/group name="engineering-team" \
    member_entity_ids="f5a8b3c2-...,d4e5f6a7-..."

# READ group details
vault read identity/group/name/engineering-team
# Key                 Value
# ---                 -----
# id                  group_xyz789
# name                engineering-team
# type                internal
# policies            [eng-policy db-read-policy]
# member_entity_ids   [f5a8b3c2... d4e5f6a7...]

# CREATE an external group (linked to LDAP)
vault write identity/group name="ldap-engineering" \
    type=external \
    policies="eng-policy" \
    metadata=ldap_dn="cn=engineering,ou=groups,dc=corp,dc=com"

# LIST groups
vault list identity/group/name
# Keys
# ----
# engineering-team
# ldap-engineering

# Check which groups an entity belongs to
vault read identity/entity/name/alice
# Look for: group_ids [...]
🔑 Policy Inheritance Rule: When an entity is a member of multiple groups, the entity's effective policies = UNION of all group policies. Vault takes the most permissive approach — if ANY group grants a capability, it's allowed. There's no "deny" policy in Vault's ACL system.

9.4 Aliases — Mapping Auth Method Identities to Entities

An Alias is the bridge between an auth method's login identity and a Vault Entity. Each alias says: "When someone logs in as X via auth method Y, they are Entity Z." Without aliases, Vault treats each auth method login as a separate, anonymous identity.

Bash — Alias Operations
# First, get the mount accessor for the auth method
vault auth list -format=json | jq '."userpass/".accessor'
# "auth_userpass_abc123def456"

# CREATE an alias: map userpass:alice → Entity:alice
vault write identity/entity-alias \
    name="alice" \
    canonical_id="f5a8b3c2-..." \
    mount_accessor="auth_userpass_abc123def456"

# Now, when "alice" logs in via userpass,
# Vault automatically recognizes her as Entity:alice
# and attaches all group policies

# CREATE another alias for the same entity (LDAP identity)
vault write identity/entity-alias \
    name="alice.smith" \
    canonical_id="f5a8b3c2-..." \
    mount_accessor="auth_ldap_xyz789abc"

# LIST all aliases for an entity
vault read identity/entity/name/alice
# Look for: aliases [...]

# AUTO-CREATION: Set on auth method role for automatic entity+alias
vault write auth/userpass/users/alice \
    password="s3cur3" \
    token_policies="user-policy"

# When entity_alias is configured on the role,
# first login auto-creates entity and alias
🔗 ALIAS — The Bridge Between Auth and Identity
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ALIAS — THE IDENTITY BRIDGE                    │
│                                                                    │
│  Without Alias:                                                    │
│  ─────────────                                                     │
│  userpass:alice → Token A (policies: user-policy)                 │
│  ldap:alice.s   → Token B (policies: ldap-policy)                 │
│  → Alice has DIFFERENT access depending on how she logs in!       │
│                                                                    │
│  With Alias:                                                       │
│  ──────────                                                        │
│  userpass:alice → Alias1 → Entity:Alice → Groups → ALL policies   │
│  ldap:alice.s   → Alias2 → Entity:Alice → Groups → ALL policies   │
│  → Alice has the SAME access regardless of auth method!           │
│                                                                    │
│  Components of an Alias:                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ name         │ The identity name in the auth method          │ │
│  │              │ (e.g., "alice" for userpass, DN for LDAP)    │ │
│  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ mount_accessor│ UUID of the auth method mount               │ │
│  │              │ (distinguishes prod-userpass from dev-userpass)│ │
│  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
│  │ canonical_id │ UUID of the Entity this alias maps to        │ │
│  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

9.5 Identity for anihpj/jobpost — Production Team Structure 🏗️

Let's design the Identity structure for the anihpj/jobpost team. We have three personas: (1) anihpj application (Kubernetes pod, machine identity), (2) developers (human operators via userpass/OIDC), (3) CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions via AppRole). All three need different levels of access, managed through groups.

🏗️ ANIHPJ/JOBPOST — Identity & Group Structure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🏗️ ANIHPJ/JOBPOST IDENTITY STRUCTURE                  │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  GROUP: anihpj-developers (internal)                          │ │
│  │  Policies: [anihpj-read-policy]                              │ │
│  │  Members: Entity:alice, Entity:bob                           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  GROUP: anihpj-admins (internal)                              │ │
│  │  Policies: [anihpj-admin-policy]                             │ │
│  │  Members: Entity:charlie (platform lead)                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  GROUP: anihpj-apps (internal)                                │ │
│  │  Policies: [anihpj-app-policy]                               │ │
│  │  Members: Entity:anihpj-app, Entity:jobpost-app              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  GROUP: ci-cd-pipelines (internal)                            │ │
│  │  Policies: [ci-cd-policy]                                    │ │
│  │  Members: Entity:github-actions                              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                    │
│  ENTITY DETAILS:                                                   │
│  ┌────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐│
│  │ Entity          │ Auth Method      │ Alias                    ││
│  ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤│
│  │ alice           │ userpass         │ userpass:alice           ││
│  │                 │ OIDC (Google)    │ oidc:alice@company.com   ││
│  ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤│
│  │ anihpj-app      │ Kubernetes       │ k8s:anihpj-sa            ││
│  │ (machine)       │                  │ (ns: anihpj)             ││
│  ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤│
│  │ github-actions  │ AppRole          │ approle:github-actions   ││
│  │ (machine)       │                  │                          ││
│  └────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘│
│                                                                    │
│  💡 All entities share the "default" policy + their group policies│
│  💡 Alice can auth via userpass OR Google OIDC — same access!     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Bash — Setting Up anihpj Identity Structure
# 1. Create entities for each team member and machine
vault write identity/entity name="alice" metadata=role=developer
vault write identity/entity name="bob" metadata=role=developer
vault write identity/entity name="charlie" metadata=role=platform_lead
vault write identity/entity name="anihpj-app" metadata=type=machine
vault write identity/entity name="jobpost-app" metadata=type=machine
vault write identity/entity name="github-actions" metadata=type=ci_cd

# 2. Create groups with policies
vault write identity/group name="anihpj-developers" \
    type=internal \
    policies="anihpj-read-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/alice),$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/bob)"

vault write identity/group name="anihpj-admins" \
    type=internal \
    policies="anihpj-admin-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/charlie)"

vault write identity/group name="anihpj-apps" \
    type=internal \
    policies="anihpj-app-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/anihpj-app),$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/jobpost-app)"

# 3. Create aliases (map auth identities to entities)
# Get mount accessors first
vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '.["userpass/"].accessor'
vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '.["kubernetes/"].accessor'

# Create aliases
vault write identity/entity-alias name="alice" \
    canonical_id="$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/alice)" \
    mount_accessor="auth_userpass_xxx"

vault write identity/entity-alias name="anihpj-sa" \
    canonical_id="$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/anihpj-app)" \
    mount_accessor="auth_kubernetes_xxx"

# 4. Verify: Alice logs in and gets all group policies
vault login -method=userpass username=alice
vault token lookup
# entity_id: ... (alice)
# policies: [anihpj-read-policy default]
# → Inherited from anihpj-developers group!

📝 Chapter 9 Practice Questions — Identity System

Q81
What is the purpose of Vault's Identity system (Entities, Aliases, Groups)?
Show Answer
Answer

The Identity system unifies multiple auth methods under a single identity. It solves the problem of a user authenticating via different methods (userpass, LDAP, OIDC) being treated as different identities. With Identity: (1) Entities represent a single person/machine, (2) Aliases map auth method logins to entities, (3) Groups organize entities and carry policies that all members inherit.

Explanation

Without Identity: Alice logs in via userpass = Identity A with policies X. Alice logs in via LDAP = Identity B with policies Y. Different access depending on auth method. With Identity: Both auth methods map to Entity:Alice via aliases → Alice always gets policies from her groups, regardless of how she authenticates.

Q82
What is the difference between an Internal and External group in Vault Identity?
Show Answer
Answer

Internal Groups: Members are managed manually within Vault using member_entity_ids. You explicitly add/remove entities. External Groups: Members are managed by an external identity provider (LDAP, Okta). Vault syncs membership from the external source. Both types carry policies that members inherit. External groups require the auth method to support group syncing (e.g., LDAP, OIDC with groups claim).

Explanation

Use internal groups when you manage team structure in Vault directly (small teams, machine identities). Use external groups when team structure is managed in your corporate directory (LDAP/AD) and you want Vault to automatically reflect changes.

Q83
How do you ensure a user has the same Vault access regardless of which auth method they use?
Show Answer
Answer

Create an Entity for the user, create Aliases for each auth method they use (pointing to the same entity), add the entity to Groups that carry the required policies. Now, when they authenticate via ANY of the configured auth methods, Vault recognizes them as the same entity and attaches all group policies.

Explanation
# Entity
vault write identity/entity name="alice"
# Alias for userpass
vault write identity/entity-alias name="alice" \
    canonical_id= mount_accessor=
# Alias for OIDC
vault write identity/entity-alias name="alice@company.com" \
    canonical_id= mount_accessor=
# Add to group
vault write identity/group name="engineers" \
    policies="eng-policy" member_entity_ids=
Q84
How do policies flow from Groups to an Entity's tokens?
Show Answer
Answer

When a token is created for an entity, Vault computes the UNION of: (1) Policies from ALL groups the entity is a member of, (2) Policies attached directly to the auth method role, (3) The "default" policy (unless token_no_default_policy=true). The resulting token has the sum of all these policies. Vault uses a most-permissive model — if ANY source grants a capability, it's allowed. There are no "deny" policies.

Explanation

Example: Alice is in group "developers" (policy: read-secrets) and group "db-admins" (policy: manage-db). Her token gets BOTH policies. She can read secrets AND manage databases. Policy inheritance is additive, never subtractive.

Q85
What is a Mount Accessor and why is it important for Aliases?
Show Answer
Answer

A Mount Accessor is a UUID that uniquely identifies each auth method mount. Aliases use the mount accessor to specify WHICH auth method mount they belong to. This is critical because you can have multiple mounts of the same auth type (e.g., prod-userpass/ and dev-userpass/) — each has a different accessor, so aliases are correctly scoped to the right mount.

Explanation

Find a mount's accessor: vault auth list -format=json | jq '."userpass/".accessor'. The accessor stays the same even if you tune the auth method, but changes if you disable and re-enable it (new accessor is assigned).

Q86
What happens when you merge two entities in Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

When you merge Entity A into Entity B: (1) All aliases from Entity A are moved to Entity B, (2) Entity A's group memberships are transferred to Entity B, (3) Entity A is deleted, (4) Entity B keeps its original aliases and groups. The merge is useful when you discover two entities represent the same person (e.g., created by different admins).

Explanation
vault write identity/entity/merge \
    from_entity_ids="old-entity-id" \
    to_entity_id="canonical-entity-id" \
    force=true

⚠️ This is irreversible — the "from" entity is permanently deleted.

Q87
Can an Entity directly have policies? How does it differ from Groups?
Show Answer
Answer

No — Entities do NOT have their own policies in standard Vault. Policies are attached to Groups, and entities inherit policies through group membership. (Note: In Vault Enterprise, entities can have direct policies via identity/entity with policies parameter, but this is an Enterprise feature. The Associate exam focuses on the open-source model: entities → groups → policies.)

Explanation

Best practice: Always use groups for policy assignment, even for a single entity. This makes it easy to add more entities later and provides a clear audit trail of who has what access.

Q88
Design the Identity structure for anihpj: 3 developers (human), 2 applications (K8s pods), and 1 CI/CD pipeline.
Show Answer
Answer
anihpj Identity Design
ENTITIES (6):
├── alice    (human, aliases: userpass, oidc)
├── bob      (human, aliases: userpass, oidc)
├── charlie  (human, aliases: userpass, ldap)
├── anihpj-app   (machine, alias: kubernetes)
├── jobpost-app  (machine, alias: kubernetes)
└── github-actions (machine, alias: approle)

GROUPS (3):
├── anihpj-developers → [alice, bob] → policy: anihpj-read
├── anihpj-admins    → [charlie]    → policy: anihpj-admin
├── anihpj-apps      → [anihpj-app, jobpost-app] → policy: anihpj-app
└── ci-cd-pipelines  → [github-actions] → policy: ci-cd
Explanation

This structure provides clear separation: developers can read secrets, admins can manage everything, apps can access their specific secrets, and CI/CD can deploy. Each entity has aliases for multiple auth methods, ensuring consistent access regardless of how they authenticate.

Q89
What are the key differences between Group policy inheritance and Token policy assignment?
Show Answer
Answer

Group policies: Inherited indirectly through entity membership. Changes to group policies affect ALL entity tokens (existing tokens continue until renewal — new policies apply on next login/renewal). Token policies: Assigned directly at token creation time (via -policy flag or auth method role). They're "baked into" the token and don't change even if the source role changes. Group policies are more dynamic and manageable at scale.

Explanation

Exam scenario: "You change a group's policies. When do existing tokens get the new policies?" Answer: On the NEXT renewal or when a NEW token is created. Existing tokens keep their original policies until they expire or are renewed.

Q90
How does Vault determine which Entity a login belongs to?
Show Answer
Answer

When a user/app authenticates: (1) Vault checks the auth method's response for an entity_alias (some auth methods like LDAP/OIDC can return this automatically), (2) Vault looks up the alias by name + mount_accessor, (3) If an alias is found, Vault resolves the canonical_id (entity ID) from the alias, (4) Vault computes the entity's effective policies from all groups. If no alias exists, a new entity may be auto-created (depending on auth method config) or the login proceeds without an entity.

Explanation

The lookup chain: Login → Alias (name + mount_accessor) → Entity → Group Memberships → Group Policies → Token policies. This happens transparently — the user just sees their token with all the right policies.

🏋️ Ch 9 Lab — Identity System (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Create entity, alias, group; verify policy inheritance
# 1. Create entity for anihpj developer
vault write identity/entity name="john-dev" metadata=team=anihpj metadata=role=developer
ENTITY_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/john-dev)

# 2. Create internal group with policies
vault write identity/group name="anihpj-devs" type=internal \
    policies="anihpj-read" metadata=team=anihpj
GROUP_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/group/name/anihpj-devs)

# 3. Add entity to group
vault write identity/group name="anihpj-devs" \
    member_entity_ids=$ENTITY_ID

# 4. Create alias (links auth method login to entity)
MOUNT_ACCESSOR=$(vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '.["userpass/"].accessor')
vault write identity/entity-alias name="john" \
    canonical_id=$ENTITY_ID mount_accessor=$MOUNT_ACCESSOR

# 5. Verify: entity now inherits group policies
vault read identity/entity/name/john-dev
# Check: group_ids includes anihpj-devs, policies=[anihpj-read]

# 6. Test: create token via userpass, check policies
# (after creating userpass user "john")
vault write auth/userpass/login username=john password=pass123
# Token should have policies: [default, anihpj-read]

Drill Check: Does the entity directly hold policies? (NO — policies come from groups). What does the alias do? (Links auth-method login to entity). Can an entity have aliases from multiple auth methods? (YES — AppRole + userpass + OIDC → same entity).

📊 Part 3: Authentication — Summary & Exam Drill

🟡 Part 3 Key Takeaways — What You Must Remember

🔑Auth ≠ AccessAuth proves WHO you are. Policies (Part 5) grant WHAT you can do.
🤖AppRole = MachinesRoleID (not secret) + SecretID (secret). Single-use by default.
☸️K8s Auth = Zero CredsPods auth via SA JWT → TokenReview API. No passwords.
🔄Lifecycle PatternEnable → Config → Roles → Test → Use. Same for ALL auth methods.
👥Identity = UnifiedEntities + Aliases unify multiple auth methods under one identity.
📋Groups Carry PoliciesEntities don't have policies. Groups do. UNION of all group policies.
🔐MFA = Per-MountNot per-user. Multi-mount pattern for tiered MFA enforcement.
⚠️Disable = IrreversibleAuth disable deletes everything. Tokens survive until expiry.
🚀 Part 3 Implementation Blueprint — Putting It All Together

Here's the complete authentication architecture for anihpj/jobpost on Kubernetes:

1
Enable K8s Auth — vault auth enable kubernetes. Configure with kubernetes_host, token_reviewer_jwt, kubernetes_ca_cert.
2
Create K8s Roles — One role per workload: anihpj-app role binds anihpj-sa in anihpj namespace. jobpost-app role binds jobpost-sa.
3
Deploy with SA — Pods reference serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa. SA JWT auto-mounted. No credentials in env vars or configmaps.
4
CI/CD via AppRole — vault auth enable approle. Create role with secret_id_ttl=10m, secret_id_num_uses=1. Deliver SecretID via response wrapping.
5
Human Ops via OIDC — vault auth enable oidc. Connect to Google/Okta/Azure AD. Bound claims restrict by email domain or group membership.
6
Identity Unification — Create entities for all users/machines. Map auth identities to entities via aliases. Add entities to groups that carry policies.
7
MFA for Privileged Access — Mount admin-userpass with TOTP enforcement. Mount dev-userpass without MFA. Different TTLs and policies per mount.
🎯 PART 3 EXAM DRILL — Auth Methods & Identity

Drill 1 — Auth Method Enable (30 seconds): Enable AppRole auth at path prod-approle, list all auth methods, then disable it.

vault auth enable -path=prod-approle approle
vault auth list
vault auth disable prod-approle/

Drill 2 — AppRole Full Setup (2 minutes): Enable, create role with 10m SecretID TTL and single-use, get RoleID, generate SecretID, login.

vault auth enable approle
vault write auth/approle/role/test-app secret_id_ttl=10m secret_id_num_uses=1 token_policies=default token_ttl=30m
vault read auth/approle/role/test-app/role-id
vault write -f auth/approle/role/test-app/secret-id
vault write auth/approle/login role_id= secret_id=

Drill 3 — K8s Auth Setup (3 minutes): Enable, configure with K8s host, create role for anihpj namespace, test login.

vault auth enable kubernetes
vault write auth/kubernetes/config kubernetes_host="https://kubernetes.default.svc:443" token_reviewer_jwt="$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" kubernetes_ca_cert=@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj policies=default ttl=1h
vault login -method=kubernetes role=anihpj

Drill 4 — Identity & Groups (2 minutes): Create entity, group, add entity to group, verify policy inheritance.

vault write identity/entity name="test-user" metadata=role=developer
vault write identity/group name="test-group" type=internal policies="default" member_entity_ids=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/test-user)
vault read identity/entity/name/test-user
# Verify group_ids includes test-group

Drill 5 — MFA Setup (2 minutes): Mount separate userpass paths, enforce TOTP MFA on admin path only.

vault auth enable -path=admin-up userpass
vault auth enable -path=dev-up userpass
vault write identity/mfa/method/totp/admin-totp issuer=vault period=30
vault write identity/mfa/login-enforcement/admin-mfa mfa_method_ids=admin-totp auth_method_accessors=$(vault auth list -format=json | jq -r '."admin-up/".accessor') auth_method_types=userpass
# Now: vault login -method=userpass -path=admin-up → MFA required
#      vault login -method=userpass -path=dev-up    → No MFA

Everything in Part 3 leads to getting a token — Part 4 teaches you how to manage them.

🟡 Part 4: Tokens — The Currency of Vault

🟡 Part 4 Overview — Token Architecture

🎫TokensResult of successful authentication
⚖️Service vs BatchStored vs Encrypted blob — #1 exam distinction

Tokens are what you earn from Part 3's authentication. Every Vault API call carries a token. Service tokens power long-lived applications (renewable, revocable, stored). Batch tokens handle high-volume workloads (not stored, not renewable — lightweight). Response wrapping securely delivers AppRole SecretIDs. Token accessors let you manage tokens without seeing their values. Part 5 covers Policies — what tokens can actually DO.

Chapter 10: Token Types and Lifecycle 🎯🎯

VA Exam Weight: 28% (Token & Policies domain)

You've proven your identity (Part 3). Now Vault gives you a token — your digital keycard. Every single Vault API call requires a token. Vault checks three things on every request: Is the token valid? What policies are attached? Has the TTL expired? Tokens are the currency of Vault — understanding them deeply is non-negotiable for the exam (28% weight!) and for production. This chapter covers every token type, their lifecycles, and the critical Service vs Batch distinction that the exam LOVES to test.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Understand what tokens are and how they flow through every Vault request
  • Master the Service vs Batch token distinction (THE #1 exam topic)
  • Learn token hierarchies: parent-child, orphan, periodic relationships
  • Understand token TTL, MaxTTL, renewal, and expiry mechanics
  • Use token accessors to manage tokens without knowing their values
  • Manage root tokens securely — generate, protect, revoke
🔗 Why This Matters for the Exam & Real Life

28% of the Vault Associate exam is Token & Policies. You WILL be asked: "Which token type is NOT stored in Vault?" (Batch), "Which token type can have children?" (Service only), "What happens when you revoke a parent token?" (All children revoked — except orphans). In production, token management is a daily operation: creating, renewing, looking up, and revoking tokens for applications, CI/CD, and human operators.

10.1 What Are Tokens? — Vault's Digital Keycard

A token is the result of successful authentication. Think of it as a hotel keycard: you prove your identity at the front desk (auth method), they give you a keycard (token), and that keycard opens specific doors (policies) for a limited time (TTL). Every single Vault API request — whether CLI, HTTP API, or SDK — carries a token in the X-Vault-Token header.

🎫 TOKENS — The Currency of Vault

📋 Token CLI Quick Reference
vault token create
Create a new service token (default)
vault token create -type=batch
Create a batch token (not stored)
vault token lookup
Inspect current token's properties
vault token renew <token>
Extend token's TTL
vault token revoke <token>
Destroy token immediately
vault token capabilities <token> <path>
Check what a token can do at a path
🔬 ANATOMY OF A VAULT TOKEN — What's Inside

When you run vault token lookup, here's what Vault knows about every token:

ids.A1b2C3d4... (the secret token string)
accessor7hS9kW2m... (management reference)
policies["default", "app-policy"]
ttlTime until expiry (e.g., 3h58m)
creation_ttlOriginal TTL at creation
explicit_max_ttlAbsolute max lifetime
entity_idIdentity entity UUID (if linked)
typeservice | batch
orphantrue | false (has parent?)
renewabletrue | false (can extend?)

The token itself is just a UUID-style string — all this metadata is stored inside Vault's internal storage (for service tokens) or encrypted within the token blob itself (for batch tokens). The token string is the key to look up this metadata.

10.2 Service Tokens vs Batch Tokens (EXAM CRITICAL) 🎯🎯🎯

THE #1 EXAM DISTINCTION — Know every difference!

This is the most tested topic in the Token domain. The exam will ask multiple questions about Service vs Batch tokens. The core distinction: Service tokens are stored in Vault's memory (they have leases, can be renewed, can be revoked, can have children). Batch tokens are encrypted blobs (not stored, no lease, cannot be renewed, cannot be revoked — they just expire).

10.2a Service Tokens — The Workhorse

Service tokens are the default token type. They're stored in Vault's internal storage, have leases, can be renewed, can be revoked by ID, and can create child tokens. Use service tokens for long-lived applications like the anihpj Django app, Vault Agent sidecars, and any workload that needs persistent, renewable access.

# Create a service token (default)
vault token create -policy=anihpj-policy -ttl=4h

# Look up any service token by its ID
vault token lookup s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...

# Renew the token
vault token renew s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...

# Revoke the token
vault token revoke s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...

# Create a child token (only service tokens can do this!)
vault token create -policy=child-policy -ttl=1h
10.2b Batch Tokens — The Lightweight Speedster

Batch tokens are encrypted blobs — Vault does NOT store them. They have no lease, no renewal, no revocation, no children. They're ideal for high-volume, short-lived operations where you don't want to burden Vault's storage. Batch tokens DO count against rate limits but NOT against the token count limit.

# Create a batch token
vault token create -type=batch -policy=read-only -ttl=30s

# Batch tokens CAN self-lookup
vault token lookup
# Shows: type=batch, policies, ttl, creation_time

# Batch tokens CANNOT be looked up by others
vault token lookup b.A1b2C3d4...  # → ERROR: bad token

# Batch tokens CANNOT be renewed
vault token renew b.A1b2C3d4...    # → ERROR

# Batch tokens CANNOT be revoked
vault token revoke b.A1b2C3d4...   # → ERROR (just wait for expiry)
10.2c Orphan Tokens — No Parent, No Inheritance

Orphan tokens are service tokens with no parent. They survive the revocation of the token that created them. Use orphans when you want a token to be independent — e.g., a long-lived application token that shouldn't die when an admin's token is revoked.

# Create an orphan token (survives parent revocation!)
vault token create -orphan -policy=app-policy -ttl=24h
10.2d Periodic Tokens — Auto-Renew Forever

Periodic tokens auto-renew indefinitely — until explicitly revoked. They have a period instead of a max_ttl. Each renewal extends the TTL by the period value. Use periodic tokens for long-running services that should never expire. Requires root/sudo to create.

# Create a periodic token (auto-renews every 24h FOREVER)
vault token create -period=24h -policy=app-policy
