│     Health check (every 30s)  → BATCH (lightweight, disposable)    │
│     CI/CD pipeline             → SERVICE (orphan, survives job end)│
│     Admin operations           → SERVICE (needs revocability)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯 EXAM TIP: The exam will ask: "Which token type does NOT count against token limits?" → BATCH. "Which token type can have children?" → SERVICE only. "Can you renew a batch token?" → NO. "Can you revoke a batch token?" → NO — just wait for TTL expiry. "Can you look up a batch token by ID?" → NO — only self-lookup works. Memorize these answers!
⚡ SPEED TIP — Memorize These 5 Differences: The Service vs Batch distinction is the most tested token topic. Memorize this chant: "Service = Stored, Renewable, Revocable, Children, Root-capable. Batch = NONE of these." In the exam lab, when you see a token question, first ask: "Is this Service or Batch?" — that usually eliminates half the wrong answers immediately.

10.3 Token Hierarchies — Parent-Child Relationships 🌳

Service tokens form a tree structure. When you create a token from another token, the new token becomes a child. The critical rule: revoking a parent token revokes ALL its children — unless the child is an orphan (no parent link). This is the "cascading revoke" pattern.

🌳 TOKEN HIERARCHY — Parent, Child, Orphan
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           🌳 TOKEN HIERARCHY — Parent, Child, Orphan               │
│                                                                    │
│       ┌──────────────────────┐                                     │
│       │   ROOT TOKEN         │  ← Created at init                  │
│       │   (bypasses all ACL) │                                     │
│       └──────────┬───────────┘                                     │
│                  │                                                  │
│       ┌──────────▼───────────┐                                     │
│       │   SERVICE TOKEN A    │  ← Created with -policy             │
│       │   TTL: 4h            │                                     │
│       │   MaxTTL: 12h        │                                     │
│       └──────────┬───────────┘                                     │
│                  │                                                  │
│    ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐                                   │
│    │             │             │                                    │
│    ▼             ▼             ▼                                    │
│  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌──────────────┐                           │
│  │Child A1│ │Child A2│ │ORPHAN (no    │  ← Created with            │
│  │TTL≤4h  │ │TTL≤4h  │ │parent link!) │    -orphan flag            │
│  │Max≤12h │ │Max≤12h │ │TTL=72h       │                           │
│  └────────┘ └────────┘ └──────────────┘                           │
│       ▲           ▲            ▲                                    │
│       │           │            │                                    │
│       └───────────┴────────────┘                                    │
│         REVOKE TOKEN A →                                            │
│         A1 & A2 DESTROYED!                                          │
│         But ORPHAN survives 💪                                      │
│                                                                    │
│  RULES:                                                             │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ ✅ Child TTL ≤ Parent TTL (can't outlive parent)            │  │
│  │ ✅ Child MaxTTL ≤ Parent MaxTTL                              │  │
│  │ ✅ Child policies ⊆ Parent policies (subset, not superset)  │  │
│  │ ✅ Revoke parent → ALL non-orphan children revoked            │  │
│  │ ✅ Orphan has no parent → survives parent revocation         │  │
│  │ ✅ Batch tokens CANNOT be parents (no children at all)       │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ GOTCHA: When you revoke a token via vault token revoke, ALL its children are recursively revoked. But when a token simply expires (TTL runs out), children are NOT automatically revoked — they continue until their own TTL expires. Revocation is cascading; expiry is not.

10.4 Periodic & Orphan Tokens — Special Purpose Tokens

👻 Orphan Tokens

No parent. Created with -orphan flag. Survives the revocation of the token that created it. Use when you need a token to be independent of its creator's lifecycle. Must be a service token (batch tokens have no parent concept).

vault token create -orphan -policy=app -ttl=72h
🔄 Periodic Tokens

Auto-renews forever. Has a period instead of max_ttl. Each renewal extends TTL by the period value. Continues until explicitly revoked. Requires root/sudo to create. Perfect for long-running services.

vault token create -period=24h -policy=service
🔑 Key Distinction: Orphan = about parent relationship (no parent). Periodic = about TTL behavior (auto-renews). A token can be BOTH orphan AND periodic: vault token create -orphan -period=24h. This creates a token with no parent that auto-renews forever — ideal for critical infrastructure services.

10.5 Token Accessors — Manage Tokens Without Knowing Their Value

A token accessor is a reference to a token. You can look up properties, renew, and revoke a token using its accessor — without ever knowing the actual token value. This is critical for separation of duties: an operator can manage tokens without seeing the secret token strings.

Bash — Token Accessor Operations
# Create a token and note the accessor
vault token create -policy=app-policy
# Key                  Value
# ---                  -----
# token                s.A1b2C3d4E5f6G7h8I9j0K1l2
# token_accessor       7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# Look up token properties using accessor (no token value needed!)
vault token lookup -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# Renew token using accessor
vault token renew -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# Revoke token using accessor
vault token revoke -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# CRITICAL: Accessor CANNOT be used to access secrets!
# It's for MANAGEMENT only — not for API calls to read data.
🎯 EXAM TIP: Token accessors are for management only — you cannot use an accessor to read secrets from Vault. Only the actual token string can do that. Accessors let operators look up, renew, and revoke tokens without seeing the secret token values — enabling separation of duties.

10.6 Root Token Management — The Nuclear Option 👑

The root token is created at Vault initialization. It bypasses ALL ACL checks — it can do anything: read/write any secret, create/delete any auth method, manage any policy. This is both its power and its danger. Best practices: never use the root token for daily operations. Generate it only when needed, use it for the specific task, then revoke it.

Bash — Root Token Management
# Generate a new root token (requires unseal keys/quorum)
vault operator generate-root -init
vault operator generate-root -nonce= 
vault operator generate-root -nonce= 
vault operator generate-root -nonce= 
vault operator generate-root -decode=
# → Root token: s.xxxxxxxxxx

# Login with root token (USE SPARINGLY!)
vault login s.xxxxxxxxxx

# Decode the root token from OTP
vault operator generate-root \
    -decode= \
    -otp=

# REVOKE the root token as soon as task is complete
vault token revoke s.xxxxxxxxxx

# BEST PRACTICE: Never store root token permanently
# Generate → Use → Revoke — within minutes!
💀 ROOT TOKEN BEST PRACTICES: (1) Never use as your daily token. (2) Generate only when needed via vault operator generate-root with quorum of unseal keys. (3) Use for the specific administration task. (4) Revoke immediately after the task is done. (5) The root token is NOT renewable — it has a TTL. (6) You can have multiple root tokens simultaneously — all must be revoked separately.
Token TypeStored?Renewable?Revocable?Children?Security LevelBest For
Root✅❌✅✅⚠️ MAXIMUM (bypasses ACL)Emergency admin, initialization
Service (Regular)✅✅✅✅🟢 StandardLong-lived apps, Vault Agent
Service (Periodic)✅✅ Auto✅✅🟡 Elevated (infinite lifetime)Infrastructure services
Service (Orphan)✅✅✅✅🟢 Standard (independent)CI/CD, isolated workloads
Batch❌❌❌❌🟢 Low-impact (self-expiring)Health checks, high-volume ops
Response Wrapping❌❌❌ (auto)❌🛡️ Tamper-proof (single-use)Credential delivery

The Golden Rule: The more powerful the token, the shorter its lifecycle should be. Root tokens: minutes. Periodic tokens: monitored. Batch tokens: seconds. Match the token's power to its exposure window — never let a high-privilege token live longer than absolutely necessary.

🔬 Deep Dive: Understanding Vault Tokens to the Core

Tokens are "the currency of Vault" — every API call, every CLI command, every secret access flows through a token. But tokens are more than just authentication strings. This section reveals the internal mechanics of token creation, storage, parent-child relationships, and the revocation cascade — the concepts that the hardest 28% of exam questions test.

🧬 Token Anatomy — What's Inside a Token

When you create a token, Vault doesn't just give you a random string. The token is a reference to a rich data structure that Vault stores internally (for service tokens) or encodes directly (for batch tokens). Understanding this structure is key to mastering tokens.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   SERVICE TOKEN — Internal Structure              │
│                                                                   │
│  Token ID:      hvs.CAESID...  (human-visible)                    │
│  Accessor:      VzN2Xk...      (management reference)             │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  TOKEN OBJECT (stored in Vault's token store)               │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │  Policies:        ["anihpj-app", "default"]                  │ │
│  │  Display Name:    "token-anihpj-app"                         │ │
│  │  Creation Time:   2025-06-12T10:00:00Z                       │ │
│  │  TTL:             3600s  (1 hour from creation)              │ │
│  │  MaxTTL:          86400s (24 hours absolute max)             │ │
│  │  Issue Time:      2025-06-12T10:00:00Z                       │ │
│  │  Expire Time:     2025-06-12T11:00:00Z  (creation + TTL)    │ │
│  │  Explicit MaxTTL: 0  (0 = use system default)                │ │
│  │  Orphan:          false                                      │ │
│  │  Renewable:       true                                       │ │
│  │  Num Uses:        0  (0 = unlimited uses)                    │ │
│  │  Entity ID:       abc-123-def-456  (linked identity entity)  │ │
│  │  Parent:          hvs.PARENT_ID...  (null if no parent)      │ │
│  │  Path:            "auth/kubernetes/login"  (creation source) │ │
│  │  Role:            "jobpost"  (auth role that created it)     │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │  CHILDREN: []  (list of child token IDs)                     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  BATCH TOKEN — Encrypted Blob (NOT stored in Vault)         │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │  [Encrypted{                                                │ │
│  │    Policies: ["health-check"],                               │ │
│  │    TTL: 60s,                                                 │ │
│  │    Creation Time: ...,                                       │ │
│  │    Expire Time: ...                                          │ │
│  │  }]  ← Encoding in the token string itself                  │ │
│  │                                                              │ │
│  │  No storage = No lookup by ID, no renewal, no revocation.   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🌳 The Token Hierarchy — Parent-Child Trees

Every service token (except orphans) lives in a tree structure. When you revoke a parent, the entire subtree dies. This is called cascading revocation and it's one of Vault's most powerful security features.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    TOKEN HIERARCHY — Parent-Child Tree            │
│                                                                   │
│                        ┌──────────┐                               │
│                        │  LOGIN   │  (User authenticates)         │
│                        │  TOKEN   │  TTL=8h, policies=[admin]    │
│                        └────┬─────┘                               │
│                             │                                     │
│              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐                     │
│              │              │              │                      │
│         ┌────▼────┐   ┌────▼────┐   ┌────▼────┐                  │
│         │ Child 1 │   │ Child 2 │   │ Orphan  │                  │
│         │ TTL=4h  │   │ TTL=2h  │   │ TTL=4h  │                  │
│         │ [app-r] │   │ [app-w] │   │ [app-x] │                  │
│         └────┬────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘                  │
│              │                     ↑                              │
│         ┌────▼────┐               │                              │
│         │Child 1.1│               │  SURVIVES!                   │
│         │ TTL=2h  │               │  No parent link              │
│         │ [app-r] │               │                               │
│         └─────────┘               │                               │
│              ↑                     │                              │
│              │                     │                              │
│  ┌───────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────┐          │
│  │  REVOKE LOGIN TOKEN (vault token revoke hvs.PARENT)│          │
│  │                                                     │          │
│  │  ❌ Login Token   → REVOKED                        │          │
│  │  ❌ Child 1       → CASCADING REVOKE               │          │
│  │  ❌ Child 1.1     → CASCADING REVOKE (grandchild!) │          │
│  │  ❌ Child 2       → CASCADING REVOKE               │          │
│  │  ✅ ORPHAN        → SURVIVES (no parent link!)     │          │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                                   │
│  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Revocation cascades through the ENTIRE subtree.  │
│  One revoke command can clean up hundreds of children instantly.  │
│  This is why you revoke the login token (root of tree) to          │
│  completely remove a user's access — one command, total cleanup.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

⚡ Token Creation — Internal Flow

When you run vault token create, Vault goes through a precise internal sequence. Understanding this helps you debug token issues and predict behavior:

1Validate Parent: Is the calling token valid? Not expired? Has create capability?
2Inherit Constraints: Child TTL ≤ Parent TTL, Child policies ⊆ Parent policies, Child MaxTTL ≤ Parent MaxTTL
3Generate ID: Create unique token ID (hvs. prefix) and accessor UUID
4Store (Service only): Write token object to token store. Add to parent's children list. Update identity if entity-linked.
5Start TTL Timer: Expiration manager starts tracking the token. When TTL expires → auto-revoke.
6Return: Return token ID + accessor to caller. The token is now active and usable.
⚠️ CRITICAL: Token Expiry vs Token Revocation — Different Behaviors!

When a parent token EXPIRES (TTL runs out naturally): children are NOT automatically revoked — they continue until their own TTLs expire.
When a parent token is EXPLICITLY REVOKED (vault token revoke): ALL children are recursively revoked immediately.
This distinction is heavily tested. Expiry = passive, individual. Revocation = active, cascading.

📝 Chapter 10 Practice Questions — Token Types & Lifecycle

Q91
What is a Vault token and what three things does Vault check on every API request?
Show Answer
Answer

A token is the result of successful authentication — it's your digital keycard. On every API request, Vault checks: (1) Is the token valid? (not expired, not revoked), (2) What policies are attached? (what capabilities does this token grant), (3) Is the path allowed? (does the policy match the requested API path). If ALL pass, the request succeeds. If ANY fail, Vault returns 403 Forbidden.

Explanation

Think of a token as a hotel keycard: it identifies you, it has a time limit, and it only opens specific doors. The token itself doesn't contain secrets — it's a reference that Vault uses to look up your identity and permissions.

Q92
What is the fundamental difference between a Service token and a Batch token?
Show Answer
Answer

Service tokens are stored in Vault's memory — they have leases, can be renewed, revoked, and can have children. Batch tokens are encrypted blobs — NOT stored in Vault. They cannot be renewed, revoked, or have children. Batch tokens can only self-lookup; they cannot be looked up by ID. Batch tokens are lightweight (don't count against token limits) but disposable (just wait for TTL expiry).

Explanation

This is the #1 exam distinction. Memorize: "Batch = NOT stored, NOT renewable, NOT revocable." The exam WILL ask: "Which token type is NOT stored in Vault?" → Batch. "Which token type can have children?" → Service only.

Q93
What happens when you revoke a parent Service token? What about orphan tokens?
Show Answer
Answer

Revoking a parent Service token recursively revokes ALL children — the entire subtree is destroyed. However, orphan tokens survive — they have no parent link, so parent revocation doesn't affect them. This is called "cascading revoke." Note: when a token simply expires (TTL runs out), children are NOT automatically revoked — expiry is not cascading.

Explanation

Cascading revoke applies to explicit vault token revoke only, not to natural TTL expiry. This distinction is important: if a parent token expires at 2 PM, its children continue until their own TTLs expire. But if you revoke the parent at 1:59 PM, all children are immediately revoked.

Q94
What are the three TTL-related constraints on child tokens?
Show Answer
Answer

When creating a child token from a parent: (1) Child TTL ≤ Parent TTL — a child cannot outlive its parent's current TTL, (2) Child MaxTTL ≤ Parent MaxTTL — a child's maximum lifetime cannot exceed the parent's, (3) Child policies ⊆ Parent policies — a child can only have a subset of the parent's policies, never additional policies the parent doesn't have.

Explanation

This enforces the principle of least privilege through the token hierarchy. A token can never create a child that is more powerful or longer-lived than itself. This prevents privilege escalation through token creation.

Q95
Can you renew a Batch token? Can you revoke a Batch token? Can you look up a Batch token by its ID?
Show Answer
Answer

NO to all three. Batch tokens cannot be renewed, cannot be revoked, and cannot be looked up by ID (only self-lookup works). If you need renewability or revocability, use a Service token. Batch tokens simply expire when their TTL runs out — there's no other way to end them early.

Explanation

Why? Batch tokens are encrypted blobs — Vault doesn't store them, so there's nothing to look up, nothing to renew, and nothing to revoke. They're designed for high-volume, short-lived, fire-and-forget operations where storage overhead would be wasteful.

Q96
What is the difference between an Orphan token and a Periodic token?
Show Answer
Answer

Orphan: About parent relationship — has no parent, survives parent revocation. Still has a normal TTL/MaxTTL. Periodic: About TTL behavior — auto-renews indefinitely until explicitly revoked. Has a period instead of MaxTTL. A token can be BOTH orphan AND periodic: vault token create -orphan -period=24h.

Explanation

Common confusion: "Orphan" and "Periodic" are orthogonal concepts. Orphan = independent from parent. Periodic = auto-renewing. You can have a non-orphan periodic token (has a parent, auto-renews) or an orphan non-periodic token (no parent, fixed TTL).

Q97
What is a Token Accessor and what can you do with it?
Show Answer
Answer

A token accessor is a reference UUID for a token. You can: look up token properties, renew the token, and revoke the token — all without knowing the actual token value. You CANNOT use an accessor to read secrets or make API calls — only the actual token string can access data. Accessors enable separation of duties: operators manage tokens without seeing secret values.

Explanation

Accessors are for token MANAGEMENT, not token USAGE. Think of it like a receipt: you can return an item (revoke), check the warranty (lookup), or extend the warranty (renew) using the receipt number — but you can't enter the store with just the receipt.

Q98
What is the root token and what are the best practices for using it?
Show Answer
Answer

The root token bypasses ALL ACL/policy checks — it can do anything in Vault. Best practices: (1) Never use as your daily token, (2) Generate only when needed via vault operator generate-root (requires quorum of unseal keys), (3) Use for the specific admin task, (4) Revoke immediately after the task, (5) Root tokens are NOT renewable, (6) Multiple root tokens can exist — all must be revoked separately.

Explanation

The root token is like a nuclear launch key — you don't carry it around daily. Generate it, use it for the one thing only root can do (like changing seal configuration), then revoke it. The vault operator generate-root process requires a quorum of unseal keys, providing accountability.

Q99
Which token type does NOT count against Vault's token count limit?
Show Answer
Answer

Batch tokens. Since batch tokens are encrypted blobs and NOT stored in Vault, they don't consume storage and don't count against token limits. Service tokens DO count against limits because they're stored in Vault's memory. This makes batch tokens ideal for high-volume scenarios where you'd otherwise hit token limits.

Explanation

Exam trick: "You have 10,000 microservices, each needing a short-lived token. Which type should you use?" → Batch. They won't overwhelm Vault's storage and won't hit token limits. They just expire naturally.

Q100
For anihpj/jobpost on Kubernetes, which token types would you use for each workload?
Show Answer
Answer
anihpj Token Strategy
WORKLOAD                 TOKEN TYPE    TTL     REASON
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
anihpj pod (Vault Agent) SERVICE      1h      Renewable, long-lived
Health check endpoint     BATCH        30s     Lightweight, disposable
CI/CD pipeline (GitHub)   SERVICE      30m     Orphan, survives job end
Admin operations          SERVICE      15m     Needs revocability
Database credential fetch BATCH        60s     High-volume, short-lived
Explanation

The anihpj pod's Vault Agent gets a service token because it needs to renew and maintain a long-lived connection. Health checks get batch tokens because they're single, short-lived operations. CI/CD gets an orphan service token so it doesn't die when the CI job's parent token expires.

🏋️ Ch 10 Lab — Token Types Hands-On (12 min)
⏱️ Target: 12 min | 🎯 Goal: Create each token type, verify hierarchy, test revocation
# 1. Create service token (default type)
vault token create -policy=default -ttl=1h
# Output: token=s.xxxxx, accessor=..., ttl=1h

# 2. Create batch token (lightweight, NOT stored)
vault token create -type=batch -policy=default -ttl=5m
# Output: token=b.xxxxx — NO lease_id, NO accessor in lookup!

# 3. Test: batch token CANNOT be renewed
vault token renew b.xxxxx    # ERROR: batch tokens cannot be renewed

# 4. Test: batch token CANNOT be revoked
vault token revoke b.xxxxx   # ERROR: batch tokens cannot be revoked

# 5. Create orphan token (survives parent)
TOKEN_A=$(vault token create -policy=default -ttl=30m -field=token)
VAULT_TOKEN=$TOKEN_A vault token create -orphan -policy=default -ttl=1h
# Revoke TOKEN_A → orphan child survives!

# 6. Create periodic token (auto-renews)
vault token create -policy=default -period=24h -explicit-max-ttl=72h
# Renews every 24h, hard-expires at 72h

# 7. Verify: list all service tokens
vault list auth/token/accessors   # Batch tokens NOT listed!

Drill Check: Which token type would you use for: (a) K8s liveness probe — BATCH, (b) Vault Agent in pod — SERVICE, (c) CI/CD deploy job — SERVICE (orphan).

Chapter 11: Token Helpers & Advanced Token Patterns 🔐

VA Exam Weight: 28% (Token & Policies domain)

Chapter 10 covered the basics — what tokens are, the Service vs Batch distinction, and token hierarchies. Now we go deeper into how tokens are used in practice: response wrapping for secure secret delivery, token accessor-based management, caching and renewal strategies, and production token patterns for anihpj/jobpost. These are the techniques that separate "I know about tokens" from "I can manage tokens in production."

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Master Response Wrapping — the tamper-proof envelope for secure secret delivery
  • Use token accessors for separation-of-duties token management
  • Implement caching and renewal strategies for long-running applications
  • Apply token best practices to anihpj/jobpost on Kubernetes

11.1 Response Wrapping — The Tamper-Proof Envelope 🎁🎯

Here's the problem: How do you securely deliver an AppRole SecretID to a new application without exposing it in transit? You can't email it, you can't put it in CI logs, and you can't store it in a shared drive. Response wrapping solves this with a brilliant pattern: Vault wraps the secret in a single-use "wrapping token." Only the intended recipient can unwrap it — and unwrapping consumes the token, proving it wasn't intercepted.

🎁 RESPONSE WRAPPING — The Tamper-Proof Envelope
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        🎁 RESPONSE WRAPPING — Secure Secret Delivery              │
│                                                                    │
│  PROBLEM: How do you securely deliver AppRole SecretID to         │
│  a new application without exposing it in transit?                │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐        │
│  │  ADMIN   │          │  VAULT   │          │  NEW APP │        │
│  └────┬─────┘          └────┬─────┘          └────┬─────┘        │
│       │                     │                      │               │
│       │ 1. Generate SecretID│                      │               │
│       │ with -wrap-ttl=300s │                      │               │
│       │────────────────────▶│                      │               │
│       │                     │ 2. Creates wrapping   │               │
│       │                     │ token: w.abc123...   │               │
│       │ 3. Returns wrapping │ (NOT the actual      │               │
│       │ token ONLY          │ SecretID!)           │               │
│       │◀────────────────────│                      │               │
│       │                     │                      │               │
│       │ 4. Share wrapping   │                      │               │
│       │ token via secure    │                      │               │
│       │ channel (PagerDuty, │                      │               │
│       │ encrypted msg)      │                      │               │
│       │─────────────────────────────────────────▶│               │
│       │                     │                      │               │
│       │                     │ 5. vault unwrap     │               │
│       │                     │    w.abc123...      │               │
│       │                     │◀────────────────────│               │
│       │                     │                      │               │
│       │                     │ 6. Returns actual    │               │
│       │                     │ SecretID + destroys  │               │
│       │                     │ wrapping token!      │               │
│       │                     │─────────────────────▶│               │
│                                                                    │
│  🛡️ SECURITY GUARANTEES:                                           │
│  • Wrapping token is SINGLE-USE (unwrapped = destroyed)             │
│  • If intercepted but already unwrapped → USELESS                   │
│  • If not unwrapped within TTL → AUTO-EXPIRES                       │
│  • Audit log shows: who created wrap, who unwrapped, when           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Bash — Response Wrapping Complete Flow
# ===== ADMIN SIDE: Create and wrap the secret =====
# Generate SecretID and wrap it with 5-minute TTL
vault write -wrap-ttl=300s \
    auth/approle/role/anihpj-app/secret-id
# Key                              Value
# ---                              -----
# wrapping_token:                  w.hB2cD4eF6gH8iJ0kL2mN4oP6qR8sT0u
# wrapping_accessor:               V2wX4yZ6aB8cD0eF2gH4iJ6kL8mN0oP
# wrapping_token_ttl:              5m
# wrapping_token_creation_time:    2026-06-13T10:30:00Z
# wrapped_accessor:                1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d

# Share ONLY the wrapping_token (w.hB2c...) with the application
# DO NOT share the actual SecretID!

# ===== APPLICATION SIDE: Unwrap to get the secret =====
VAULT_TOKEN=w.hB2cD4eF6gH8iJ0kL2mN4oP6qR8sT0u vault unwrap
# Key                  Value
# ---                  -----
# secret_id            hvs.CAESIKmR8oQMli...
# secret_id_accessor   1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d

# The wrapping token is now DESTROYED — single use!
# Any attempt to unwrap again → ERROR: wrapping token is not valid

# ===== CHEAT: Wrap ANY Vault response =====
vault write -wrap-ttl=600s secret/data/anihpj/db password="s3cr3t"
# Returns wrapping token, not the actual db password!
🔑 When to Use Response Wrapping: (1) Delivering AppRole SecretIDs to new applications or CI/CD pipelines, (2) Distributing initial bootstrap credentials to operators, (3) Sharing any secret where you need proof that only one recipient received it (single-use guarantee), (4) Reducing exposure — the wrapping token has its own TTL independent of the wrapped secret's TTL.
🎯 EXAM TIP: The exam LOVES response wrapping. Know: (1) -wrap-ttl sets the wrapping token's own TTL (not the wrapped secret's TTL), (2) vault unwrap consumes the wrapping token — it's single-use, (3) The wrapping token is a special token type (not service, not batch), (4) If the wrapping TTL expires, the wrapped secret is NOT deleted from Vault — only the wrapping token expires. The secret still exists and can be accessed by its actual path.

11.2 Token Accessors Deep Dive — Separation of Duties

Token accessors enable a powerful pattern: one team creates tokens, another team manages them — without sharing the actual token values. An operator can renew or revoke tokens using only accessors, never seeing the secret token strings. This is critical for compliance (SOC2, HIPAA) where access to credentials must be strictly controlled.

Bash — Accessor-Based Token Management Workflow
# ===== TEAM A: Creates tokens, shares accessors with Team B =====
vault token create -policy=app-policy -ttl=24h
# token:                s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...
# token_accessor:       7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI  ← Share THIS only

# Share the accessor with Team B (operations)
# Team B NEVER sees s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...

# ===== TEAM B: Manages tokens using only accessors =====
# Look up token properties
vault token lookup -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI
# Shows: policies, TTL, creation_time, entity_id
# Does NOT show: the actual token value

# Renew the token (if service token)
vault token renew -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# Revoke the token
vault token revoke -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI

# CANNOT do this:
vault kv get secret/anihpj -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8nQ3cR6tY1uI
# → ERROR: Accessor is for MANAGEMENT only, not for data access!

11.3 Caching & Renewal Strategies — Keeping Tokens Alive

Long-running applications (like anihpj Django pods) can't re-authenticate every time their token expires. They need token renewal. Vault supports pattern-based renewal where you renew before the TTL expires, extending the token's life up to its MaxTTL.

🔄 TOKEN LIFECYCLE — Renew Before Expiry
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          🔄 TOKEN LIFECYCLE — Renew Before Expiry                  │
│                                                                    │
│  Token TTL = 1 hour, MaxTTL = 24 hours                            │
│                                                                    │
│  ──┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────▶      │
│    │0         │1h        │2h        │3h        │...24h           │
│    │          │          │          │          │                  │
│    │ Create   │ Renew    │ Renew    │ Renew    │ MAX TTL          │
│    │ token    │ (before  │ (before  │ (before  │ reached =        │
│    │ TTL=1h   │ expiry)  │ expiry)  │ expiry)  │ MUST re-auth     │
│    │          │ TTL→1h   │ TTL→1h   │ TTL→1h   │                  │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 Vault Agent handles ALL of this AUTOMATICALLY!                 │
│  💡 vault token renew  → extends TTL by original value      │
│  💡 Best practice: Renew at TTL/2 (renew when 50% of TTL remains) │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ RENEWAL PATTERNS:                                            │ │
│  │                                                               │ │
│  │ vault token renew           # Extend TTL by 1 value   │ │
│  │ vault token renew -increment=2h  # Extend by specific time│ │
│  │ vault lease renew        # Renew dynamic secret    │ │
│  │                                                               │ │
│  │ AUTOMATIC: Vault Agent sidecar handles renewal automatically │ │
│  │ AUTOMATIC: Periodic tokens auto-renew indefinitely           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Bash — Token Renewal Operations
# Renew current token (extends TTL by its original value)
vault token renew

# Renew a specific token
vault token renew s.A1b2C3d4...

# Renew by a specific increment (must be ≤ original TTL)
vault token renew -increment=30m s.A1b2C3d4...

# Check how much TTL remains
vault token lookup | grep ttl
# ttl: 52m34s  ← time remaining before expiry

# MaxTTL check — has the token hit its maximum lifetime?
vault token lookup | grep explicit_max_ttl
# explicit_max_ttl: 23h58m  ← total lifetime limit

# If MaxTTL reached → renewal FAILS → MUST re-authenticate!
⚠️ GOTCHA: When a token hits its MaxTTL, renewal fails. The token will expire naturally at its TTL. After MaxTTL, the only option is to re-authenticate — get a brand new token from an auth method. This is by design: MaxTTL forces periodic re-authentication, limiting the blast radius of a compromised token.
🤖 VAULT AGENT AUTO-AUTH PATTERN: In production (especially on Kubernetes), you should never write token renewal logic in your application code. Instead, use Vault Agent as a sidecar. Vault Agent: (1) Authenticates using the pod's SA JWT (Kubernetes Auth), (2) Writes the resulting token to a shared sink file, (3) Automatically renews the token before expiry, (4) If renewal fails, it re-authenticates from scratch, (5) The application simply reads the token from the sink file — no Vault logic needed. This pattern is covered in detail in Part 6 (Chapter 14: Vault on Kubernetes).

11.4 Token Best Practices for anihpj 🏗️

Here's the recommended token strategy for the anihpj application running on Kubernetes:

☸️anihpj Pod (Vault Agent)Service token, TTL=1h, MaxTTL=24h. Vault Agent sidecar handles auto-renewal and writes secrets to a shared volume. Token is never exposed to the application container.
🏥Health Check EndpointBatch token, TTL=30s. Lightweight, fire-and-forget. Doesn't need renewal or revocation. Doesn't contribute to token count limits.
🔧CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions)Orphan Service token, TTL=30m. Orphan ensures the token survives the CI job's parent. SecretID delivered via response wrapping.
👤Admin OperationsService token, TTL=15m. Short-lived for security. Revocable if compromised. Accessor shared with audit team for compliance monitoring.

11.5 Token Best Practices for anihpj/jobpost — Production Summary 🏗️

🚀 Production Token Strategy Checklist
1
Use Service tokens for long-lived apps — They're renewable, revocable, and manageable. Vault Agent handles renewal automatically.
2
Use Batch tokens for high-volume, short-lived ops — Health checks, one-time config reads, API probes. They don't bloat Vault's storage.
3
Deliver credentials via Response Wrapping — AppRole SecretIDs, initial bootstrap tokens. Single-use guarantee proves no interception.
4
Use token accessors for separation of duties — Ops team manages tokens without seeing values. Compliance team audits via accessors.
5
Set appropriate TTLs — Short TTL (15m-1h) for human operators. Longer TTL (1h-24h) for automated services. MaxTTL forces periodic re-auth.
6
Revoke root tokens immediately after use — Generate → Use → Revoke. Never store root tokens. Generate new ones as needed via quorum.
7
Never share token values — share accessors — For management operations (renew, revoke, lookup), accessors are sufficient. Token values stay secret.

📝 Chapter 11 Practice Questions — Token Helpers & Advanced Patterns

Q101
What is Response Wrapping and what problem does it solve?
Show Answer
Answer

Response Wrapping creates a single-use "wrapping token" that contains a secret. The recipient uses vault unwrap to retrieve the secret. Unwrapping consumes and destroys the wrapping token — so any eavesdropper who tries to unwrap will fail (already consumed). It solves the secure secret delivery problem: how to send a secret (like AppRole SecretID) to an application without exposing it in transit.

Explanation

Think of it as a tamper-proof envelope: if you receive an unopened envelope, you know the secret is inside. If the envelope is already opened, you know it was intercepted. The wrapping token IS the envelope — opening it (unwrap) destroys it.

Q102
What happens when you unwrap a wrapping token? What if someone else already unwrapped it?
Show Answer
Answer

When you vault unwrap <wrapping_token>, Vault returns the original secret (e.g., the SecretID) and destroys the wrapping token. If someone else already unwrapped it, you'll get an error: "wrapping token is not valid or does not exist" — because it was already consumed. This single-use property is the core security guarantee: you can detect interception.

Explanation

This is why response wrapping is superior to just encrypting the secret and sending it. With encryption, an attacker could decrypt and re-encrypt, and you'd never know. With wrapping, the token is consumed on first use — there's no way to "re-wrap" it.

Q103
What is the difference between the wrapping token's TTL and the wrapped secret's TTL?
Show Answer
Answer

The wrapping token TTL (-wrap-ttl) controls how long the envelope is valid — how long the recipient has to unwrap it. The wrapped secret's own TTL (e.g., SecretID TTL) is independent. If the wrapping TTL expires, the wrapping token is destroyed but the secret still exists in Vault at its original path. The wrapping token expiring does NOT delete the underlying secret.

Explanation

Key exam nuance: Expired wrapping token ≠ deleted secret. The secret (e.g., SecretID) still exists at auth/approle/role/anihpj-app/secret-id and can be accessed by its accessor. Only the delivery envelope expired.

Q104
How do you securely deliver an AppRole SecretID to a new application using response wrapping?
Show Answer
Answer
# Admin: Generate SecretID and wrap it
vault write -wrap-ttl=300s auth/approle/role/anihpj-app/secret-id
# → wrapping_token: w.hB2cD4eF6...

# Admin: Send ONLY w.hB2cD4eF6... to the application
# (via secure channel: encrypted message, PagerDuty, etc.)

# Application: Unwrap to get the SecretID
VAULT_TOKEN=w.hB2cD4eF6... vault unwrap
# → secret_id: hvs.CAESI...
# → secret_id_accessor: 1a2b3c...

# Application: Now login with RoleID + SecretID
vault write auth/approle/login \
    role_id= secret_id=hvs.CAESI...
Q105
What is the relationship between token accessors and separation of duties?
Show Answer
Answer

Token accessors enable separation of duties: Team A creates tokens (knows token values). Team B manages tokens (uses only accessors — cannot read secrets). Team B can look up, renew, and revoke tokens without ever seeing the actual token strings. Accessors are for management only — they cannot be used to access secrets in Vault.

Explanation

This pattern is critical for compliance: the team that handles token lifecycle management doesn't have access to the secrets those tokens protect. Accessors are the bridge that makes this possible.

Q106
What happens when a Service token reaches its MaxTTL? How is this different from TTL expiry?
Show Answer
Answer

When a token reaches its MaxTTL, renewal fails. The token continues to work until its current TTL expires (naturally), but you cannot extend its life further. MaxTTL is the absolute lifetime limit. TTL expiry means the token is dead — it can no longer be used for any Vault operation. After MaxTTL, the only option is to re-authenticate and get a brand new token.

Explanation

Analogy: TTL = your hotel checkout time (can extend). MaxTTL = the maximum stay limit (cannot extend beyond this — must check out and check back in). This forces periodic re-authentication, limiting how long a compromised token remains useful.

Q107
What is the recommended token renewal strategy for production applications?
Show Answer
Answer

Renew at TTL/2 — when 50% of the TTL remains, renew the token. This provides a safety buffer: if renewal fails (network issue, Vault temporarily unavailable), you have another 50% of the TTL to retry before the token expires. For automated renewal, use Vault Agent sidecar — it handles the entire lifecycle: authenticate, renew, and write secrets to a shared volume.

Explanation

Vault Agent uses a configurable retry block for renewal failures. If renewal fails repeatedly, Vault Agent can be configured to re-authenticate from scratch — ensuring the application always has a valid token.

Q108
Can you use a token accessor to read secrets from Vault?
Show Answer
Answer

NO. Token accessors are for token management only: lookup properties, renew, revoke. You cannot use an accessor to read secrets, write data, or perform any path-based Vault operation. Only the actual token string (s.xxxxx or hvs.xxxxx) can access secrets. This is by design — accessors are safe to share with ops/audit teams.

Explanation

Accessors can do: vault token lookup -accessor <id>, vault token renew -accessor <id>, vault token revoke -accessor <id>. Accessors CANNOT do: vault kv get secret/foo (or any data operation).

Q109
What is the difference between vault token renew and vault lease renew?
Show Answer
Answer

vault token renew extends a token's TTL (the authentication credential). vault lease renew extends a dynamic secret's lease (e.g., database credentials generated by the DB secrets engine). Tokens are for authentication; leases are for dynamic secrets. They're separate concepts — a token can be alive while a lease expires, and vice versa.

Explanation

From Chapter 5 (Secrets Engines): Dynamic secrets have leases. You renew leases to keep database credentials alive. Tokens are what let you call Vault at all. You renew tokens to stay authenticated. Both need renewal, but they're independent.

Q110
Design a complete token strategy for anihpj/jobpost covering: pod authentication, health checks, CI/CD, admin access, and credential delivery.
Show Answer
Answer
anihpj/jobpost Complete Token Strategy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🎫 ANIHPJ/JOBPOST — Complete Token Strategy               │
│                                                                    │
│  WORKLOAD            TOKEN    TTL     DELIVERY      RENEWAL        │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│  anihpj pod          SERVICE  1h      K8s Auth      Vault Agent    │
│  (Vault Agent)                Max24h  (SA JWT)      auto-renew     │
│                                                                    │

│  (orphan)                     Max4h   (wrapped      survives job   │
│                                       SecretID)     end            │
│                                                                    │

🏋️ Ch 11 Lab — Response Wrapping & Accessors (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Wrap a SecretID, unwrap it, use token accessor
# 1. Generate SecretID and wrap it (single-use envelope)
vault write -wrap-ttl=5m -f auth/approle/role/myapp/secret-id
# Output: wrapping_token: hvs.xxxxx (valid for 5 min)

# 2. Unwrap (consume the wrapping token)
WRAP_TOKEN=hvs.xxxxx
vault unwrap $WRAP_TOKEN
# Output: secret_id, secret_id_accessor, ...
# The wrapping token is DESTROYED — cannot unwrap again!

# 3. Try to unwrap again → FAILS (single-use)
vault unwrap $WRAP_TOKEN  # ERROR: wrapping token is not valid

# 4. Token accessor: manage without knowing token value
TOKEN=$(vault token create -policy=default -field=token)
ACCESSOR=$(vault token lookup $TOKEN | grep accessor | awk '{print $2}')
vault token lookup -accessor $ACCESSOR   # Works!
vault token renew -accessor $ACCESSOR    # Works!
vault token revoke -accessor $ACCESSOR   # Revoke by accessor!
# But: vault kv get -header="X-Vault-Token: $ACCESSOR" secret/app → FAILS

Drill Check: Why can't you unwrap twice? (Single-use security — prevents eavesdropper). Can accessor read secrets? (NO — management only).

📊 Part 4: Tokens — Summary & Exam Drill

🟡 Part 4 Key Takeaways — What You Must Remember

🎫Token = Authentication ResultEvery Vault API call carries a token. Valid + Policies + TTL = Access.
⚖️Service ≠ BatchService stored/renewable/revocable. Batch NOT stored/NOT renewable/NOT revocable.
🌳Parent Revoke = CascadingRevoke parent → ALL children destroyed. Orphans survive. Expiry is NOT cascading.
👻Orphan ≠ PeriodicOrphan = no parent. Periodic = auto-renew. They're orthogonal (can be both).
🎁Wrap = Tamper-ProofSingle-use envelope. Unwrap consumes token. Detect interception.
🔑Accessors ≠ SecretsAccessors manage tokens. Only token strings access data. Separation of duties.
⏱️Renew at TTL/2Renew when 50% TTL remains. MaxTTL forces re-auth. Vault Agent auto-handles.
👑Root = NuclearGenerate → Use → Revoke. Never store. Requires quorum of unseal keys.
🚀 Part 4 Implementation Blueprint — Token Strategy for anihpj/jobpost

Here's how tokens flow through the complete anihpj stack:

1
Pod authenticates via K8s Auth — SA JWT → Vault verifies → Returns Service token (TTL=1h, MaxTTL=24h). Vault Agent stores it in sink file.
2
Vault Agent auto-renews — At TTL/2 (30 min), Vault Agent renews the token. On MaxTTL, it re-authenticates automatically. Application never manages tokens directly.
3
Health checks use Batch tokens — Readiness probes get disposable 30s batch tokens via K8s Auth. No storage, no renewal, no cleanup needed.
4
CI/CD gets Orphan Service token — GitHub Actions pipeline authenticates via AppRole. SecretID delivered via response wrapping. Orphan token survives pipeline job completion.
5
Admins auth via OIDC — Human operators get short-lived Service tokens (15m). Revocable if compromised. Accessors shared with audit team — never token values.
6
Root token used only for emergencies — Generate via quorum, use for the specific task (e.g., changing seal config), revoke immediately. Never stored.
🎯 PART 4 EXAM DRILL — Token Types & Management

Drill 1 — Create All Token Types (1 minute): Create service, batch, orphan, and periodic tokens.

# Service (default)
vault token create -policy=default -ttl=1h

# Batch (not stored, not renewable, not revocable)
vault token create -type=batch -policy=default -ttl=60s

# Orphan (no parent, survives parent revocation)
vault token create -orphan -policy=default -ttl=72h

# Periodic (auto-renews forever)
vault token create -period=24h -policy=default

Drill 2 — Token Lookup & Renewal (1 minute): Look up, check TTL, renew, verify TTL extended.

vault token create -policy=default -ttl=1h  # Note the token
vault token lookup                    # Check properties
vault token renew                     # Extend TTL
vault token lookup  | grep ttl        # Verify extended
vault token revoke                    # Clean up

Drill 3 — Parent-Child Hierarchy (2 minutes): Create parent, create children, revoke parent, verify orphans survive.

# Create parent token
vault token create -policy=default -ttl=4h  # Note: PARENT_TOKEN
VAULT_TOKEN=

# Create child (inherits from parent)
vault token create -policy=default -ttl=1h  # Note: CHILD_TOKEN

# Create orphan (no parent link)
vault token create -orphan -policy=default -ttl=72h  # Note: ORPHAN_TOKEN

# Revoke parent → child destroyed, orphan survives!
vault token revoke 
vault token lookup    # → ERROR (revoked)
vault token lookup    # → Works! (survives)

Drill 4 — Response Wrapping Flow (2 minutes): Wrap a secret, unwrap it, verify single-use.

# Create a test secret and wrap it
vault write -wrap-ttl=120s secret/data/test db_user=anihpj db_pass=s3cr3t
# Note: wrapping_token: w.xxxxx

# Unwrap to get the secret
VAULT_TOKEN=w.xxxxx vault unwrap
# Returns: { data: { db_user: "anihpj", db_pass: "s3cr3t" } }

# Try unwrapping again → FAILS (single-use consumed)
VAULT_TOKEN=w.xxxxx vault unwrap
# ERROR: wrapping token is not valid or does not exist

Drill 5 — Token Accessor Management (1 minute): Create token, manage via accessor only, verify accessor can't read secrets.

# Create token and capture accessor
vault token create -policy=default -ttl=1h
# token_accessor: 7hS9kW2mX5vB8...  ← Note this

# Manage using ONLY the accessor
vault token lookup -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8...  # ✅ Works
vault token renew -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8...    # ✅ Works
vault token revoke -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8...   # ✅ Works

# Try to read secrets with accessor → FAILS
vault kv get -accessor 7hS9kW2mX5vB8... secret/test
# ERROR: Accessor is for management only!

🟡 Part 5: Policies — Controlling Access

Chapter 12: Vault Policies — The ACL System 🎯🎯🎯

Tokens (Part 4) get you in the door. Policies determine which rooms you can enter. This is the most important concept in Vault — it's 28% of the exam, merged with tokens. A policy is an ACL (Access Control List) written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) or JSON. It answers one question: "Should THIS caller be allowed to do THIS operation on THIS path?" Default rule: DENY ALL. If a policy doesn't explicitly allow it, it's denied.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 VA 28% Domain 🏗️ anihpj Lab

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What Vault policies are and how the DENY ALL default works
  • ✅ Master policy syntax — path patterns, wildcards (*, **, +), and capabilities
  • ✅ Understand the UNION model: multiple policies combine, most permissive wins
  • ✅ Write production-grade policies for anihpj/jobpost
  • ✅ Manage policies: write, read, list, delete, format
  • ✅ Test policies before deploying to production
🎓 VAULT ASSOCIATE RELEVANCE
Domain 1: Token & Policies 28% Domain 2: Secrets Engines 25%

12.1 What Are Policies? — The Foundation of Vault Access Control

At its core, a Vault policy is a document that says: "WHO can do WHAT on WHICH path." Every token in Vault has one or more policies attached. When a request arrives, Vault checks ALL policies attached to the token. If ANY policy allows the operation, it's granted. If NONE allow it, it's denied. This is the UNION model — most permissive wins.

HOW POLICIES WORK — The Decision Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🎫 HOW VAULT POLICIES WORK — Complete Flow           │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 1: User/App authenticates                                    │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  TOKEN: s.A1b2C3d4E5f6...                                   │  │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │ Attached Policies: [app-policy, db-read, default]     │  │  │
│  │  │ Identity: Entity → alice → Groups → [engineers]       │  │  │
│  │  │ Group Policies: [eng-policy]                          │  │  │
│  │  │ ────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │  │  │
│  │  │ EFFECTIVE POLICIES (UNION):                            │  │  │
│  │  │ [app-policy + db-read + default + eng-policy]          │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  STEP 2: App tries: vault read anihpj/data/database                │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  POLICY CHECK — Vault iterates ALL policies                  │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  │  CHECK 1: app-policy                                          │  │
│  │    path "anihpj/data/*" {                                     │  │
│  │      capabilities = ["read"]                                  │  │
│  │    }                                                          │  │
│  │    → Path "anihpj/data/database" matches anihpj/data/*       │  │
│  │    → "read" capability IS granted                             │  │
│  │    → ✅ ACCESS GRANTED (stop checking)                        │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  │  If NO policy matched: → ❌ PERMISSION DENIED                 │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 KEY: Vault checks until ONE policy says YES.                   │
│     If NO policy says YES → DENY. Default = DENY ALL.            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 The Golden Rule of Vault Policies

DENY ALL by default. When Vault starts, nothing is accessible — not even listing enabled secrets engines. The default policy (automatically attached to all tokens) provides minimal functionality like token lookup and cubbyhole access. Every other permission must be explicitly granted through policies.

📜 Policy Language: HCL vs JSON

Policies can be written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language — recommended) or JSON. HCL is more human-readable. Vault stores all policies as JSON internally, so HCL is converted on write.

✅ HCL (RECOMMENDED)
HCL
# Human-friendly syntax
path "anihpj/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

path "database/creds/anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
⚠️ JSON (ALSO SUPPORTED)
JSON
{
  "path": {
    "anihpj/data/*": {
      "capabilities": ["read","list"]
    }
  }
}
🎓 EXAM TIP: The Default Policy

The default policy is attached to EVERY token unless explicitly excluded with token_no_default_policy=true. It grants basic permissions: token lookup, token renew, cubbyhole access, and listing auth methods. The exam may ask: "Which policy allows a token to look up its own properties?" — Answer: default.

⚡ SPEED TIP: The Fastest Way to Write a Policy

During the exam (and in daily work), use heredoc syntax to write policies in ONE command — no editor, no file cleanup:

vault policy write app-policy - <<EOF
  path "secret/data/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF

This saves 30-60 seconds per policy compared to: vim → type → save → vault policy write → rm file. With 5-10 policies in the exam, that's 5-10 minutes saved! Practice this pattern until it's muscle memory.

12.2 Policy Syntax — HCL Reference 🎯🎯

Every policy rule has three components: a path (which API endpoint), capabilities (which operations), and optional parameters (fine-grained restrictions).

📋 Path Wildcard Patterns — Every Variation Explained

PatternMatchesDoes NOT MatchUse Case
secret/*secret/anihpj, secret/dbsecret/a/b, secret/x/y/zOne level deep
secret/**secret/anihpj, secret/a/b/c/d(matches ALL depths)All nested paths
secret/+/dbsecret/anihpj/db, secret/prod/dbsecret/a/b/db, secret/dbExactly one segment
["secret/data","secret/metadata"]Exactly secret/data, secret/metadatasecret/data/x, secret/metadata/xExact path list (KV v2)
secret/data/+/+secret/data/anihpj/dbsecret/data/anihpjTwo segments deep
WILDCARD VISUAL — See the Difference
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   WILDCARD PATTERNS VISUALIZED                     │
│                                                                    │
│  VAULT PATH TREE:                                                  │
│  secret/                                                           │
│  ├── data/                                                         │
│  │   ├── anihpj/        ← secret/data/*     (matches this)        │
│  │   │   ├── database   ← secret/data/**    (matches this too)    │
│  │   │   └── api        ← secret/data/+/+  (does NOT match this)  │
│  │   └── jobpost/                                                    │
│  │       └── config                                                  │
│  └── metadata/                                                       │
│      └── anihpj/                                                     │
│                                                                    │
│  COMPARISON:                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ PATTERN      │ WHAT IT COVERS UNDER secret/                  │  │
│  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│  │ secret/*     │ Only direct children (data/, metadata/)       │  │
│  │ secret/**    │ EVERYTHING — all depths                       │  │
│  │ secret/+/db  │ data/db, metadata/db — exactly 1 level then db│  │
│  └──────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 Capabilities — The CRUD Mapping

CapabilityHTTP VerbCLI EquivalentWhat It Allows
createPOST / PUTvault writeCreate new resources at this path
readGETvault readRead data from this path
updatePUT / PATCHvault writeModify existing resources
deleteDELETEvault deleteRemove resources at this path
listLISTvault listEnumerate resources
sudo——Access root-protected paths
deny——Explicitly block (overrides everything)

⚠️ EXAM GOTCHA — The "deny" Capability

deny is the only capability that overrides all others. Even if 5 policies say "read" and 1 policy says "deny" — the deny wins. This is the exception to the UNION model. Use deny sparingly — it can lock you out of Vault entirely if applied to critical paths like sys/*.

📝 Required Parameters — Fine-Grained Control

Beyond path + capabilities, policies can restrict operations with required_parameters — the request MUST include these keys/values:

HCL — Parameter Restrictions
# Only allow creating tokens with max 1-hour TTL
path "auth/token/create" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
  required_parameters = ["policies"]
  # Reject tokens with TTL > 1h
}

# Only allow listing specific key prefix
path "secret/metadata/anihpj/*" {
  capabilities = ["list"]
  # The listing starts at this prefix
}

12.3 Capabilities Deep Dive — Policy Management Commands

📋 Policy CRUD — Complete Command Reference

Bash — Policy Management Commands
# CREATE / UPDATE a policy (from file)
vault policy write anihpj-app anihpj-app-policy.hcl

# CREATE / UPDATE a policy (inline via heredoc)
vault policy write anihpj-app - <<EOF
path "anihpj/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
EOF

# READ a policy (view its content)
vault policy read anihpj-app
# path "anihpj/data/*" {
#   capabilities = ["read", "list"]
# }

# LIST all policies
vault policy list
# anihpj-app
# anihpj-admin
# default
# root

# DELETE a policy (IRREVERSIBLE — affects all tokens with this policy!)
vault policy delete anihpj-app

# FORMAT policy as JSON
vault policy read -format=json anihpj-app

🔍 Testing Policies — Check Token Capabilities

Before assigning a policy to a real application, always test it. Vault provides tools to verify what a token can do:

Bash — Testing Policies
# Create a test token with the policy
vault token create -policy=anihpj-app -ttl=10m
# Key                  Value
# ---                  -----
# token                s.A1b2C3d4E5f6G7h8
# token_policies       ["anihpj-app","default"]

# Check what a token can do on a specific path
export TEST_TOKEN=s.A1b2C3d4E5f6G7h8
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/database
# read, list

# Check multiple paths at once
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN \
    anihpj/data/database \
    sys/auth \
    secret/data/anihpj
# anihpj/data/database: read, list
# sys/auth: deny
# secret/data/anihpj: deny

# Revoke test token when done
vault token revoke $TEST_TOKEN

✅ Policy Testing Checklist

  • ✅ Create a test token with vault token create -policy=<name>
  • ✅ Check capabilities with vault token capabilities <token> <path>
  • ✅ Actually RUN the command with the test token
  • ✅ Verify DENIED operations are indeed denied
  • ✅ Test edge cases: deep paths, parent paths, sibling paths
  • ✅ Revoke the test token after testing

12.4 Writing Policies for anihpj/jobpost 🎯🏗️

Here is the complete least-privilege policy set for the anihpj/jobpost project. Each role gets EXACTLY the permissions it needs — nothing more.

ANIHJP POLICY ARCHITECTURE — Least Privilege Design
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           🔐 ANIHJP/JOBPOST — COMPLETE POLICY ARCHITECTURE        │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ROLE: Django Application Pods                               │  │
│  │  POLICY: anihpj-app-policy                                   │  │
│  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                       │  │
│  │  path "anihpj/data/database"      → [read]                   │  │
│  │  path "anihpj/data/api"           → [read]                   │  │
│  │  path "database/creds/anihpj-role"→ [read]  (dynamic creds)  │  │
│  │  path "transit/encrypt/anihpj-key"→ [create,update]          │  │
│  │  path "transit/decrypt/anihpj-key"→ [create,update]          │  │

│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ROLE: DevOps / SRE Team                                     │  │
│  │  POLICY: anihpj-admin-policy                                 │  │
│  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                       │  │
│  │  path "anihpj/*"                   → [create,read,update,    │  │
│  │                                       delete,list]           │  │
│  │  path "database/roles/anihpj-role"  → [create,read,update,   │  │
│  │                                       delete]                │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ROLE: Monitoring / Dashboard (read-only)                    │  │
│  │  POLICY: anihpj-ro-policy                                    │  │
│  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                       │  │
│  │  path "anihpj/data/*"              → [read, list]            │  │
│  │  path "sys/health"                 → [read]                  │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
