│     via the auth method role (K8s role, AppRole role, etc.)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
anihpj-app-policy.hcl
# ─── anihpj-app-policy.hcl ───
# For: Django application pods (anihpj + jobpost)
# Principle: LEAST PRIVILEGE — only what the app needs

# Read static KV secrets (database config, API keys)
path "anihpj/data/database" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "anihpj/data/api" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Generate dynamic database credentials
path "database/creds/anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Encrypt sensitive data with Transit engine
path "transit/encrypt/anihpj-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}

# Decrypt data with Transit engine
path "transit/decrypt/anihpj-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}
anihpj-admin-policy.hcl
# ─── anihpj-admin-policy.hcl ───
# For: DevOps / SRE team
# Full management of anihpj secrets + DB role configuration

# Full control over all anihpj secrets
path "anihpj/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

# Manage database roles (create, modify, delete DB roles)
path "database/roles/anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete"]
}

# View audit logs
path "sys/audit" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
Bash — Apply & Test Policies
# Write policies to Vault
vault policy write anihpj-app anihpj-app-policy.hcl
vault policy write anihpj-admin anihpj-admin-policy.hcl
vault policy write anihpj-ro anihpj-readonly-policy.hcl

# Verify policies exist
vault policy list
# anihpj-admin
# anihpj-app
# anihpj-ro
# default
# root

# Test anihpj-app policy
vault token create -policy=anihpj-app -ttl=10m
export TEST_TOKEN=s.xxxxxxxxxx

# These SHOULD work (allowed by policy)
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/database
# → read

# These SHOULD fail (not in policy)
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/database
# For delete: → deny
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN sys/auth
# → deny

# Clean up
vault token revoke $TEST_TOKEN
💡 The "Secrets Are Not Code" Principle

Notice that nowhere in the application code are database passwords, API keys, or encryption keys. The app only knows where to find secrets (Vault paths), not the secrets themselves. Policies ensure the app can only read what it needs — even if the app is compromised, the attacker can't access other secrets or modify Vault configuration.

⏱️ 5 minutes
Scenario: Your First Policy — Write & Test

You're the DevOps engineer for anihpj. The development team needs a new microservice called jobpost-worker that needs to:

  1. Read database credentials from anihpj/data/jobpost-worker
  2. Generate dynamic PostgreSQL credentials from database/creds/jobpost-worker-role
  3. Read the anihpj API key from anihpj/data/api
  4. NOT be able to modify or delete anything

Your task: Write the policy, test it, and verify permissions.

💡 Hint: Start with vault policy write using heredoc. Use vault token capabilities to verify. Remember — least privilege means ONLY "read" for KV paths.
▼ Solution (Click to Reveal)
Step 1: Write the Policy
vault policy write jobpost-worker - <<EOF
# Policy for jobpost-worker microservice
# Least privilege: read-only access to specific paths

path "anihpj/data/jobpost-worker" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "anihpj/data/api" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "database/creds/jobpost-worker-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF
Step 2: Test the Policy
# Create a test token
vault token create -policy=jobpost-worker -ttl=10m
export TEST_TOKEN=s.xxxxxxxxxx

# Verify capabilities (should ALL show "read")
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/jobpost-worker
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/api
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN database/creds/jobpost-worker-role

# Verify DENIED operations
vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN anihpj/data/database
# → deny (not in policy!)

vault token capabilities $TEST_TOKEN sys/auth
# → deny (definitely not allowed!)

# Clean up
vault token revoke $TEST_TOKEN
Step 3: Attach to a Real Role
# If using Kubernetes auth:
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/jobpost-worker \
    bound_service_account_names=jobpost-worker-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    policies=jobpost-worker \
    ttl=1h

# If using AppRole:
vault write auth/approle/role/jobpost-worker \
    secret_id_ttl=10m \
    token_policies=jobpost-worker \
    token_ttl=1h

12.5 Policy Management — Complete Operational Guide

🔍 Inspecting Policies

Bash — Policy Inspection Commands
# Read a policy's full HCL content
vault policy read anihpj-app

# Read in JSON format
vault policy read -format=json anihpj-app

# List all policies in the system
vault policy list

# Check which policies a specific token has
vault token lookup <token> | grep policies
# token_policies: [anihpj-app default]

# Check which entities/groups reference a policy
# (requires identity lookup)
vault list identity/entity/name
vault read identity/entity/name/<entity>
⚠️ WARNING: Deleting a Policy is Immediate and Global

When you delete a policy, it affects ALL tokens that have that policy — immediately on their next renewal. Existing tokens keep their current permissions until their TTL expires or they're renewed. Always test the impact before deleting a production policy.

📊 Policy Audit — Who Uses What

Bash — Policy Audit Script
#!/bin/bash
# Audit: which policies are attached to which auth roles?

echo "=== Kubernetes Auth Roles ==="
vault list auth/kubernetes/role
for role in $(vault list -format=json auth/kubernetes/role | jq -r '.[]'); do
    echo "Role: $role"
    vault read -field=token_policies auth/kubernetes/role/$role
done

echo "=== AppRole Auth Roles ==="
vault list auth/approle/role
for role in $(vault list -format=json auth/approle/role | jq -r '.[]'); do
    echo "Role: $role"
    vault read -field=token_policies auth/approle/role/$role
done

echo "=== Identity Groups ==="
vault list identity/group/name
for group in $(vault list -format=json identity/group/name | jq -r '.[]'); do
    echo "Group: $group"
    vault read -field=policies identity/group/name/$group
done

🔬 Deep Dive: Understanding Vault Policies to the Core

This section takes you beyond the syntax — into the internal mechanics of how Vault evaluates policies. Understanding these internals is what separates a passing score from a perfect score on the 28% of exam questions related to policies and tokens.

🧠 The Policy Evaluation Engine — How Vault Decides "Allow" or "Deny"

Policy Evaluation Algorithm — Step by Step
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           VAULT POLICY EVALUATION — INTERNAL ALGORITHM           │
│                                                                   │
│  INPUT: Token + Requested Path + Requested Operation              │
│                                                                   │
│  STEP 1: COLLECT ALL POLICIES                                     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ • Token policies (directly attached)                        │  │
│  │ • Identity entity policies (via entity)                     │  │
│  │ • Identity group policies (via group membership)            │  │
│  │ • All policies are flattened into ONE list                  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 2: FIND MATCHING PATHS                                      │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ For EACH policy, check:                                     │  │
│  │   "Does any path pattern MATCH the requested path?"         │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │ Requested: secret/data/anihpj/db                            │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ Policy A: path "secret/data/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } │  │
│  │   → MATCHES (anihpj/db matches *)                           │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ Policy B: path "secret/data/anihpj/*" { caps = ["list"] }  │  │
│  │   → DOES NOT MATCH (db doesn't match * for this level)      │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ Policy C: path "secret/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }       │  │
│  │   → MATCHES data/anihpj/db                                  │  │
│  │   → BUT * only spans ONE level — anihpj/db is below data/   │  │
│  │   → ACTUALLY: secret/* matches secret/data but NOT          │  │
│  │     secret/data/anihpj because * doesn't span slashes!       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 3: COLLECT CAPABILITIES (UNION — Most Permissive Wins!)     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ From ALL matching path rules across ALL policies:           │  │
│  │   Policy A: ["read"]                                        │  │
│  │   Policy D: ["read", "list"]                                │  │
│  │   → UNION = ["read", "list"]                                │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │ ⚠️ EXCEPTION: If ANY policy has "deny" → IMMEDIATE DENY    │  │
│  │   "deny" is the KING — it overrides everything.            │  │
│  │   Even if 99 policies say "allow", 1 "deny" = DENIED.      │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 4: CHECK REQUESTED OPERATION                                │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Requested: "read" on secret/data/anihpj/db                  │  │
│  │ Collected capabilities: ["read", "list"]                    │  │
│  │ → "read" IS in the set → ALLOW                             │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │ Requested: "delete" on secret/data/anihpj/db                │  │
│  │ Collected capabilities: ["read", "list"]                    │  │
│  │ → "delete" NOT in the set → DENY                           │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 5: CHECK PARAMETERS (Optional)                               │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ If the path rule has required_parameters or                 │  │
│  │ allowed_parameters, check those too.                        │  │
│  │ Example:                                                    │  │
│  │   path "secret/data/*" {                                    │  │
│  │     capabilities = ["read"]                                 │  │
│  │     required_parameters = ["version"]                       │  │
│  │   }                                                         │  │
│  │   → Must specify ?version=X in the URL or it's DENIED       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                   │
│  RESULT: ALLOW (operation permitted) or DENY (403 Forbidden)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔍 Wildcard Matching — The #1 Exam Trap

Wildcards in Vault policies follow glob-style matching, but with specific rules that are heavily tested:

* (Single-Level Wildcard)

* matches any characters within a single path segment (between slashes).

path "secret/data/*" { ... }
Matches: secret/data/app     ✅
Matches: secret/data/db      ✅
NOT:     secret/data/app/db  ❌  (crosses /)

Exam Trap: path "secret/*" does NOT match secret/data/app because * doesn't span slashes! You need path "secret/data/*" for KV v2 secrets.

+ (Single-Segment Required)

+ matches exactly one non-empty path segment.

path "secret/data/+/db" { ... }
Matches: secret/data/app/db    ✅
Matches: secret/data/prod/db   ✅
NOT:     secret/data/db        ❌  (missing segment)
NOT:     secret/data/app/x/db  ❌  (extra segment)

Use case: Match any app name but only the "db" sub-path: secret/data/+/db matches app1/db, app2/db, etc.

** (Recursive Wildcard)

** matches everything including slashes — any number of path segments.

path "secret/data/**" { ... }
Matches: secret/data/app           ✅
Matches: secret/data/app/db        ✅
Matches: secret/data/a/b/c/d/e     ✅
Matches: secret/data/              ⚠️ (depends on Vault version)
KV v2 Policy — The Critical Pattern

KV v2 has TWO path types that need separate policy rules:

# Data path (the actual secrets)
path "secret/data/anihpj/*" {
  capabilities = ["create","read","update","delete"]
}

# Metadata path (version info, listing)
path "secret/metadata/anihpj/*" {
  capabilities = ["list","read"]
}

# ⚠️ Without the metadata rule, listing fails!
# ⚠️ Without /data/ in the path, reading fails!

📊 Capability Resolution — The Full Matrix

When multiple policies attach to the same token, Vault combines them using the UNION model — the most permissive combination wins. EXCEPT for deny, which always overrides.

Policy APolicy BEffectiveReason
["read"]["list"]["read","list"]UNION of both
["read"]["read","write"]["read","write"]UNION (write added)
["read"]["deny"]DENIEDdeny ALWAYS wins
["read","write"]["deny"]DENIEDEven though write exists, deny overrides
["create","read"]["update","delete"]["create","read","update","delete"]Full CRUD via UNION
["sudo"]["read"]["sudo","read"]sudo + any other = allowed
No matchNo matchDENIEDDefault: DENY ALL
⚠️ CRITICAL GOTCHA: "list" ≠ "read"

The list capability lets you enumerate keys (vault kv list secret/) but does NOT let you read the values. Conversely, read lets you get values but does NOT let you list. You often need BOTH in policies. This is one of the most common exam traps.

🔄 Policy Inheritance and Precedence

When a token authenticates, policies come from multiple sources. Vault merges them ALL — there's no "order" and no "first match wins." Here's the complete inheritance chain:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              POLICY INHERITANCE CHAIN                        │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
│  │ 1. Token Policies     │ ← Directly on the token           │
│  │    (token_policies)   │    vault token create -policy=X   │
│  └──────────┬───────────┘                                    │
│             │  UNION (combine all)                           │
│  ┌──────────▼───────────┐                                    │
│  │ 2. Identity Policies  │ ← From entity attached to token   │
│  │    (entity.policies)  │    vault write identity/entity    │
│  └──────────┬───────────┘      policies=A,B                 │
│             │  UNION                                         │
│  ┌──────────▼───────────┐                                    │
│  │ 3. Group Policies     │ ← Groups the entity belongs to    │
│  │    (group.policies)   │    vault write identity/group     │
│  └──────────┬───────────┘      member_entity_ids=...         │
│             │  UNION                                         │
│  ┌──────────▼───────────┐                                    │
│  │ 4. Internal Policies  │ ← Vault-internal (no user access) │
│  │    (e.g., cubbyhole)  │                                    │
│  └──────────┬───────────┘                                    │
│             │                                                │
│             ▼                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐                                    │
│  │  FINAL EFFECTIVE      │                                    │
│  │  PERMISSION SET       │ ← ALL of the above, UNIONed       │
│  │  (UNION model)        │                                    │
│  │  EXCEPT: deny in ANY  │                                    │
│  │  policy = DENY ALL    │                                    │
│  └──────────────────────┘                                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 How to Think About Policy Evaluation

Don't think "which policy wins." Think: "Does ANY policy allow this operation on this path, and does NO policy deny it?" Vault checks every policy simultaneously and takes the most permissive result, except that deny acts as an immediate veto. This is fundamentally different from firewall rules or IAM policies that use "first match wins" or "explicit deny overrides implicit allow." In Vault, the default is DENY ALL, and you build up permissions through additive UNION across all policies.

📊 Chapter 12 — Recap

📜Policy = ACLPath + capabilities + optional parameters
🚫Default = DENY ALLExplicit allow only — nothing granted by default
🔗UNION ModelMultiple policies combine — most permissive wins
🗂️Wildcards* (one level), ** (all levels), + (one segment)
🔑7 Capabilitiescreate/read/update/delete/list/sudo/deny
⚠️deny = KINGOnly capability that overrides all others

⚡ Policy Management — Command Quick Reference Card

TaskCommandExam Notes
Write policyvault policy write <name> <file>Use - + heredoc for speed
Read policyvault policy read <name>Shows HCL; -format=json for JSON
List policiesvault policy listNames only; need root or sudo
Delete policyvault policy delete <name>⚠️ Immediate! Affects next token renewal
Test capabilitiesvault token capabilities <token> <path>READ-ONLY — always safe to run
Create test tokenvault token create -policy=<name> -ttl=10mAlways test before deploying to roles
Check token policiesvault token lookup <token>Shows token_policies, entity_id, TTL
Force renewalvault token renew <token>Re-evaluates policies on renewal

📝 Chapter 12 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q111
What is the default access model in Vault, and what policy is automatically attached to all tokens?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Vault's default access model is DENY ALL — if no policy explicitly grants access, the operation is denied. The default policy is automatically attached to every token (unless token_no_default_policy=true). It grants basic permissions: token lookup, token renew, cubbyhole operations, and listing auth methods.

EXPLANATION

This is the foundation of Vault's security model. Unlike systems where a default "user" role grants broad access, Vault starts locked and you explicitly open doors. The default policy provides just enough permissions for a token to be usable (self-inspection, renewal) without granting access to any secrets.

Q112
How do multiple policies combine on a single token?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Multiple policies combine as a UNION — the most permissive capability wins. If Policy A grants "read" and Policy B grants "create, read, update", the effective capability is "create, read, update". The only exception is the deny capability, which overrides all others — if ANY policy says deny, access is denied regardless of what other policies allow.

EXPLANATION

Think of it as: Vault checks ALL policies. If ANY says "yes" (and none say "deny"), it's allowed. The check is optimistic — find one policy that grants it, and you're in. This is why careful policy design is crucial: a permissive policy attached accidentally can grant unintended access.

Q113
What does each wildcard pattern match? secret/* vs secret/** vs secret/+/db
Show Answer
ANSWER

secret/*: Matches exactly ONE level — secret/anihpj, secret/db. Does NOT match secret/a/b.
secret/**: Matches ALL levels — secret/anihpj, secret/a/b/c/d/e.
secret/+/db: Matches exactly ONE segment between secret/ and /db — secret/anihpj/db, secret/prod/db. Does NOT match secret/a/b/db (2 segments) or secret/db (0 segments).

EXPLANATION

These wildcards are critical for the exam. * = "any characters in this one path segment." ** = "this and everything below." + = "exactly one path segment." A common exam trap: using secret/* expecting it to cover secret/data/anihpj — it doesn't! Use secret/** or secret/+/anihpj instead.

Q114
Write a policy that allows a Django app to read database config, generate dynamic DB credentials, and encrypt/decrypt data — nothing more.
Show Answer
ANSWER
HCL
path "anihpj/data/database" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "database/creds/anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "transit/encrypt/anihpj-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}

path "transit/decrypt/anihpj-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}
EXPLANATION

This policy grants exactly 4 permissions — nothing more. The app can read its own KV secrets, generate database credentials (dynamic), and use the Transit engine for encryption. It cannot list secrets, delete anything, or access other apps' data. This is the principle of least privilege in action.

Q115
What command tests whether a token can perform an operation on a specific path?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault token capabilities <token> <path> — it outputs which capabilities (if any) the token has on that path. You can test multiple paths at once by listing them after the token. This is the safest way to verify policies before deploying to production — no actual Vault operations are performed.

EXPLANATION
vault token capabilities s.A1b2C3d4 anihpj/data/database sys/auth
# anihpj/data/database: read, list
# sys/auth: deny

This is read-only — it does not modify anything in Vault. Always test your policies with this command before assigning them to real workloads.

Q116
What happens when you delete a policy that is being used by active tokens?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The policy is immediately removed from Vault. Existing tokens keep their current permissions until their next renewal (or until their TTL expires, whichever comes first). At renewal, Vault re-evaluates policies — the deleted policy is no longer attached, so those permissions are lost. New tokens created after the deletion will NOT have the policy.

EXPLANATION

This is a critical operational detail: deleting a policy does NOT immediately revoke access for existing tokens. If you need immediate revocation, you must also revoke the affected tokens with vault token revoke <token>. This is why token lifecycle management (Part 4) and policy management go hand-in-hand.

Q117
How do you write a Vault policy inline (without a file)?
Show Answer
ANSWER
vault policy write my-policy - <<EOF
path "secret/data/myapp/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
EOF

The - tells Vault to read from stdin. The heredoc (<<EOF ... EOF) provides the policy content. This is the FASTEST way to write policies during the exam — no need to create files!

EXPLANATION

This saves precious seconds on the exam. Instead of: vim policy.hcl → type content → vault policy write name policy.hcl → rm policy.hcl, you can do it in one command. Practice this pattern until it's muscle memory.

Q118
What is the difference between create and update capabilities?
Show Answer
ANSWER

create: Allows creating NEW resources at a path. Typically maps to HTTP POST.
update: Allows modifying EXISTING resources at a path. Typically maps to HTTP PUT/PATCH.
In practice, the Vault CLI's vault write command may require both capabilities depending on the operation — creating a new secret requires "create", while overwriting an existing one requires "update". Many policies grant both: capabilities = ["create", "update"].

EXPLANATION

For the exam: if you want to allow vault write (which can both create and overwrite), grant both create and update. If you only want to allow reading without modification, grant only read. The distinction matters more in API usage than CLI usage.

Q119
Design a complete policy set for a three-tier application: app-pods (need DB + API keys), CI/CD pipeline (needs to write secrets), and monitoring (read-only).
Show Answer
ANSWER
HCL — Three Policies
# Policy 1: app-pods (least privilege)
path "anihpj/data/database" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
path "database/creds/anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Policy 2: cicd-pipeline (write secrets only)
path "anihpj/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update"]
}

# Policy 3: monitoring-ro (read-only everything)
path "anihpj/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
path "sys/health" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EXPLANATION

Notice the separation: app-pods can only READ their specific paths — they can't list or modify. CI/CD can write secrets but can't delete them. Monitoring can read and list but can't change anything. No policy has unnecessary permissions. Attach these policies to different K8s auth roles or AppRole roles.

Q120
How do you list all Vault policies and read a specific policy's content?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# List all policies
vault policy list
# anihpj-app
# default
# root

# Read a specific policy
vault policy read anihpj-app

# Read as JSON
vault policy read -format=json anihpj-app
EXPLANATION

vault policy list shows policy names only. vault policy read <name> shows the full HCL content. You need the "read" capability on sys/policies/acl/<name> to read a policy — the root token and tokens with "sudo" on sys/policies/* can read any policy.

🏋️ Ch 12 Lab — Policy Writing Mastery (12 min)
⏱️ Target: 12 min | 🎯 Goal: Write 3 policies from scratch, test with token capabilities
# 1. Write a read-only KV policy (least privilege!)
vault policy write read-only-kv - <<EOF
path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
path "secret/metadata/app/*" { capabilities = ["list"] }
EOF

# 2. Write a DB+KV policy (application access)
vault policy write app-access - <<EOF
path "secret/data/app/*" { capabilities = ["read","list"] }
path "database/creds/app-role" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF

# 3. Test: create token and verify capabilities
TOKEN=$(vault token create -policy=app-access -field=token)
vault token capabilities $TOKEN secret/data/app/config
# Output: ["read","list"]
vault token capabilities $TOKEN database/creds/app-role
# Output: ["read"]
vault token capabilities $TOKEN sys/mounts
# Output: ["deny"] (not in policy!)

# 4. Test the deny capability
vault policy write deny-secrets - <<EOF
path "secret/*" { capabilities = ["deny"] }
EOF
# Attach BOTH app-access + deny-secrets to token → secret access DENIED!

Drill Check: Does * span slashes? (NO — secret/* matches secret/app but NOT secret/data/app). What beats allow? (deny overrides everything).

13.1 Fine-Grained Parameter Control — Restricting HOW, Not Just WHERE

Basic policies control which paths can be accessed. Fine-grained control goes further: it restricts what parameters can be used in the request. For example, you might allow token creation but only with specific policies and a maximum TTL of 1 hour.

🎯 Why This Matters — The Privilege Escalation Problem

Imagine you grant a junior admin the ability to create tokens via auth/token/create. Without parameter control, they can create a token with root policy and 768-hour TTL — effectively becoming a root user for 32 days. Fine-grained control prevents this by locking down: which policies the created token can have, maximum TTL, allowed CIDR ranges, and whether the token can be orphan. This is the difference between delegation and abdication.

HCL — Parameter Control Examples
# Example 1: Restrict token creation
# Allow creating tokens, but ONLY with specific policies and max TTL
path "auth/token/create" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
  # Token MUST have these policies (no arbitrary policies)
}

# Example 2: Restrict KV write to specific keys
path "anihpj/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
  # Only allow writing specific keys
}

# Example 3: Restrict DB role creation
path "database/roles/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
  # DB roles must have TTL between 1h and 24h
}

# Example 4: Restrict AppRole SecretID generation
path "auth/approle/role/anihpj-app/secret-id" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
  # SecretID must have CIDR binding
  # SecretID must have max 10m TTL
}
📖 What Fine-Grained Control Gives You

Without parameter control: "You can create tokens" → user creates a token with root policy and 768h TTL. With parameter control: "You can create tokens with ONLY these 3 policies, and max 1h TTL" → user cannot escalate privileges. This is the difference between ACL and true authorization.

🎓 EXAM TIP

The exam may ask: "How do you prevent a user from creating tokens with arbitrary policies?" The answer is fine-grained parameter control — restricting the policies parameter at auth/token/create or using AppRole roles with token_policies instead of letting users choose policies at token creation time.

13.2 Templated Policies — Dynamic Access with {{...}} 🎯

Imagine you have 50 teams, each needing access to their own secrets at secret/data/teams/team-name/*. Without templates, you'd need 50 separate policies — a maintenance nightmare. With templated policies, you write ONE policy that dynamically resolves the team name from the entity's metadata.

📊 The Math — Why Templates Are Inevitable at Scale

A company with 50 teams, 2 environments each (dev/prod), and 3 types of access per team (app, admin, readonly):
Without templates: 50 × 2 × 3 = 300 policies to write, version, review, and audit.
With templates: 3 policies (app, admin, readonly) — the environment and team name come from entity metadata at runtime.
Adding a 51st team? Without templates: 6 new policies. With templates: create one entity, add to group — done. This isn't just convenience — it's the only way to maintain security consistency at scale. When 300 policies diverge over time, security gaps are inevitable.

TEMPLATED POLICIES — One Policy, 50 Teams
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           📝 TEMPLATED POLICIES — Dynamic Path Resolution          │
│                                                                    │
│  WITHOUT TEMPLATES:                                                │
│  ──────────────────                                                │
│  Team Alpha policy: path "secret/data/teams/alpha/*" {...}        │
│  Team Beta  policy: path "secret/data/teams/beta/*"  {...}        │
│  Team Gamma policy: path "secret/data/teams/gamma/*" {...}        │
│  ... × 50 policies → maintenance hell                             │
│                                                                    │
│  WITH TEMPLATES:                                                   │
│  ───────────────                                                   │
│  ONE policy for ALL teams:                                         │
│                                                                    │
│  path "secret/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" {            │
│    capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "list"]            │
│  }                                                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  HOW IT RESOLVES AT RUNTIME:                                       │
│  ─────────────────────────────                                     │
│  Entity "team-alpha" requests:                                     │
│    secret/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/db                  │
│                    ↓ RESOLVES TO                                   │
│    secret/data/teams/team-alpha/db  ✅ ALLOWED                     │
│                                                                    │
│  Entity "team-alpha" tries to access team-beta's data:            │
│    secret/data/teams/team-beta/db  ← HARDCODED path, no template!  │
│                    ↓                                               │
│    NOT covered by templated path → DENIED ✅                        │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 EACH TEAM ONLY SEES THEIR OWN DATA — one policy, automatic     │
│     isolation. Entity name becomes the access boundary.            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📋 Available Template Parameters

ParameterResolves ToExample Value
{{identity.entity.id}}Entity's unique IDf5a8b3c2-1d4e-5f6a-7b8c-9d0e1f2a3b4c
{{identity.entity.name}}Entity's human-readable nameteam-alpha
{{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}}Entity metadata value{{identity.entity.metadata.department}} → "engineering"
{{identity.groups.names.<index>}}Group name by index{{identity.groups.names.0}} → "engineers"
{{identity.groups.ids.<index>}}Group ID by index{{identity.groups.ids.0}} → "group_xyz789"
HCL — Templated Policy for Multi-Tenant anihpj
# ─── team-policy.hcl ───
# ONE policy for ALL anihpj teams
# Each team gets their own namespace based on entity name

# Each team can CRUD their own KV secrets
path "anihpj/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

# Each team can generate their own dynamic DB creds
path "database/creds/{{identity.entity.name}}-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Each team can encrypt/decrypt with their own Transit key
path "transit/encrypt/{{identity.entity.name}}-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}

path "transit/decrypt/{{identity.entity.name}}-key" {
  capabilities = ["create", "update"]
}

# READ-ONLY: teams can see their own config, not others'
# The template ensures team-alpha can ONLY read team-alpha/*
Bash — Setup Multi-Tenant Teams
# 1. Write the templated policy ONCE
vault policy write team-policy team-policy.hcl

# 2. Create entities for each team
vault write identity/entity name="team-alpha" \
    metadata=department="engineering"
vault write identity/entity name="team-beta" \
    metadata=department="data-science"
vault write identity/entity name="team-gamma" \
    metadata=department="platform"

# 3. Create ONE group with the templated policy
vault write identity/group name="all-teams" \
    type=internal \
    policies="team-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="<alpha-id>,<beta-id>,<gamma-id>"

# 4. Now team-alpha can access:
#    anihpj/data/teams/team-alpha/* ✅
# But NOT:
#    anihpj/data/teams/team-beta/*   ❌ Denied

# 5. Add a new team — no policy changes needed!
vault write identity/entity name="team-delta"
vault write identity/group name="all-teams" \
    member_entity_ids="...,<delta-id>"
# team-delta IMMEDIATELY gets access to:
#    anihpj/data/teams/team-delta/* ✅
💡 KEY INSIGHT: Scaling Secret Management

Without templates, adding a new team means: creating a new policy, applying it, attaching it to roles/groups, testing it. With templates, adding a new team is ONE command: create the entity and add it to the group. The templated policy automatically resolves the entity name, and isolation is guaranteed by the template itself. This is how enterprises manage thousands of teams with a handful of policies.

⚠️ EXAM GOTCHA — Template Variables Are NOT Magic

Template variables resolve from the ENTITY associated with the token. If a token has NO entity (e.g., tokens created with vault token create without an entity alias), {{identity.entity.name}} resolves to an empty string, and the resulting path may match nothing — effectively denying all access. Always ensure tokens are associated with entities when using templated policies.

13.3 Sentinel Policies — Policy-as-Code Beyond ACL (Enterprise) 🔐

Sentinel is HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework, available in Vault Enterprise. While ACL policies control who can access what, Sentinel controls under what conditions access is granted. Sentinel can enforce rules that ACL alone cannot express — like "no tokens can be created on weekends" or "only allow reading secrets from the production IP range."

✅ ACL Policies (Open Source)

• Path-based: "Can read secret/*"

• Capability-based: "create, read, update, delete, list"

• Parameter restrictions: "token_policies must be X"

• UNION model: most permissive wins

• Syntax: HCL or JSON

⚠️ ACL Limitations (Why Sentinel Exists)

• Cannot check: "Is it Monday-Friday?"

• Cannot check: "Is this IP in the allowed range?"

• Cannot check: "Has the requestor completed 2FA?"

• Cannot check: "Is the secret value a valid JSON?"

• Cannot combine: time + IP + user attributes

Sentinel — Example Policies (Enterprise)
# Example 1: Restrict token creation to business hours
import "time"
main = rule {
    time.now.hour >= 9 and time.now.hour <= 17
}
# → Tokens can only be created between 9 AM and 5 PM

# Example 2: Only allow access from production CIDR
import "sockaddr"
main = rule {
    sockaddr.is_contained(request.connection.remote_addr,
                          "10.244.0.0/16")
}
# → Access only from the Kubernetes pod network

# Example 3: Enforce minimum TTL on tokens
main = rule {
    request.data.token_ttl >= 3600
}
# → Tokens must have at least 1-hour TTL

# Example 4: Prevent creation of root-protected paths
deny_root_path = rule {
    not request.path matches "sys/*"
}
📖 Sentinel for Vault Associate Exam

The Vault Associate exam expects you to know what Sentinel is and when you'd need it, but NOT write Sentinel policies from scratch. Key exam points: (1) Sentinel is Enterprise-only, (2) It provides conditional access control beyond ACL, (3) It can inspect request data, time, IP, and entity metadata, (4) Common use cases: time-based access, IP restrictions, value validation.

13.4 Policy Best Practices — Production-Ready Rules

These best practices come from real production incidents. Each one prevents a specific class of mistake that has caused outages.

🎯
1. Least Privilege FIRST

Start with the absolute minimum permissions. Add capabilities only when the application breaks. It's easier to add than to remove.

📝
2. Descriptive Naming

Name policies for WHAT they do, not WHO uses them. read-anihpj-db not alice-policy. Roles change — the access needed doesn't.

✅
3. ALWAYS Test First

Create a test token with vault token create -policy=<name>. Run vault token capabilities. Actually execute the commands. Only THEN attach to real roles.

📂
4. Version Control

Store policy files in Git alongside application code. Review policy changes in PRs just like code changes. Use vault policy write from CI/CD, never manually.

🚫
5. Avoid "sudo" Capability

sudo grants access to root-protected paths. It should be reserved for Vault administrators. Never attach sudo to application policies.

📊
6. Audit Policy Usage

Regularly review which policies are actually used. Remove orphaned policies. Use vault policy list and cross-reference with auth roles and identity groups.

🔄
7. Use Templates for Scale

When you have >3 teams with similar access patterns, use templated policies. One policy beats 50 nearly-identical copies.

⚠️
8. "deny" is Nuclear

Use deny sparingly — it overrides ALL other policies. A single deny on a critical path can lock you out of Vault.

✅ Policy Deployment Checklist

  • ✅ Policy file is in version control
  • ✅ Policy has been reviewed in a pull request
  • ✅ Test token created and capabilities verified
  • ✅ Actual commands tested with the test token
  • ✅ Negative tests: verify denied operations ARE denied
  • ✅ Policy applied with vault policy write
  • ✅ Auth role/group updated to reference the policy
  • ✅ Test token revoked after testing
  • ✅ Audit log shows expected access pattern

13.5 anihpj Multi-Tenant Policy Design 🏗️

Here's the complete multi-environment policy architecture for anihpj/jobpost — dev, staging, and production — all from one set of templated policies with environment-specific isolation.

│  │  ENVIRONMENT: STAGING                                        │  │
│  │  ─────────────────                                            │  │
│  │  Entity groups: anihpj-staging-team, anihpj-staging-apps     │  │
│  │  Policies:      staging-team (CRUD anihpj/data/staging/*)    │  │
│  │                 staging-app (read anihpj/data/staging/*,     │  │
│  │                              DB creds for staging-db)         │  │
│  │  Paths:          anihpj/data/staging/database                │  │
│  │                  database/creds/staging-anihpj-role          │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ENVIRONMENT: PRODUCTION                                     │  │
│  │  ─────────────────                                            │  │
│  │  Entity groups: anihpj-prod-admin, anihpj-prod-apps          │  │
│  │  Policies:      prod-admin (CRUD anihpj/data/prod/*)         │  │
│  │                 prod-app  (read-ONLY anihpj/data/prod/*,     │  │
│  │                            DB creds for prod-db)              │  │
│  │  NOTE: prod-app can ONLY read — can't write/delete!           │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
│  🔒 ISOLATION GUARANTEE:                                           │
│  ─────────────────────                                             │
│  dev-app CANNOT read staging/* or prod/*                           │
│  staging-app CANNOT read dev/* or prod/*                           │
│  prod-app CANNOT read dev/* or staging/*                           │
│                                                                    │
│  → Each environment's secrets are ISOLATED by path prefix         │
│  → Templated policies make this scalable:                          │
│    path "anihpj/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}/*" {...}     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
HCL — Multi-Environment Templated Policy
# ─── env-app-policy.hcl ───
# ONE policy for ALL environments (dev, staging, prod)
# Environment resolved from entity metadata

# Read static KV secrets for this environment
path "anihpj/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

# Generate dynamic DB credentials for this environment
path "database/creds/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}-anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# PRODUCTION: Applications CANNOT write or delete secrets
# → Only "read" and "list" in the policy above

# ADMIN policy (separate — for DevOps/SRE only):
path "anihpj/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}
Bash — Setup Multi-Environment Entities
# Create entities with environment metadata
vault write identity/entity name="anihpj-dev-app" \
    metadata=env="dev"
vault write identity/entity name="anihpj-staging-app" \
    metadata=env="staging"
vault write identity/entity name="anihpj-prod-app" \
    metadata=env="prod"

# Create groups
vault write identity/group name="anihpj-apps" \
    type=internal \
    policies="env-app-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="<dev-id>,<staging-id>,<prod-id>"

# Now:
# anihpj-dev-app token → can read anihpj/data/dev/* ✅
# anihpj-dev-app token → can read anihpj/data/prod/* ❌
# (template resolves to dev, path prod doesn't match)
#
# PRODUCTION ISOLATION: achieved with ONE policy + entity metadata
✅ Multi-Tenant Design Benefits
  • ✅ 1 policy serves ALL environments — no copy-paste drift
  • ✅ Isolation guaranteed by template resolution — dev can't touch prod
  • ✅ Adding a new environment = create entity with metadata, add to group
  • ✅ Policy changes apply to ALL environments simultaneously
  • ✅ Environment-specific roles (admin vs app) are separate policies
🎓 EXAM TIP: Multi-Tenant Design

The Vault Associate exam expects you to understand how to isolate teams/environments using policies. The three approaches are: (1) Separate policies per environment (simple but doesn't scale), (2) Path-based prefixes (dev/*, staging/*, prod/*), (3) Templated policies with entity metadata (scales to any number of environments). Know when to use each approach.

⏱️ 8 minutes
Scenario: Multi-Tenant Policy from Scratch

You're the platform engineer. The anihpj project has grown from 1 team to 10 teams. Each team needs:

  1. CRUD access to their own KV path: anihpj/data/teams/<team-name>/*
  2. Read access to database credentials: database/creds/<team-name>-role
  3. Each team must be completely isolated from other teams
  4. Adding a new team should require zero policy changes

Your task: Write the templated policy, create entities for 3 teams (alpha, beta, gamma), and verify isolation.

💡 Hint: Use {{identity.entity.name}} in paths. Entity metadata is not needed here — the entity name IS the team name.
▼ Solution (Click to Reveal)
Step 1: Write ONE Templated Policy
vault policy write team-access - <<EOF
# ONE policy for ALL teams
# Team name resolved from entity name at runtime

path "anihpj/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "database/creds/{{identity.entity.name}}-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF
Step 2: Create Entities & Group
# Create entities (one per team)
vault write identity/entity name="team-alpha"
vault write identity/entity name="team-beta"
vault write identity/entity name="team-gamma"

# Get entity IDs
ALPHA_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/team-alpha)
BETA_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/team-beta)
GAMMA_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/team-gamma)

# Create ONE group with the templated policy
vault write identity/group name="all-teams" \
    type=internal \
    policies="team-access" \
    member_entity_ids="$ALPHA_ID,$BETA_ID,$GAMMA_ID"
Step 3: Verify Isolation
# Create test tokens (one per team)
# (In reality, tokens come from auth methods — this is for testing)
ALPHA_TOKEN=$(vault token create -entity-id=$ALPHA_ID -ttl=10m -field=token)
BETA_TOKEN=$(vault token create -entity-id=$BETA_ID -ttl=10m -field=token)

# ALPHA should be able to access alpha's data
VAULT_TOKEN=$ALPHA_TOKEN vault token capabilities $ALPHA_TOKEN \
    anihpj/data/teams/team-alpha/config
# → create, read, update, delete, list ✅

# ALPHA should NOT be able to access beta's data
VAULT_TOKEN=$ALPHA_TOKEN vault token capabilities $ALPHA_TOKEN \
    anihpj/data/teams/team-beta/config
# → deny ✅ (template resolves to team-alpha, path doesn't match)

# BETA should NOT be able to access alpha's DB creds
VAULT_TOKEN=$BETA_TOKEN vault token capabilities $BETA_TOKEN \
    database/creds/team-alpha-role
# → deny ✅

# Clean up
vault token revoke $ALPHA_TOKEN
vault token revoke $BETA_TOKEN

📝 Chapter 13 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q121
What problem do templated policies solve, and what parameter would you use to give each team access to only their own secrets?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Templated policies solve the N×M policy explosion problem — without templates, each team needs its own policy for each path. With templates, ONE policy serves all teams by dynamically resolving identity parameters. Use {{identity.entity.name}} or {{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}} to give each team access to only their own path prefix.

EXPLANATION

Example: path "secret/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" { capabilities = ["read"] } — for entity "team-alpha", this resolves to secret/data/teams/team-alpha/*. Team-alpha can NEVER access team-beta's data because the template resolves team-alpha into the path, and team-beta's path doesn't match.

Q122
What happens when a token without an associated entity uses a templated policy?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Template variables like {{identity.entity.name}} resolve to an empty string. The resulting path likely matches nothing — effectively denying all access. For example, path "secret/data/teams/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" becomes path "secret/data/teams/*", which does NOT match secret/data/teams/team-alpha/db (it requires one more segment). The token gets no access.

EXPLANATION

This is why tokens used with templated policies MUST have an associated entity. Auth methods that support entity aliases (Kubernetes, AppRole with bind_secret_id, LDAP, OIDC) automatically create entity associations. Tokens created with vault token create have NO entity unless explicitly associated via -entity-id.

Q123
What is Sentinel and when would you need it instead of ACL policies?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Sentinel is HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework (Vault Enterprise only). You need Sentinel when ACL policies cannot express the condition — for example: "allow access only during business hours" (time-based), "allow access only from the production IP range" (network-based), "prevent token creation with TTL > 24h" (value validation), or "require multi-factor authentication before reading production secrets." ACL controls WHO can do WHAT on WHICH path. Sentinel controls UNDER WHAT CONDITIONS.

EXPLANATION

Exam-relevant: Sentinel is Enterprise-only. It provides conditional, context-aware access control. ACL = static rules. Sentinel = dynamic rules based on request context (time, IP, data values, entity attributes).

Q124
What are the 8 policy best practices for production?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Least privilege first — start minimal, add as needed. 2. Descriptive naming — name for WHAT (read-anihpj-db), not WHO (alice-policy). 3. Always test with vault token capabilities. 4. Version control policies in Git. 5. Avoid sudo in application policies. 6. Audit policy usage regularly. 7. Use templates when you have >3 teams. 8. deny is nuclear — use sparingly.

EXPLANATION

These aren't just theory — each one prevents a specific production incident. For example, "Always test" prevents the "I deployed a policy and now nothing works" scenario. "Avoid sudo" prevents application tokens from accessing Vault's internal configuration.

Q125
Design a multi-tenant policy that isolates dev, staging, and prod environments using entity metadata.
Show Answer
ANSWER
# ONE templated policy for all environments
path "anihpj/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

path "database/creds/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}-anihpj-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

Entity setup: vault write identity/entity name="app-dev" metadata=env="dev". vault write identity/entity name="app-staging" metadata=env="staging". vault write identity/entity name="app-prod" metadata=env="prod". The template resolves {{identity.entity.metadata.env}} to "dev", "staging", or "prod" — each entity only accesses its own environment.

EXPLANATION

This is the cleanest approach: 1 policy, unlimited environments. Adding a new environment = create entity with metadata, add to group. Zero policy changes. Isolation is guaranteed by the template resolution — app-dev resolves to paths containing "dev", which don't match "staging" or "prod" paths.

Q126
How does fine-grained parameter control improve security beyond basic path-based ACL?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Basic ACL says: "You can access path X." Fine-grained control says: "You can access path X, but ONLY with these parameters." For example, allowing auth/token/create without parameter control means the user can create tokens with ANY policy (including root) and ANY TTL. With parameter control, you restrict: which policies can be attached to created tokens, maximum TTL, whether the token is orphan, and which CIDR ranges are allowed.

EXPLANATION

This prevents privilege escalation: a user who can create tokens can't grant themselves more privileges than you've allowed. Fine-grained control is configured at the auth method role level (e.g., token_policies in AppRole/K8s role) and within policy definitions using required_parameters.

Q127
What are the available template parameters and what does each resolve to?
Show Answer
ANSWER
ParameterResolves To
{{identity.entity.id}}Entity's UUID
{{identity.entity.name}}Entity's human-readable name
{{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}}Specific metadata value (e.g., metadata.department)
{{identity.groups.names.<index>}}Group name at index 0, 1, 2...
{{identity.groups.ids.<index>}}Group ID at index 0, 1, 2...
EXPLANATION

{{identity.entity.name}} is the most commonly used — it's human-readable and maps directly to team names. {{identity.entity.metadata.<key>}} is the most flexible — you can store any key-value pairs (environment, cost-center, region) and use them in policy paths.

Q128
When should you use separate policies per environment vs templated policies?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Separate policies: Use when each environment has fundamentally different access patterns (e.g., dev allows CRUD, prod allows read-only) AND the policy content is different enough that templates don't simplify it. Best for ≤3 environments.
Templated policies: Use when all environments follow the same pattern, just with different path prefixes. Best for ≥3 environments or when environments are added/removed frequently. Templated policies reduce maintenance overhead and eliminate copy-paste errors.

EXPLANATION

Hybrid approach (recommended): Use templated policies for environment-specific paths (secrets, DB creds) and separate policies for role-specific permissions (admin vs app). This gives you both scalability and clarity.

Q129
Why is the deny capability called "nuclear" and when should you use it?
Show Answer
ANSWER

deny is "nuclear" because it overrides ALL other policies — even if 10 policies say "read" and 1 says "deny", the deny wins. If applied to a critical path like sys/* or auth/token/*, it can lock ALL users out of Vault, including administrators. Use deny only when you need to explicitly block a specific operation that would otherwise be allowed by the UNION of other policies — and always test on a non-production Vault first.

EXPLANATION

Safer alternative: Instead of deny, restructure your policies so the unwanted operation is simply not granted by any policy. The default DENY ALL model already blocks everything — you only need deny when multiple policies combine to accidentally grant something you don't want.

Q130
Configure a complete multi-tenant Vault setup: 3 teams (alpha, beta, gamma) across 2 environments (dev, prod) with full isolation.
Show Answer
ANSWER
# ─── team-policy.hcl ───
# 1 policy for 3 teams × 2 environments = 6 combinations
path "anihpj/data/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}/{{identity.entity.name}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}
path "database/creds/{{identity.entity.metadata.env}}-{{identity.entity.name}}-role" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
# Setup entities (6 total)
vault write identity/entity name="alpha-dev" \
    metadata='{"env":"dev","team":"alpha"}'
vault write identity/entity name="alpha-prod" \
    metadata='{"env":"prod","team":"alpha"}'
vault write identity/entity name="beta-dev" \
    metadata='{"env":"dev","team":"beta"}'
# ... (beta-prod, gamma-dev, gamma-prod)

# One group with the templated policy
vault write identity/group name="all-apps" \
    type=internal policies="team-policy" \
    member_entity_ids="<all 6 entity IDs>"

# Now:
# alpha-dev → anihpj/data/dev/alpha/* ✅
# alpha-dev → anihpj/data/prod/alpha/* ❌
# beta-dev → anihpj/data/dev/beta/* ✅
# alpha-prod → anihpj/data/dev/alpha/* ❌
# → 6 isolated namespaces, 1 policy, 0 drift!
EXPLANATION

This is the gold standard of multi-tenant Vault design. The policy uses TWO template variables ({{identity.entity.metadata.env}} and {{identity.entity.name}}) to create a 2D isolation matrix. Adding a 4th team or 3rd environment requires only entity creation — zero policy changes. The template guarantees no cross-team or cross-environment access.

🧯 Common Policy Mistakes & Lockout Recovery — What Every Admin Must Know

Policies are the most powerful — and most dangerous — part of Vault. A single mistake can lock you out of your own Vault instance. Here are the most common mistakes and exactly how to recover from each.

💀 MISTAKE #1: Deleting the Default Policy

Symptom: All tokens suddenly lose basic functionality — can't look up their own properties, can't renew, can't list auth methods. Vault appears to be "broken."
Why it happens: The default policy is attached to every token. If deleted, tokens lose cubbyhole access, self-lookup, and renewal capabilities.
Recovery: Use the root token to recreate the default policy:

# Login with root token (the ONLY token that works without default policy)
vault login <root-token>

# Recreate the default policy
vault policy write default - <<EOF
# Allow tokens to look up their own properties
path "auth/token/lookup-self" {
    capabilities = ["read"]
}
# Allow tokens to renew themselves
path "auth/token/renew-self" {
    capabilities = ["update"]
}
# Allow tokens to revoke themselves
path "auth/token/revoke-self" {
    capabilities = ["update"]
}
# Allow listing and managing cubbyhole secrets
path "cubbyhole/*" {
    capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}
# Allow listing visible auth methods
path "sys/auth" {
    capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF

💀 MISTAKE #2: Using deny on sys/* (Locking Yourself Out)

Symptom: Even the root token can't access Vault configuration. You're completely locked out.
Why it happens: A policy with path "sys/*" { capabilities = ["deny"] } was attached to your token. The deny capability overrides everything — even root.
Recovery: You need physical access to the Vault server. Restart Vault and modify the storage backend directly:

# 1. Stop Vault
systemctl stop vault

# 2. If using Raft storage, use vault operator to remove the policy
vault operator raft list-peers  # Verify raft is healthy

# 3. Restart Vault and use root token BEFORE the bad policy
#    is evaluated (root token created during init bypasses policies
#    for emergency recovery)

# 4. IMMEDIATELY delete the bad policy
vault login <root-token>
vault policy delete bad-policy

# ⚠️ If even root is blocked, you need to restore from backup
#    or manually edit the Raft snapshot (advanced, last resort)

💀 MISTAKE #3: Wildcard Gone Wrong — secret/* instead of secret/data/*

Symptom: Applications can't read KV v2 secrets despite having "read" on secret/*.
Why it happens: KV v2 stores data at secret/data/<path> and metadata at secret/metadata/<path>. The path secret/* matches secret/data (the directory itself) but NOT secret/data/anihpj (which is 2 levels deep). You need secret/data/* for one level or secret/** for all levels.
Fix:

# ❌ WRONG: secret/* only matches secret/data (1 level)
path "secret/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# ✅ CORRECT: secret/data/* matches secret/data/anihpj (2 levels)
path "secret/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# ✅ ALSO CORRECT: secret/** matches everything at all depths
path "secret/**" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

💀 MISTAKE #4: Forgetting That Policy Changes Don't Affect Existing Tokens

Symptom: You updated a policy to remove access, but the application still has access.
Why it happens: Policy changes only affect tokens on their next renewal. Existing tokens keep their old permissions until TTL expiry or renewal. If TTL is 768h, the app keeps old permissions for 32 days!
Fix:

# If you need immediate revocation:
# 1. Find all tokens with the old policy
vault list auth/token/accessors  # List all token accessors
# (Or use identity entities to find affected tokens)

# 2. Revoke the affected tokens
vault token revoke <token>

# 3. OR: Force renew to pick up new policy (if you want to keep the token)
vault token renew <token>
# After renewal, the token picks up the updated policy
🛡️ PREVENTION CHECKLIST — Before Deploying ANY Policy

✅ Never delete the default policy — modify it if needed, but never delete
✅ Always test with vault token create -policy=<name> before attaching to roles
✅ Check capabilities with vault token capabilities <token> <path>
✅ Actually RUN the intended commands with the test token
✅ Verify DENIED operations are correctly denied (negative testing)
✅ Save root token in a secure offline location (physical safe recommended)
✅ Keep audit logs enabled — they're your "black box" for debugging access issues
✅ For production: deploy policies via CI/CD with mandatory code review
✅ Use deny only when absolutely necessary — and test on a dev Vault first
✅ Always have a separate recovery path (root token, unseal keys) stored securely

🚀 Part 5 Implementation Blueprint — Putting Policies into Production

Here is the complete step-by-step workflow for deploying Vault policies in a real environment. Follow this blueprint and you'll never lock yourself out.

1
DESIGN

Map out who needs what access. Write policies for roles, not people.

2
WRITE

Create .hcl files in version control. Start with least privilege.

3
TEST

Create test token. Verify capabilities. Run actual commands.

4
REVIEW

PR review by another team member. Check for over-permissive paths.

5
DEPLOY

CI/CD runs vault policy write. Apply to auth roles and groups.

6
VERIFY

Monitor audit logs. Verify apps can access what they need.

7
AUDIT

Monthly review: remove unused policies, tighten overly broad rules.

📋 Part 5 — Key Takeaways for the Exam

  • ✅ Default = DENY ALL — If no policy explicitly grants it, it's denied
  • ✅ UNION model — Multiple policies combine, most permissive wins (except deny)
  • ✅ deny is king — Overrides ALL other capabilities across ALL policies
  • ✅ Wildcards: * = one level, ** = all levels, + = exactly one segment
  • ✅ Capabilities: create, read, update, delete, list, sudo, deny
  • ✅ Templates: {{identity.entity.name}} enables 1 policy for unlimited teams
  • ✅ Sentinel: Enterprise only — conditional access (time, IP, value-based)
  • ✅ Testing: vault token capabilities before deploying ANY policy
  • ✅ Policy changes affect tokens on next RENEWAL, not immediately
  • ✅ KV v2 paths: Use secret/data/* not secret/* (v2 adds /data/ prefix)
🏋️ Ch 13 Lab — Templated Policies & Multi-Tenant (10 min)
⏱️ Target: 10 min | 🎯 Goal: Create templated policy, entities with metadata, verify isolation
# 1. Create templated policy (ONE policy for all teams!)
vault policy write team-access - <<'EOF'
path "secret/data/teams/{{identity.entity.metadata.team}}/*" {
  capabilities = ["create","read","update","delete","list"]
}
EOF

# 2. Create entities with team metadata
vault write identity/entity name="alice" metadata='{"team":"alpha"}'
vault write identity/entity name="bob" metadata='{"team":"beta"}'

# 3. Create groups with the templated policy
vault write identity/group name="all-devs" type=internal policies="team-access"

# 4. Add entities to group → they inherit team-access
ALICE_ID=$(vault read -field=id identity/entity/name/alice)
vault write identity/group name="all-devs" member_entity_ids=$ALICE_ID

# 5. Test: Alice's token → resolves to secret/data/teams/alpha/*
# Bob's token → resolves to secret/data/teams/beta/*
# Alice CANNOT see beta's secrets! Bob CANNOT see alpha's!
# Template {{identity.entity.metadata.team}} auto-resolves!

Drill Check: How many policies needed for 10 teams? (ONE — templated!). What if entity has no metadata.team? (Resolves to empty string → denies all access).

Master these 20 items and you've secured nearly 1/3 of your passing score:
