14.1 Why Vault on Kubernetes? — The Security Gap

Kubernetes has a built-in Secret resource. Many beginners think: "K8s has Secrets — why do I need Vault?" The answer is in one word: encryption. K8s Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone with kubectl access can decode them. Vault provides AES-256 encryption, dynamic secrets, audit logging, and fine-grained policies — things K8s simply cannot do.

K8s SECRETS vs VAULT — The Security Gap (Why Vault is Essential)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│     ⚠️ K8s SECRETS vs HASHICORP VAULT — The Security Reality      │
│                                                                    │
│  K8s SECRET (base64 obfuscation — NOT encryption):                │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────                      │
│  $ kubectl create secret generic db-secret \                      │
│      --from-literal=password=s3cr3t                               │
│                                                                    │
│  $ kubectl get secret db-secret -o yaml                           │
│  apiVersion: v1                                                    │
│  data:                                                             │
│    password: czNjcjN0    ← base64, NOT encrypted!                 │
│                                                                    │
│  $ echo 'czNjcjN0' | base64 -d                              │
│  → s3cr3t  ← ANYONE with kubectl access can read this!           │
│                                                                    │
│  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════  │
│                                                                    │
│  VAULT SECRET (AES-256-GCM96 encrypted at rest):                  │
│  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
│  $ vault kv get secret/database                                   │
│  → Access controlled by: Token + Policy + Identity                │
│  → Every access LOGGED in immutable audit trail                   │
│  → Can be DYNAMIC (auto-generated, auto-expired with TTL)         │
│  → Can be auto-ROTATED without application restart                │
│  → Policies enforce LEAST PRIVILEGE per path                      │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 K8s Secrets = "PLEASE DON'T LOOK" (obfuscation)           │
│     Vault Secrets = "YOU CAN'T LOOK" (encryption + ACL)      │
│                                                                    │
│  REALITY CHECK:                                                    │
│  ──────────────                                                    │
│  • 67% of organizations have suffered a secret leak               │
│  • Average cost of a credential leak: $4.45 million               │
│  • K8s Secrets in etcd: encoded, not encrypted by default         │
│  • With Vault: encrypted at rest, in transit (TLS), per-path ACL  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔍 A Real Day Without Vault on K8s — And With It

WITHOUT Vault: A developer commits a .env file with the production database password to Git. The password spreads to 5 developers' laptops, the CI/CD pipeline logs it in build output, and a contractor with temporary kubectl access decodes the K8s Secret in 2 seconds. Six months later, nobody has rotated the password — it's the same one from day one.

WITH Vault: The database password never exists as plaintext. Vault generates dynamic credentials with a 1-hour TTL — each pod gets unique credentials. If a pod is compromised, the credentials auto-expire. The audit log shows exactly who accessed what and when. When the contractor leaves, you revoke their token — instant, complete, audited.

🎓 EXAM TIP

The Vault Associate exam expects you to know: (1) K8s Secrets are base64-encoded, NOT encrypted, (2) etcd encryption-at-rest only protects the storage layer — anyone with kubectl access can still read decoded secrets, (3) Vault adds: dynamic secrets, lease management, audit logging, and per-path ACL policies that K8s RBAC cannot replicate at the secret level.

14.2 Pattern 1: Vault Agent Sidecar Injector 🎯🏗️

The Vault Agent Sidecar is the most popular and flexible pattern. A second container (the "sidecar") runs alongside your application container. It authenticates to Vault, fetches secrets, renders them to a shared volume, and continuously renews tokens and leases. Your application simply reads files — it doesn't even know Vault exists.

VAULT AGENT SIDECAR — Complete Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        🏗️ PATTERN 1: VAULT AGENT SIDECAR INJECTOR                 │
│        How anihpj pods get secrets without knowing Vault exists    │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  ANIHJP POD (namespace: anihpj)                              │  │
│  │                                                               │  │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │  │
│  │  │  APP CONTAINER       │    │  VAULT AGENT CONTAINER       │ │  │
│  │  │  (Django + Gunicorn) │    │                               │ │  │
│  │  │                     │    │  auto_auth:                    │ │  │
│  │  │  Reads secrets      │    │    method: kubernetes          │ │  │
│  │  │  from files:        │    │    role: anihpj-app            │ │  │
│  │  │  /vault/secrets/    │    │                               │ │  │
│  │  │                     │    │  template files:               │ │  │
│  │  │  • database.json    │    │    1. Auth to Vault (K8s SA)  │ │  │
│  │  │  • api-keys.json    │    │    2. Fetch secrets            │ │  │
│  │  │  • django.env       │    │    3. Render templates         │ │  │
│  │  │                     │    │    4. Write to /vault/secrets/ │ │  │
│  │  │  App NEVER talks    │    │    5. Auto-renew token         │ │  │
│  │  │  to Vault directly  │    │    6. Auto-renew DB lease      │ │  │
│  │  └────────┬────────────┘    └──────────────┬──────────────┘ │  │
│  │           │                                 │                 │  │
│  │           └─────────────┬───────────────────┘                 │  │
│  │                         │                                     │  │
│  │               ┌─────────▼─────────┐                           │  │
│  │               │  SHARED VOLUME     │                           │  │
│  │               │  /vault/secrets/   │  ← emptyDir (memory)     │  │
│  │               │  ├── database.json │  ← Agent writes          │  │
│  │               │  ├── apikeys.json  │  ← App reads             │  │
│  │               │  └── django.env    │                           │  │
│  │               └───────────────────┘                           │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                    │
│  FLOW:                                                             │
│  1. Pod starts → Init container? No (Agent handles auth)          │
│  2. Agent authenticates to Vault via K8s ServiceAccount JWT       │
│  3. Vault validates JWT via TokenReview API                       │
│  4. Vault returns token with anihpj-app policy                    │
│  5. Agent fetches secrets: database/creds/anihpj-role             │
│  6. Agent renders templates to /vault/secrets/                    │
│  7. Django app reads /vault/secrets/database.json → connects!    │
│  8. Agent auto-renews token at 66% of TTL                        │
│  9. Agent auto-renews database lease before expiry                │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 The app NEVER has Vault credentials — just reads files.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.2a Agent Injector — How It Works

The Vault Agent Injector is a mutating admission webhook. When you deploy a pod with specific annotations, the webhook automatically modifies the pod spec to add the Vault Agent sidecar container and shared volume. You don't manually add the sidecar — the injector does it for you.

YAML — anihpj Deployment with Agent Annotations
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
      annotations:
        # ══════ VAULT AGENT INJECTOR ANNOTATIONS ══════
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
        vault.hashicorp.com/role: "anihpj-app"
        
        # Secret 1: Static KV — database config
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-database: "anihpj/data/database"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-database: |
          {{- with secret "anihpj/data/database" -}}
          {
            "engine": "{{ .Data.data.engine }}",
            "host": "{{ .Data.data.host }}",
            "port": "{{ .Data.data.port }}"
          }
          {{- end }}
        
        # Secret 2: Dynamic DB credentials
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db-creds: "database/creds/anihpj-role"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-db-creds: |
          {{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
          {
            "username": "{{ .Data.username }}",
            "password": "{{ .Data.password }}"
          }
          {{- end }}
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa  # K8s auth requires this
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: anihpj/anihpj:latest
        # App reads from /vault/secrets/ — no Vault config needed!

14.2b Template Rendering — How Secrets Become Files

The Agent uses Go's text/template syntax to transform Vault API responses into application-friendly formats. This is the bridge between Vault's JSON API and your app's config files.

Template Syntax Reference
# Access KV v2 data:
{{- with secret "secret/data/anihpj" -}}
KEY={{ .Data.data.key_name }}
{{- end }}

# Access dynamic DB credentials:
{{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
DB_USER={{ .Data.username }}
DB_PASS={{ .Data.password }}
LEASE_DURATION={{ .LeaseDuration }}
LEASE_ID={{ .LeaseID }}
{{- end }}

# Access PKI certificate:
{{- with secret "pki/issue/anihpj" "common_name=anihpj.local" -}}
{{ .Data.certificate }}
{{ .Data.private_key }}
{{ .Data.ca_chain }}
{{- end }}

# Range over lists:
{{- range secrets "secret/metadata/anihpj/" -}}
{{ . }}
{{- end }}

# Conditional logic:
{{- if .Data.data.feature_flag -}}
FEATURE_ENABLED=true
{{- else -}}
FEATURE_ENABLED=false
{{- end }}

14.2c Auto-Auth Methods — How the Agent Authenticates

The Agent supports multiple auto-auth methods. For Kubernetes, the agent reads the pod's ServiceAccount JWT from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token and authenticates to Vault using the Kubernetes auth method. No credentials are stored in the pod spec — identity comes from the platform.

☸️
Kubernetes Auth

Pod's SA JWT → Vault validates via TokenReview API. Best for workloads ON K8s. Zero credentials in the pod.

🤖
AppRole Auth

RoleID (in config) + SecretID (wrapped). Best for workloads OUTSIDE K8s (VMs, bare metal, CI/CD runners).

☁️
AWS/GCP/Azure Auth

Uses cloud instance identity documents or signed metadata. Best for cloud-native workloads with IAM roles.

🔐
JWT/OIDC Auth

Agent presents a signed JWT from an OIDC provider. Best for workloads with existing identity tokens.

⚡ SPEED TIP: Quick Sidecar Test

To verify the sidecar is working: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent -- cat /vault/secrets/database.json. If you see your secrets rendered correctly, the integration is working! Check the agent logs: kubectl logs deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent.

🧠 The Three Patterns — A Physical Analogy to Remember Forever

Think of your applications as apartments in a building:
Sidecar: Each apartment has its own personal concierge (the Agent container). The concierge goes to the vault, retrieves what you need, and places it on your table. Most personal, most flexible, but uses extra space.
CSI: The building has a central mailroom (the CSI driver). Packages appear in your mailbox slot — no concierge needed, but you get exactly what was sent, in exactly the format it arrived.
VSO: The building has a bulletin board (K8s Secrets). Important notices are posted there — everyone with access to the board can read them. Convenient, familiar, but visible to anyone in the building with permission.

14.3 Pattern 2: Vault CSI Provider 🎯

The Container Storage Interface (CSI) Provider mounts Vault secrets as a volume in your pod — no sidecar container needed. Secrets appear as regular files in the pod's filesystem. The CSI driver (a DaemonSet on every node) handles authentication and secret retrieval transparently.

VAULT CSI PROVIDER — No Sidecar Required
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           📂 PATTERN 2: VAULT CSI PROVIDER                         │
│           Secrets as files — no extra container needed             │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐    │
│  │  anihpj Pod  │      │  CSI Driver   │      │  Vault       │    │
│  │              │      │  (DaemonSet)  │      │  Server      │    │
│  │  volumeMount │      │               │      │              │    │
│  │  /mnt/secrets│─────▶│  1. Kubelet   │      │              │    │
│  │              │      │     requests  │─────▶│  2. Auth via │    │
│  │  Files appear│      │     mount     │      │  K8s SA JWT  │    │
│  │  as regular  │◀─────│  3. CSI writes│◀─────│  3. Fetch    │    │
│  │  files!      │      │     secrets   │      │  secrets     │    │
│  └─────────────┘      └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘    │
│                                                                    │
│  ADVANTAGES:                                                       │
│  ✅ No sidecar container — less resource overhead                  │
│  ✅ Kubernetes-native — uses standard CSI interface                │
│  ✅ Secrets appear as files — app reads like any other file        │
│  ✅ Secrets are in-memory (tmpfs) — never touch disk              │
│                                                                    │
│  LIMITATIONS:                                                      │
│  ⚠️ No template rendering — raw JSON output                        │
│  ⚠️ No auto-renewal of dynamic secrets (CSI v1.x limitation)      │
│  ⚠️ Less flexible than Agent for complex secret orchestration     │
│  ⚠️ Requires CSI driver DaemonSet on every node                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
YAML — SecretProviderClass for CSI
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: vault-database
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  provider: vault
  parameters:
    vaultAddress: "https://vault.vault.svc:8200"
    roleName: "anihpj-app"
    objects: |
      - objectName: "db-creds"
        secretPath: "database/creds/anihpj-role"
        secretKey: ""
      - objectName: "db-config"
        secretPath: "anihpj/data/database"
        secretKey: ""
      - objectName: "api-key"
        secretPath: "anihpj/data/api"
        secretKey: ""
---
# Pod referencing the CSI volume
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-csi
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: anihpj/anihpj:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: secrets
      mountPath: /mnt/secrets
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: secrets
    csi:
      driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
      readOnly: true
      volumeAttributes:
        secretProviderClass: "vault-database"

14.4 Kubernetes Auth Method for Vault — Deep Dive 🎯

The Kubernetes auth method is the bridge between K8s and Vault. When a pod tries to authenticate, Vault calls the TokenReview API to validate the pod's ServiceAccount JWT. This means Vault trusts Kubernetes to vouch for the pod's identity — a powerful and secure pattern.

Bash — K8s Auth: Inside vs Outside Cluster
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# SCENARIO A: Vault INSIDE K8s (Helm)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    kubernetes_host="https://kubernetes.default.svc:443" \
    token_reviewer_jwt="$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt"
# Auto-resolves — everything available from mounted SA

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# SCENARIO B: Vault OUTSIDE K8s (VM/Bare Metal)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# Step 1: Create a long-lived ServiceAccount for Vault to use
kubectl create sa vault-reviewer -n vault
kubectl create clusterrolebinding vault-reviewer \
    --clusterrole=system:auth-delegator \
    --serviceaccount=vault:vault-reviewer

# Step 2: Get the SA token and CA cert
REVIEWER_JWT=$(kubectl create token vault-reviewer -n vault --duration=87600h)
kubectl get secret $(kubectl get sa vault-reviewer -n vault -o jsonpath='{.secrets[0].name}') -n vault -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > k8s-ca.pem

# Step 3: Configure Vault
vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    kubernetes_host="https://k8s-api.company.com:6443" \
    token_reviewer_jwt="$REVIEWER_JWT" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@k8s-ca.pem"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# Both scenarios: Create roles
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj-app \
    bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    policies=anihpj-policy \
    ttl=1h

⚠️ EXAM GOTCHA: External Vault

When Vault runs OUTSIDE Kubernetes, you MUST provide kubernetes_host (the external API server URL), token_reviewer_jwt (a long-lived ServiceAccount JWT), and kubernetes_ca_cert (the K8s API CA cert). The exam frequently tests this scenario — many candidates fail because they use the in-cluster defaults when Vault is external.

14.5 Deploying Vault HA on Kubernetes 🏗️

The recommended way to deploy Vault on Kubernetes is via the official Helm chart. It configures HA mode with Raft storage, TLS, and the Agent Injector automatically.

Bash — Deploy Vault HA on K8s with Helm
# Add HashiCorp Helm repo
helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
helm repo update

# Install Vault in HA mode with Raft
helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault \
    --create-namespace \
    --set server.ha.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.raft.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.raft.setNodeId=true \
    --set server.ha.replicas=3 \
    --set injector.enabled=true \
    --set ui.enabled=true \
    --set ui.serviceType=ClusterIP

# Wait for pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=vault -n vault --timeout=120s

# Initialize Vault (only on vault-0)
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator init \
    -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3 \
    -format=json > cluster-keys.json

# Unseal each pod (3 unseal keys each)
for i in 0 1 2; do
    kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault operator unseal $(jq -r '.unseal_keys_b64[0]' cluster-keys.json)
    kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault operator unseal $(jq -r '.unseal_keys_b64[1]' cluster-keys.json)
    kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault operator unseal $(jq -r '.unseal_keys_b64[2]' cluster-keys.json)
done

# Verify HA status
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator raft list-peers
# Node       Address              State     Voter
# vault-0    vault-0.vault:8201   leader    true
# vault-1    vault-1.vault:8201   follower  true
# vault-2    vault-2.vault:8201   follower  true

# Login and enable K8s auth
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault login $(jq -r '.root_token' cluster-keys.json)
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault auth enable kubernetes
🏗️ Production Vault on K8s — What You Now Have

After these steps, you have: (1) 3-node Vault HA cluster with Raft consensus, (2) Agent Injector automatically adding sidecars to annotated pods, (3) UI accessible via port-forward, (4) TLS between all components, (5) Ready for anihpj integration with K8s auth + policies.

🔬 Deep Dive: Kubernetes Auth — Understanding the Injection to the Core

The Vault Agent Injector pattern looks like magic — add an annotation, and secrets appear in your pod. But what's actually happening? This section peels back the curtain on the mutating webhook, the JWT authentication flow, and the shared volume mechanism — the internals that power Vault on Kubernetes.

🔍 The Complete Injection Flow — 8 Steps from Annotation to Secret

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        VAULT AGENT INJECTOR — COMPLETE INJECTION FLOW            │
│                                                                   │
│  STEP 1: YOU CREATE A POD                                        │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ apiVersion: v1                                              │  │
│  │ kind: Pod                                                   │  │
│  │ metadata:                                                   │  │
│  │   annotations:                                              │  │
│  │     vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"                │  │
│  │     vault.hashicorp.com/role: "jobpost"                     │  │
│  │     vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db: |           │  │
│  │       {{- with secret "database/creds/jobpost-role" -}}     │  │
│  │       DB_USER={{ .Data.username }}                           │  │
│  │       DB_PASS={{ .Data.password }}                           │  │
│  │       {{- end }}                                            │  │
│  │ spec:                                                       │  │
│  │   serviceAccountName: jobpost-sa                            │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 2: K8S API SERVER RECEIVES POD CREATION REQUEST            │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Before the pod is persisted to etcd, the API server calls  │  │
│  │ ALL registered mutating admission webhooks.                │  │
│  │ The Vault Agent Injector webhook is one of them.           │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 3: WEBHOOK INSPECTS ANNOTATIONS                             │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Webhook reads:                                              │  │
│  │ • vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject → "true" → INTERVENE    │  │
│  │ • vault.hashicorp.com/role → "jobpost"                        │  │
│  │ • vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-* → template cnfg │  │
│  │                                                            │  │
│  │ Webhook MODIFIES the pod spec BEFORE it's created:          │  │
│  │ 1. Adds Vault Agent container (vault:latest image)          │  │
│  │ 2. Adds shared emptyDir volume (/vault/secrets)             │  │
│  │ 3. Mounts SA token volume for JWT auth                     │  │
│  │ 4. Sets env vars: VAULT_ADDR, AGENT_CONFIG                  │  │
│  │ 5. Writes Agent config file with template + auto_auth       │  │
│  │ 6. Optionally adds init container (if init annotation set)  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 4: POD IS CREATED (NOW WITH EXTRA SIDECAR)                 │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Pod Spec (after webhook mutation):                          │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ containers:                                                 │  │
│  │ - name: anihpj              ← YOUR APP (unchanged)          │  │
│  │   image: anihpj/jobpost:latest                              │  │
│  │   volumeMounts:                                             │  │
│  │   - name: vault-secrets                                     │  │
│  │     mountPath: /vault/secrets   ← Shared with Agent         │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ - name: vault-agent          ← INJECTED by webhook          │  │
│  │   image: hashicorp/vault:latest                             │  │
│  │   args: ["agent", "-config=/etc/vault/agent-config.hcl"]    │  │
│  │   env:                                                      │  │
│  │   - name: VAULT_ADDR                                        │  │
│  │     value: https://vault.vault:8200                          │  │
│  │   volumeMounts:                                             │  │
│  │   - name: vault-secrets                                     │  │
│  │     mountPath: /vault/secrets   ← Writes secrets here       │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ volumes:                                                    │  │
│  │ - name: vault-secrets         ← emptyDir (shared memory)    │  │
│  │   emptyDir:                                                 │  │
│  │     medium: Memory             ← RAM-backed (never on disk) │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 5: VAULT AGENT STARTS + AUTHENTICATES                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Agent reads its config file (written by webhook):           │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ auto_auth {                                                 │  │
│  │   method "kubernetes" {                                     │  │
│  │     mount_path = "auth/kubernetes"                          │  │
│  │     config = {                                              │  │
│  │       role = "jobpost"                                      │  │
│  │     }                                                       │  │
│  │   }                                                         │  │
│  │ }                                                           │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ 1. Agent reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/SA/token      │  │
│  │ 2. Agent POSTs to Vault: auth/kubernetes/login (JWT + role) │  │
│  │ 3. Vault calls K8s TokenReview API to validate JWT          │  │
│  │ 4. K8s confirms: "Yes, this is jobpost-sa in anihpj ns"     │  │
│  │ 5. Vault issues token with policies: ["jobpost-k8s"]        │  │
│  │ 6. Agent stores token in sink file (optional)               │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 6: AGENT FETCHES SECRETS + RENDERS TEMPLATES                │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ For EACH template (agent-inject-secret-*):                   │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ Template: DB_USER={{ .Data.username }}                      │  │
│  │           DB_PASS={{ .Data.password }}                       │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ 1. Agent resolves: database/creds/jobpost-role              │  │
│  │ 2. Agent calls: vault read database/creds/jobpost-role      │  │
│  │    → Vault generates a new PostgreSQL user                   │  │
│  │    → Returns: username=v-token-abc, password=A1bC2dE3       │  │
│  │    → Creates lease (TTL=1h, lease_id=...)                   │  │
│  │ 3. Agent renders template:                                  │  │
│  │    DB_USER=v-token-abc                                      │  │
│  │    DB_PASS=A1bC2dE3                                         │  │
│  │ 4. Agent writes to: /vault/secrets/db.env                   │  │
│  │ 5. Agent chmod 0400 (owner read-only)                       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 7: YOUR APP READS THE SECRET FILE                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ The anihpj container simply reads:                          │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │   import os                                                 │  │
│  │   DB_USER = open('/vault/secrets/db.env').read()            │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ The app has NO Vault library, NO Vault token, NO awareness. │  │
│  │ It just reads files — same as any config file.              │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                           │                                       │
│                           ▼                                       │
│  STEP 8: AGENT CONTINUOUSLY RENEWS IN BACKGROUND                  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ • Token renewal: At TTL/2, Agent renews Vault token         │  │
│  │ • Lease renewal: At TTL/2, Agent renews DB lease            │  │
│  │ • Template re-render: On renewal, Agent re-fetches secrets  │  │
│  │   and updates /vault/secrets/db.env with new credentials    │  │
│  │ • Signal app: Optional — send SIGHUP to app container       │  │
│  │   so it reloads config with new credentials                 │  │
│  │                                                             │  │
│  │ ⏱️ 90% reduction in Vault API calls via Agent caching       │  │
│  │ 🔄 Credentials can be rotated every hour automatically      │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 Why Shared Volumes Matter — The Security Architecture

The shared volume between the Vault Agent and your app container is an emptyDir with medium: Memory — it exists only in RAM, never touches disk, and is destroyed when the pod stops. This is critical for security: even if someone gains physical access to the node's hard drive, they find nothing. The secrets live only in the pod's memory, and different pods (even on the same node) have isolated tmpfs mounts — one pod cannot read another pod's secrets.

⚠️ CRITICAL: JWT Expiry in Kubernetes 1.22+

Since Kubernetes 1.22, ServiceAccount tokens have a 1-hour default expiry (bound tokens, not legacy secrets). If your Vault Agent doesn't renew its token within 1 hour, it loses authentication and can't fetch new secrets. The Vault Agent handles this automatically via auto_auth renewal, but if you're writing custom integration code, you must handle token rotation. Always use the vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-token: "true" annotation to mount the latest JWT.

📝 Chapter 14 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q131
Why are Kubernetes Secrets alone insufficient for production secret management?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, NOT encrypted. Anyone with kubectl access to the namespace can read and decode them in 2 seconds. K8s Secrets also lack: dynamic secrets (auto-generated + TTL), per-path ACL policies, full audit logging of every access, automatic rotation, and cross-cluster secret sharing. etcd encryption-at-rest only protects the storage layer — not application-level access.

EXPLANATION

Think of K8s Secrets as a "keep out" sign — it works against casual observers but not against anyone with access. Vault adds cryptographic guarantees, identity-based access control, and full lifecycle management.

Q132
Describe the Vault Agent Sidecar Injector pattern — how does anihpj get its database credentials?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The mutating admission webhook reads pod annotations (vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true") and automatically injects a Vault Agent sidecar container. The Agent: (1) authenticates to Vault using the pod's K8s ServiceAccount JWT, (2) fetches specified secrets, (3) renders them via templates to a shared volume at /vault/secrets/, (4) continuously renews the token and leases. The anihpj container simply reads files from the shared volume — it never talks to Vault directly.

EXPLANATION

Key benefit: The application code has ZERO Vault awareness. It reads /vault/secrets/database.json just like any other config file. If you switch from Vault to another secret manager (or back to K8s Secrets), the application code doesn't change — only the pod annotations change.

Q133
What are the key differences between Vault Agent Sidecar and CSI Provider patterns?
Show Answer
ANSWER
FeatureSidecar InjectorCSI Provider
Extra container?✅ Yes (sidecar)❌ No (CSI driver)
Template rendering?✅ Full Go templates❌ Raw JSON only
Auto-renewal?✅ Token + leases⚠️ Limited (v1.x)
ComplexityMediumLower
Best forComplex config, dynamic secrets, PKIStatic secrets, simple KV
EXPLANATION

Choose Sidecar when you need template rendering, dynamic secret renewal, or multi-source secret aggregation. Choose CSI when you want the simplest setup and only need static KV secrets mounted as files.

Q134
What three parameters are required when configuring Kubernetes auth for Vault OUTSIDE the cluster?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. kubernetes_host: External K8s API endpoint (e.g., https://k8s-api.company.com:6443). 2. token_reviewer_jwt: A long-lived ServiceAccount JWT that Vault uses to call the TokenReview API. 3. kubernetes_ca_cert: The K8s API server's CA certificate for TLS verification. All three are provided to vault write auth/kubernetes/config.

EXPLANATION

When Vault is inside K8s, these auto-resolve from the mounted ServiceAccount at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/. Outside the cluster, you must provide all three explicitly, and the K8s API must be network-reachable from Vault.

Q135
What does the Agent template {{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}} do?
Show Answer
ANSWER

It fetches dynamic database credentials from Vault's DB secrets engine at the path database/creds/anihpj-role. The {{- with secret ... -}} block: (1) makes a Vault API call to read the secret, (2) stores the response in the . (dot) context variable, (3) makes .Data.username and .Data.password available inside the block, (4) the {{- syntax strips whitespace. After the block, Vault automatically manages the lease — renewing before expiry.

EXPLANATION

This is the magic of dynamic secrets: the application gets fresh, unique credentials every time, and Vault automatically revokes them when the lease expires. No hardcoded passwords, no manual rotation.

Q136
How do you deploy a 3-node Vault HA cluster on Kubernetes?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Use the HashiCorp Helm chart with: --set server.ha.enabled=true --set server.ha.raft.enabled=true --set server.ha.replicas=3. After deployment: initialize on vault-0, unseal all 3 pods with 3 of 5 unseal keys each, verify with vault operator raft list-peers (should show 1 leader + 2 followers). Raft handles leader election and log replication automatically.

EXPLANATION

The Helm chart configures: Raft storage (integrated — no external dependency), TLS between nodes, auto-join for new nodes, and the Agent Injector. For production, also configure: resource limits, anti-affinity (spread across nodes), PVC for Raft data, and Prometheus monitoring.

Q137
How does the Vault Agent handle token and lease renewal automatically?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The Agent runs a background renewal loop: (1) It renews the Vault token at 66% of TTL (configurable), (2) For each dynamic secret with a lease (DB creds, PKI certs), it renews the lease before expiry, (3) If renewal fails (e.g., token revoked, Vault unreachable), the Agent retries with exponential backoff, (4) When secrets are successfully renewed, the Agent re-renders templates and writes updated files atomically. The application never notices credential rotation — it just reads the latest file.

EXPLANATION

This is what makes Vault "set and forget" — once configured, the Agent handles the entire credential lifecycle. Developers don't need to implement renewal logic in their applications.

Q138
What annotations trigger Vault Agent sidecar injection?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# Required: Enable injection
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
# Required: Vault role (maps to K8s auth role)
vault.hashicorp.com/role: "anihpj-app"
# Per-secret annotations:
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-<name>: "path/to/secret"
vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-<name>: |
  Template content here
EXPLANATION

The webhook watches for agent-inject: "true". When found, it adds: a vault-agent init container (for pre-start secrets), a vault-agent sidecar container, a shared emptyDir volume, and volume mounts at /vault/secrets/. Each agent-inject-secret-<name> annotation maps to a rendered file at /vault/secrets/<name>.

Q139
How does the Kubernetes auth flow work from a pod's perspective?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Pod starts with serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa. 2. K8s mounts the SA JWT at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. 3. Agent (or app) sends this JWT to Vault with the role name: vault write auth/kubernetes/login role=anihpj-app jwt=<token>. 4. Vault calls K8s TokenReview API with the JWT — K8s validates it and returns the SA name + namespace + UID. 5. Vault matches against role: bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa, bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj. 6. If matched, Vault returns a token with anihpj-policy.

EXPLANATION

Key insight: Vault doesn't trust the pod directly — it trusts Kubernetes to vouch for the pod. The TokenReview API is the trust bridge. This is why token_reviewer_jwt must have system:auth-delegator ClusterRole — without it, Vault can't call TokenReview.

Q140
Configure a complete anihpj deployment with Vault Agent sidecar for database credentials and API keys.
Show Answer
ANSWER
YAML — Complete Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
        vault.hashicorp.com/role: "anihpj-app"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db: "database/creds/anihpj-role"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-db: |
          {{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
          DATABASE_URL=postgres://{{ .Data.username }}:{{ .Data.password }}@postgres:5432/anihpj
          {{- end }}
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-api: "anihpj/data/api"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-api: |
          {{- with secret "anihpj/data/api" -}}
          SENDGRID_KEY={{ .Data.data.sendgrid_key }}
          {{- end }}
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: anihpj/anihpj:latest
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          valueFrom:
            file: /vault/secrets/db
EXPLANATION

This single YAML configures: dynamic DB credentials (auto-renewed), static API keys (from KV v2), all rendered to files at /vault/secrets/. The app reads DATABASE_URL from a file — no Vault code in the application. The Agent handles authentication, fetching, rendering, and renewal automatically.

⏱️ 10 minutes
Scenario: Deploy Vault HA on K8s and Configure anihpj Sidecar

You have a fresh Kubernetes cluster. Your task:

  1. Deploy Vault in HA mode (3 replicas) with Helm
  2. Initialize and unseal all 3 pods
  3. Enable Kubernetes auth and create an anihpj role
  4. Write an anihpj policy that allows reading anihpj/data/*
  5. Create a ServiceAccount anihpj-sa in the anihpj namespace
  6. Verify the role accepts authentication from a test pod
💡 Hint: Remember to unseal ALL three pods. Use vault operator raft list-peers to verify HA is working before configuring auth.
▼ Solution (Click to Reveal)
Step 1: Deploy Vault HA
helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
helm repo update
helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault --create-namespace \
    --set server.ha.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.raft.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.replicas=3 \
    --set injector.enabled=true \
    --set ui.enabled=true
Step 2: Init + Unseal
# Init
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault operator init \
    -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3 -format=json > keys.json

# Unseal ALL three pods
for i in 0 1 2; do
    for j in 0 1 2; do
        kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault operator unseal \
            $(jq -r ".unseal_keys_b64[$j]" keys.json)
    done
done

# Verify: all should show sealed=false
for i in 0 1 2; do
    kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault status | grep Sealed
done
Step 3-5: Auth + Policy + Role
# Login
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault login $(jq -r .root_token keys.json)

# Enable K8s auth + create role
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault auth enable kubernetes
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
    kubernetes_host="https://kubernetes.default.svc:443" \
    token_reviewer_jwt="$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" \
    kubernetes_ca_cert="@/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt"

# Write policy
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault policy write anihpj-app - <<EOF
path "anihpj/data/*" { capabilities = ["read"] }
EOF

# Create K8s auth role
kubectl exec -n vault vault-0 -- vault write auth/kubernetes/role/anihpj-app \
    bound_service_account_names=anihpj-sa \
    bound_service_account_namespaces=anihpj \
    policies=anihpj-app \
    ttl=1h

# Create SA and test
kubectl create ns anihpj
kubectl create sa anihpj-sa -n anihpj
kubectl run test-pod -n anihpj --image=hashicorp/vault:latest \
    --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"anihpj-sa"}}' \
    -- vault login -method=kubernetes role=anihpj-app
# → Success! Token with anihpj-app policy

Chapter 15: Vault Agent Templates and Configuration 🎯

In Chapter 14 you saw the Agent sidecar pattern from the outside. Now we go inside the Agent — the config file, template syntax, auto-auth, caching, and performance tuning. This is the knowledge that separates "I deployed Vault" from "I mastered Vault on Kubernetes." When you understand Agent templates, you can make secrets appear in ANY format your app needs — env files, JSON, YAML, XML, or custom config formats.

🧠 Why Templates Matter — The Config Format Mismatch Problem

Your Django app needs DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db. Vault returns {"data": {"username": "v-token-xxx", "password": "abc123"}}. These are completely different formats. Templates are the translator. They take Vault's JSON API responses and reshape them into whatever format your application expects — .env files for Django, JSON for Node.js, YAML for Go apps, XML for legacy systems. Without templates, every application would need custom Vault client code. With templates, the Agent handles all format conversion — your app just reads files.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🎯 VA Exam Topic 🏗️ Full Agent Lab

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Write complete Vault Agent configuration files from scratch
  • ✅ Master the Agent template syntax — every directive and function
  • ✅ Configure auto-auth for K8s, AppRole, AWS, GCP, and Azure
  • ✅ Enable Agent caching for performance and Vault resiliency
  • ✅ Build the complete anihpj Agent configuration for production

15.1 Vault Agent Configuration File — Full Reference

The Agent config file controls everything: how the Agent authenticates, which secrets to fetch, how to render them, and where to write the output. It's written in HCL (same as policies) and typically stored in a ConfigMap or as a file on disk.

anihpj-agent-config.hcl — Full Annotated Config
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# VAULT AGENT CONFIG — anihpj Production
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Vault server connection
vault {
  address = "https://vault.vault.svc:8200"
  # ca_cert = "/vault/config/ca.crt"  # For custom CA
}

# Auto-authentication (how the agent logs in)
auto_auth {
  method "kubernetes" {
    mount_path = "auth/kubernetes"
    role       = "anihpj-app"
    # Agent reads SA JWT from pod filesystem automatically
  }

  # Where to store the Vault token (shared with app if needed)
  sink "file" {
    path = "/vault/token/.vault-token"
    mode = 0644
  }
}

# Cache — reduces Vault load, enables offline access
cache {
  use_auto_auth_token = true
  # persist "kubernetes" { path = "/vault/cache" }  # Disk cache
}

# Template 1: Database credentials (dynamic)
template {
  source      = "/vault/templates/database.ctmpl"
  destination = "/vault/secrets/database.env"
  # command     = "kill -HUP $(cat /vault/pid/anihpj.pid)"  # SIGHUP app
}

# Template 2: API keys (static KV)
template {
  source      = "/vault/templates/apikeys.ctmpl"
  destination = "/vault/secrets/apikeys.env"
}

# Template 3: Django settings (multi-source)
template {
  source      = "/vault/templates/django.ctmpl"
  destination = "/vault/secrets/django.env"
}

# PID file for signalling app on secret change
pid_file = "/vault/pid/agent.pid"

15.2 Agent Template Syntax — Deep Dive

The Agent uses Go's text/template with Vault-specific functions. The most important function is secret — it fetches a secret from Vault and makes its data available in the template.

VAULT AGENT TEMPLATES — From Vault API to Files
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        📝 AGENT TEMPLATE — How Secrets Become Files               │
│                                                                    │
│  TEMPLATE FILE: database.ctmpl                                     │
│  ─────────────────────────────                                     │
│  {{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}                │
│  DB_USER_DYNAMIC={{ .Data.username }}                             │
│  DB_PASS_DYNAMIC={{ .Data.password }}                             │
│  DB_LEASE={{ .LeaseDuration }}                                    │
│  {{- end }}                                                        │
│                                                                    │
│                    ↓ Agent processes template                      │
│                                                                    │
│  1. Agent calls: vault read database/creds/anihpj-role            │
│  2. Vault returns:                                                 │
│     {                                                              │
│       "data": {                                                    │
│         "username": "v-token-anihpj-x9F2kL",                     │
│         "password": "dynamic-pw-abc123"                           │
│       },                                                           │
│       "lease_duration": 3600,                                      │
│       "lease_id": "database/creds/anihpj-role/abc123"             │
│     }                                                              │
│  3. Template renders:                                              │
│                                                                    │
│  RENDERED FILE: /vault/secrets/database.env                        │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────                            │
│  DB_USER_DYNAMIC=v-token-anihpj-x9F2kL                           │
│  DB_PASS_DYNAMIC=dynamic-pw-abc123                                │
│  DB_LEASE=3600                                                     │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 Agent auto-renews lease at 66% of TTL (40 min)                │
│  💡 File written atomically — app never sees partial writes       │
│  💡 Agent can send SIGHUP to app on template change               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Template Functions Reference
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# CORE SECRET FUNCTIONS
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Fetch a single secret (KV v2 — note /data/ path)
{{- with secret "secret/data/anihpj" -}}
{{ .Data.data.key_name }}
{{- end }}

# Fetch a dynamic secret (DB, PKI, etc.)
{{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
{{ .Data.username }}  # Dynamic credential data
{{ .LeaseDuration }}  # TTL in seconds
{{ .LeaseID }}        # Lease identifier
{{- end }}

# Fetch a PKI certificate
{{- with secret "pki/issue/anihpj" "common_name=anihpj.local" "ttl=720h" -}}
{{ .Data.certificate }}
{{ .Data.private_key }}
{{ .Data.ca_chain }}
{{ .Data.serial_number }}
{{- end }}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# HELPER FUNCTIONS
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Range over a list of secrets
{{- range secrets "secret/metadata/anihpj/" -}}
{{ . }}  # Each item is a secret path
{{- end }}

# Conditionals
{{- if .Data.data.feature_flag -}}
FEATURE_ENABLED=true
{{- else -}}
FEATURE_ENABLED=false
{{- end }}

# Write to a file (useful for certificate files)
{{- with secret "pki/issue/anihpj" "common_name=anihpj.local" -}}
{{- file.Write "/vault/secrets/tls.crt" .Data.certificate }}
{{- file.Write "/vault/secrets/tls.key" .Data.private_key }}
{{- end }}

# Base64 encoding (for K8s Secrets or binary data)
{{ .Data.data.raw_key | base64Encode }}

# String manipulation
{{ .Data.data.host | replaceAll "localhost" "db.anihpj.svc" }}
⚡ SPEED TIP: Vault Agent Debugging — 5 Commands That Solve 90% of Issues

1. kubectl logs deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent — shows auth status, secret fetches, template renders.
2. kubectl exec deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent -- cat /vault/secrets/database.env — check rendered output.
3. kubectl exec deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent -- wget -qO- localhost:9090/metrics — Agent Prometheus metrics (if listener enabled).
4. kubectl describe pod anihpj-xxx | grep -A20 "vault.hashicorp" — verify injector annotations applied.
5. kubectl exec deploy/anihpj -c vault-agent -- cat /vault/token/.vault-token | xargs -I{} vault token lookup {} — verify token has correct policies.
These 5 commands will resolve 90% of Agent issues without needing to escalate.

15.3 Auto-Auth Methods for Agent

The Agent supports multiple auto-auth methods — choose based on where your workload runs.

Auto-Auth Configurations
# ═══ KUBERNETES (for pods) ═══
auto_auth {
  method "kubernetes" {
    mount_path = "auth/kubernetes"
    role       = "anihpj-app"
    # JWT auto-read from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  }
}

# ═══ APPROLE (for VMs / CI/CD) ═══
auto_auth {
  method "approle" {
    mount_path = "auth/approle"
    role_id_file_path   = "/vault/config/role-id"
    secret_id_file_path = "/vault/config/secret-id"
    # Or use response wrapping:
    # secret_id_response_wrapping_path = "/vault/config/wrapped-secret-id"
  }
}

# ═══ AWS (for EC2 instances) ═══
auto_auth {
  method "aws" {
    mount_path = "auth/aws"
    role       = "anihpj-ec2-role"
    type       = "ec2"
    # Uses instance identity document automatically
  }
}

# ═══ GCP (for GCE instances) ═══
auto_auth {
  method "gcp" {
    mount_path = "auth/gcp"
    role       = "anihpj-gce-role"
    type       = "gce"
  }
}

# ═══ AZURE (for Azure VMs) ═══
auto_auth {
  method "azure" {
    mount_path = "auth/azure"
    role       = "anihpj-azure-role"
    resource   = "https://management.azure.com/"
  }
}

15.4 Agent Caching and Performance

The Agent can cache secrets locally, reducing load on Vault and enabling limited offline operation. When Vault is unreachable, the Agent serves from cache — your app keeps running.

AGENT CACHE FLOW — App → Agent → Cache → Vault (only on miss)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🔄 AGENT CACHE — Reduces Vault Calls                  │
│                                                                    │
│  APP requests database.env                                         │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐                                          │
│  │  AGENT CACHE CHECK   │                                          │
│  │  Is secret cached?   │                                          │
│  └─────────┬───────────┘                                          │
│            │                                                        │
│     ┌──────┴──────┐                                                │
│     │             │                                                 │
│  ✅ HIT         ❌ MISS                                              │
│     │             │                                                 │
│     ▼             ▼                                                 │
│  Serve from    Call Vault                                           │
│  cache         ↓                                                    │
│  (instant)     Store in cache                                       │
│                ↓                                                    │
│                Serve                                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  CACHE CONFIG:                                                      │
│  ─────────────                                                      │
│  cache {                                                            │
│    use_auto_auth_token = true                                       │
│    persist "kubernetes" {                                           │
│      path = "/vault/cache"                                          │
│      keep_after_import = true                                       │
│      exit_on_err = false  # Don't crash if cache fails            │
│    }                                                                │
│  }                                                                  │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 If Vault is DOWN: Agent serves from cache (stale, but workable)│
│  💡 Persist across Agent restarts (disk-backed cache)              │
│  💡 Reduces Vault API calls by 90%+ in steady state               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.5 anihpj Complete Agent Configuration 🏗️

Here's the complete, production-ready Agent setup for anihpj — config file, templates, and K8s deployment with all annotations.

anihpj-agent-config.hcl — Production Complete
vault {
  address = "https://vault.vault.svc:8200"
}

auto_auth {
  method "kubernetes" {
    mount_path = "auth/kubernetes"
    role       = "anihpj-app"
  }
  sink "file" { path = "/vault/token/.vault-token" }
}

cache {
  use_auto_auth_token = true
}

# Template 1: Dynamic DB credentials
template {
  source = <<EOT
{{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
DATABASE_URL=postgres://{{ .Data.username }}:{{ .Data.password }}@postgres.anihpj.svc:5432/anihpj
LEASE_DURATION={{ .LeaseDuration }}
{{- end }}
  EOT
  destination = "/vault/secrets/database.env"
}

# Template 2: Static API keys
template {
  source = <<EOT
{{- with secret "anihpj/data/api" -}}
SENDGRID_KEY={{ .Data.data.sendgrid_key }}
TWILIO_SID={{ .Data.data.twilio_sid }}
{{- end }}
  EOT
  destination = "/vault/secrets/apikeys.env"
}

# Template 3: Django settings
template {
  source = <<EOT
{{- with secret "anihpj/data/django" -}}
SECRET_KEY={{ .Data.data.secret_key }}
DEBUG={{ .Data.data.debug }}
ALLOWED_HOSTS={{ .Data.data.allowed_hosts }}
{{- end }}
  EOT
  destination = "/vault/secrets/django.env"
}

pid_file = "/vault/pid/agent.pid"

📝 Chapter 15 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q141
What are the four main sections of a Vault Agent configuration file?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. vault: Vault server address, CA cert, TLS settings. 2. auto_auth: How the agent authenticates (method + sink). 3. template: Source template + destination file path (multiple allowed). 4. cache: Local caching for performance and resiliency. Optional: pid_file for signalling, exit_after_auth for one-shot mode, listener for Agent API.

EXPLANATION

Think of the config as: WHERE is Vault (vault), HOW do I log in (auto_auth), WHAT secrets do I need (template), and HOW do I optimize (cache).

Q142
What does {{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}} do, and what variables become available?
Show Answer
ANSWER

It fetches the secret at the given path and sets the response as the template context (.). Available variables: .Data.username, .Data.password (dynamic credentials), .LeaseDuration (TTL in seconds), .LeaseID (unique lease identifier), .Renewable (boolean), .RequestID (audit correlation ID). The {{- strips leading whitespace.

EXPLANATION

For KV v2: use {{- with secret "secret/data/anihpj" -}} and access with {{ .Data.data.key_name }} (note the extra .data). For DB/PKI: use {{ .Data.username }} (single .data). This is a common exam gotcha!

Q143
How does Agent caching work, and why is it important for production?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The Agent cache intercepts secret requests: if the secret is in cache and not expired, serve from cache (instant). If not cached or expired, call Vault, store in cache, then serve. Benefits: (1) Reduces Vault API load by 90%+ in steady state, (2) Enables limited offline operation — if Vault is temporarily down, apps still get secrets from cache, (3) Persistent cache survives Agent restarts. Configure with cache { persist "kubernetes" { path = "/vault/cache" } }.

EXPLANATION

Critical for production: without caching, 100 pods refreshing secrets every 20 minutes = 300 Vault API calls/hour. With caching, each unique secret is fetched ONCE and served from cache to all pods sharing the same Agent.

Q144
How do you configure Agent auto-auth for a workload running on AWS EC2?
Show Answer
ANSWER
auto_auth {
  method "aws" {
    mount_path = "auth/aws"
    role       = "anihpj-ec2-role"
    type       = "ec2"
    # Uses EC2 instance identity document (PKCS7 signature)
    # No credentials needed — identity from AWS metadata service
  }
}
EXPLANATION

The AWS auth method uses the EC2 instance's signed identity document — a cryptographically signed statement from AWS saying "this is instance i-abc123." Vault verifies the signature against AWS's public certificate. Zero credentials are stored on the instance.

Q145
What is the difference between .Data.data and .Data in Agent templates?
Show Answer
ANSWER

KV v2: Use {{ .Data.data.key_name }} — KV v2 wraps data in an extra data layer. The API path is secret/data/anihpj and the response structure is .Data.data.<key>. DB / PKI / Other engines: Use {{ .Data.username }} — no extra wrapping. The API path is database/creds/anihpj-role and the response structure is .Data.username. The double .Data.data for KV v2 is the #1 Agent template mistake.

EXPLANATION

Memory trick: KV v2 = 2 dots (.Data.data), other engines = 1 dot (.Data). This is tested on the exam — candidates mix them up and wonder why templates render empty.

Q146
What happens when the Agent's Vault token expires?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The Agent automatically re-authenticates using the configured auto_auth method. It detects the expired token, uses the same credentials (K8s SA JWT, AppRole SecretID, etc.) to get a new Vault token, then resumes fetching and rendering secrets. This is transparent to the application — at most, there's a brief delay while the new token is obtained. The sink file is updated with the new token.

EXPLANATION

This is why auto_auth is critical — without it, an expired token means the Agent stops working until manually restarted. With auto_auth, the Agent handles the entire re-authentication flow without human intervention.

Q147
How can the Agent signal an application that secrets have changed?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Use the command directive in the template block, combined with pid_file: the Agent writes its PID to pid_file, and the command can use this to signal the app. Example: command = "kill -HUP $(cat /vault/pid/app.pid)" sends SIGHUP to the app, which can reload its configuration. Alternatively, the app can watch the secret files for changes using inotify/kqueue.

EXPLANATION

Best practice: use file watching instead of signals. The Agent writes files atomically (write to temp, then rename), so file watchers detect the change reliably. Django, for example, doesn't reload on SIGHUP by default — file watching is more universal.

Q148
Write a complete Agent template that creates a Django settings.py-compatible environment file from three secret sources.
Show Answer
ANSWER
{{- with secret "anihpj/data/django" -}}
SECRET_KEY={{ .Data.data.secret_key }}
DEBUG={{ .Data.data.debug }}
ALLOWED_HOSTS={{ .Data.data.allowed_hosts }}
{{- end }}

{{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
DATABASE_URL=postgres://{{ .Data.username }}:{{ .Data.password }}@db:5432/anihpj
{{- end }}

{{- with secret "anihpj/data/api" -}}
SENDGRID_KEY={{ .Data.data.sendgrid_key }}
TWILIO_SID={{ .Data.data.twilio_sid }}
{{- end }}
EXPLANATION

This single template pulls from three sources: KV v2 (static Django settings), DB engine (dynamic credentials), and KV v2 (API keys). The Agent fetches all three, renders them into one file, and auto-renews the DB lease. The Django app reads /vault/secrets/django.env — done.

Q149
How do you configure the Agent for one-shot mode (exit after rendering)?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Use exit_after_auth = true in the top-level config. The Agent authenticates, fetches all secrets, renders all templates, and exits. This is useful for: (1) Init containers that prepare secrets before the app starts, (2) CI/CD pipelines that need secrets for one job, (3) Batch jobs that run to completion. For continuous operation (sidecar), omit this setting or set to false.

EXPLANATION

One-shot vs continuous: One-shot = fetch once, exit. Continuous = fetch, render, watch for changes, auto-renew. Use one-shot for init containers and batch jobs. Use continuous for long-running application sidecars.

Q150
Configure a complete Vault Agent with caching, two templates, and Kubernetes auto-auth for anihpj production.
Show Answer
ANSWER
vault { address = "https://vault.vault.svc:8200" }

auto_auth {
  method "kubernetes" { mount_path = "auth/kubernetes" role = "anihpj-app" }
  sink "file" { path = "/vault/token/.vault-token" }
}

cache {
  use_auto_auth_token = true
  persist "kubernetes" { path = "/vault/cache" }
}

template {
  source = <<EOT
{{- with secret "database/creds/anihpj-role" -}}
DB_USER={{ .Data.username }}
DB_PASS={{ .Data.password }}
{{- end }}
  EOT
  destination = "/vault/secrets/database.env"
}

template {
  source = <<EOT
{{- with secret "anihpj/data/api" -}}
SENDGRID={{ .Data.data.sendgrid_key }}
{{- end }}
  EOT
  destination = "/vault/secrets/api.env"
}
EXPLANATION

This config: authenticates via K8s SA, caches secrets on disk (survives restarts), renders two templates (dynamic DB + static API), and auto-renews. Store this as a ConfigMap and mount it at /vault/config/agent.hcl in the pod. The Agent reads it on startup automatically.

Chapter 16: Vault Secrets Operator and CSI Deep Dive 🎯

Beyond the Agent sidecar, HashiCorp provides two more Kubernetes-native integration patterns: the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) — a Kubernetes operator that syncs Vault secrets to native K8s Secrets using CRDs, and the CSI Provider — which mounts secrets directly as volumes. This chapter compares all three patterns and gives you the decision framework to choose the right one for any scenario.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🎯 VA Exam Topic 🔐 Ops Pro Bridge

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) and its CRDs
  • ✅ Master the CSI Provider configuration for file-based secrets
  • ✅ Compare all three patterns: Sidecar vs CSI vs VSO — when to use each
  • ✅ Build a production anihpj setup using all three patterns

16.1 Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) 🎯

The Vault Secrets Operator is a Kubernetes operator that watches Custom Resources (CRDs) and synchronizes Vault secrets into native Kubernetes Secrets. If your apps already consume K8s Secrets (via envFrom.secretRef or secretKeyRef), VSO lets you keep that pattern while getting Vault's security benefits.

YAML — VSO CRDs for anihpj
# ═══ VaultStaticSecret — Static KV v2 secrets ═══
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultStaticSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-database-config
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  vaultAuthRef: vault-auth
  mount: anihpj
  type: kv-v2
  path: database
  destination:
    name: anihpj-db-secret  # Creates this K8s Secret
    create: true
  refreshAfter: 1h          # Re-sync hourly

---
# ═══ VaultDynamicSecret — Dynamic DB credentials ═══
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultDynamicSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-creds
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  vaultAuthRef: vault-auth
  mount: database
  path: creds/anihpj-role
  destination:
    name: anihpj-db-dynamic
    create: true
  renewalPercent: 67  # Renew at 67% of TTL

---
# ═══ VaultPKISecret — TLS certificates ═══
apiVersion: secrets.hashicorp.com/v1beta1
kind: VaultPKISecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-tls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  vaultAuthRef: vault-auth
  mount: pki
  role: anihpj
  commonName: anihpj.local
  destination:
    name: anihpj-tls-cert
    create: true
  renewalPercent: 67
🎓 EXAM TIP

VSO creates native K8s Secrets from Vault. Key difference from Sidecar/CSI: secrets exist as K8s Secret objects (visible via kubectl get secrets). This means: (1) Apps using secretKeyRef work without changes, (2) Secrets are still base64-encoded in etcd (like any K8s Secret), (3) VSO continuously reconciles — if Vault secret changes, K8s Secret updates automatically.

16.2 CSI Provider Configuration — Full Setup

The CSI Provider was introduced in 14.3. Here's the complete setup from installation to pod configuration.

Bash — CSI Provider Installation
# Install CSI driver via Helm
helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver \
    https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver/charts
helm install csi secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver \
    --namespace kube-system

# Install Vault CSI Provider
helm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com
helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault \
    --set injector.enabled=true \
    --set csi.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.enabled=true \
    --set server.ha.replicas=3

# Verify CSI driver pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=secrets-store-csi-driver
kubectl get pods -n vault -l app.kubernetes.io/name=vault-csi-provider

16.3 Sidecar vs CSI vs Operator — Choosing the Right Pattern

📦 The Delivery Service Analogy — Three Ways to Get Secrets

Sidecar = Personal Shopper: You hire a dedicated assistant who goes to the warehouse (Vault), picks exactly what you need, wraps it the way you like (template rendering), and brings it to your desk. Most expensive, most personalized.
CSI = Locker Delivery: Packages appear in your assigned locker (volume mount). No assistant needed — the central delivery system (CSI driver) puts it there. You get what was sent, in the original packaging.
VSO = Bulletin Board: Important notices are posted on a shared board (K8s Secrets). Everyone with access can see them. Simple, familiar, but visible to anyone authorized for that board. Choose based on: how much you value personalization vs simplicity vs familiarity.

FeatureSidecar InjectorCSI ProviderVault Secrets Operator
Extra container?✅ Yes (sidecar)❌ No (CSI driver)❌ No (operator syncs)
Template rendering?✅ Full Go templates❌ Raw JSON/values❌ Raw K8s Secret keys
Auto-renewal?✅ Token + leases⚠️ Limited (v1.x)✅ CRD-specified
Output formatFiles in shared volumeFiles via CSI volumeK8s Secret objects
App changes needed?Read files from /vault/secrets/Read files from mountPath✅ None (uses K8s Secrets)
Secret visibilityOnly in pod memoryOnly in pod memoryIn etcd (base64)
ComplexityMediumLowMedium
Best forComplex config, dynamic secrets, multi-sourceStatic secrets, simple KVK8s-native apps, existing Secret consumers
🎯 DECISION TREE — Which Pattern Should You Use?

Sidecar: You need template rendering (env files, JSON configs), dynamic secret renewal, or multi-source aggregation. The most flexible option.
CSI: You want the simplest setup — static secrets as files, no extra containers, Kubernetes-native volumes.
VSO: Your apps already consume K8s Secrets (secretKeyRef) and you don't want to change application code. Easiest migration path.
HYBRID (recommended for production): Sidecar for complex applications (anihpj), VSO for simple services, CSI for one-off static secrets.

16.4 Production anihpj Vault Integration — End-to-End 🏗️

Here's the recommended production architecture: Sidecar for anihpj (complex Django app with dynamic DB + static KV + encryption keys), VSO for monitoring tools (Prometheus, Grafana — they need K8s Secrets), and CSI for simple config (nginx frontend that just needs a TLS cert).
