📝 Chapter 16 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q151
What is the Vault Secrets Operator and how does it differ from the Agent Sidecar?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The Vault Secrets Operator (VSO) is a Kubernetes operator that watches CRDs (VaultStaticSecret, VaultDynamicSecret, VaultPKISecret) and synchronizes Vault secrets into native K8s Secret objects. Key difference from Sidecar: VSO creates K8s Secrets (visible in etcd via kubectl get secrets), while Sidecar renders secrets to files in a pod-local volume (never stored in etcd). VSO is best for apps that already consume K8s Secrets.

EXPLANATION

VSO = "Make Vault look like K8s Secrets." Sidecar = "Make Vault secrets appear as files in my pod." CSI = "Mount Vault secrets as a volume." Three different approaches, three different trade-offs.

Q152
What are the three CRD types provided by the Vault Secrets Operator?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. VaultStaticSecret: Syncs static KV v1/v2 secrets to a K8s Secret. 2. VaultDynamicSecret: Syncs dynamic secrets (DB, cloud) with automatic renewal. 3. VaultPKISecret: Syncs PKI certificates with automatic renewal. Each CRD specifies a Vault path and a destination K8s Secret name. VSO continuously reconciles — changes in Vault are pushed to K8s.

EXPLANATION

The naming follows Vault's engine types: Static = KV (fixed values), Dynamic = DB/Cloud (short-lived, auto-renewed), PKI = certificates (auto-issued, auto-renewed).

Q153
Compare all three Vault-K8s integration patterns across: resource overhead, template support, and secret visibility.
Show Answer
ANSWER
AspectSidecarCSIVSO
Resource overhead1 extra container/pod1 DaemonSet/node1-2 operator pods/cluster
Template supportFull Go templatesNone — raw valuesNone — raw K8s keys
Secret visibilityPod memory onlyPod memory onlyK8s etcd (base64)
Best forComplex appsSimple staticK8s-native apps
EXPLANATION

The resource overhead difference matters at scale: 100 pods with sidecars = 200 containers. 100 pods with CSI = 100 containers + 1 DaemonSet per node. 100 pods with VSO = 100 containers + 2 operator pods total. Choose based on your tolerance for extra containers vs need for template rendering.

Q154
How does VSO handle dynamic secret renewal?
Show Answer
ANSWER

VSO continuously watches the Vault lease. The renewalPercent setting (default 67%) tells VSO to renew the lease when 67% of TTL has elapsed. On successful renewal, VSO updates the K8s Secret with the new credentials. If renewal fails (e.g., Vault unreachable), VSO retries and updates the CRD status. The K8s Secret is always kept in sync with Vault's current credential state.

EXPLANATION

VSO handles the entire dynamic secret lifecycle: create → sync to K8s Secret → monitor TTL → renew at 67% → update K8s Secret → repeat. Apps using secretKeyRef may need a restart or config reload to pick up new values — this is a K8s limitation, not VSO's.

Q155
When would you choose CSI Provider over Agent Sidecar?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Choose CSI when: (1) You want the simplest possible setup — no extra container per pod, (2) You only need static KV secrets (no dynamic renewal needed), (3) Your app can read raw JSON/files without template formatting, (4) Resource efficiency is critical (no sidecar overhead per pod), (5) You're running simple microservices or batch jobs that just need a few static values.

EXPLANATION

CSI is the "lightweight" option. It's perfect for nginx configs, static API keys in simple services, or TLS certificates where the file format is already what you need. For complex multi-source secret aggregation with .env formatting — use Sidecar.

Q156
What is the recommended hybrid architecture for production Vault on Kubernetes?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Use all three patterns based on workload needs: Sidecar for complex applications needing template rendering and dynamic secrets (e.g., anihpj Django app), VSO for Kubernetes-native tools that consume K8s Secrets (e.g., Prometheus, Grafana, cert-manager), and CSI for simple static secrets as files (e.g., nginx TLS certs, static config files). One Vault cluster serves all three patterns simultaneously.

EXPLANATION

Don't force one pattern on everything — match the pattern to the workload. This is the "right tool for the job" approach that HashiCorp recommends for production deployments.

Q157
What is the security trade-off of VSO creating native K8s Secrets?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Advantage: Apps consume secrets via standard K8s mechanisms (secretKeyRef, envFrom) — no application code changes needed. Disadvantage: Secrets exist as K8s Secret objects in etcd — they're base64-encoded (not encrypted) and visible to anyone with kubectl get secret -o yaml access in the namespace. Compare: Sidecar/CSI secrets only exist in pod memory and the shared volume (tmpfs) — never stored in etcd.

EXPLANATION

This is the fundamental trade-off: convenience (K8s-native Secrets) vs security (in-memory only). For highly sensitive secrets, use Sidecar/CSI. For lower-sensitivity config that's already managed via K8s Secrets, VSO is a great migration path to Vault.

Q158
How do you install the Vault CSI Provider on Kubernetes?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# Install Secrets Store CSI Driver
helm repo add secrets-store-csi-driver \
    https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/secrets-store-csi-driver/charts
helm install csi secrets-store-csi-driver/secrets-store-csi-driver \
    --namespace kube-system --set syncSecret.enabled=true

# Install Vault with CSI enabled
helm install vault hashicorp/vault \
    --namespace vault --create-namespace \
    --set csi.enabled=true
EXPLANATION

The Secrets Store CSI Driver is a Kubernetes project that provides the generic CSI interface. The Vault CSI Provider is a plugin that implements the provider-specific logic (auth, fetching, renewal). Both must be installed.

Q159
What happens when Vault is unreachable — how do the three patterns behave differently?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Sidecar: Agent serves from cache (if configured). App continues with last-known secrets. Agent retries Vault in background.
CSI: Existing mounts continue working from tmpfs cache. New pods fail to start (can't mount volume).
VSO: Last-synced K8s Secrets remain in etcd. Apps continue working. VSO retries reconciliation in background. New secrets won't be created/updated until Vault is reachable.

EXPLANATION

Resiliency ranking: VSO (K8s Secrets persist independently) > Sidecar with disk cache > Sidecar without cache > CSI. For maximum resiliency, use Sidecar with persistent cache OR VSO — both survive Vault outages gracefully.

Q160
Design a complete Vault-on-K8s architecture for anihpj: Django app (needs dynamic DB + static KV), Prometheus (needs K8s Secret), and nginx (needs TLS cert). Choose the right pattern for each.
Show Answer
ANSWER

anihpj Django: Agent Sidecar — needs template rendering (DATABASE_URL format), dynamic DB renewal, and multi-source aggregation (DB + KV + Transit).
Prometheus: Vault Secrets Operator — consumes K8s Secrets natively via secretKeyRef, zero code changes.
nginx: CSI Provider — just needs TLS cert as files at /etc/nginx/ssl/, simplest setup, no sidecar overhead.
ONE Vault HA cluster (3 nodes, Raft) with Kubernetes auth serves all three patterns simultaneously.

EXPLANATION

This is the production gold standard: match the pattern to the workload, not one-size-fits-all. Each pattern addresses a different need — and they all coexist on the same Vault cluster with the same policies, audit, and authentication.

🧯 Common Vault-on-Kubernetes Mistakes — And How to Avoid Them

💀 MISTAKE #1: Forgetting to Unseal All Vault Pods

Symptom: After deploying Vault HA on K8s, only vault-0 works. vault-1 and vault-2 show "sealed" status.
Why: In HA mode with Raft, EVERY pod must be unsealed individually. Unsealing vault-0 does NOT unseal vault-1 or vault-2.
Fix: Run vault operator unseal on each pod. For automation, use auto-unseal with cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CKMS, Azure Key Vault) or a Transit engine on a separate Vault cluster.

# Check seal status on ALL pods
for i in 0 1 2; do
    echo "vault-$i: $(kubectl exec -n vault vault-$i -- vault status -format=json | jq -r .sealed)"
done
# vault-0: false ✅
# vault-1: true  ❌ Still sealed!
# vault-2: true  ❌ Still sealed!

💀 MISTAKE #2: Agent Annotations on the Wrong Object

Symptom: Agent sidecar is NOT injected despite setting annotations.
Why: Annotations must be in spec.template.metadata.annotations (the Pod template), NOT in the Deployment's top-level metadata.annotations. The webhook modifies Pod specs, not Deployments.
Fix: Place annotations under spec.template.metadata.annotations:

# ❌ WRONG — annotations at Deployment level (ignored!)
metadata:
  annotations:
    vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"

# ✅ CORRECT — annotations at Pod template level
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"

💀 MISTAKE #3: K8s Auth Role Not Matching ServiceAccount

Symptom: Agent fails to authenticate: "service account name not authorized."
Why: The K8s auth role's bound_service_account_names and bound_service_account_namespaces must EXACTLY match the pod's ServiceAccount. A typo in the SA name or namespace = auth failure.
Fix: Verify with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}' and ensure it matches the Vault role.

💀 MISTAKE #4: Using VSO Without Understanding the Security Trade-off

VSO creates native K8s Secrets — they're base64-encoded, visible via kubectl get secret -o yaml, and stored in etcd. If you use VSO for highly sensitive secrets (database passwords, API keys), you're back to the same base64 problem that K8s Secrets have. VSO is best for medium-sensitivity config where convenience matters more than maximum secrecy. For high-security secrets, use Sidecar or CSI — secrets never touch etcd.

🛡️ PART 6 PRODUCTION CHECKLIST — Deploying Vault on K8s Safely

✅ Vault deployed in HA mode (3+ nodes, Raft)
✅ All pods unsealed (verify with vault status on each)
✅ K8s auth configured and tested from inside a pod
✅ Pod annotations at correct level (spec.template.metadata.annotations)
✅ ServiceAccount names match between K8s and Vault roles
✅ Policies follow least privilege per workload
✅ Agent caching enabled for resiliency
✅ Audit devices enabled on Vault (file + socket)
✅ Backup strategy in place (Raft snapshots — see Part 7)
✅ Resource limits set on Vault pods (CPU: 500m-2000m, Memory: 512Mi-2Gi)

Follow this step-by-step blueprint to go from zero to production-ready Vault on Kubernetes.

📋 Part 6 — Key Takeaways for the Exam

  • ✅ K8s Secrets = base64, NOT encrypted — Vault adds encryption, ACL, audit, rotation
  • ✅ Three patterns: Sidecar (flexible), CSI (lightweight), VSO (K8s-native Secrets)
  • ✅ Agent Injector: Mutating webhook, triggered by pod annotations
  • ✅ Agent Auto-Auth: K8s SA JWT → TokenReview API → Vault token
  • ✅ Templates: KV v2 = .Data.data, dynamic = .Data — know the difference!
  • ✅ K8s Auth external: Need host + reviewer_jwt + ca_cert explicitly
  • ✅ HA deploy: Helm, 3 replicas, Raft, unseal ALL pods individually
  • ✅ Cache: Enables offline operation, reduces Vault load by 90%+
  • ✅ Hybrid approach: Match pattern to workload — Sidecar for complex, VSO for simple
  • ✅ Never commit: Secrets stay in Vault — apps read from files, K8s Secrets, or CSI mounts

17.1 Vault CLI — Complete Command Reference

🔐 Operator Commands — Cluster Administration

Bash — Operator Commands with Context
# INITIALIZE: Creates encryption keys + root token (do ONCE)
vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3
# Unseal Keys: 5 total, 3 needed to unseal
# Root Token: s.xxxxxxxxxx (SAVE SECURELY!)

# UNSEAL: Required after every restart
vault operator unseal <unseal-key-1>
vault operator unseal <unseal-key-2>
vault operator unseal <unseal-key-3>
# → Sealed: false — Vault is now operational

# SEAL: Emergency lockdown (stops ALL access)
vault operator seal
# → Sealed: true — ALL operations blocked

# RAFT: Manage the integrated storage cluster
vault operator raft list-peers
# Node       Address              State     Voter
# vault-0    vault-0.vault:8201   leader    true
# vault-1    vault-1.vault:8201   follower  true

vault operator raft remove-peer vault-2
# Remove a failed node from the cluster

# STEP-DOWN: Force leader to become follower
vault operator step-down
# → Current leader steps down, election triggered

# ROTATE: Rotate the encryption key (re-encrypts all data)
vault operator rotate
# → New key becomes active, old keys retained for decryption

# DIAGNOSE: Check for cluster issues
vault operator diagnose
# Checks: TLS, storage, HA status, clock skew

🔌 Secrets Engine Commands — Managing Secret Backends

Bash — Secrets Engine Management
# ENABLE: Activate a secrets engine
vault secrets enable kv              # Default path: kv/
vault secrets enable -path=anihpj kv-v2  # Custom path
vault secrets enable -path=pki pki       # PKI at pki/
vault secrets enable database            # DB at database/

# LIST: See all enabled engines
vault secrets list
# Path          Type         Description
# anihpj/       kv           n/a
# cubbyhole/    cubbyhole    per-token private storage
# database/     database     n/a
# secret/       kv           key/value v2
# sys/          system       system endpoints

# TUNE: Modify engine configuration
vault secrets tune -default-lease-ttl=1h database/
vault secrets tune -max-lease-ttl=24h database/
vault secrets tune -description="anihpj production secrets" anihpj/

# MOVE: Rename an engine (preserves data)
vault secrets move anihpj/ anihpj-v2/
# → All secrets at anihpj/ now at anihpj-v2/

# DISABLE: Remove an engine (IRREVERSIBLE — deletes ALL data!)
vault secrets disable anihpj-old/
# ⚠️ All secrets at this path are PERMANENTLY deleted!
⚡ SPEED TIP: The 5 Commands You'll Run Daily

vault status — Is Vault sealed? Healthy?
vault secrets list — What engines are enabled?
vault auth list — What auth methods exist?
vault operator raft list-peers — Is the cluster healthy?
vault audit list — Are audit devices enabled?
Run these 5 commands every morning and you'll catch 90% of issues before users notice.

17.2 Vault API — HTTP Reference

Everything the CLI does, the HTTP API also does. The API is RESTful, uses JSON, and requires a Vault token in the X-Vault-Token header. Knowing the API is essential for automation, CI/CD, and custom integrations.

Bash — Vault API via curl
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# API BASICS — Authentication Header
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
export VAULT_ADDR="https://vault.anihpj.com:8200"
export VAULT_TOKEN="s.xxxxxxxxxx"

# Every API call requires the token header:
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# READ SECRETS (GET requests)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# KV v2 read
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/anihpj/data/database

# Dynamic DB credentials
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/database/creds/anihpj-role

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# WRITE SECRETS (POST/PUT requests)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Write KV v2 secret
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -X POST \
     -d '{"data":{"db_user":"anihpj","db_host":"postgres"}}' \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/anihpj/data/database

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# SYSTEM ENDPOINTS
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Health check
curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health
# {"initialized":true,"sealed":false,"standby":false,...}

# Seal status
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/seal-status

# List auth methods
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/auth

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# RESPONSE WRAPPING (via API)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
curl -H "X-Vault-Token: $VAULT_TOKEN" \
     -H "X-Vault-Wrap-TTL: 60s" \
     -X POST \
     $VAULT_ADDR/v1/auth/approle/role/anihpj-app/secret-id
# Returns wrapping token instead of raw secret
📋 API vs CLI vs UI — When to Use Each

CLI: Interactive operations, debugging, manual administration. Faster for one-off commands.
API: Automation scripts, CI/CD pipelines, custom applications, monitoring integrations.
UI: Visual exploration, quick status checks, secret browsing, policy inspection. Great for learning and demonstrations.

17.2b Vault Web UI — Visual Management Interface

The Vault UI is a web-based interface that ships with Vault (no extra installation needed). It provides a visual way to manage secrets, auth methods, policies, and monitor cluster health. It's enabled by adding ui = true to your Vault config file.

🖥️ Enable the UI
# In vault-config.hcl:
listener "tcp" {
  address = "0.0.0.0:8200"
  tls_cert_file = "/etc/vault.d/cert.pem"
  tls_key_file  = "/etc/vault.d/key.pem"
}

ui = true  # ← Enable the Web UI

# Access: https://vault-server:8200/ui
🧭 UI Capabilities
  • Secrets: Browse, create, edit, and delete secrets in any engine
  • Access: Manage auth methods, entities, groups, and policies
  • Policies: Visual policy editor with ACL template hints
  • Tokens: Create, lookup, and revoke tokens
  • Monitoring: View cluster health, seal status, Raft peers
  • Tools: Wrap/unwrap data, generate TOTP codes
💡 UI for Exam Preparation

While the exam is CLI/API-focused, using the UI during study helps visualize concepts. Seeing policies visually, browsing the secrets engines hierarchy, and watching the seal/unseal flow in the UI reinforces your mental model. The UI also helps verify your CLI operations — write a secret via CLI, then confirm it appears in the UI.

⚠️ UI Authentication

The UI authenticates the same way as the CLI — you need a valid Vault token. The UI login screen supports all enabled auth methods: Token, AppRole, Kubernetes, OIDC, Userpass, etc. After login, your browser stores the token in memory (not localStorage) for security. Refreshing the page requires re-authentication.

17.3 Monitoring Vault — Health Checks and Metrics

Monitoring Vault is about answering three questions: Is it up? (health check), Is it sealed? (seal status), Is it performing? (metrics).

Bash — Health & Monitoring Commands
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# HEALTH CHECKS
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Quick status
vault status
# Key             Value
# Seal Type       shamir
# Initialized     true
# Sealed          false
# HA Enabled      true
# HA Mode         active
# Version         1.18.0

# Health endpoint (200 = healthy, 429 = unsealed/standby, 501 = not init)
curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health
curl "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health?standbyok=true"  # Accept standby
curl "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health?perfstandbyok=true"  # Accept perf standby

# Raft peer health
vault operator raft list-peers
# Verify: all voters show "true", leader identified

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# KEY METRICS (enabled in config)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# In vault config:
# telemetry {
#   prometheus_retention_time = "30s"
#   disable_hostname = true
# }

# Scrape endpoint:
curl http://vault:8200/v1/sys/metrics?format=prometheus
# vault_core_unsealed 1
# vault_core_handle_request_count{...}
# vault_runtime_alloc_bytes 1.2e+08
# vault_raft_leader 1
🟢
Critical Metrics to Alert On

vault_core_unsealed != 1 → Vault is sealed!
vault_core_handle_request_count sudden drop → Possible outage
vault_raft_leader no node = 1 → No leader elected
vault_runtime_alloc_bytes trend up → Memory leak?

📊
Recommended Dashboards

• Vault Cluster Overview (seal status, HA mode, peers)
• Vault Request Rate (by path, method, status code)
• Vault Token Operations (create, renew, revoke rate)
• Vault Storage (Raft snapshot size, commit index)
• Vault Audit (events/sec, file size)

17.4 Vault Logs and Debugging

When Vault misbehaves, the audit log tells you what happened and the server log tells you why. Together they provide complete forensic visibility.

Bash — Log & Debug Commands
# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# AUDIT LOGS (every request — who, what, when)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# Enable audit device
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log

# Enable socket audit (→ Splunk, Logstash, Elasticsearch)
vault audit enable socket address=logstash:9090 socket_type=tcp

# View audit log
tail -f /var/log/vault/audit.log | jq .
# {
#   "time": "2025-01-15T10:30:00Z",
#   "type": "response",
#   "auth": {
#     "client_token": "s.xxxxxxxxxx",
#     "policies": ["anihpj-app", "default"],
#     "metadata": {"service_account_name": "anihpj-sa"}
#   },
#   "request": {
#     "path": "anihpj/data/database",
#     "operation": "read"
#   },
#   "response": {"data": {"data": {...}}}
# }

# ═══════════════════════════════════════
# SERVER LOGS (Vault process output)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════

# systemd journal
journalctl -u vault -f

# Docker / K8s
kubectl logs -n vault vault-0 -f

# Increase log level for debugging
# In config: log_level = "debug"  (or "trace" for maximum)
# Default: "info"

⚠️ GOTCHA: Audit Logs Are Tamper-Proof

Vault audit logs are append-only — you cannot delete or modify entries. This is a security feature (tamper-proof audit trail), but it means logs grow indefinitely. Always configure log rotation: log_rotation_max_files=10 log_rotation_bytes=104857600 (100 MB × 10 files = 1 GB max).

17.5 Resource Quotas and Rate Limiting

In production, Vault needs to protect itself from noisy neighbors — one misconfigured application should not degrade Vault for everyone. Rate limiting controls how many requests per second a client can make.

HCL — Rate Limiting Configuration
# In Vault config file:
# Limit: Maximum 100 requests/second
# Burst: Allow short bursts up to 200

api_proxy {
  use_auto_auth_token = true
}

# Rate limiting for specific paths
# Priority: most specific → general
limit {
  rate  = 100   # Requests per second (sustained)
  burst = 200   # Burst allowance (temporary spike)
}

# Per-path rate limiting (Enterprise):
# path "sys/*" {
#   rate  = 10
#   burst = 20
# }

✅ Operations Health Check — Daily Checklist

  • ✅ vault status — Sealed: false, Initialized: true
  • ✅ vault operator raft list-peers — All peers healthy, leader elected
  • ✅ vault audit list — Audit devices enabled and logging
  • ✅ Check disk usage: du -sh /vault/data/ — below 80% capacity
  • ✅ Verify backup ran: check S3/GCS for latest snapshot
  • ✅ vault token lookup — Test token still valid
  • ✅ Check Prometheus: no active alerts for Vault

17.6 Vault Configuration Parameters — Production Essentials

Beyond the basic storage and listener stanzas, Vault has dozens of configuration parameters that control its behavior. Understanding these is critical for both the exam and production operations.

🔑 Essential Configuration Parameters

ParameterDefaultPurposeExam Note
default_lease_ttl768h (32 days)Default TTL for tokens and secrets when not specifiedCan be overridden per mount via vault secrets tune
max_lease_ttl768h (32 days)Absolute ceiling — no token or secret can exceed thisSet lower in production (e.g., 720h = 30 days)
disable_mlockRequiredWhen true, disables the mlock() syscallMUST be true with Raft/BoltDB! See gotcha below.
cache_size131072 entriesSize of physical storage read cacheLarger = faster reads, more RAM used
disable_cachefalseDisables ALL caches — severe performance impactOnly for debugging, never in production
log_level"info"Log verbosity: trace, debug, info, warn, errorCan be changed at runtime via SIGHUP
log_format"standard"Log output format: "standard" or "json"Use "json" for log aggregation systems
default_max_request_duration90sMaximum time before Vault cancels a requestPrevents hung requests from exhausting resources
pid_file""Path to write the Vault process PIDUseful for systemd and monitoring scripts
cluster_nameauto-generatedHuman-readable cluster identifierAppears in telemetry metrics as a label
enable_response_header_hostnamefalseAdds X-Vault-Hostname header to responsesUseful for identifying which node served a request
enable_response_header_raft_node_idfalseAdds X-Vault-Raft-Node-ID header to responsesShows which Raft node handled the request
raw_storage_endpointfalseEnables sys/raw — raw barrier decryptionHighly privileged! Never enable in production.
uifalseEnables the built-in Web UI at /uiBrowser auto-redirects from API address to /ui
⚠️ CRITICAL: disable_mlock and Raft/BoltDB

With integrated storage (Raft), you MUST set disable_mlock = true. Raft uses BoltDB, which memory-maps files. When mlock is enabled with BoltDB, the entire dataset gets loaded into resident memory — causing out-of-memory crashes when data exceeds available RAM. Even when mlock is disabled, data in BoltDB remains encrypted at rest. On Linux, to use mlock (for non-Raft setups), run: sudo setcap cap_ipc_lock=+ep $(which vault). For systemd, add LimitMEMLOCK=infinity to the [Service] section.

🔊 Listener Types — TCP and Unix Socket

🌐 TCP Listener (Production Standard)
listener "tcp" {
  address       = "0.0.0.0:8200"
  tls_cert_file = "/etc/vault.d/cert.pem"
  tls_key_file  = "/etc/vault.d/key.pem"
  tls_min_version = "tls12"
  
  # Optional: rate limiting per listener
  max_request_size = 33554432  # 32MB
  max_request_duration = "90s"
  
  # Proxy protocol support (behind load balancer)
  proxy_protocol_behavior = "use_always"
}
🔌 Unix Socket Listener (Local Only)
listener "unix" {
  path         = "/var/run/vault/vault.sock"
  mode         = "0600"
  user         = "vault"
  group        = "vault"
  
  tls_disable  = true  # Local only, TLS optional
}

# Use with CLI:
# export VAULT_ADDR="unix:///var/run/vault/vault.sock"
# vault status

Use case: Sidecar communication on the same host. No network exposure, no TLS overhead, secure by filesystem permissions. Ideal for Vault Agent on the same machine.

📊 Telemetry Providers — Prometheus, StatsD, and More

ProviderConfig ParameterBest For
Prometheusprometheus_retention_time = "30s"Modern monitoring stacks, Grafana dashboards
StatsDstatsd_address = "statsd:8125"Legacy monitoring, Datadog agent
DogStatsDdogstatsd_addr = "127.0.0.1:8125"Datadog with tags support
Circonuscirconus_api_token = "..."Circonus monitoring platform
Stackdriverstackdriver_project_id = "my-project"Google Cloud Monitoring
Prometheus Metric Filtering (Vault 1.15+)
telemetry {
  prometheus_retention_time = "30s"
  disable_hostname = true
  
  # Filter which metrics to include/exclude
  filter_default = false  # Start with nothing
  prefix_filter = [
    "+vault.core",          # Include core metrics
    "+vault.token",         # Include token metrics
    "+vault.expire",        # Include lease metrics
    "+vault.raft",          # Include Raft metrics
    "-vault.core.lock"      # Exclude lock metrics
  ]
}

📝 Chapter 17 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q161
What are the five main command categories in the Vault CLI?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. vault operator: Cluster administration (init, unseal, seal, raft, step-down, rotate, diagnose). 2. vault secrets: Secrets engine management (enable, disable, list, tune, move). 3. vault auth: Auth method management (enable, disable, list, tune, login). 4. vault token: Token lifecycle (create, lookup, renew, revoke, capabilities). 5. vault policy: Policy management (write, read, list, delete, fmt).

EXPLANATION

Think of them as: operator = "admin the cluster", secrets = "manage secret backends", auth = "manage login methods", token = "manage access tokens", policy = "manage ACL rules".

Q162
What does vault operator unseal do and how many keys are typically needed?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault operator unseal provides a Shamir unseal key to decrypt the master key in memory. The number of keys needed depends on the -key-threshold set during vault operator init. For a -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3 setup, you need 3 out of 5 unseal keys. After providing the threshold number of keys, Vault transitions from "Sealed: true" to "Sealed: false" and becomes operational.

EXPLANATION

In HA mode, EVERY node must be unsealed individually. Unsealing vault-0 does NOT unseal vault-1. For production with auto-unseal (cloud KMS), this process is automated — Vault unseals itself on startup by calling the KMS API.

Q163
How do you check Vault's health via the HTTP API?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# Basic health check (no auth needed)
curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health
# HTTP 200 = healthy (initialized, unsealed, active)
# HTTP 429 = unsealed but standby node
# HTTP 501 = not initialized
# HTTP 503 = sealed

# Accept standby nodes as healthy
curl "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health?standbyok=true"

# Accept performance standby as healthy
curl "$VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health?perfstandbyok=true"
EXPLANATION

The health endpoint is designed for load balancers. A load balancer should use ?standbyok=true to route to standby nodes (they can handle read requests) but prefer the active node. The response body includes: initialized, sealed, standby, performance_standby, replication_dr_mode, version.

Q164
What is the difference between vault operator seal and Vault sealing on restart?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault operator seal: Manual emergency lockdown. Discards the master key from memory, immediately blocking ALL operations. Used when a security incident is suspected — instant, irreversible without unseal keys.
Seal on restart: Automatic — Vault always starts sealed. The master key is only in memory, so a restart clears it. Normal operation — unseal with keys to resume.

EXPLANATION

Key exam point: vault operator seal is an emergency action. It does NOT stop the Vault process — Vault keeps running but rejects all requests. To resume, you must unseal again with the threshold number of keys. Think of it as "panic button" for the Vault operator.

Q165
How do you view the Vault audit log and what information does it contain?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Each audit log entry is a JSON object containing: time (timestamp), type (request/response), auth (client_token, policies, metadata, entity_id), request (path, operation, remote_address, data — sensitive fields HMAC'ed), response (data — sensitive fields HMAC'ed, auth info), error (if any). The audit log is append-only and tamper-proof — you cannot modify or delete entries.

EXPLANATION

HMAC'ing sensitive fields means you can verify "was this value accessed?" without storing the actual secret in plaintext in the audit log. The HMAC is computed with the audit device's HMAC key — only someone with access to the audit log AND the HMAC key can verify values.

Q166
What are the critical Prometheus metrics to monitor for Vault?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault_core_unsealed: MUST = 1 (alert if 0 — Vault is sealed!). vault_core_handle_request_count: Track request rate. vault_raft_leader: Exactly 1 node should have this = 1. vault_runtime_alloc_bytes: Memory usage — watch for steady increase (leak). vault_route_create_ metrics: Token/create, secret/create rates — spot abnormal patterns.

EXPLANATION

Set up alerts: (1) vault_core_unsealed == 0 → CRITICAL — Vault is sealed, all operations blocked. (2) vault_raft_leader no node with value 1 → CRITICAL — no leader elected. (3) Request rate drops to 0 → WARNING — possible connectivity issue.

Q167
How do you enable an audit device and what types are available?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# File audit (local disk)
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log

# Socket audit (→ Splunk, Logstash, Elasticsearch)
vault audit enable socket address=logstash:9090 socket_type=tcp

# Syslog audit (→ SIEM)
vault audit enable syslog tag="vault" facility="AUTH"

# List enabled audit devices
vault audit list
# Path     Type    Description
# file/    file    n/a
# socket/  socket  n/a
EXPLANATION

Best practice: Enable at least TWO audit devices — one file (local, always available) and one socket (remote, for centralized logging). If either fails to write, Vault stops processing requests (audit is a critical path).

Q168
What happens when Vault runs out of disk space for the Raft storage?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Vault's Raft storage writes to /vault/data/. If the disk fills up: (1) Raft log compaction fails, (2) The Raft log grows unbounded, (3) Eventually Vault cannot accept new writes — it becomes read-only, (4) In extreme cases, the node crashes and may not restart. Prevention: monitor disk usage, set up alerts at 80% capacity, configure automated Raft snapshotting which triggers log compaction.

EXPLANATION

Raft snapshotting is both a backup mechanism AND a log compaction mechanism. After a snapshot, Raft truncates the log — freeing disk space. Run vault operator raft snapshot save regularly to keep the Raft log compact.

Q169
How does the Vault HTTP API handle authentication?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Every API request requires the X-Vault-Token header with a valid Vault token. The token is validated on every request — Vault checks: (1) Token exists and is not revoked, (2) Token has not expired (TTL), (3) Token's policies allow the requested operation on the requested path. If any check fails, Vault returns HTTP 403 Forbidden. For login endpoints, the token header is not required — the response includes a new token.

EXPLANATION

The API mirrors the CLI exactly — vault read secret/foo = curl -H "X-Vault-Token: ..." $VAULT_ADDR/v1/secret/data/foo. The /v1/ prefix is the API version. All API paths match CLI paths with /v1/ prepended.

Q170
Perform a complete health assessment: check seal status, raft peers, audit devices, and token validity.
Show Answer
ANSWER
# 1. Seal status
vault status
# → Sealed: false, Initialized: true ✅

# 2. Raft peers
vault operator raft list-peers
# → All peers present, leader elected ✅

# 3. Audit devices
vault audit list
# → file/ + socket/ enabled ✅

# 4. Token validity
vault token lookup
# → TTL > 0, policies listed ✅

# 5. Secrets engines
vault secrets list
# → All expected engines present ✅

# 6. Auth methods
vault auth list
# → All expected methods enabled ✅

# 7. API health
curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health
# → HTTP 200 ✅
EXPLANATION

This 7-step health assessment should be automated and run every 5 minutes in production. If ALL checks pass, Vault is operational. If ANY check fails: (1) seal → unseal, (2) raft peer missing → investigate node, (3) audit missing → re-enable, (4) token invalid → re-authenticate.

⏱️ 5 minutes
Scenario: Production Health Assessment

You receive a PagerDuty alert: "Vault may be degraded." Run a complete 7-point health assessment and determine if Vault is operational.

  1. Check seal status
  2. Verify Raft peers
  3. Confirm audit devices
  4. Test token validity
  5. List secrets engines
  6. List auth methods
  7. Hit the health endpoint
💡 Hint: vault status, vault operator raft list-peers, vault audit list, vault token lookup, vault secrets list, vault auth list, curl $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health
▼ Solution
echo "=== HEALTH ASSESSMENT ==="
vault status && echo "✅ Status OK"
vault operator raft list-peers && echo "✅ Raft OK"
vault audit list && echo "✅ Audit OK"
vault token lookup && echo "✅ Token OK"
vault secrets list && echo "✅ Engines OK"
vault auth list && echo "✅ Auth OK"
curl -s $VAULT_ADDR/v1/sys/health && echo "✅ API OK"
echo "=== ALL CHECKS PASSED ==="

Chapter 18: Vault Backup, Restore, and Disaster Recovery 🎯🔐

If Vault holds all your secrets, losing Vault means losing everything — database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, encryption keys. This chapter covers the three pillars of Vault resilience: Raft snapshots (backup), raft restore (recovery), and DR replication (continuous protection across regions). This is not optional knowledge — it's survival knowledge.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 VA Exam Topic 🔐 Ops Pro Critical

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Create Raft snapshots for backup — manual and automated (K8s CronJob)
  • ✅ Restore Vault from a Raft snapshot — complete step-by-step procedure
  • ✅ Configure Disaster Recovery (DR) replication across regions
  • ✅ Understand Performance replication and when to use it
  • ✅ Build an automated backup strategy with retention policies
  • ✅ Design the complete anihpj backup and DR strategy
🎓 VAULT ASSOCIATE RELEVANCE
Domain 5: Operations 12% Domain 4: Architecture 15%

18.1 Raft Snapshots — Backup Strategy 🎯

💡 The Two Insurance Policies You Need

Think of Vault backup like insurance for your house. You need TWO policies: Snapshots = Fire Insurance (recover everything after catastrophic loss — restore the entire Vault state). DR Replication = Moving to a Hotel (immediately continue operations from another location when your primary is unavailable). You wouldn't own a house worth millions without insurance. Don't run Vault with all your secrets without both backups AND DR.

A Raft snapshot is a point-in-time copy of Vault's entire state — all secrets, policies, tokens, identities, and configuration. Snapshots are encrypted with Vault's barrier key, so the snapshot file itself is protected even if stored in an untrusted location.

RAFT SNAPSHOT BACKUP — Complete Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              💾 RAFT SNAPSHOT BACKUP — The Safe Way                │
│                                                                    │
│  $ vault operator raft snapshot save /backup/vault.snap           │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  VAULT-1      │                    │  BACKUP STORAGE          │ │
│  │  (Active)     │                    │                          │ │
│  │               │                    │  S3 / GCS / NFS / MinIO  │ │
│  │  Raft DB      │──── snapshot ────▶│                          │ │
│  │  ┌─────────┐  │                    │  vault-20250115-1030.snap│ │
│  │  │Secrets  │  │                    │  vault-20250115-1630.snap│ │
│  │  │Policies │  │                    │  vault-20250116-1030.snap│ │
│  │  │Tokens   │  │                    │  ...                     │ │
│  │  │Identity │  │                    └──────────────────────────┘ │
│  │  │Config   │  │                                                 │
│  │  └─────────┘  │                                                 │
│  └──────────────┘                                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  WHAT'S IN THE SNAPSHOT:                                         │
│  ───────────────────────                                           │
│  ✅ All KV secrets (every version in KV v2)                        │
│  ✅ All policies + auth methods + roles                            │
│  ✅ All service tokens (batch tokens NOT included — they're not  │
│     stored in Vault)                                               │
│  ✅ All identity entities + groups + aliases                       │
│  ✅ All configuration (listeners, storage, seals, audit)           │
│  ✅ Encryption keys (still encrypted by the Vault barrier)         │
│                                                                    │
│  ⚠️ WHAT's NOT in the snapshot:                                  │
│  ───────────────────────────                                       │
│  ❌ Unseal keys (you MUST have these separately!)                  │
│  ❌ Batch tokens (not stored — encrypted in the token itself)      │
│  ❌ External storage data (Consul, integrated storage only)        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
YAML — K8s CronJob for Automated Backups
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: vault-backup
  namespace: vault
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"    # Every 6 hours
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 7
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: vault-backup-sa
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: hashicorp/vault:latest
            env:
            - name: VAULT_ADDR
              value: "https://vault-0.vault:8200"
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              vault login -method=kubernetes role=vault-backup
              vault operator raft snapshot save \
                /backup/vault-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).snap
              # Upload to S3 (if configured)
              aws s3 cp /backup/ s3://vault-backups/ --recursive
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
🎓 EXAM TIP

The exam expects you to know: (1) Raft snapshots are taken on the active node (leader), (2) Snapshots are encrypted with Vault's barrier — safe to store anywhere, (3) Batch tokens are NOT included in snapshots (they're not stored), (4) Unseal keys are NEVER in the snapshot — you must store them separately.

18.2 Raft Restore Procedures 🎯

Restoring from a snapshot is a destructive operation — it replaces ALL existing data. This is for disaster recovery, not for selective data recovery.

RAFT RESTORE — Complete Step-by-Step Procedure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🔄 RAFT RESTORE — Step-by-Step Recovery               │
│                                                                    │
│  SCENARIO: Vault cluster corrupted — need full restore            │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 1: STOP ALL VAULT NODES                                     │
│  ─────────────────────────────                                     │
│  $ kubectl scale sts vault --replicas=0 -n vault                  │
│  (or: systemctl stop vault on each node)                          │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 2: CLEAR EXISTING DATA (on ALL nodes)                       │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────                        │
│  $ rm -rf /vault/data/*                                           │
│  ⚠️ This deletes ALL current Vault data — make sure you have      │
│     the snapshot file accessible!                                  │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 3: RESTORE SNAPSHOT (on node that will be new leader)       │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────          │
│  $ vault operator raft snapshot restore \                         │
│      -force /backup/vault-20250115-1030.snap                      │
│  → Restored snapshot into /vault/data/                            │
│  → This node is now initialized with snapshot data                │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 4: START VAULT (on restored node only)                      │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────                      │
│  $ kubectl scale sts vault --replicas=1 -n vault                  │
│  (or: systemctl start vault)                                      │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 5: UNSEAL VAULT (NEED unseal keys from original cluster!)   │
│  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────        │
│  $ vault operator unseal <key1>                                  │
│  $ vault operator unseal <key2>                                  │
│  $ vault operator unseal <key3>                                  │
│  → Sealed: false — Vault is operational                            │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 6: JOIN OTHER NODES (scale up to desired replicas)          │
│  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
│  $ kubectl scale sts vault --replicas=3 -n vault                  │
│  → New nodes auto-join the restored leader                        │
│                                                                    │
│  ⚠️ CRITICAL: Without unseal keys = CANNOT restore = DATA LOST    │
│  ⚠️ Root token in snapshot = root token works after restore       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

💀 CRITICAL: Unseal Keys Are NOT in the Snapshot

The snapshot contains all Vault data encrypted by the barrier. To decrypt it, you need the unseal keys from the original cluster. If you lose BOTH the snapshot AND the unseal keys → complete data loss. If you lose the unseal keys but have the snapshot → cannot restore. Store unseal keys and snapshots in DIFFERENT secure locations.

18.3 Disaster Recovery (DR) Replication 🔐

DR replication continuously streams data from a primary cluster to one or more secondary clusters in different regions. If the primary region fails, you promote a secondary to become the new primary. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): seconds. RTO (Recovery Time Objective): minutes.

DR REPLICATION — Primary → Secondary Topology
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🌍 DISASTER RECOVERY REPLICATION — Multi-Region Setup      │
│                                                                    │
│  REGION: us-east-1 (PRIMARY)        REGION: eu-west-1 (SECONDARY) │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐    │       │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐    │   │
│  │ │Active │ │Standby│    │  DR   │ │Standby│ │Standby│    │   │
│  │ │ Vault │ │ Vault │    │ ────▶ │ │ Vault │ │ Vault │    │   │
│  │ │  🟢   │ │  ⚪   │    │stream │ │  ⚪   │ │  ⚪   │    │   │
│  │ └───────┘ └───────┘    │       │ └───────┘ └───────┘    │   │
│  │     Raft Cluster       │       │     Raft Cluster       │   │
│  └─────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                    │
│  CHARACTERISTICS:                                                  │
│  ────────────────                                                  │
│  ✅ ALL data replicated: secrets, policies, tokens, identity      │
│  ✅ Async replication (near real-time, typically <1 second lag)  │
│  ✅ Secondary is READ-ONLY (cannot write locally)                 │
│  ✅ PROMOTE: vault write -f sys/replication/dr/promote            │
│     → Secondary becomes PRIMARY (takes over all traffic)          │
│  ⚠️ Requires Vault Enterprise license                             │
│                                                                    │
│  SETUP COMMANDS:                                                   │
│  ───────────────                                                   │
│  # On PRIMARY:                                                     │
│  vault write sys/replication/dr/primary/enable                     │
│  vault write sys/replication/dr/primary/secondary-token \         │
│      id=eu-dr-secondary ttl=1h                                     │
│                                                                    │
│  # On SECONDARY:                                                   │
│  vault write sys/replication/dr/secondary/enable \                │
│      token=<secondary-token> \                                    │
│      primary_api_addr=https://vault-primary:8200                   │
│                                                                    │
│  🚨 DR PROMOTION (when primary region is DOWN):                    │
│  vault write -f sys/replication/dr/promote                        │
│  → eu-west-1 secondary is NOW the primary!                        │
│  → Update DNS: vault.anihpj.com → eu-west-1 IP                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

18.4 Performance Replication 🔐

Performance replication is for reducing latency, not disaster recovery. Secondaries handle read requests locally, reducing cross-region latency for global applications.

FeatureDR ReplicationPerformance Replication
PurposeDisaster recovery (survive region failure)Reduce latency (serve global users faster)
Secondary writes?❌ Read-only❌ Read-only (routed to primary)
Local reads?❌ No (must go to primary)✅ Yes (served from local)
Promotable?✅ Can become primary❌ Cannot become primary
Use caseRegion failure, data center outageGlobal apps, multi-region read scaling

18.5 Automated Backup Strategies

A manual backup is a forgotten backup. Automate it with a K8s CronJob (shown in 18.1) or a systemd timer. The key is: backup frequently, verify backups work, and retain according to a policy.

📦 Recommended Backup Retention Policy

Hourly: Keep 24 (last 24 hours) — vault-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.snap
Daily: Keep 7 (last week) — retained from the 00:00 backup each day
Weekly: Keep 4 (last month) — retained from Sunday backups
Monthly: Keep 3 (last quarter) — retained from the 1st of each month
Total: ~38 snapshots at any time, ~100 MB each with compression ≈ 4 GB total storage.

18.6 anihpj Backup and DR Strategy 🏗️

ANIHJP VAULT — Complete Backup & DR Strategy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        🛡️ anihpj/jobpost — Vault Backup & DR Strategy             │
│                                                                    │
│  BACKUP:                                                           │
│  ───────                                                           │
│  • Raft snapshot every 6 hours → S3 bucket (vault-backups)        │
│  • Retention: 7 daily + 4 weekly + 3 monthly                      │
│  • Encrypted: S3 SSE-KMS + Vault barrier encryption (dual layer)  │
│  • Automated: K8s CronJob (shown in 18.1)                         │
│  • Alert: If no backup in last 7 hours → PagerDuty critical       │
│                                                                    │
│  DISASTER RECOVERY:                                                │
│  ─────────────────                                                 │
│  • DR secondary in eu-west-1 (different AWS region)               │
│  • Async replication (typically <5 second lag)                   │
│  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): <5 seconds                     │
│  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): <15 minutes                     │
│                                                                    │
│  QUARTERLY DR DRILL:                                               │
│  ────────────────────                                              │
│  1. Simulate primary region failure (us-east-1 down)              │
│  2. Promote DR secondary → primary                                │
│  3. Update DNS: vault.anihpj.com → eu-west-1 IP                   │
│  4. Verify: anihpj pods auto-reconnect to new Vault primary       │
│  5. Verify: All secrets readable, DB dynamic creds work            │
│  6. Document: Time taken, issues found, improvements needed       │
│  7. Rollback: Demote → re-establish replication                   │
│                                                                    │
│  ⚠️ UNTESTED BACKUP = NO BACKUP. Test quarterly.                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 18 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q171
What does a Raft snapshot contain, and what is NOT included?
Show Answer
ANSWER

INCLUDED: All KV secrets (every version), all policies + auth methods + roles, all service tokens, all identity entities + groups + aliases, all configuration (listeners, storage, seals, audit), encryption keys (still encrypted by barrier). NOT INCLUDED: Unseal keys (you MUST store these separately!), batch tokens (not stored in Vault), external storage data.

EXPLANATION

The snapshot is a complete Vault state — but it's encrypted. Without the unseal keys, you cannot decrypt it. This is why storing unseal keys separately from snapshots is critical.

Q172
What are the 6 steps to restore Vault from a Raft snapshot?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Stop ALL Vault nodes. 2. Clear existing data (rm -rf /vault/data/*) on ALL nodes. 3. Restore snapshot on one node: vault operator raft snapshot restore -force <file>. 4. Start Vault on the restored node. 5. Unseal Vault with original unseal keys (3 of 5 threshold). 6. Join other nodes to the new cluster.

EXPLANATION

Critical points: (1) ALL nodes must be stopped and cleared — not just the leader, (2) The -force flag is required because restore is destructive, (3) You NEED the original unseal keys — they're not in the snapshot.

Q173
How does DR replication differ from Performance replication?
Show Answer
ANSWER

DR Replication: For disaster recovery. Secondary is read-only, can be promoted to primary when the primary region fails. All data replicated asynchronously.
Performance Replication: For reducing latency. Secondary can serve local reads but CANNOT be promoted to primary. Writes are forwarded to the primary. Best for global applications where users need fast read access from multiple regions.

EXPLANATION

Memory trick: DR = "can take over" (promotable). Performance = "can serve locally" (not promotable). If you need both, deploy DR replication for disaster recovery and add performance secondaries on top for read scaling.

Q174
How do you automate Raft snapshot backups on Kubernetes?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Use a Kubernetes CronJob that: (1) Runs a Vault container, (2) Authenticates via Kubernetes auth, (3) Runs vault operator raft snapshot save, (4) Uploads to S3/GCS. Schedule every 6 hours. The CronJob needs a ServiceAccount with a Vault policy allowing operator raft snapshot save (requires sudo or root).

EXPLANATION

Alternative: Use vault operator raft snapshot save from outside the cluster via a CI/CD pipeline. The key is that backups must be AUTOMATED — manual backups are forgotten backups.

Q175
What is the promotion process for a DR secondary when the primary fails?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Run vault write -f sys/replication/dr/promote on the DR secondary. This: (1) Makes the secondary writable, (2) Generates a new root token (optional), (3) Updates the secondary to primary status. After promotion: update DNS to point to the new primary, update application configurations, and (optionally) set up reverse replication if the old primary comes back online.

EXPLANATION

Promotion is a one-way operation — once promoted, the secondary becomes an independent primary. There's no automatic "failback" — you must manually re-establish replication if the old primary recovers.

Q176
What is the recommended backup retention policy for Vault snapshots?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Hourly: Keep 24 (last 24 hours). Daily: Keep 7 (last week). Weekly: Keep 4 (last month). Monthly: Keep 3 (last quarter). Total: ~38 snapshots. This balances recovery granularity with storage cost. Automate cleanup — delete snapshots older than the retention window.

EXPLANATION

Why this policy? If a secret was accidentally deleted 3 days ago, you can restore from the daily backup. If corruption was introduced 2 weeks ago, the weekly backup has a clean copy. If you discover a long-running issue, the monthly backup from last quarter is your last resort.

Q177
How do you test that your Vault backup actually works?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Quarterly DR drill: (1) Deploy a fresh Vault instance in an isolated environment, (2) Restore the latest snapshot, (3) Unseal with a copy of the unseal keys (test key accessibility!), (4) Verify: login with root token from snapshot, read test secrets, create a new secret and verify it persists, (5) Document results and any issues. If you haven't tested your restore, you don't have a backup — you have a hope.

EXPLANATION

Common findings during drills: (1) Unseal keys are in a safe that nobody remembers the combination to, (2) Snapshot file is corrupted (test integrity!), (3) Restore takes longer than expected (measure RTO!), (4) New Vault version is incompatible with old snapshot format.

Q178
What happens if you lose your unseal keys but have a Raft snapshot?
Show Answer
ANSWER

You cannot restore. The snapshot is encrypted with Vault's barrier key, which is protected by the unseal keys. Without the unseal keys, the snapshot is an encrypted blob — completely useless. This is why unseal keys must be stored in a DIFFERENT secure location from the snapshots. Losing both = complete, irreversible data loss.

EXPLANATION

Best practice: Store unseal keys in a physical safe, a Hardware Security Module (HSM), or a cloud KMS with strict access controls. Use auto-unseal in production to eliminate the manual unseal key management problem entirely.

Q179
Design an automated backup strategy for Vault on Kubernetes with S3 storage and alerting.
Show Answer
ANSWER
# CronJob (every 6 hours):
schedule: "0 */6 * * *"
# Job steps:
# 1. vault login -method=kubernetes role=vault-backup
# 2. vault operator raft snapshot save /tmp/vault-$(date).snap
# 3. aws s3 cp /tmp/vault-$(date).snap s3://vault-backups/
# 4. Cleanup: delete snapshots older than retention

# Alert: Prometheus alert if no snapshot in 7 hours
# Alert: AWS CloudWatch alarm if S3 bucket has no new objects
EXPLANATION

Two layers of alerting: (1) Prometheus watches the CronJob success/failure metric, (2) S3 lifecycle policy ensures old snapshots are auto-deleted while CloudWatch monitors for new objects. If both alert → investigate immediately.

Q180
Create a complete anihpj DR plan: backup schedule, DR region, promotion steps, and quarterly test procedure.
Show Answer
ANSWER

Backup: Raft snapshot every 6 hours → S3 (vault-backups bucket, SSE-KMS). Retention: 24h + 7d + 4w + 3m.
DR: Secondary cluster in eu-west-1. Async DR replication from us-east-1 primary.
Promotion: vault write -f sys/replication/dr/promote on secondary, update DNS, verify anihpj connects.
Quarterly test: Simulate primary failure, promote secondary, verify all 5 anihpj secret types (KV, DB dynamic, API keys, Transit keys, TLS certs) are accessible, time the process, document findings. RPO target: <5 seconds. RTO target: <15 minutes.

EXPLANATION

This is a production-grade DR plan. The key insight: DR replication gives you seconds of RPO (near-real-time data), while snapshots give you point-in-time recovery for logical errors (accidental deletion, corruption). Both are needed for complete coverage.

⏱️ 10 minutes
Scenario: Take a Backup and Verify Restore Works

You must prove that Vault backups are working. Take a snapshot, then restore it to a fresh Vault instance and verify data integrity.

  1. Take a Raft snapshot on the active node
  2. Write a test secret AFTER the snapshot (to verify restore point)
  3. Restore the snapshot to a fresh Vault dev instance
  4. Verify the pre-snapshot data exists
  5. Verify the post-snapshot secret does NOT exist (proves restore point)
💡 Hint: vault operator raft snapshot save /tmp/test.snap. For restore test, use a dev Vault — never test restore on production!
▼ Solution
# On PRODUCTION Vault:
# 1. Write a secret BEFORE snapshot
vault kv put secret/test value=before-snapshot

# 2. Take snapshot
vault operator raft snapshot save /tmp/test-$(date +%s).snap
echo "Snapshot taken at $(date)"

# 3. Write a secret AFTER snapshot
vault kv put secret/test value=after-snapshot

# On DEV Vault (fresh instance):
# 4. Restore snapshot
vault operator raft snapshot restore -force /tmp/test-*.snap
vault operator unseal <keys>

# 5. Verify: pre-snapshot data EXISTS
vault kv get secret/test
# → value=before-snapshot ✅

# 6. Verify: post-snapshot data does NOT exist
# (It was written after the snapshot point)
# → If it shows "after-snapshot", you restored the wrong file!

echo "✅ Backup verified — restore works!"

Chapter 19: Vault Upgrades and Maintenance 🔐

Vault follows semantic versioning. Upgrades within a major version (e.g., 1.17 → 1.18) are straightforward. Upgrading Vault in a high-availability cluster without downtime requires a specific procedure: upgrade standby nodes first, failover, then upgrade the old primary. This chapter covers the complete rolling upgrade process, node management, and maintenance best practices.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🔐 Ops Pro Critical

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand Vault's versioning and upgrade compatibility
  • ✅ Perform a zero-downtime rolling upgrade of a Vault HA cluster
  • ✅ Manage nodes in an HA cluster: add, remove, replace
  • ✅ Apply maintenance best practices for production Vault

19.1 Upgrade Procedures — Version Compatibility

Vault uses semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). You can upgrade from version N to N+1 directly. You CANNOT skip major versions — must upgrade sequentially through each major version.

Bash — Pre-Upgrade Checklist
# 1. Check current version
vault status | grep Version

# 2. Read release notes for the target version
# https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/release-notes

# 3. Take a Raft snapshot (safety net!)
vault operator raft snapshot save /backup/vault-pre-upgrade.snap

# 4. Verify snapshot was created successfully
ls -la /backup/vault-pre-upgrade.snap

# 5. Check cluster health
vault operator raft list-peers
# All peers should be healthy, leader elected

# 6. Upgrade path: vault → vault (same binary name)
# The binary replaces in-place — Vault reads existing data

19.2 Rolling Upgrades in HA — Zero-Downtime Procedure

The key to zero-downtime upgrades: upgrade followers first, then failover, then upgrade the old leader.

🧠 Why This Order Matters — The Orchestra Analogy

Imagine Vault is an orchestra. The leader node is the conductor — actively directing the performance. The standby nodes are musicians — ready to play but waiting for their cue. You would never tap the conductor on the shoulder mid-symphony and say "time for your break!" You'd replace the musicians first, then have the conductor hand the baton to someone already prepared. That's exactly what the rolling upgrade does: upgrade the musicians (standbys), then have the conductor step down and hand the baton to an upgraded musician (failover), then upgrade the ex-conductor who's now just a musician. The symphony never stops.

ROLLING VAULT UPGRADE — Zero-Downtime Procedure
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        🔄 ROLLING VAULT UPGRADE — Zero-Downtime Procedure          │
│                                                                    │
│  INITIAL: vault-1(Active/v1.17), vault-2(Standby/v1.17),         │
│           vault-3(Standby/v1.17)                                  │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 1: UPGRADE STANDBY NODES FIRST                              │
│  ──────────────────────────────────                                │
│  # On vault-2 (standby):                                          │
│  systemctl stop vault                                             │
│  [replace binary: v1.17 → v1.18]                                  │
│  systemctl start vault                                            │
│  vault operator unseal  # Use unseal keys                         │
│  → vault-2 now on v1.18 (standby)                                 │
│                                                                    │
│  # Repeat for vault-3                                             │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 2: FAILOVER TO UPGRADED STANDBY                             │
│  ────────────────────────────────────                              │
│  vault operator step-down                                         │
│  → vault-1 steps down                                             │
│  → Raft elects vault-2 (v1.18) as new leader                     │
│  → vault-2 is now ACTIVE on v1.18                                 │
│  → Zero downtime — requests served by vault-3 during election     │
│                                                                    │
│  STEP 3: UPGRADE OLD PRIMARY                                      │
│  ─────────────────────────────                                     │
│  # On vault-1 (now standby):                                      │
│  systemctl stop vault                                             │
│  [replace binary: v1.17 → v1.18]                                  │
│  systemctl start vault                                            │
│  vault operator unseal                                             │
│                                                                    │
│  RESULT: All 3 nodes on v1.18                                     │
│  vault-2(Active/v1.18), vault-3(Standby/v1.18),                  │
│  vault-1(Standby/v1.18)                                          │
│                                                                    │
│  ⏱️ TOTAL DOWNTIME: ZERO — failover during Raft election is       │
│     sub-second. Clients retry and connect to new leader.          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚡ SPEED TIP: K8s Rolling Upgrade (Helm)

With Helm: helm upgrade vault hashicorp/vault --set server.image.tag=1.18.0. Kubernetes StatefulSet does a rolling update — one pod at a time. After each pod restarts, you must unseal it (unless using auto-unseal). If using auto-unseal with cloud KMS, the upgrade is fully automatic — the pod restarts, auto-unseals, and rejoins the cluster without human intervention.

19.3 Node Management in HA — Add, Remove, Replace

Bash — Node Management Commands
# LIST PEERS: See current cluster members
vault operator raft list-peers
# Node       Address              State     Voter
# vault-0    vault-0.vault:8201   leader    true
# vault-1    vault-1.vault:8201   follower  true
# vault-2    vault-2.vault:8201   follower  true

# ADD A NODE (from the new node):
vault operator raft join https://vault-0.vault:8200
# → New node joins as a voter

# REMOVE A NODE (from any existing node):
vault operator raft remove-peer vault-2
# → vault-2 is removed from the cluster

# REPLACE A FAILED NODE:
# 1. Remove the failed peer
vault operator raft remove-peer vault-2
# 2. Deploy a new node with the same node ID
# 3. New node joins the cluster
vault operator raft join https://vault-0.vault:8200

# ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Never remove more than (N/2 - 1) nodes
# For a 3-node cluster, you can only lose 1 node
# For a 5-node cluster, you can lose 2 nodes
# If you lose quorum, the cluster becomes unavailable!

19.4 Maintenance Best Practices

✅ Vault Maintenance Checklist

  • ✅ Before any maintenance: Take a Raft snapshot
  • ✅ Upgrade order: Standby → Failover → Old primary
  • ✅ Never skip versions: 1.17 → 1.18 → 1.19, not 1.17 → 1.19
  • ✅ Check release notes: Look for breaking changes, deprecated features
  • ✅ Test in dev/staging first: Never upgrade production directly
  • ✅ Monitor during upgrade: Watch vault operator raft list-peers
  • ✅ Never remove the leader: Step down first, then remove
  • ✅ Maintain quorum: 3-node → max 1 down. 5-node → max 2 down
  • ✅ Automate unseal: Use auto-unseal (cloud KMS) to survive restarts
  • ✅ Backup post-upgrade: Take a snapshot after successful upgrade

⚠️ GOTCHA: Quorum Loss on 3-Node Cluster

With 3 nodes, quorum = 2 (N/2 + 1). If 2 nodes fail simultaneously, the cluster becomes unavailable — the remaining node cannot form quorum and stops accepting writes. This is why production clusters should have 5 nodes (can survive 2 failures) or use auto-unseal to recover quickly from restarts.

📊 Chapter 19 — Recap

🔄Rolling UpgradeStandby first → failover → old primary
⏱️Zero DowntimeRaft election <1 second during failover
🔢Semantic VersioningN → N+1 only — never skip versions
🔧Node MgmtAdd/remove/replace via raft commands
⚖️Quorum = Survival3-node: max 1 down. 5-node: max 2 down
✅10 Best PracticesSnapshot before, test in dev, monitor during

📝 Chapter 19 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q181
What is the correct order for a zero-downtime rolling upgrade of a Vault HA cluster?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Take a Raft snapshot (safety net). 2. Upgrade standby nodes first (one at a time). 3. After all standbys are upgraded: vault operator step-down on the current leader. 4. Raft elects an upgraded standby as the new leader. 5. Upgrade the old leader (now a standby). Result: All nodes upgraded with zero downtime.

EXPLANATION

Why this order? The leader is actively serving requests — you never want to stop it while it's the leader. Upgrading standbys first, then failing over to an upgraded node, ensures there's always an active Vault serving traffic.

Q182
Can you upgrade Vault from 1.15 directly to 1.18?
Show Answer
ANSWER

No. Vault requires sequential upgrades through each major version: 1.15 → 1.16 → 1.17 → 1.18. You cannot skip versions. Each major version may introduce breaking changes that require intermediate steps. Always check the release notes for the recommended upgrade path.

EXPLANATION

This is a common exam question. Vault's upgrade policy is: must upgrade through each major version sequentially. The same applies to the storage backend — Raft data format changes between versions are only compatible with the previous version.

Q183
What happens to Vault's quorum if 2 out of 3 nodes fail?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The remaining node cannot form quorum (needs 2 of 3 = N/2+1). It stops accepting write operations entirely. The cluster is effectively unavailable — reads may still work from the surviving node's local state, but no secrets can be created, updated, or deleted. Recovery requires bringing at least 1 more node back online.

EXPLANATION

This is why 5-node clusters are recommended for production — they can survive 2 node failures (quorum = 3, 5-2=3 ≥ 3). With 3 nodes, losing 2 means the cluster is down. Use auto-unseal to minimize the time nodes spend sealed after restarts.

Q184
How do you add a new node to an existing Vault HA cluster?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Deploy the new Vault node with the same configuration (but different node_id). 2. Start Vault on the new node. 3. From the new node, run: vault operator raft join https://<leader-address>:8200. 4. The new node joins the Raft cluster as a voter. 5. Verify: vault operator raft list-peers shows the new node.

EXPLANATION

The new node must have a unique node_id in its config. It joins by contacting the current leader. After joining, Raft replicates the log to the new node — it syncs all existing data automatically.

Q185
What must you do BEFORE any Vault maintenance operation?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Take a Raft snapshot. vault operator raft snapshot save /backup/vault-pre-maintenance.snap. This gives you a rollback point if the maintenance goes wrong. Also: verify the snapshot was created successfully, note the current leader, and ensure unseal keys are accessible.

EXPLANATION

"Snapshot before maintenance" is the Vault equivalent of "save before editing." It takes 30 seconds and can save you from complete data loss if an upgrade corrupts the Raft log or a configuration change locks you out.

Q186
How do you remove a failed node from a Vault HA cluster?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault operator raft remove-peer <node-id>. This removes the node from the Raft cluster. The removed node's data is no longer part of the consensus group. If the node was the leader, Raft will elect a new leader automatically (this may cause a brief unavailability during election).

EXPLANATION

Never remove the leader directly — step down first with vault operator step-down, then remove. Removing a node when you're at the minimum quorum (e.g., 3 nodes → remove 1 = 2 nodes, quorum still 2) is safe. Removing below quorum makes the cluster unavailable.

Q187
What is the recommended cluster size for production Vault and why?
Show Answer
ANSWER

5 nodes is recommended for production. Reasons: (1) Can survive 2 simultaneous node failures (quorum = 3, 5-2=3 ≥ 3), (2) Can perform rolling upgrades without losing quorum (upgrade 1 node at a time, 4 remain), (3) Can remove a failed node without risk (5-1=4 ≥ 3), (4) Better read scalability — any node can serve reads. 3 nodes is acceptable for staging/dev. 1 node is for development only.

EXPLANATION

Cluster sizes must be odd (3, 5, 7) for Raft quorum to work correctly. Even numbers provide no additional fault tolerance — a 4-node cluster still only survives 1 failure (quorum = 3, 4-1=3 ≥ 3, 4-2=2 < 3).

Q188
What is the purpose of vault operator step-down?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault operator step-down forces the current active (leader) node to become a standby (follower). This triggers a Raft leader election — another node becomes the new leader. Use this: (1) Before upgrading the leader, (2) To rebalance the cluster, (3) When the current leader is experiencing issues. The election is typically sub-second, causing no noticeable downtime.

EXPLANATION

During step-down and the subsequent election, Vault briefly cannot process write requests (the Raft cluster needs a leader for writes). Reads may be served by standby nodes during this window if ?standbyok=true is used.

Q189
How does auto-unseal simplify upgrades and maintenance?
Show Answer
ANSWER

With auto-unseal (cloud KMS: AWS KMS, GCP CKMS, Azure Key Vault, or Transit engine), Vault automatically unseals on startup — no manual unseal key entry needed. This means: after a restart (upgrade, crash, maintenance), Vault comes back online automatically. Rolling upgrades become: stop → upgrade binary → start → Vault auto-unseals → rejoins cluster. Zero human intervention for unsealing.

EXPLANATION

Without auto-unseal: every restart requires a human to provide 3 of 5 unseal keys. In a 5-node cluster upgrade, that's 15 key entries. With auto-unseal: zero key entries. This is why auto-unseal is strongly recommended for production.

Q190
Perform a complete rolling upgrade of a 3-node Vault cluster from v1.17 to v1.18 with zero downtime.
Show Answer
ANSWER
# 0. Pre-upgrade snapshot
vault operator raft snapshot save /backup/pre-upgrade.snap
vault operator raft list-peers  # Note leader

# 1. Upgrade vault-1 (standby)
systemctl stop vault
[install vault v1.18]
systemctl start vault
vault operator unseal <key1> <key2> <key3>

# 2. Upgrade vault-2 (standby, same as step 1)

# 3. Failover to upgraded standby
vault operator step-down
# → vault-0 steps down, vault-1 becomes leader

# 4. Upgrade vault-0 (now standby)
systemctl stop vault
[install vault v1.18]
systemctl start vault
vault operator unseal <key1> <key2> <key3>

# 5. Verify
vault status  # Version: 1.18.0 ✅
vault operator raft list-peers  # All healthy ✅
EXPLANATION

Total downtime: ZERO. During step-down, the Raft election takes <1 second. Vault clients with retry logic won't even notice. If using auto-unseal, skip the unseal steps entirely — Vault unseals itself automatically on restart.

🧯 Common Vault Operations Mistakes — And How to Recover

💀 MISTAKE #1: Forgetting to Take a Snapshot Before an Upgrade

Scenario: You upgrade Vault from 1.17 to 1.18. The upgrade corrupts the Raft log. You have no snapshot. All data is lost.
Prevention: vault operator raft snapshot save /backup/pre-upgrade.snap — ALWAYS run this first. It takes 30 seconds and is the difference between a 5-minute rollback and complete data loss.

💀 MISTAKE #2: Losing Quorum During Node Maintenance

Scenario: You have 3 nodes. You stop vault-1 for maintenance, then vault-2 crashes. vault-3 is alone — quorum lost, cluster unavailable.
Prevention: Use 5 nodes for production (survives 2 failures). Never perform maintenance on more than 1 node at a time in a 3-node cluster. Always check vault operator raft list-peers before and after each maintenance action.

💀 MISTAKE #3: Disabling an Audit Device Without a Replacement

Scenario: You disable the file audit device, intending to replace it with a socket audit. The socket configuration is wrong. Now Vault has NO audit device — and by default, Vault blocks ALL requests if any audit device fails to write. You're locked out.
Prevention: Always enable the new audit device BEFORE disabling the old one. Vault supports multiple simultaneous audit devices.

💀 MISTAKE #4: Relying on a Single Backup Location

Scenario: Your CronJob backs up to S3 in us-east-1. us-east-1 has a region-wide outage. You can't access your backups during the outage.
Prevention: Store backups in at least TWO locations — primary S3 bucket + cross-region replication, or S3 + GCS, or S3 + local NFS. Test restore from ALL locations quarterly.

🛡️ PART 7 PRODUCTION CHECKLIST — Daily, Weekly, Monthly

DAILY: vault status, raft list-peers, audit list, check Prometheus alerts, verify last backup succeeded.
WEEKLY: Review audit logs for anomalies, check disk usage trend, rotate audit log files, verify token & lease counts are normal.
MONTHLY: Test restore from latest snapshot, review and remove unused policies, check for Vault version updates, update documentation.
QUARTERLY: Full DR drill — promote secondary, verify all secrets, time the process, document findings.
