📋 Part 7 — Key Takeaways for the Exam

  • ✅ vault operator commands manage the cluster — init, unseal, seal, raft, step-down
  • ✅ Health endpoint: sys/health — 200=OK, 429=standby, 501=not init, 503=sealed
  • ✅ Raft snapshots: Point-in-time backup, encrypted, safe to store anywhere
  • ✅ Restore = 6 steps: Stop → Clear → Restore → Start → Unseal → Join
  • ✅ DR replication: Async cross-region, secondary is read-only, promotable
  • ✅ Rolling upgrade: Standby nodes first → failover → old primary last
  • ✅ Quorum: 3 nodes survive 1 failure. 5 nodes survive 2 failures. Never go below quorum
  • ✅ Audit logs: Append-only, tamper-proof — enable at least 2 devices
  • ✅ Snapshot before EVERY maintenance: It's your undo button
  • ✅ Untested backup = no backup: Test restore quarterly

🟡 Part 8: Encryption & Advanced Secrets Engines

Chapter 20: Transit Secrets Engine — Encryption Deep Dive 🎯

The Transit engine is Vault's Encryption-as-a-Service. It performs cryptographic operations without the encryption keys ever leaving Vault. Your application sends plaintext → Vault encrypts it and returns ciphertext. Your application sends ciphertext → Vault decrypts it and returns plaintext. The application never sees the encryption key. This is a game-changer for data security: even if your database is breached, the encrypted data is useless without Vault.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🎯 VA 25% Domain 🔐 Ops Pro Bridge

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand Transit as Encryption-as-a-Service — keys never leave Vault
  • ✅ Perform encrypt, decrypt, rewrap, HMAC, sign, and verify operations
  • ✅ Rotate encryption keys without re-encrypting data (key versioning)
  • ✅ Use convergent encryption for deduplication-safe encryption
  • ✅ Integrate Transit with anihpj for field-level encryption
🎓 VAULT ASSOCIATE RELEVANCE
Domain 2: Secrets Engines 25%
🔍 Before Transit vs After Transit — The Data Breach Scenario

BEFORE: anihpj stores user emails as plaintext in PostgreSQL. A SQL injection vulnerability exposes the users table. Attacker downloads all 50,000 emails — GDPR fine: €20 million or 4% of global revenue. AFTER TRANSIT: Same SQL injection. Attacker downloads the users table. Every email is vault:v1:8SDd3WHw9cHKd.... Attacker has terabytes of ciphertext — completely useless without Vault access. To read a single email, they must: (1) have a valid Vault token, (2) have the transit/decrypt/anihpj-key policy, (3) get past Vault's IP restrictions, and (4) leave an audit trail of every decryption attempt. Transit turns a catastrophic breach into a non-event.

⚡ SPEED TIP: One-Liner Encrypt/Decrypt

ENCRYPTED=$(echo -n "$SECRET" | base64 | xargs -I{} vault write -field=ciphertext transit/encrypt/anihpj-key plaintext={})
DECRYPTED=$(vault write -field=plaintext transit/decrypt/anihpj-key ciphertext="$ENCRYPTED" | base64 -d)
These one-liners save you from writing scripts for quick operations. Practice them until they're muscle memory.

20.1 Transit Engine Architecture — Encryption as a Service

The Transit engine follows one principle: "Keys stay in Vault. Vault does the crypto." It supports AES-256-GCM96, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA-2048/4096, and ECDSA.

TRANSIT ENGINE — Complete Encrypt/Decrypt Data Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        🔒 TRANSIT ENGINE — Encryption as a Service (EaaS)         │
│        "Keys stay in Vault. Vault does the crypto."               │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  APPLICATION  │                    │  VAULT TRANSIT ENGINE     │ │
│  │  (anihpj)     │                    │                           │ │
│  │               │                    │  Has: Encryption keys     │ │
│  │  Has:          │    ── TLS ──▶     │  NEVER stores plaintext   │ │
│  │  Plaintext     │                    │  Keys NEVER leave Vault   │ │
│  │  data          │◀─── TLS ────     │                           │ │
│  └───────┬───────┘                    └──────────┬───────────────┘ │
│          │                                       │                 │
│          │  ENCRYPT: POST /transit/encrypt/key   │                 │
│          │  { plaintext: base64(data) }          │                 │
│          │──────────────────────────────────────▶│                 │
│          │                                       │ Vault encrypts   │
│          │                                       │ with AES-256-   │
│          │                                       │ GCM96 key       │
│          │  { ciphertext: "vault:v1:abc123..." } │                 │
│          │◀──────────────────────────────────────│                 │
│          │                                       │                 │
│          │  App stores ciphertext in DB/file     │                 │
│          │  🔑 Key NEVER left Vault!             │                 │
│          │                                       │                 │
│          │  DECRYPT: POST /transit/decrypt/key   │                 │
│          │  { ciphertext: "vault:v1:abc123..." } │                 │
│          │──────────────────────────────────────▶│                 │
│          │                                       │ Vault decrypts   │
│          │                                       │ with SAME key    │
│          │  { plaintext: base64(data) }          │                 │
│          │◀──────────────────────────────────────│                 │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 IF DATABASE IS BREACHED: ciphertext is USELESS without Vault  │
│  💡 ALL operations AUDITED — who encrypted/decrypted what, when   │
│  💡 Key rotation is transparent — ciphertext prefix tracks version │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 Why This Architecture is Revolutionary

Traditional encryption: Your app holds the key → if app is breached, key is stolen → ALL data decryptable. Transit model: Your app NEVER has the key → if app is breached → attacker has ciphertext they CANNOT decrypt → they must ALSO breach Vault (which has audit logging, MFA, IP restrictions). This is defense in depth applied to encryption.

20.1a Encrypt / Decrypt

Bash — Encrypt & Decrypt Operations
# Enable Transit engine
vault secrets enable transit

# Create an encryption key (AES-256-GCM96 default)
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-key
# → Key created. All encrypt/decrypt uses this key.

# ENCRYPT: Plaintext MUST be base64-encoded
PLAINTEXT=$(echo -n "DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t" | base64)
vault write transit/encrypt/anihpj-key plaintext="$PLAINTEXT"
# ciphertext: vault:v1:8SDd3WHw9cHKd...

# DECRYPT: Returns base64 plaintext
vault write transit/decrypt/anihpj-key \
    ciphertext="vault:v1:8SDd3WHw9cHKd..."
# plaintext: REJfUEFTU1dPUkQ9czNjcjN0
echo "REJfUEFTU1dPUkQ9czNjcjN0" | base64 -d
# → DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t

20.1b Rewrap — Re-encrypt with Latest Key Version

# After rotating the key (see 20.3), old ciphertext still works.
# Rewrap: decrypt with OLD key version, encrypt with LATEST.
vault write transit/rewrap/anihpj-key \
    ciphertext="vault:v1:old-ciphertext..."
# ciphertext: vault:v2:new-ciphertext...
# → Now encrypted with v2 key. No plaintext exposure!

20.1c HMAC / Verify

# HMAC: Create a cryptographic fingerprint of data
vault write transit/hmac/anihpj-key \
    input="$(echo -n 'user-id-12345' | base64)"
# hmac: vault:v1:abc123def456...

# VERIFY: Check if data matches the HMAC
vault write transit/verify/anihpj-key \
    input="$(echo -n 'user-id-12345' | base64)" \
    hmac="vault:v1:abc123def456..."
# valid: true  ← Data matches!

20.1d Sign / Verify

# Create a signing key (ECDSA)
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-sign-key type=ecdsa-p256

# SIGN: Create a digital signature
vault write transit/sign/anihpj-sign-key \
    input="$(echo -n 'contract-data' | base64)"
# signature: vault:v1:MEUCIFfK...

# VERIFY SIGNATURE: Check authenticity
vault write transit/verify/anihpj-sign-key \
    input="$(echo -n 'contract-data' | base64)" \
    signature="vault:v1:MEUCIFfK..."
# valid: true  ← Signature is authentic!

20.2 Encrypt/Decrypt Operations — Complete Reference

OperationAPI PathInputOutputUse Case
Encrypttransit/encrypt/<key>Base64 plaintextCiphertext (vault:vN:...)Encrypt PII before storing in DB
Decrypttransit/decrypt/<key>CiphertextBase64 plaintextRead encrypted data from DB
Rewraptransit/rewrap/<key>Ciphertext (any version)Ciphertext (latest version)Rotate keys without exposing data
HMACtransit/hmac/<key>Base64 inputHMAC fingerprintVerify data integrity
Verifytransit/verify/<key>Input + HMACvalid: true/falseCheck data hasn't been tampered
Signtransit/sign/<key>Base64 inputDigital signatureProve data authenticity

20.3 Key Rotation and Versioning 🎯

Transit keys support automatic versioning. When you rotate a key, a new version is created. Old ciphertext (encrypted with v1) still decrypts correctly — Vault tracks which version was used. Rewrap updates ciphertext to the latest version without exposing plaintext.

# Rotate key (creates new version, old versions retained)
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-key/rotate
# → Key rotated. New version: 2

# List key versions
vault read transit/keys/anihpj-key
# latest_version: 2
# min_decryption_version: 1
# → v2 is used for NEW encryptions
# → v1 can still DECRYPT old ciphertexts

# Set minimum decryption version (disable v1)
vault write transit/keys/anihpj-key/config \
    min_decryption_version=2
# → v1 can no longer decrypt — all data must use v2+

# Trim old versions (permanently delete v1)
vault write transit/keys/anihpj-key/trim \
    min_available_version=2
# ⚠️ v1 keys deleted — old ciphertext can NEVER be decrypted!

⚠️ GOTCHA: Don't Trim Too Aggressively

If you trim old key versions before rewrap-ping all your data, any ciphertext encrypted with the trimmed version becomes permanently undecryptable. Always rewrap BEFORE trimming. The safe workflow: Rotate → Rewrap ALL data → Verify → Trim old versions.

20.4 Convergent Encryption — Deduplication-Friendly

Convergent encryption produces the same ciphertext for identical plaintext — enabling deduplication while maintaining encryption. Use for data-at-rest where deduplication matters (backup systems, file storage).

# Create a convergent encryption key
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-convergent \
    derived=true convergent_encryption=true

# Same plaintext → SAME ciphertext (deterministic!)
vault write transit/encrypt/anihpj-convergent \
    plaintext="$(echo 'user@email.com' | base64)" \
    context="$(echo 'user-emails' | base64)"
# ciphertext: vault:v1:xyz789...
# Run again → SAME ciphertext!

20.5 Transit for anihpj — Field-Level Encryption 🏗️

anihpj stores user PII (email, phone numbers). With Transit, we encrypt these fields before storing in PostgreSQL. Even if the database is breached, all PII is ciphertext — useless without Vault.

Python — anihpj Transit Integration Example
import hvac  # Vault Python client
import base64

client = hvac.Client(url='https://vault:8200')
client.auth.kubernetes.login(role='anihpj-app')

def encrypt_field(plaintext: str) -> str:
    """Encrypt PII before storing in DB"""
    b64 = base64.b64encode(plaintext.encode()).decode()
    resp = client.secrets.transit.encrypt_data(
        name='anihpj-key',
        plaintext=b64
    )
    return resp['data']['ciphertext']

def decrypt_field(ciphertext: str) -> str:
    """Decrypt PII when reading from DB"""
    resp = client.secrets.transit.decrypt_data(
        name='anihpj-key',
        ciphertext=ciphertext
    )
    return base64.b64decode(resp['data']['plaintext']).decode()

# Usage in Django model:
# user.email_encrypted = encrypt_field(user.email)
# user.save()
# print(decrypt_field(user.email_encrypted))
# → "user@example.com"

📝 Chapter 20 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q191
What is the core principle of the Vault Transit secrets engine?
Show Answer
ANSWER

The Transit engine provides Encryption-as-a-Service (EaaS). The core principle is: encryption keys NEVER leave Vault. Applications send plaintext to Vault, Vault encrypts it with its internal keys and returns ciphertext. Applications send ciphertext to Vault, Vault decrypts it and returns plaintext. The application never possesses or sees the encryption key — only Vault does.

EXPLANATION

This is fundamentally different from traditional encryption where the application holds the key. With Transit: if your app is breached → attacker gets ciphertext they can't decrypt → they must ALSO breach Vault. Two separate systems must be compromised — defense in depth.

Q192
What six cryptographic operations does the Transit engine support?
Show Answer
ANSWER

1. Encrypt: Plaintext → ciphertext. 2. Decrypt: Ciphertext → plaintext. 3. Rewrap: Decrypt with old key + encrypt with latest key (no plaintext exposure). 4. HMAC: Create cryptographic fingerprint. 5. Verify: Check if input matches HMAC. 6. Sign/Verify: Digital signatures with ECDSA/RSA keys.

EXPLANATION

Rewrap is the most commonly tested operation — it allows key rotation without exposing plaintext. The ciphertext is decrypted and re-encrypted inside Vault, and only the new ciphertext is returned.

Q193
How does Transit key rotation work and why doesn't it require re-encrypting all data?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Transit keys are versioned. When you rotate, a new version (e.g., v2) is created. Old ciphertext is prefixed with vault:v1: — Vault knows which key version to use for decryption. New encryptions use the latest version. Old ciphertext continues to work because Vault keeps old key versions for decryption. Rewrap updates ciphertext to the latest version without exposing plaintext.

EXPLANATION

The ciphertext prefix (vault:v1:...) acts as a version tracker. Vault reads it, loads the correct key version, and decrypts. This is why rotation is instant — old keys are retained, new encryptions use the new key.

Q194
What is rewrap and when should you use it?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Rewrap decrypts ciphertext with the old key version and re-encrypts it with the latest key version — all inside Vault, no plaintext exposed. Use it: (1) After key rotation — update old ciphertext to use the new key, (2) Before trimming old key versions, (3) When a key version is suspected compromised (rewrap everything to a new key).

EXPLANATION

Rewrap is critical before trimming old keys. If you trim v1 without rewrap-ping v1 ciphertext, that data becomes permanently undecryptable. Safe sequence: Rotate → Rewrap all data → Verify → Trim.

Q195
How does HMAC differ from encryption in the Transit engine?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Encryption: Reversible — ciphertext can be decrypted back to plaintext. HMAC: One-way — creates a fixed-size fingerprint that CANNOT be reversed. Use HMAC when you need to verify data integrity without storing the original value (e.g., "has this user ID been seen before?" without storing the actual user ID). HMAC produces the same output for the same input (deterministic).

EXPLANATION

HMAC is not encryption — it's a cryptographic hash with a key. Think of it as a "signature" for data. Same input always produces the same HMAC, but you cannot derive the input from the HMAC.

Q196
What is convergent encryption and when is it useful?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Convergent encryption produces the same ciphertext for identical plaintext. This enables deduplication — if two users have the same email, they produce the same encrypted value, so the storage system can deduplicate. Enable with derived=true convergent_encryption=true. Use for: backup systems, file storage, email deduplication. Don't use for: data where uniqueness reveals information (an attacker can tell if two ciphertexts came from the same plaintext).

EXPLANATION

The tradeoff: convergent encryption leaks "same plaintext" information. If an attacker sees two identical ciphertexts, they know the plaintext was the same — even though they can't decrypt it. This is acceptable for deduplication use cases but not for highly sensitive data.

Q197
What happens if you trim old key versions without rewrapping first?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Any ciphertext encrypted with the trimmed key version becomes permanently undecryptable. The key material is deleted — Vault can no longer decrypt that ciphertext. This is irreversible data loss. Always rewrap all ciphertext to the latest version BEFORE trimming old versions.

EXPLANATION

Safe rotation workflow: (1) Rotate key → (2) Rewrap ALL affected ciphertext → (3) Verify old ciphertext no longer exists in your data stores → (4) Trim old versions. Skipping step 3 or 4 without step 2 = permanent data loss.

Q198
How would you implement field-level encryption for anihpj user emails using Transit?
Show Answer
ANSWER
# Enable: vault secrets enable transit
# Create key: vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-key

# Encrypt before storing:
b64 = base64.b64encode(email.encode()).decode()
cipher = vault.secrets.transit.encrypt_data(
    name='anihpj-key', plaintext=b64)
user.email_encrypted = cipher['data']['ciphertext']

# Decrypt when reading:
plain = vault.secrets.transit.decrypt_data(
    name='anihpj-key',
    ciphertext=user.email_encrypted)
email = base64.b64decode(plain['data']['plaintext'])
EXPLANATION

The application stores vault:v1:abc123... in the database instead of the email. If the database is breached, the attacker sees only ciphertext. To read emails, the attacker must ALSO breach Vault and have a valid token with the transit/decrypt/anihpj-key policy.

Q199
What encryption algorithms does Transit support and which is the default?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Default: AES-256-GCM96 (symmetric). Also supported: ChaCha20-Poly1305 (symmetric), RSA-2048/4096 (asymmetric), ECDSA-P256/P384/P521 (signing). Keys default to symmetric AES-256. Use type=ecdsa-p256 for signing keys, type=rsa-4096 for asymmetric encryption.

EXPLANATION

AES-256-GCM96 is the default because it provides authenticated encryption (GCM mode = encryption + integrity verification). The "96" refers to the nonce size in bits. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is preferred for environments without AES hardware acceleration.

Q200
Configure a complete Transit setup for anihpj: create an encryption key, encrypt a password, rotate the key, rewrap the data, and verify.
Show Answer
ANSWER
vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-key
CIPHER=$(vault write -field=ciphertext transit/encrypt/anihpj-key \
    plaintext="$(echo -n 's3cr3t-p@ss' | base64)")
vault write -f transit/keys/anihpj-key/rotate
NEW_CIPHER=$(vault write -field=ciphertext transit/rewrap/anihpj-key \
    ciphertext="$CIPHER")
echo "v1 cipher: $CIPHER"    # vault:v1:...
echo "v2 cipher: $NEW_CIPHER" # vault:v2:...
# Decrypt both → same plaintext ✅
EXPLANATION

Both v1 and v2 ciphertext decrypt to the same plaintext — proving key rotation is transparent. The old key (v1) is retained for decryption only, and new encryptions use v2.

Chapter 21: Transform Secrets Engine & Advanced Patterns

The Transform engine provides data masking, tokenization, and format-preserving encryption — protecting sensitive data while preserving its format. KMIP (Enterprise) enables Vault to act as a key management server for external systems. This chapter covers these advanced engines and when to use each.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🔐 Enterprise Features

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Transform engine for data masking and tokenization
  • ✅ Know KMIP and when it's needed for external key management
  • ✅ Compare encryption approaches: Transit vs Transform vs KMIP

21.1 Transform Secrets Engine — Data Masking & Tokenization

🎭 The "Test Data" Problem — Why Transform Exists

Your production database has real credit card numbers. You need to copy data to a test environment. You can't use real cards (PCI violation), but your test system validates credit card format (Luhn checksum). Transit would turn 4111-1111-1111-1111 into vault:v1:abc... — the test system rejects it as "not a card number." Transform turns it into 8456-7823-9012-3456 — still a valid card format, but completely fake. Test system accepts it, PCI auditors are happy, and the original value is recoverable via Vault if needed. Transform solves the format-preservation problem that pure encryption cannot.

While Transit encrypts data into opaque ciphertext, Transform preserves the original format. A 16-digit credit card number becomes another 16-digit number. An email keeps looking like an email. This is critical when downstream systems expect specific formats.

✅ Transit (Encryption)

4111-1111-1111-1111
→ vault:v1:8SDd3WHw9cHKd...

Data is SECURE but format is lost. Good for: storage, backups, PII in databases.

⚠️ Transform (Masking)

4111-1111-1111-1111
→ 8456-7823-9012-3456

Format preserved — looks like a valid card number. Good for: test environments, analytics, format-sensitive systems.

Bash — Transform Engine Operations
vault secrets enable transform

# Create a transformation (format-preserving encryption)
vault write transform/transformations/fpe/ccn \
    template="builtin/creditcardnumber" \
    tweak_source=internal

# Encode (mask) a credit card number
vault write transform/encode/ccn value=4111-1111-1111-1111
# encoded_value: 8456-7823-9012-3456  ← Same format!

# Decode (unmask) back to original
vault write transform/decode/ccn value=8456-7823-9012-3456
# decoded_value: 4111-1111-1111-1111
📖 Transform vs Transit — When to Use Which

Transit: Maximum security — the output bears no resemblance to the input. Use for data-at-rest encryption.
Transform: Format preservation — the output looks valid to downstream systems. Use for test data, analytics pipelines, legacy systems that validate format.

21.2 KMIP Secrets Engine (Enterprise) 🔐

The Key Management Interoperability Protocol (KMIP) engine allows Vault to act as a KMIP server — external systems (databases, storage arrays, HSMs) can request encryption keys from Vault using the KMIP standard protocol.

🎯 When You Need KMIP

Use KMIP when you have systems that speak KMIP natively but not Vault's API — Oracle databases, NetApp storage, VMware vSphere, Thales HSMs. Vault becomes the central key manager for your entire infrastructure — not just your applications.

21.3 Advanced Key Management — Choosing the Right Engine

EngineWhat It DoesKey LocationBest For
TransitEncrypt/decrypt dataKeys in Vault onlyApp-level encryption, PII protection
TransformFormat-preserving maskingKeys in Vault onlyTest data, tokenization, analytics
KMIP (Enterprise)Key management serverVault manages, external usesDatabase TDE, storage encryption
PKIX.509 certificate managementKeys in Vault onlyTLS certificates, mTLS

📋 Encryption Engine Decision Guide

  • ✅ App encrypting PII before DB insert? → Transit
  • ✅ Need same ciphertext for same plaintext (dedup)? → Transit (convergent)
  • ✅ Test data that looks real but isn't? → Transform
  • ✅ Oracle/VMware needs encryption keys? → KMIP (Enterprise)
  • ✅ Need TLS certificates for services? → PKI (Chapter 6)

Q201
What is the key difference between Transit and Transform engines?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Transit: Produces opaque ciphertext (e.g., vault:v1:abc123...) — maximum security, format is lost.
Transform: Produces format-preserving output (e.g., credit card → another valid credit card number) — useful when downstream systems expect specific formats.

EXPLANATION

Memory trick: Transit = "destroy the format" (like shredding a document). Transform = "disguise but keep the shape" (like wearing a mask).

Q202
What is KMIP and when would you use it?
Show Answer
ANSWER

KMIP (Key Management Interoperability Protocol) is a standard protocol for key management. Vault's KMIP engine (Enterprise) lets Vault act as a KMIP server — external systems (Oracle, VMware, NetApp) can request keys from Vault using standard KMIP. Use it when you have systems that natively speak KMIP but not Vault's HTTP API.

EXPLANATION

KMIP is an Enterprise feature (not in open-source). The exam expects you to know what it is and when it's needed, but not detailed KMIP configuration.

Q203
Which Vault engine would you use for: encrypting PII in a database, masking credit cards for a test environment, and managing Oracle TDE keys?
Show Answer
ANSWER

PII in database: Transit — maximum security, opaque ciphertext.
Credit card masking: Transform — format-preserving, looks like real cards.
Oracle TDE keys: KMIP (Enterprise) — Oracle natively speaks KMIP.

EXPLANATION

This is the decision framework you'll use in real life: Transit for security, Transform for compatibility, KMIP for enterprise systems, PKI for certificates.

Q204
What does format-preserving encryption mean in the context of the Transform engine?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Format-preserving encryption (FPE) encrypts data while maintaining the same format and length as the input. A 16-digit credit card number encrypts to another 16-digit number. An SSN (XXX-XX-XXXX) encrypts to the same format. This is critical when downstream systems validate data format (payment processors, government systems, legacy databases).

EXPLANATION

Without FPE: a system expecting a 16-digit number receives vault:v1:8SDd3... — rejected. With FPE: the system receives 8456-7823-9012-3456 — accepted, processed, and the original value can be recovered via Vault when needed.

🧯 Common Transit Engine Mistakes — And How to Avoid Them

💀 MISTAKE #1: Forgetting to Base64-Encode Plaintext

Symptom: "error: illegal base64 data at input byte..."
Fix: Transit REQUIRES base64-encoded input. Always: PLAINTEXT=$(echo -n "$data" | base64) before encrypt, and echo "$result" | base64 -d after decrypt.
Why: Transit operates on arbitrary bytes — base64 ensures binary-safe transport over JSON.

💀 MISTAKE #2: Trimming Keys Before Rewrap

Symptom: Some ciphertexts fail to decrypt after key rotation.
Fix: ALWAYS rewrap before trimming. Sequence: Rotate → Rewrap ALL → Verify → Trim.
Why: Trimming deletes the key material. Any ciphertext still using that version becomes permanently undecryptable.

💀 MISTAKE #3: Using the Wrong Key Type for Signing

Symptom: "unsupported operation: sign" on a default key.
Fix: Default keys are AES-256 (symmetric, encryption only). For signing, create: vault write -f transit/keys/sign-key type=ecdsa-p256. AES keys encrypt; ECDSA/RSA keys sign.

🛡️ PART 8 PRODUCTION CHECKLIST — Encryption Best Practices

✅ Always base64-encode plaintext before Transit operations
✅ Create separate keys for separate purposes (encrypt, HMAC, sign)
✅ Set min_decryption_version after rotating and rewrapping
✅ NEVER trim without verifying all data is rewrapped first
✅ Use convergent encryption ONLY when deduplication is required
✅ Audit all encrypt/decrypt operations — audit logs are your forensic trail
✅ Rotate keys on schedule: quarterly for high-security, annually for standard
✅ Test decrypt with old ciphertext after every rotation to verify

⏱️ 8 minutes
Scenario: Full Transit Lifecycle — Encrypt, Rotate, Rewrap, Verify

Your task: (1) Create a Transit key, (2) Encrypt "anihpj-db-password", (3) Rotate the key, (4) Prove the old ciphertext still decrypts, (5) Rewrap to the new key, (6) Verify both versions decrypt to the same plaintext.

💡 Hint: The ciphertext prefix (vault:v1: vs vault:v2:) tells you which key version was used. After rewrap, the prefix changes.
▼ Solution
vault secrets enable transit
vault write -f transit/keys/test-key

# Encrypt with v1
C1=$(vault write -field=ciphertext transit/encrypt/test-key \
    plaintext="$(echo -n 'anihpj-db-password' | base64)")
echo "v1 cipher: $C1"  # vault:v1:...

# Rotate
vault write -f transit/keys/test-key/rotate

# v1 ciphertext STILL decrypts
vault write transit/decrypt/test-key ciphertext="$C1" | \
    jq -r .data.plaintext | base64 -d
# → anihpj-db-password ✅

# Rewrap to v2
C2=$(vault write -field=ciphertext transit/rewrap/test-key \
    ciphertext="$C1")
echo "v2 cipher: $C2"  # vault:v2:...

# Both decrypt to same value
echo "✅ Rotation transparent — no data loss!"

📋 Part 8 — Key Takeaways for the Exam

  • ✅ Transit = EaaS: Keys NEVER leave Vault — app sends data, Vault does crypto
  • ✅ 6 operations: encrypt, decrypt, rewrap, hmac, verify, sign
  • ✅ Rewrap: Updates ciphertext to latest key WITHOUT plaintext exposure
  • ✅ Key rotation = versioning: Old keys retained for decryption, new for encryption
  • ✅ Base64 REQUIRED: All Transit input/output is base64-encoded
  • ✅ Transform = FPE: Format-preserving — output looks like input
  • ✅ KMIP = Enterprise: External key management for Oracle, VMware, NetApp
  • ✅ Never trim before rewrap: Permanent data loss if you do

🟡 Part 9: Monitoring & Audit

Chapter 22: Audit Devices — Logging Everything 🎯

Audit devices are Vault's CCTV cameras. Every single request to Vault — successful or failed — passes through the audit broker and gets logged. This is your forensic trail: who accessed what, when, from where, and what happened. Audit logs are append-only and tamper-proof — you cannot modify or delete entries. If a security incident occurs, the audit log is your primary evidence source.

🔍 Without Audit: Flying Blind — With Audit: The Truth is Known

WITHOUT AUDIT: Monday 3 AM. Your production database password is used from an unknown IP. Was it a scheduled backup? A rogue employee? A compromised pod? You have no idea — there's no record of who accessed what. You spend 8 hours checking Kubernetes logs, cloud trails, and application logs — all inconclusive.
WITH AUDIT: Monday 3 AM. You check the audit log: {"time":"03:00:01","auth":{"metadata":{"service_account_name":"backup-sa"}},"request":{"path":"database/creds/anihpj-role","operation":"read","remote_address":"10.244.3.42"}}. It was the backup CronJob. Case closed in 30 seconds. That's the power of audit.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🎯 VA 12% Domain 🛡️ Security Critical

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand how the audit broker captures every Vault request
  • ✅ Enable and configure File, Socket, and Syslog audit devices
  • ✅ Read and analyze audit log entries to detect suspicious patterns
  • ✅ Know how HMAC protects sensitive fields in audit logs
🎓 VAULT ASSOCIATE RELEVANCE
Domain 5: Operations 12%

22.1 What Are Audit Devices? — "CCTV for Vault"

Every request to Vault flows through the Audit Broker — a non-blocking middleware that sends a copy of each request and response to all enabled audit devices.

AUDIT DEVICES — Complete Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              📋 AUDIT DEVICES — "CCTV for Vault"                  │
│                                                                    │
│  Every request to Vault goes through the Audit Broker:            │
│                                                                    │
│  ┌─────────┐                                                      │
│  │ Request │                                                      │
│  └────┬────┘                                                      │
│       │                                                            │
│       ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    AUDIT BROKER (Non-blocking!)               │  │
│  │  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐                │  │
│  │  │   FILE    │  │  SOCKET   │  │  SYSLOG   │                │  │
│  │  │ /var/log/ │  │ TCP:9090  │  │ AUTH      │                │  │
│  │  │ vault.log │  │           │  │ facility  │                │  │
│  │  └─────┬─────┘  └─────┬─────┘  └─────┬─────┘                │  │
│  └────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────────────┘  │
│           │              │              │                          │
│           ▼              ▼              ▼                          │
│     ┌─────────┐   ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐                  │
│     │Log file │   │Logstash   │   │syslog-ng  │                  │
│     │on disk  │   │→ ES/Splunk│   │→ SIEM     │                  │
│     └─────────┘   └───────────┘   └───────────┘                  │
│                                                                    │
│  WHAT'S IN EACH AUDIT LOG ENTRY (JSON):                          │
│  ───────────────────────────────────────                            │
│  {                                                                  │
│    "time": "2025-01-15T12:00:00Z",                                 │
│    "type": "request",                                               │
│    "auth": {                                                        │
│      "client_token": "hmac-sha256:abc...",  ← HMAC'ed!           │
│      "policies": ["anihpj-policy"],                                │
│      "metadata": {"service_account_name": "anihpj-sa"}            │
│    },                                                               │
│    "request": {                                                     │
│      "path": "anihpj/data/database",                               │
│      "operation": "read",                                           │
│      "remote_address": "10.244.1.5",                               │
│      "data": {"key": "hmac-sha256:def..."}  ← Sensitive HMAC'ed  │
│    },                                                               │
│    "response": {"data": {"data": "hmac-sha256:ghi..."}}            │
│  }                                                                  │
│                                                                    │
│  💡 HMAC protects sensitive fields — you can verify "was this     │
│     value accessed?" without storing the value in plaintext.      │
│  💡 Append-only — entries CANNOT be modified or deleted.          │
│  💡 If ANY audit device fails → Vault STOPS processing requests.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

22.1a File Audit Device

Writes audit logs to a local file. Simplest setup, always available. Best as the primary audit device.

vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
# Config: log_rotation_max_files=10 log_rotation_bytes=104857600

22.1b Socket Audit Device

Streams audit logs to a TCP/UDP/Unix socket — perfect for real-time log aggregation (Splunk, Logstash, Elasticsearch).

vault audit enable socket address=logstash:9090 socket_type=tcp

22.1c Syslog Audit Device

Sends audit logs via syslog protocol — integrates directly with SIEM systems.

vault audit enable syslog tag="vault" facility="AUTH"

22.2 Audit Device Configuration 🎯

# Enable all three device types
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log
vault audit enable socket address=127.0.0.1:9090 socket_type=tcp log_raw=true
vault audit enable syslog tag=vault facility=AUTH

# List enabled devices
vault audit list
# Path     Type    Description
# file/    file    n/a
# socket/  socket  n/a
# syslog/  syslog  n/a

# Disable a device
vault audit disable file

# ⚠️ ALWAYS enable audit BEFORE doing anything in production!

22.3 File Audit Device — Configuration & Rotation

File audit is the most common setup. Configure rotation to prevent disk exhaustion:

# In Vault config file:
# log_rotation {
#   max_files = 10
#   max_file_size_mb = 100
# }

22.4 Socket Audit Device — Streaming Logs

Socket audit sends each log entry as a JSON line to a TCP/UDP socket. The receiving end (Logstash, Fluentd, Splunk) parses and indexes the entries.

22.5 Syslog Audit Device — SIEM Integration

Syslog audit sends logs using standard syslog protocol — any SIEM (Splunk ES, QRadar, ArcSight) can ingest these logs natively.

22.6 Audit Log Analysis — Detecting Suspicious Patterns

# Find all failed requests (potential attack)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.error != "")' | jq '{time, path, error}'

# Find requests from unexpected IPs
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.request.remote_address != "10.244.0.0/16")'

# Find token creation events (privilege escalation?)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.request.path | startswith("auth/token/create"))'

# Find policy changes (who changed what?)
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.request.path | startswith("sys/policies"))'

⚠️ GOTCHA: Audit Device Failure = Vault Stops

If an audit device fails to write (disk full, socket disconnected), Vault stops processing ALL requests. This is by design — audit is a critical security component. Always have at least one file audit device (local disk) that won't fail due to network issues. Configure disk alerts at 80% capacity.

⚡ SPEED TIP: Audit Analysis One-Liners

jq -s 'group_by(.request.path) | map({path: .[0].request.path, count: length})' audit.log — Top paths by request count.
jq 'select(.error!="") | {time,path,error}' audit.log | tail -20 — Last 20 errors.
jq -s 'group_by(.auth.metadata.service_account_name) | map({sa: .[0].auth.metadata.service_account_name, count: length})' — Which SAs are most active?
These one-liners turn raw JSON into actionable intelligence in seconds.

📊 Chapter 22 — Recap

📋3 Device TypesFile (local), Socket (streaming), Syslog (SIEM)
🔐HMAC ProtectionSensitive fields hashed — verifiable, not readable
🚫Append-OnlyEntries cannot be modified or deleted — tamper-proof
⚠️Failure = StopIf audit device fails, Vault stops all requests

📝 Chapter 22 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q206
What are the three types of Vault audit devices and their use cases?
Show Answer
ANSWER

File: Writes to local disk — always available, simplest. Socket: Streams to TCP/UDP/Unix socket — real-time log aggregation (Splunk, Logstash). Syslog: Uses syslog protocol — SIEM integration. Best practice: enable at least TWO (file + socket) for redundancy.

Q207
What happens if an audit device fails to write?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Vault stops processing ALL requests. This is a security feature — Vault refuses to operate without a working audit trail. Recovery: fix the audit device (free disk space, reconnect socket) or disable it with vault audit disable <path> (requires a working audit device to disable — circular!).

Recovery Commands
# When audit device is full → Vault STOPS all requests
# Recovery options:
ssh vault-node && gzip /var/log/vault/audit.log

# Better: add redundancy BEFORE failure
vault audit enable socket address=logstash:9090 socket_type=tcp

# Prevent with rotation in vault-config.hcl:
log_rotate_max_files = 10
log_rotate_bytes = 104857600
Q208
How does HMAC protect sensitive fields in audit logs?
Show Answer
ANSWER

HMAC replaces sensitive values (tokens, secret data) with a cryptographic hash. You can verify "was X accessed?" by computing HMAC(X) and comparing — but you cannot derive X from the HMAC. The audit device has its own HMAC key — only someone with that key can verify values.

HMAC Verification
# Verify "Was token X used in this audit entry?"
vault write sys/audit-hash/file input="hvs.REAL_TOKEN"
# Returns HMAC hash → compare with audit log entry
# Match = token was used. No match = different token.
Q209
How do you enable a file audit device and list all enabled devices?
Show Answer
ANSWER
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
vault audit list
# Path     Type    Description
# file/    file    n/a
Q210
What information does each audit log entry contain?
Show Answer
ANSWER

time: Timestamp. type: request/response. auth: token (HMAC'ed), policies, metadata. request: path, operation, remote_address, data (sensitive fields HMAC'ed). response: data, auth info. error: error message if request failed.

Chapter 23: Telemetry, Metrics, and Monitoring 🎯

Audit logs tell you what happened. Telemetry tells you how Vault is performing. Together they give you complete observability. This chapter covers Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, health checks, and Kubernetes probes for Vault.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🎯 VA 12% Domain

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Configure Vault telemetry for Prometheus scraping
  • ✅ Understand key Vault metrics and what they reveal
  • ✅ Set up health monitoring and Kubernetes probes
  • ✅ Build Grafana dashboards for Vault observability
🔍 Audit = "Who did it?" | Telemetry = "Is it working?" — Both Are Essential

Audit answers forensic questions: "Who read the database password at 3 AM from IP 10.244.3.42?" This is your security camera footage — reviewed AFTER an incident. Telemetry answers operational questions: "Is Vault using 90% memory?" "Is the request rate plummeting?" "Has the leader changed 5 times in the last hour?" This is your dashboard — watched IN REAL TIME to prevent incidents. Without telemetry, you discover Vault is sealed when users complain. With telemetry, you get a PagerDuty alert 5 seconds after it happens.

23.1 Telemetry Configuration

# In Vault config file:
telemetry {
  prometheus_retention_time = "24h"
  disable_hostname          = true
  # Statsd, DogStatsD, and Circonus also supported
}

# Scrape endpoint:
# curl http://vault:8200/v1/sys/metrics?format=prometheus

23.2 Key Vault Metrics — What to Watch

MetricWhat It RevealsAlert If
vault_core_unsealedIs Vault operational?!= 1 (CRITICAL!)
vault_core_handle_request_countRequest rateSudden drop to 0
vault_raft_leaderIs leader elected?No node = 1
vault_runtime_alloc_bytesMemory usageSteady increase (leak)
vault_token_count_by_ttlToken distributionSudden spike
vault_expire_num_leasesActive lease countRapid increase

23.3 Health Monitoring — K8s Probes

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["vault", "status"]
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /v1/sys/health?standbyok=true
    port: 8200
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 5

23.4 Prometheus & Grafana Integration

# Prometheus ServiceMonitor for Vault
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: vault
spec:
  endpoints:
  - interval: 30s
    path: /v1/sys/metrics
    params:
      format: [prometheus]
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: vault
📊 Recommended Grafana Panels

• Seal Status (gauge), • Request Rate (graph), • Raft Leader (gauge), • Memory Usage (graph), • Token Count (gauge), • Lease Count (gauge), • Audit Events/sec (graph)

🔔Critical AlertsSealed, no leader, memory leak
🏥K8s ProbesLiveness: vault status. Readiness: sys/health
📈Grafana7 recommended panels for full visibility

📝 Chapter 23 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q211
How do you configure Vault to expose Prometheus metrics?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Add a telemetry stanza to Vault's config file with prometheus_retention_time. Metrics are available at /v1/sys/metrics?format=prometheus. No authentication needed for the metrics endpoint.

Q212
What is the most critical Vault metric to alert on?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault_core_unsealed — if this is 0, Vault is sealed and ALL operations are blocked. This is a P0/critical alert. Also critical: vault_raft_leader (no leader = cluster unavailable) and sudden request rate drops (possible connectivity issue).

Q213
What Kubernetes probes should you configure for Vault pods?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Liveness: exec: ["vault", "status"] — restart if vault process is unresponsive. Readiness: httpGet: /v1/sys/health?standbyok=true — only route traffic if Vault is initialized and unsealed.

Q214
What are the key Vault metrics to monitor for performance?
Show Answer
ANSWER

vault_core_handle_request_count (request rate), vault_runtime_alloc_bytes (memory), vault_token_count_by_ttl (token distribution), vault_expire_num_leases (active leases), vault_merkle_flush_duration (storage write time).

Q215
How do audit logs and telemetry complement each other?
Show Answer
ANSWER

Audit logs: Tell you WHO did WHAT and WHEN — forensic trail for security incidents. Telemetry: Tells you HOW Vault is performing — request rates, memory, latency. Audit = "what happened" (security). Telemetry = "how it's going" (operations). Both are needed for complete observability.

🚀 Part 9 Implementation Blueprint — Observability in Production

✅ The Complete Observability Stack — What Good Looks Like

Audit Layer: File audit on local disk (always available) + Socket audit → Logstash → Elasticsearch (searchable, dashboard-ready). Rotate every 100 MB, keep 10 files.
Metrics Layer: Prometheus scrapes every 30s → Grafana dashboard with seal status, request rate, raft health, and memory.
Alerting Layer: PagerDuty for: vault_core_unsealed=0, no raft leader, disk >80%, no backup in 7 hours.
K8s Probes: Liveness (vault status), Readiness (/v1/sys/health?standbyok=true).

📋
Audit: Your Forensic Trail

Every request recorded. Append-only. Tamper-proof. Answer: who accessed what, when, from where. Enable audit FIRST — before using Vault.

📊
Telemetry: Your Dashboard

Real-time metrics. Answer: is Vault healthy, performing well, under attack? Alert on sealed + no leader + memory leak.

⚠️ GOTCHA: The "No Audit, No Vault" Rule

If all audit devices fail (disk full + socket down + syslog unreachable), Vault stops ALL operations. This is a security feature — Vault refuses to process unlogged requests. Always have at least one file audit device (local disk, no network dependency) as your safety net. Set disk alerts at 70% capacity so you never hit 100%.

  • ✅ Audit failure = Vault stops: Always have at least 2 devices
  • ✅ Critical alert: vault_core_unsealed != 1 — Vault is sealed
  • ✅ K8s probes: Liveness = vault status, Readiness = sys/health?standbyok=true
  • ✅ Prometheus: /v1/sys/metrics?format=prometheus — no auth needed
