📝 Chapter 25 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q241Which Vault component is typically the biggest performance bottleneck?
A. The HTTP listener
B. Policy evaluation engine
C. The storage backend (Raft/Consul)
D. TLS handshake processing
Answer: C. The storage backend is the most common bottleneck. Every read and write hits storage, and Raft requires fsync on every write. Slow storage directly translates to slow Vault responses.

Explanation: Storage I/O is the slowest layer. Policy evaluation is in-memory (fast), TLS handshakes are one-time costs, and listeners rarely bottleneck before storage does. Always benchmark your storage first when troubleshooting Vault performance.

Q242What is the minimum TLS version required for a production Vault listener?
A. TLS 1.0
B. TLS 1.1
C. TLS 1.2
D. TLS 1.3
Answer: C. TLS 1.2 is the minimum version for production. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated and vulnerable. TLS 1.3 is recommended where supported but not required.

Explanation: Vault's tls_min_version should always be set to "tls12". The listener stanza lets you control this explicitly. In exam scenarios, any answer suggesting TLS 1.0 or 1.1 is wrong.

listener "tcp" {
  tls_min_version = "tls12"   # Minimum for production
  # tls_min_version = "tls13" # Recommended when possible
}
Q243Why should Vault NEVER run as the root user in production?
A. Root users cannot use TLS certificates
B. If Vault is compromised, the attacker gains root access to the entire host
C. The root user has insufficient memory for mlock
D. Vault's license forbids running as root
Answer: B. Running as root violates the principle of least privilege. If an attacker compromises Vault (via API vulnerability or plugin exploit), they gain root-level host access — they can read all files, install backdoors, and pivot to other systems.

Explanation: Always create a dedicated vault OS user with minimal permissions. The vault user should only have read access to config/certs and write access to data/audit directories. This limits the blast radius if Vault itself is compromised.

Q244What does the mlock() system call do for Vault?
A. Encrypts secrets before writing to disk
B. Prevents Vault's memory from being swapped to disk
C. Locks the Vault binary to prevent tampering
D. Restricts network access to localhost only
Answer: B. mlock() locks Vault's memory pages in RAM, preventing the OS from swapping them to disk. Without mlock, secrets in memory could be written to swap and later recovered from disk.

Explanation: Swap is a security risk for any secrets management tool. If Vault's memory gets swapped, decrypted secrets could persist on disk indefinitely. mlock() is enabled by default (disable_mlock = false). If it fails, Vault refuses to start.

Q245What is the recommended minimum memory for a small production Vault instance?
A. 256 MB
B. 512 MB
C. 2-4 GB
D. 16 GB
Answer: C. 2-4 GB is recommended for small production workloads. While Vault can run with less (dev mode uses ~256MB), production needs caching, Raft overhead, and headroom for request bursts.

Explanation: Vault's memory usage scales with: number of secrets cached, number of concurrent connections, Raft log size, and policy complexity. 2GB is a safe minimum; 4GB provides comfortable headroom.

Q246Which parameter controls how aggressively Raft batches write operations?
A. max_entry_size
B. performance_multiplier
C. batch_interval
D. raft_snapshot_threshold
Answer: B. performance_multiplier (0-10) controls Raft write batching. Higher values batch more writes together, increasing throughput at the cost of slightly higher risk of losing uncommitted entries on crash.

Explanation: performance_multiplier = 0 (default) is safe — one write per Raft log entry. performance_multiplier = 1 gives ~30-50% throughput boost for SSD-backed production. Don't go above 5 without understanding the crash-consistency implications.

storage "raft" {
  performance_multiplier = 1   # 0=safe, 1-5=faster (SSD only!)
}
Q247What is the purpose of max_lease_ttl in Vault configuration?
A. Sets the maximum time Vault can run before requiring restart
B. Sets the absolute maximum TTL for any lease or token in the system
C. Limits how long audit logs are retained
D. Controls the TLS certificate renewal interval
Answer: B. max_lease_ttl is a hard ceiling — no token or secret lease can exceed this value, regardless of what individual roles or mounts specify. It's a global safety limit.

Explanation: Even if a DB role specifies ttl="90d" and the system max_lease_ttl is "768h" (32 days), the actual TTL will be capped at 32 days. This prevents infinite-lived secrets from accumulating.

Q248In the 15-point hardening checklist, which item prevents secrets from being recovered from disk after Vault restarts?
A. TLS 1.2 on all listeners
B. Dedicated OS user
C. Disable swap (mlock)
D. Rate limiting
Answer: C. Disabling swap and using mlock() ensures Vault's memory (which may contain unencrypted secrets) never gets written to disk as swap. Without this, an attacker with disk access could recover secrets from swap files.

Explanation: This is one of the most critical hardening items. Even with TLS (A), a dedicated user (B), and rate limiting (D), if secrets hit swap, they persist on disk unencrypted. mlock is your last line of defense against memory-to-disk leakage.

Q249How often should Raft snapshots be taken in production?
A. Once per day
B. Every 6 hours
C. Once per week
D. Only before upgrades
Answer: B. Every 6 hours is recommended for production. More frequent snapshots prevent Raft log from growing too large (which impacts performance) and reduce data loss window in DR scenarios.

Explanation: Snapshots compact the Raft log. Without regular snapshots, the log grows indefinitely, slowing down restarts and degrading write performance. A CronJob or systemd timer running vault operator raft snapshot save every 6 hours is standard practice.

# Kubernetes CronJob for Raft snapshots (every 6 hours)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
spec:
  schedule: "0 */6 * * *"     # Every 6 hours
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: snapshot
            image: vault:latest
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              vault operator raft snapshot save \
                /backups/vault-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).snap
Q250You receive an error: "failed to lock memory: cannot allocate memory" when starting Vault. What is the most likely cause?
A. The Vault binary is corrupted
B. The vault user lacks CAP_IPC_LOCK capability
C. The storage backend is full
D. TLS certificates are expired
Answer: B. The mlock() call requires the CAP_IPC_LOCK capability. Without it, Vault cannot lock memory pages and refuses to start. This is commonly missing when running as a non-root user without proper systemd configuration.

Explanation: Fix: add LimitMEMLOCK=infinity to the systemd unit, or grant CAP_IPC_LOCK to the vault user. Never use disable_mlock = true in production — it's a security risk.

[Service]
LimitMEMLOCK=infinity    # Required for mlock

🔌 Chapter 26: Plugins and Extensibility

Vault ships with over 20 built-in secrets engines and auth methods — but what if you need something custom? Maybe your organization uses a proprietary database, a homegrown authentication system, or a hardware security module that Vault doesn't natively support. Vault's plugin system lets you extend Vault with your own secrets engines and auth methods, written in Go and loaded at runtime. This chapter demystifies the plugin architecture, shows you how plugins work under the hood, and walks through building, registering, and managing custom plugins — a skill that bridges the gap from Vault Associate to Vault Authorship certification.

🎯 What You'll Learn in This Chapter

  • ✅ Understand Vault's plugin architecture and gRPC communication model
  • ✅ Register, enable, and manage custom plugins
  • ✅ Understand the plugin development lifecycle with the Go SDK
  • ✅ Explore community and ecosystem plugins
  • ✅ Debug and troubleshoot plugin issues
📋 Exam Relevance — Vault Associate (003) + Authorship

Associate: Know that Vault supports custom plugins, understand plugin registration commands, and recognize plugin security boundaries (~3% of exam). Authorship: This chapter is foundational — the Vault Authorship cert is entirely about building, testing, and distributing custom plugins. Master these concepts before diving into the Go SDK.

26.1 Vault Plugin System — Custom Auth and Secrets Engines

🔌 What IS a Vault Plugin?

A Vault plugin is a standalone Go binary that communicates with Vault's core via gRPC over a local Unix socket. Vault spawns the plugin as a child process, and all API requests to that plugin's mount point are forwarded through gRPC. The plugin never accesses Vault's storage directly — it goes through Vault's barrier. This means plugins inherit Vault's encryption, audit logging, and authentication — they can't bypass security controls.

🔌 Vault Plugin Architecture — Communication Flow
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                    VAULT PLUGIN ARCHITECTURE                     │
     │                                                                  │
     │   ┌──────────┐     HTTP/API      ┌──────────────────────────┐   │
     │   │  CLIENT  │ ───────────────▶  │     VAULT CORE           │   │
     │   │  (vault  │                   │                          │   │
     │   │   CLI)   │                   │  ┌────────────────────┐  │   │
     │   └──────────┘                   │  │  Plugin Catalog     │  │   │
     │                                  │  │  (registry)         │  │   │
     │                                  │  └────────┬───────────┘  │   │
     │                                  │           │               │   │
     │                                  │  ┌────────▼───────────┐  │   │
     │                                  │  │  gRPC over Unix     │  │   │
     │                                  │  │  Socket (local)     │  │   │
     │                                  │  └────────┬───────────┘  │   │
     │                                  └───────────┼──────────────┘   │
     │                                              │                  │
     │                                  ┌───────────▼──────────────┐   │
     │                                  │   CUSTOM PLUGIN BINARY   │   │
     │                                  │   (Go, compiled)         │   │
     │                                  │                          │   │
     │                                  │  • secrets engine        │   │
     │                                  │  • auth method           │   │
     │                                  │  • Runs as child process  │   │
     │                                  │  • No direct storage     │   │
     │                                  │  • Inherits Vault's      │   │
     │                                  │    encryption & audit    │   │
     │                                  └──────────────────────────┘   │
     │                                                                  │
     │   🔒 PLUGIN ISOLATION:                                           │
     │   • Plugin runs as SEPARATE process (process isolation)           │
     │   • Plugin communicates ONLY via gRPC (no shared memory)          │
     │   • Plugin cannot access Vault's storage directly                 │
     │   • Plugin crash does NOT crash Vault core                        │
     │   • Plugins are scoped to mounting namespace                      │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📦 Plugin Types
  • Secrets Engine Plugin: Custom secret engines (e.g., custom DB backend)
  • Auth Method Plugin: Custom authentication (e.g., custom MFA provider)
  • Both compiled as Go binaries implementing Vault's plugin interfaces
🔒 Plugin Security Model
  • Process isolation: Separate process, no shared memory
  • gRPC communication: All API calls proxied through gRPC
  • Barrier protection: Storage goes through Vault's encryption
  • Permission scoping: Plugin can't bypass ACL policies
  • Audit inclusion: Plugin operations ARE audited
🔌 Plugin Loading Sequence — What Happens When You Register & Enable
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │              PLUGIN LOADING SEQUENCE — STEP BY STEP              │
     │                                                                  │
     │  STEP 1: REGISTRATION (vault plugin register)                    │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
     │  │ • Vault reads the binary from plugin_directory           │    │
     │  │ • Computes SHA256 of binary                              │    │
     │  │ • Compares with provided -sha256 flag → MUST MATCH       │    │
     │  │ • Stores {name, type, sha256, command, args} in catalog  │    │
     │  │ • Binary is NOT executed at this stage                   │    │
     │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
     │                           │                                      │
     │                           ▼                                      │
     │  STEP 2: ENABLING (vault secrets enable -plugin-name=...)        │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
     │  │ • Vault looks up plugin in catalog by name               │    │
     │  │ • Re-verifies SHA256 of binary on disk                   │    │
     │  │ • Creates mount point entry in storage                   │    │
     │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
     │                           │                                      │
     │                           ▼                                      │
     │  STEP 3: FIRST REQUEST (or plugin reload)                        │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
     │  │ • Vault spawns the plugin binary as a CHILD PROCESS      │    │
     │  │ • Creates a local Unix socket for gRPC communication     │    │
     │  │ • Plugin calls back to Vault to establish gRPC connection │    │
     │  │ • Mutual TLS handshake over Unix socket                  │    │
     │  │ • Vault sends ServeConfig (system info, storage barrier) │    │
     │  │ • Plugin initializes its backend (Factory function)      │    │
     │  │ • Plugin registers its API paths with Vault Core         │    │
     │  │ • Plugin is now LIVE — accepting requests                │    │
     │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
     │                                                                  │
     │  STEP 4: REQUEST HANDLING (every subsequent API call)            │
     │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
     │  │ • Client → Vault HTTP API → matched to mount path        │    │
     │  │ • Vault Core → gRPC → Plugin (with storage context)      │    │
     │  │ • Plugin processes request (may call req.Storage)        │    │
     │  │ • Plugin → gRPC response → Vault Core → HTTP response    │    │
     │  │ • Audit log records the operation (transparent)          │    │
     │  │ • All storage I/O goes through Vault's barrier (encrypted)│    │
     │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
     │                                                                  │
     │  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The plugin binary is IDLE until the first       │
     │  request arrives. Registration and enabling are just metadata    │
     │  operations — the process spawn happens LAZILY on first use.     │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Plugin Lifecycle — Registration to Mounting
# Step 1: Register the plugin binary in Vault's plugin catalog
vault plugin register \
    -sha256=$(sha256sum /opt/vault/plugins/vault-plugin-secrets-mycloud | cut -d' ' -f1) \
    secret \
    mycloud-plugin

# Step 2: Enable the plugin as a secrets engine
vault secrets enable \
    -path=mycloud \
    -plugin-name=mycloud-plugin \
    plugin

# Step 3: Configure the plugin (plugin-specific config)
vault write mycloud/config \
    api_key="abc123" \
    region="us-east-1"

# Step 4: Use the plugin — same as any built-in engine!
vault read mycloud/creds/app-role

# ─── MANAGING PLUGINS ───
vault plugin list                                    # List all registered plugins
vault plugin list secret                             # List only secret engine plugins
vault plugin list auth                               # List only auth method plugins

vault plugin info secret mycloud-plugin              # Get plugin details

# Reload a plugin (after updating the binary)
vault plugin reload -plugin mycloud-plugin
# Or reload all plugins on a mount
vault plugin reload -mounts mycloud
⚠️ GOTCHA: Plugin Reload is Manual

When you update a plugin binary, Vault doesn't automatically pick up the new version. You must run vault plugin reload -plugin <name> or -mounts <path>. During reload, the plugin process is killed and restarted — but in-flight requests are held until the new plugin is ready. Plan for brief (1-2 second) unavailability during reload.

🧪 Plugin Testing Strategies — Before Production

Custom plugins handle secrets — testing is non-negotiable. Follow this testing staircase:

  1. Unit tests (Go): Test each path handler with mock storage. The Vault SDK provides logicaltest.TestBackend for this — it creates an in-memory backend and runs your paths through real Vault request/response cycles without a real Vault server. Aim for >80% coverage.
  2. Integration tests: Start a real vault server -dev, register your plugin, and run end-to-end tests. Use Go's testing package with os/exec to manage the dev server lifecycle.
  3. Acceptance tests: HashiCorp provides github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/helper/pluginutil with acceptance test helpers. These spin up real Vault clusters (using the vault package) and validate plugin behavior in a cluster environment.
  4. Chaos testing: Kill the plugin process mid-operation. Verify Vault core stays healthy. Verify audit logs show the failure. Restart and verify recovery. Test with large payloads, concurrent requests, and expired tokens.

Golden Rule: If your plugin crashes, Vault should NEVER crash. If your plugin leaks memory, Vault should survive OOM. Test the failure modes before testing the happy path.

🏋️ PRACTICE DRILL: Plugin Versioning Workflow

Scenario: You have v1.0 of mycloud-plugin running. You've built v1.1 with a critical bug fix. How do you deploy it safely?
Step 1: Register v1.1 as a SEPARATE plugin name: vault plugin register -sha256=<new_hash> secret mycloud-plugin-v1.1
Step 2: Enable v1.1 on a test path: vault secrets enable -path=mycloud-test -plugin-name=mycloud-plugin-v1.1 plugin
Step 3: Run your test suite against mycloud-test/ — verify no regressions
Step 4: Disable the old mount path, enable v1.1 on the production path. OR: update the binary in-place and run vault plugin reload -plugin mycloud-plugin (if backward compatible).
Golden Rule: Never overwrite a production plugin binary without a rollback plan. Keep the old binary and hash saved.

26.2 Building Custom Plugins — Go SDK and Plugin Registration

🛠️ Plugin Development Prerequisites
  • Go 1.19+: Plugins are written in Go and compiled to a single binary
  • Vault Go SDK: github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk provides plugin interfaces
  • Plugin interfaces: Implement SecretsEngine or AuthMethod interface
  • gRPC: Communication protocol (handled by SDK, no direct gRPC coding needed)
  • Binary output: Compile to a single static binary, place in plugin directory
Minimal Custom Secrets Engine (Go)
// vault-plugin-secrets-mycloud/main.go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "os"
    
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/framework"
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/logical"
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/plugin"
)

// mycloudBackend implements the logical.Backend interface
type mycloudBackend struct {
    *framework.Backend
}

// Factory returns a new backend instance
func Factory(ctx context.Context, conf *logical.BackendConfig) (logical.Backend, error) {
    b := &mycloudBackend{}
    b.Backend = &framework.Backend{
        BackendType: logical.TypeLogical,
        Help:        "MyCloud Secrets Engine — generates API tokens for MyCloud service",
        Paths: []*framework.Path{
            {
                Pattern: "creds/" + framework.GenericNameRegex("name"),
                Fields: map[string]*framework.FieldSchema{
                    "name": {
                        Type:        framework.TypeString,
                        Description: "Name of the credential set",
                    },
                },
                Operations: map[logical.Operation]framework.OperationHandler{
                    logical.ReadOperation: &framework.PathOperation{
                        Callback: b.pathCredsRead,
                    },
                },
            },
            {
                Pattern: "config",
                Fields: map[string]*framework.FieldSchema{
                    "api_key": {
                        Type:        framework.TypeString,
                        Description: "MyCloud API Key",
                    },
                },
                Operations: map[logical.Operation]framework.OperationHandler{
                    logical.CreateOperation: &framework.PathOperation{
                        Callback: b.pathConfigWrite,
                    },
                    logical.UpdateOperation: &framework.PathOperation{
                        Callback: b.pathConfigWrite,
                    },
                    logical.ReadOperation: &framework.PathOperation{
                        Callback: b.pathConfigRead,
                    },
                },
            },
        },
    }
    return b, nil
}

func (b *mycloudBackend) pathCredsRead(ctx context.Context, req *logical.Request, d *framework.FieldData) (*logical.Response, error) {
    // Read config to get API key
    config, err := req.Storage.Get(ctx, "config")
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if config == nil {
        return logical.ErrorResponse("plugin not configured — write to mycloud/config first"), nil
    }
    
    // Generate a dynamic API token (in real life: call MyCloud API)
    token := "mc-token-" + generateRandomString(32)
    
    return &logical.Response{
        Data: map[string]interface{}{
            "token":      token,
            "expires_at": "2026-06-14T00:00:00Z",
        },
    }, nil
}

func main() {
    apiClientMeta := &plugin.APIClientMeta{}
    flags := apiClientMeta.FlagSet()
    flags.Parse(os.Args[1:])
    
    tlsConfig := apiClientMeta.GetTLSConfig()
    tlsProviderFunc := plugin.VaultPluginTLSProvider(tlsConfig)
    
    plugin.Serve(&plugin.ServeOpts{
        BackendFactoryFunc: Factory,
        TLSProviderFunc:    tlsProviderFunc,
    })
}
🔄 Plugin Development Lifecycle — Step by Step
1Scaffold: Clone the Vault plugin template repo or start from SDK examples
2Implement: Code your Backend with paths, fields, and operation handlers
3Build: go build -o vault-plugin-secrets-mycloud . — single binary
4Place: Copy binary to Vault's plugin directory (e.g., /opt/vault/plugins/)
5Register: vault plugin register -sha256=<sum> secret mycloud-plugin
6Enable: vault secrets enable -path=mycloud -plugin-name=mycloud-plugin plugin
7Configure: vault write mycloud/config api_key="..."
8Test: vault read mycloud/creds/test-role — verify it works
💡 EXAM TIP: Plugin Directory Configuration

The plugin directory is set in Vault's config file with plugin_directory = "/opt/vault/plugins". Vault ONLY loads plugins from this directory. The vault process must have read+execute permissions on this directory and the plugin binaries. In Kubernetes, this is typically a mounted volume or init container that downloads the plugin binary.

26.3 Community and Ecosystem Plugins

🌍 Notable Community & Ecosystem Plugins
PluginTypePurposeUse Case
vault-plugin-auth-kerberos Auth Method Kerberos/Active Directory authentication Windows-heavy enterprises, legacy AD integration
vault-plugin-secrets-gcp Secrets Engine Generate GCP service account keys (built-in now) GCP-native deployments, dynamic IAM
vault-plugin-auth-oidc Auth Method OIDC authentication (built-in now) SSO with Google, Okta, Azure AD
vault-plugin-database-mongodbatlas Secrets Engine MongoDB Atlas dynamic credentials Cloud MongoDB deployments
vault-plugin-secrets-artifactory Secrets Engine JFrog Artifactory access tokens CI/CD pipeline artifact access
🔍 How to Find & Vet Community Plugins
  • HashiCorp Plugin Registry: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/plugins
  • GitHub Topic: Search topic:vault-plugin on GitHub
  • Vet checklist: Check stars, last commit date, test coverage, and maintainer responsiveness
  • Security audit: Review the code before running in production — plugins have access to secrets!
  • Pin SHA256: Always register plugins with their SHA256 hash to prevent tampering
🛠️ Real-World Scenario: anihpj Custom Plugin

Your organization's anihpj platform uses a legacy internal authentication system that Vault doesn't natively support. Instead of migrating all users, you build a custom auth plugin:

# Register the custom auth plugin
vault plugin register \
    -sha256=$(sha256sum /opt/vault/plugins/vault-plugin-auth-anihpj | cut -d' ' -f1) \
    auth \
    anihpj-auth

# Enable it as an auth method
vault auth enable \
    -path=anihpj \
    -plugin-name=anihpj-auth \
    plugin

# Configure the plugin to talk to legacy auth system
vault write auth/anihpj/config \
    legacy_api_url="https://auth.anihpj.internal" \
    legacy_api_key="shared-secret-key"

# Now users can login with legacy credentials!
vault login -method=anihpj username=john_doe

# Create a role mapping legacy roles to Vault policies
vault write auth/anihpj/role/developer \
    legacy_role="anihpj-developer" \
    token_policies="jobpost-reader"
⚡ SPEED TIP: Plugin Troubleshooting

If a plugin fails: (1) Check vault plugin info secret <name> — shows SHA256 mismatch, version, args. (2) Check Vault server logs for plugin crash details. (3) Run plugin binary directly with VAULT_PLUGIN_LOG_LEVEL=trace ./plugin-binary — plugins log to stderr, Vault captures these. (4) Verify plugin_directory path exists and vault user can read+execute. (5) After updating: vault plugin reload -plugin <name> is required.

26.4 Advanced Plugin Development — Secrets Engine Deep Dive for Vault Authorship 🔐

This section bridges Associate-level plugin knowledge to Vault Authorship certification level. We'll build a complete, production-quality secrets engine plugin with credential lifecycle management (create, renew, revoke), configuration persistence, path-help documentation, versioning, and comprehensive testing. This is the level of depth the Authorship exam expects.

🏭 Complete Secrets Engine Backend — Production Template

Below is a complete, compilable secrets engine backend skeleton showing every pattern you need for the Authorship exam: Factory function, path registration, CRUD operations with barrier storage, secret lifecycle (create/renew/revoke), configuration management, and health checks.

backend.go — Complete Secrets Engine Backend (Authorship-Level)
package myengine

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "time"

    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/framework"
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/logical"
)

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// BACKEND STRUCT — The Core
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
type myEngineBackend struct {
    *framework.Backend
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// FACTORY — Entry point called by Vault
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
func Factory(ctx context.Context, conf *logical.BackendConfig) (logical.Backend, error) {
    b := &myEngineBackend{}
    b.Backend = &framework.Backend{
        Help: `
The MyEngine secrets engine generates dynamic API tokens for the
MyCloud platform. Each token is unique, time-limited, and automatically
revoked when its lease expires.

CONFIGURATION:
    Write to myengine/config to set the API key and default TTL.

CREDENTIALS:
    Read from myengine/creds/:name to generate a new API token.
    Tokens are auto-revoked on lease expiry.

ROTATION:
    Write to myengine/rotate/:name to rotate an existing token.
`,
        Paths: framework.PathAppend(
            b.pathConfig(),
            b.pathConfigList(),
            b.pathCreds(),
            b.pathCredsList(),
            b.pathInfo(),
        ),
        Secrets: []*framework.Secret{
            b.credentialSecret(),
        },
        BackendType: logical.TypeLogical,
        // PeriodicFunc is called at regular intervals — use for cleanup
        PeriodicFunc: b.periodicCleanup,
        // Invalidate is called on events like policy changes
        Invalidate: b.invalidate,
        // Initialize is called once when backend is first mounted
        Initialize: b.initialize,
    }

    if err := b.Setup(ctx, conf); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return b, nil
}

func (b *myEngineBackend) initialize(ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.InitializationRequest) error {
    // Run once when mount is created or Vault starts
    b.Logger().Info("MyEngine backend initialized",
        "mount", req.MountPoint)
    return nil
}

func (b *myEngineBackend) invalidate(ctx context.Context,
    key string) {
    // Called when storage changes externally (e.g., policy change)
    b.Logger().Debug("invalidate called", "key", key)
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// PERIODIC CLEANUP — Runs every PeriodicFunc interval
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
func (b *myEngineBackend) periodicCleanup(ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.Request) error {
    // Example: Check for expired tokens, clean up stale configs
    // This is optional — only implement if your plugin needs
    // background tasks
    return nil
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// CREDENTIAL SECRET — Lifecycle Management
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
const credentialSecretType = "myengine_creds"

func (b *myEngineBackend) credentialSecret() *framework.Secret {
    return &framework.Secret{
        Type: credentialSecretType,
        // Fields returned when reading this secret
        Fields: map[string]*framework.FieldSchema{
            "token": {
                Type:        framework.TypeString,
                Description: "MyCloud API token",
            },
            "username": {
                Type:        framework.TypeString,
                Description: "MyCloud username for this credential",
            },
        },
        // Revoke is called when the lease expires or is manually revoked
        Revoke: b.credentialRevoke,
        // Renew is called when a client requests lease renewal
        Renew: b.credentialRenew,
        // Optional: called when Vault rolls back a failed operation
        Rollback: b.credentialRollback,
    }
}

func (b *myEngineBackend) credentialRevoke(ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.Request, d *framework.FieldData) (*logical.Response, error) {

    // InternalData contains metadata stored when the secret was created
    credName, ok := req.Secret.InternalData["cred_name"]
    if !ok {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("missing cred_name in internal data")
    }

    // Read the API key from config to delete the credential
    config, err := b.readConfig(ctx, req.Storage)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if config == nil {
        // Config was deleted — nothing to clean up
        return nil, nil
    }

    // Call external API to delete/revoke the credential
    err = b.revokeExternalCredential(ctx,
        config["api_key"].(string),
        credName.(string))
    if err != nil {
        // Log but don't fail — the lease will retry
        b.Logger().Error("failed to revoke external credential",
            "cred_name", credName, "error", err)
    }

    return nil, nil
}

func (b *myEngineBackend) credentialRenew(ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.Request, d *framework.FieldData) (*logical.Response, error) {

    config, err := b.readConfig(ctx, req.Storage)
    if err != nil || config == nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("config not found — cannot renew")
    }

    ttl := time.Duration(config["ttl"].(int)) * time.Second
    resp := &logical.Response{Secret: req.Secret}
    resp.Secret.TTL = ttl
    resp.Secret.MaxTTL = ttl * 2

    // Optionally rotate the external credential on renewal
    // b.rotateExternalCredential(...)

    return resp, nil
}

func (b *myEngineBackend) credentialRollback(ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.Request, kind string, data interface{}) error {
    // Called if a WAL (Write-Ahead Log) operation fails
    // Clean up any partially created resources
    b.Logger().Warn("rollback triggered", "kind", kind)
    return nil
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// HELPER: Read configuration from storage
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
func (b *myEngineBackend) readConfig(ctx context.Context,
    storage logical.Storage) (map[string]interface{}, error) {

    entry, err := storage.Get(ctx, "config")
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if entry == nil {
        return nil, nil
    }

    var config map[string]interface{}
    if err := entry.DecodeJSON(&config); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return config, nil
}

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
// STUB: External API integration
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════
func (b *myEngineBackend) revokeExternalCredential(ctx context.Context,
    apiKey, credName string) error {
    // In production: make HTTP call to MyCloud API
    // DELETE https://api.mycloud.com/v1/tokens/{credName}
    // Authorization: Bearer {apiKey}
    return nil
}
🗂️ Complete Path Definitions
func (b *myEngineBackend) pathCreds() *framework.Path {
    return &framework.Path{
        Pattern: "creds/" + framework.GenericNameRegex("name"),
        Fields: map[string]*framework.FieldSchema{
            "name": {Type: framework.TypeString,
                Description: "Credential set name"},
            "ttl": {Type: framework.TypeDurationSecond,
                Description: "Override default TTL",
                Default: 3600},
        },
        Operations: map[logical.Operation]framework.OperationHandler{
            logical.ReadOperation: &framework.PathOperation{
                Callback: b.pathCredsRead,
                // Summary appears in vault path-help output
                Summary: "Generate a new MyCloud API token",
                Description: `Creates a unique, time-limited API 
token for the specified credential set. The token 
is automatically revoked when the lease expires.`,
                // Example gives users a quick start
                Examples: []framework.RequestExample{{
                    Description: "Generate a token",
                    Data: map[string]interface{}{
                        "name": "my-app",
                        "ttl":  3600,
                    },
                }},
                // Responses documents the API contract
                Responses: map[logical.ResponseCode]framework.ResponseFields{
                    http.StatusOK: {
                        Description: "Credential created",
                        Fields: map[string]*framework.FieldSchema{
                            "token":    {Type: framework.TypeString},
                            "username": {Type: framework.TypeString},
                        },
                    },
                },
            },
        },
    }
}
🔑 Credential Generation Handler
func (b *myEngineBackend) pathCredsRead(
    ctx context.Context,
    req *logical.Request,
    d *framework.FieldData) (*logical.Response, error) {

    name := d.Get("name").(string)
    ttlOverride := d.Get("ttl").(int)

    // 1. Read config (API key + default TTL)
    config, err := b.readConfig(ctx, req.Storage)
    if err != nil || config == nil {
        return logical.ErrorResponse(
            "engine not configured"), nil
    }

    // 2. Determine TTL
    ttl := time.Duration(config["ttl"].(int)) * time.Second
    if ttlOverride > 0 {
        ttl = time.Duration(ttlOverride) * time.Second
    }

    // 3. Call external API to create credential
    token, username, err := b.createExternalCredential(
        ctx, config["api_key"].(string), name)
    if err != nil {
        return logical.ErrorResponse(
            "failed to create credential: %v", err), nil
    }

    // 4. Build response with SECRET (lease-based!)
    resp := b.Secret(credentialSecretType).Response(
        // Response data (returned to caller)
        map[string]interface{}{
            "token":    token,
            "username": username,
        },
        // Internal data (stored with lease, for revoke/renew)
        map[string]interface{}{
            "cred_name":  name,
            "api_key":    config["api_key"],
        },
    )

    resp.Secret.TTL = ttl
    resp.Secret.MaxTTL = ttl * 2
    // Renewable=true means clients can extend the lease
    resp.Secret.Renewable = true

    return resp, nil
}
🧪 Plugin Testing — Authorship Exam Essential

The Authorship exam expects you to know how to test plugins at multiple levels. Here's the complete testing strategy:

plugin_test.go — Unit Tests with In-Memory Storage
package myengine

import (
    "context"
    "testing"
    "time"

    "github.com/hashicorp/go-hclog"
    "github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk/logical"
)

// getTestBackend creates a backend with in-memory storage for testing
func getTestBackend(t *testing.T) (logical.Backend, logical.Storage) {
    t.Helper()
    config := &logical.BackendConfig{
        Logger: hclog.New(&hclog.LoggerOptions{
            Level: hclog.Trace,
        }),
        System: &logical.StaticSystemView{
            DefaultLeaseTTLVal: 1 * time.Hour,
            MaxLeaseTTLVal:     24 * time.Hour,
        },
        StorageView: &logical.InmemStorage{},
    }
    b, err := Factory(context.Background(), config)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatalf("failed to create backend: %v", err)
    }
    return b, config.StorageView
}

// TestConfigCRUD tests the config write/read/delete cycle
func TestConfigCRUD(t *testing.T) {
    b, storage := getTestBackend(t)

    // Test write
    resp, err := b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.UpdateOperation,
        Path:      "config",
        Storage:   storage,
        Data: map[string]interface{}{
            "api_key": "test-key-abc-123",
            "ttl":     7200,
        },
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if resp != nil && resp.IsError() {
        t.Fatal(resp.Error())
    }

    // Test read
    resp, err = b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.ReadOperation,
        Path:      "config",
        Storage:   storage,
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if resp.Data["ttl"].(int) != 7200 {
        t.Fatalf("expected ttl=7200, got %v", resp.Data["ttl"])
    }
    // API key should NOT be returned in plaintext
    if _, ok := resp.Data["api_key"]; ok {
        t.Fatal("api_key should NOT be returned in config read")
    }
}

// TestCredsWithoutConfig tests error handling
func TestCredsWithoutConfig(t *testing.T) {
    b, storage := getTestBackend(t)

    resp, err := b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.ReadOperation,
        Path:      "creds/my-app",
        Storage:   storage,
    })
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if !resp.IsError() {
        t.Fatal("expected error when config not set")
    }
}

// TestCredsFullCycle tests create → renew → revoke
func TestCredsFullCycle(t *testing.T) {
    b, storage := getTestBackend(t)

    // 1. Write config
    b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.UpdateOperation,
        Path:      "config",
        Storage:   storage,
        Data: map[string]interface{}{
            "api_key": "test-key",
            "ttl":     3600,
        },
    })

    // 2. Create credential
    resp, err := b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.ReadOperation,
        Path:      "creds/test-app",
        Storage:   storage,
    })
    if err != nil || resp == nil {
        t.Fatal("failed to create credential")
    }
    if resp.Secret == nil {
        t.Fatal("expected secret response with lease")
    }
    if resp.Data["token"] == "" {
        t.Fatal("expected token in response")
    }

    // 3. Renew lease
    renewReq := &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.RenewOperation,
        Storage:   storage,
        Secret:    resp.Secret,
        Data:      map[string]interface{}{},
    }
    renewResp, err := b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), renewReq)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal("renew failed:", err)
    }
    if renewResp.Secret.TTL == 0 {
        t.Fatal("renewed TTL should be > 0")
    }

    // 4. Revoke lease
    revokeReq := &logical.Request{
        Operation: logical.RevokeOperation,
        Storage:   storage,
        Secret:    resp.Secret,
    }
    _, err = b.HandleRequest(context.Background(), revokeReq)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal("revoke failed:", err)
    }
}
💡 AUTHORSHIP EXAM TIP: Test Coverage Requirements

The Authorship exam expects you to know that plugins should have: (1) Unit tests using logical.InmemStorage{} for isolated testing, (2) Path-level tests for every CRUD operation, (3) Secret lifecycle tests (create → renew → revoke), (4) Error path tests (no config, bad input, expired TTL), (5) Concurrent access tests (multiple goroutines hitting the same path). HashiCorp recommends >80% code coverage for published plugins.

🚨 Error Response Patterns
// User-friendly error (4xx) — returns to client
return logical.ErrorResponse(
    "config not found — write to %s/config first",
    req.MountPoint)

// Permission error
return logical.RespondWithStatusCode(
    &logical.Response{Data: map[string]interface{}{
        "error": "insufficient permissions",
    }}, req, http.StatusForbidden)

// System error (5xx) — logged, generic to client
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf(
        "storage failure: %w", err)
}
// ↑ Returns 500 to client, logs full error

// CodedError with specific error code
return nil, logical.CodedError(
    http.StatusBadRequest,
    "invalid TTL: must be between 60 and 86400")
📋 Logging Best Practices
// Structured logging — use key=value pairs
b.Logger().Info("creating credential",
    "cred_name", name,
    "ttl", ttl.String())

b.Logger().Debug("calling external API",
    "endpoint", "https://api.mycloud.com/v1/tokens",
    "method", "POST")

b.Logger().Error("external API failure",
    "error", err,
    "retry_count", retries,
    "cred_name", name)

b.Logger().Warn("credential revocation delayed",
    "cred_name", credName,
    "reason", "external API timeout")

// NEVER log secrets or API keys!
// ❌ b.Logger().Info("api_key", apiKey)
// ✅ b.Logger().Info("using api_key",
//     "key_prefix", apiKey[:4]+"...")
📦 Plugin Distribution — Build, Package, Ship

For Vault Authorship, you need to know how to build and distribute plugins professionally. Here's the Makefile and release process:

Makefile — Build, Test, Package
# Plugin metadata
NAME     := vault-plugin-secrets-myengine
VERSION  := 1.0.0
SHA      := $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD)
BUILD    := $(shell date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

# Go build flags for version injection
LDFLAGS  := -s -w \
  -X main.Version=$(VERSION) \
  -X main.BuildDate=$(BUILD) \
  -X main.GitCommit=$(SHA)

# ─── BUILD ───────────────────────────────
.PHONY: build
build:
	@echo "Building $(NAME) v$(VERSION)..."
	go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o $(NAME) .

# ─── TEST ────────────────────────────────
.PHONY: test
test:
	go test -v -race -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
	go tool cover -func=coverage.out | grep total

# ─── LINT ────────────────────────────────
.PHONY: lint
lint:
	golangci-lint run ./...

# ─── VULNERABILITY CHECK ────────────────
.PHONY: vuln
vuln:
	govulncheck ./...

# ─── MULTI-ARCH RELEASE ─────────────────
.PHONY: release
release: test lint
	GOOS=linux   GOARCH=amd64 go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o dist/$(NAME)-linux-amd64
	GOOS=linux   GOARCH=arm64 go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o dist/$(NAME)-linux-arm64
	GOOS=darwin  GOARCH=amd64 go build -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" -o dist/$(NAME)-darwin-amd64
	cd dist && sha256sum * > SHA256SUMS
	cd dist && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
	@echo "Release files in dist/"

# ─── CLEAN ───────────────────────────────
.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f $(NAME) coverage.out
	rm -rf dist/

26.5 Vault Authorship Certification — Exam Overview & Bridge from Associate 🔐

🎯 Vault Authorship — What It Tests
  • Plugin Architecture: gRPC communication, process isolation, TLS, barrier integration
  • Secrets Engine Development: Implementing logical.Backend, path schema, CRUD operations, credential lifecycle
  • Auth Method Development: Implementing logical.AuthMethod, login flows, token creation
  • Testing: Unit tests with InmemStorage, acceptance tests with TestCluster
  • Debugging: Plugin logs, dlv debugger, SHA256 verification, reload workflows
  • Security: SHA256 integrity, mTLS, least privilege, audit compliance, secret handling
  • Distribution: Multi-arch builds, SHA256SUMS, README, GitHub releases

📝 Chapter 26 — Vault Associate Practice Questions

Q251How does Vault communicate with a custom plugin at runtime?
A. HTTP REST API over localhost
B. Shared memory (mmap)
C. gRPC over a local Unix socket
D. Standard input/output (stdin/stdout)
Answer: C. Vault communicates with plugins via gRPC over a local Unix socket. The plugin runs as a child process and all API calls are proxied through this gRPC connection. This provides process isolation while maintaining high performance.

Explanation: The gRPC-over-Unix-socket model is key to Vault's plugin security. The plugin never listens on a network port (no external access possible), and all communication is local and encrypted. The SDK abstracts away the gRPC details — plugin developers work with Go interfaces, not raw gRPC.

Q252What command registers a custom plugin in Vault's plugin catalog?
A. vault secrets enable -plugin-name=myplugin plugin
B. vault plugin register -sha256=<hash> secret myplugin
C. vault write sys/plugins/catalog/myplugin binary=<path>
D. vault plugin install myplugin
Answer: B. vault plugin register adds the plugin to Vault's catalog with its SHA256 hash. Option A enables the plugin (after registration). There is no vault plugin install command.

Explanation: Registration and enabling are separate steps. First register (add to catalog with SHA256 for integrity), then enable (mount as a secrets engine or auth method). The SHA256 ensures the binary hasn't been tampered with.

Q253Where must custom plugin binaries be placed for Vault to load them?
A. Any directory — Vault searches PATH
B. The directory specified by plugin_directory in Vault's config
C. /usr/local/bin/
D. The /opt/vault/data/plugins/ directory (hardcoded)
Answer: B. Vault's config file specifies a plugin_directory (e.g., /opt/vault/plugins). Vault ONLY loads plugins from this directory. The path is not hardcoded — it must be explicitly configured.

Explanation: This is a security measure — Vault won't load arbitrary binaries from anywhere on the system. The plugin directory should have restricted permissions (only vault user can write to it) to prevent unauthorized plugin injection.

# In vault-config.hcl
plugin_directory = "/opt/vault/plugins"

# Permissions
# chown vault:vault /opt/vault/plugins
# chmod 750 /opt/vault/plugins
Q254What happens when a custom plugin process crashes?
A. Vault core also crashes (cascading failure)
B. The plugin is automatically restarted and requests are retried
C. Requests to that plugin's mount point fail, but Vault core continues running
D. Vault automatically disables the plugin mount
Answer: C. Plugin crashes are isolated — Vault core continues running unaffected. However, any requests to that plugin's mount point will return errors until the plugin is manually reloaded with vault plugin reload.

Explanation: This is the benefit of process isolation. A buggy plugin can't take down Vault. However, Vault does NOT auto-restart crashed plugins — you must reload them. This is by design — a crashing plugin may have a bug that would cause an infinite crash loop.

Q255Which programming language is used to write Vault plugins?
A. Python
B. JavaScript/Node.js
C. Go
D. Java
Answer: C. Vault plugins must be written in Go. The Vault SDK (github.com/hashicorp/vault/sdk) provides Go interfaces and the gRPC plugin protocol. While you could theoretically use any language that supports gRPC, HashiCorp only supports Go plugins.

Explanation: Go is required because Vault itself is written in Go and the plugin protocol is built on Go's plugin system + gRPC. The plugin compiles to a single static binary — no runtime dependencies needed on the Vault server.

Q256You updated a custom plugin binary. What command makes Vault use the new version?
A. vault plugin update -plugin myplugin
B. systemctl restart vault
C. vault plugin reload -plugin myplugin
D. Vault auto-detects binary changes — no command needed
Answer: C. vault plugin reload -plugin <name> kills the old plugin process and starts a new one with the updated binary. Vault does NOT auto-detect plugin binary changes — reload must be triggered manually.

Explanation: Plugin reload is graceful — in-flight requests are held until the new plugin instance is ready. You can also reload all plugins for a specific mount: vault plugin reload -mounts mycloud. Restarting Vault (B) also works but causes unnecessary downtime for other mounts.

Q257Can a custom plugin access Vault's underlying storage (Raft/Consul) directly?
A. Yes — plugins have full filesystem access
B. No — all storage access goes through Vault's barrier via the SDK
C. Yes — but only if configured with a storage path
D. No — plugins cannot store any data at all
Answer: B. Plugins use req.Storage (provided by the SDK) to read/write data. This goes through Vault's encryption barrier — the plugin never sees raw storage. This ensures plugins can't bypass Vault's encryption or access other engines' data.

Explanation: req.Storage.Get(ctx, "key") and req.Storage.Put(ctx, &logical.StorageEntry{Key: "key", Value: data}) are the only ways a plugin reads/writes data. These calls go through Vault's barrier, which encrypts data before writing to the physical backend. The plugin sees plaintext; the storage backend sees ciphertext.

Q258Why is SHA256 verification required when registering a plugin?
A. To compress the plugin binary for faster loading
B. To ensure the plugin binary hasn't been tampered with or corrupted
C. To check the plugin is compatible with the current Vault version
D. To verify the plugin was compiled with the correct Go version
Answer: B. The SHA256 hash acts as an integrity check — if the binary is modified (maliciously or accidentally), the hash won't match and Vault will refuse to load it. This is a critical security control for plugin supply chain security.

Explanation: Always generate the SHA256 from a trusted binary: sha256sum /opt/vault/plugins/myplugin. Store this hash in your deployment pipeline. If someone replaces the binary with a backdoored version, the hash mismatch will be detected.

Q259What are the two types of Vault plugins?
A. Secrets engine plugins and audit device plugins
B. Auth method plugins and secrets engine plugins
C. Storage backend plugins and listener plugins
D. Policy plugins and token plugins
Answer: B. Vault supports two plugin types: secrets engine plugins and auth method plugins. Audit devices, storage backends, and listeners are not currently pluggable via the plugin system.

Explanation: When registering, you specify either secret or auth as the plugin type. Secrets engine plugins generate and manage secrets; auth method plugins verify identities and issue tokens. The plugin type determines which Vault interfaces the plugin must implement.

Q260A plugin is registered but not working. The vault plugin info command shows "sha256: mismatched." What does this mean?
A. The plugin is too old for this Vault version
B. The plugin binary has been modified or replaced since registration
C. The plugin requires a license key
D. The plugin directory permissions are incorrect
Answer: B. "sha256: mismatched" means the binary on disk no longer matches the hash stored during registration. Someone (or something) has modified the binary. Fix: re-register with the new hash, or restore the original binary.

Explanation: This is your supply chain security at work. Don't ignore SHA256 mismatches — investigate why the binary changed. If it was an intentional update, re-register with the new hash. If it's unexpected, treat it as a potential security incident.

# Check current state
vault plugin info secret mycloud-plugin

# If SHA256 mismatched, re-register with new hash
NEW_SHA=$(sha256sum /opt/vault/plugins/mycloud-plugin | cut -d' ' -f1)
vault plugin register -sha256=$NEW_SHA secret mycloud-plugin
vault plugin reload -plugin mycloud-plugin

🔴 Part 10 — Key Takeaways: Advanced Topics

🏢 Ch24: Namespaces
  • ✅ Enterprise feature — isolated tenants in one cluster
  • ✅ Each namespace has OWN secrets, auth, policies, audit
  • ✅ Parent sees children; siblings are isolated
  • ✅ Hybrid Team/Env pattern is best for enterprise
  • ✅ Delete is permanent — always snapshot first
⚡ Ch25: Performance & Hardening
  • ✅ Storage is #1 bottleneck — use SSD, ≥3000 IOPS
  • ✅ 15-point hardening checklist — TLS to DR drills
  • ✅ mlock() prevents secrets from swapping to disk
  • ✅ Dedicated OS user (never root) + resource limits
  • ✅ Raft snapshots every 6h, stored offsite encrypted
🔌 Ch26: Plugins
  • ✅ Go binaries communicating via gRPC/Unix socket

Integration Example — anihpj/jobpost Enterprise Setup: Create anihpj/dev, anihpj/staging, anihpj/prod namespaces (Ch24) → Harden each with TLS 1.2+, mlock, resource limits (Ch25) → Extend with a custom auth plugin for legacy anihpj SSO (Ch26). This architecture maps directly to Vault Ops Pro and Vault Authorship certification paths.

💡 EXAM TIP: The "Mark for Review" Strategy

The exam software lets you flag questions and come back later. Use this aggressively: if you don't know the answer within 45 seconds, flag it and move on. Fast, confident answers on the easy questions give you a time buffer for the hard ones. Do NOT get stuck on question 12 and run out of time at question 55. Answer what you know first, then loop back.

🖥️ What the Online Proctoring Experience is REALLY Like

You'll use PSI Secure Browser — it locks your computer so you can only see the exam. Before starting, a proctor (real person via webcam) will: (1) verify your government ID matches your face, (2) ask you to slowly pan your webcam around the room — walls, ceiling, floor, desk surface, (3) check your ears (for hidden earpieces), wrists, and pockets, (4) confirm no other monitors, phones, smartwatches, or papers are in reach. This takes 5-10 minutes and is NOT part of your 75 minutes. The proctor watches you via webcam the entire time — they can see your face, eyes, and hands. If you look away from the screen repeatedly, cover your mouth, or someone enters the room, they will pause the exam and warn you. Stay calm, stay still, stay focused.

🚫 Top 5 Exam Day Mistakes (From People Who Failed)
  1. Not reading the FULL question: "Which of the following is NOT..." — the word NOT changes everything. Read every word.
  2. Second-guessing correct answers: Your first instinct is usually right. Only change an answer if you're CERTAIN it's wrong.
  3. Spending 5 minutes on one question: That's 4 questions you didn't answer. FLAG IT and move on.
  4. Leaving blanks: NO penalty for wrong answers! With 30 seconds left, quickly mark any unanswered questions — even random guesses.
  5. Panicking after a hard question: The exam has easy, medium, and hard questions. A hard Q at #7 doesn't mean the rest are hard. Reset after each question.
🧠 Multiple Choice Strategy — The Elimination Method

When you don't know the answer immediately, eliminate wrong options first — don't hunt for the right one. Most Vault Associate questions have 1-2 obviously wrong answers:

  • "Always"/"Never" absolutes: Options with words like "always," "never," "only," or "must" are often wrong — Vault is flexible and has exceptions.
  • Wrong terminology: If an option says "Vault namespace" but you're reading about "namespaces" (Enterprise feature), check if they're using the right term. Options that say "vault encrypt" instead of "vault write transit/encrypt" are wrong.
  • Too specific: "KV v2 stores exactly 10 versions" — sounds right (default is 10) but it's configurable, making the "exactly" claim false.
  • Too broad: "The root token can do everything including bypass audit" — root token is powerful but audit is NOT bypassed. Over-broad claims are usually traps.

After eliminating 2 options, you have a 50/50 chance. Trust your training and pick the one that aligns with Vault's design philosophy: secure by default, least privilege, everything is audited.

🔬 What "Lab/Simulation" Questions Actually Look Like

Vault Associate includes lab-style questions where you're given a scenario and must pick the correct sequence of commands, or identify the correct configuration snippet. These are NOT live terminals (unlike CKA) — they're multiple-choice questions that test your ability to reason about real Vault operations. Example: "A developer reports they cannot read secrets from secret/data/app. Their policy is: path 'secret/*' { capabilities = ['read'] }. What is the most likely cause?" — You must know that KV v2 uses /data/ prefix. These questions test applied knowledge, not memorization. The best preparation? Actually run the commands from Chapters 1-26. There's no substitute for hands-on practice.

27.2 Domain-by-Domain Study Plan — Prioritize Your Remaining Time

🎯 The Pareto Principle for Vault Studying

28% of the exam (Tokens & Policies) + 25% (Secrets Engines) = 53% of your score. If you master these two domains alone, you're more than halfway to passing. The remaining 47% is split across Auth, Architecture, and Operations. Spend your time where the points are.

🏆 Domain 1: Tokens & Policies (28%)
  • Study Ch 10-13: Token types, policy syntax
  • Must know: Service vs Batch, periodic, orphan, response wrapping, HCL capabilities

🥈 Domain 2: Secrets Engines (25%)
  • Study Ch 4-6: KV v1/v2, DB dynamic, PKI, Transit
  • Must know: KV v2 versioning/destroy, DB config→role→creds flow, PKI root→intermediate
  • Practice: Enable KV v2, write versioned secrets, destroy specific versions
  • CLI drill: vault secrets enable, vault kv put/get/destroy
  • Time: ~19 hours (25% of 75-hour total study plan)
🥉 Domain 3: Auth Methods (20%)
  • Study Ch 7-9: AppRole, K8s auth, OIDC, Identity
  • Must know: AppRole RoleID/SecretID flow, K8s JWT review, entity/group mapping
  • Practice: Configure K8s auth from scratch, create AppRole with token policies
  • CLI drill: vault write auth/kubernetes/config, vault write auth/approle/role/...
  • Time: ~15 hours (20% of 75-hour total study plan)
4️⃣ Domain 4: Architecture (15%)
  • Study Ch 1-3: Architecture, seal/unseal, storage
  • Must know: Shamir key threshold, auto-unseal (KMS/HSM), Raft vs Consul

  • Time: ~11 hours (15% of 75-hour total study plan)
5️⃣ Domain 5: Operations (12%)
  • Study Ch 17-23: CLI, DR, snapshots, audit, telemetry

⌨️ 15 CLI Commands You MUST Memorize for Exam Day

These commands appear in 70%+ of Vault Associate questions. You should be able to type them from memory — no hesitating, no looking up:

Essential Vault CLI — Typed From Memory
# ─── CORE OPS (know these COLD) ───
vault status                    # Is Vault sealed? Initialized?
vault operator init             # First-time setup
vault operator unseal           # Provide unseal key (3 of 5)
vault login                     # Authenticate with token

# ─── SECRETS ENGINES ───
vault secrets enable -path=kv kv-v2     # Enable KV v2
vault kv put secret/app key=value       # Write a secret
vault kv get secret/app                 # Read a secret
vault kv destroy -versions=2 secret/app # Permanently delete version

# ─── AUTH METHODS ───
vault auth enable approle               # Enable AppRole
vault write auth/approle/role/myrole token_policies=myapp
vault write auth/kubernetes/config kubernetes_host=...
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/myrole bound_service_account_names=...

# ─── TOKENS & POLICIES ───
vault token create -policy=myapp        # Create token with policy
vault token capabilities <token> <path>  # What can this token do?
vault policy write myapp myapp.hcl       # Create/update policy
vault policy read myapp                  # View policy

# ─── OPERATIONS ───
vault operator raft snapshot save backup.snap  # Backup
vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log

Each question has 4 options, one correct answer, and a detailed explanation. Set a timer for 62 minutes (proportional to the real 75 min for 60 questions).
